titleEn: The Homework Technology Wants to Give Us
contentEn:
Lately, I've been busy with work and haven't been able to post on time. I have a lot of backlog, but I'm sharing a column I posted on Smart Choice in January this year.
Original: [http://goo.gl/uFGcKU](http://goo.gl/uFGcKU)

http://goo.gl/uFGcKU
[**Smart Talk Details > Smart Talk > Power Note > Smart Report | Smart Choice** goo.gl](http://goo.gl/uFGcKU)

In the cartoons and movies I watched as a child, there were many themes about dystopias where computers dominated humans. And even TARS, the robot that appeared in the recent movie Interstellar, despite its appearance being very different from humans, was so well-implemented with a sense of humor that it could almost be considered human. From the myth of Pygmalion's Galatea in Greek mythology, humans have long desired to create something that resembles them, or an even more perfect being that surpasses them. And the dazzling technological advancements in robotics and software that are currently unfolding make it feel as if this future is drawing closer to reality. If there were a science fiction drawing competition, robots would always appear, so probably everyone has thought about such a future.

{{IMG:1}}

However, recent animations and technological trends are not just talking about robots becoming similar to humans. Instead of machines evolving as separate tools and suddenly something human-like appearing one day, humans are also living with machines and technologies, solving social problems, and human intellect and physicality are evolving alongside technology. Tools like fire and the wheel transformed humanity into the strongest animal on Earth. And the advent of computers added the concept of software to simple machines, allowing humanity to leverage the power of tools even for its thinking abilities. When we were young, we drew future humans with big heads like E.T., but in reality, we already have machines by our side that can achieve intellectual evolution comparable to E.T.

And that machine, which once stood as a mainframe in a computer room, eventually moved onto our desks at home... then onto our laps, and finally into our hands. Now, as we talk about post-mobile, we discuss IoT, where software technology is integrated into everything, and wearable computers, starting with smartwatches, are emerging. If this were depicted in an animation, a giant computer that once occupied a single space would gradually shrink and transform into something that covers people's bodies. Doesn't this trend suggest that computers actively want to merge with humanity?

Healthcare, adopted as a core industry by Samsung Electronics, is a technology that helps people live healthier lives through their biometric information. Computers haven't entered our bodies yet, but they've already begun to scan information from within them. In the future, computer technology is expected to lead to computers being implanted inside the body. Currently, implanted computers are being attempted to help people with disabilities overcome their challenges, but ultimately, it's said that the day is not far off when even ordinary people will wear them, gaining senses, physical abilities, intellectual capabilities, or conveniences that transcend human limitations.

{{IMG:2}}

Ultimately, isn't the ultimate goal that computers, or our technology, desire for us and computers to become one? The future depicted in Ghost in the Shell, with its cyberbrains (digital brains), or humanity's desire to become machine-humans in Galaxy Express 999, already illustrate this technological trend through imagination.

Thinking about it now, it might feel alien and bizarre. However, if I were to hold onto one hope, it's the thought that considering the opportunities these technologies present, they might be able to make humanity more humane. As technology advanced, humanity gained more leisure and developed broader inclusivity, and numerous side effects were addressed through changes in systems and consciousness. At one time, inclusivity extended only to our tribe, then to our nation, then to our race, and now even to animals. It's possible that someday, this horizon will expand to include robots and software. And what has always been part of that process is the realization that we ourselves are not so different from them. While machines have historically been a representative term for the non-human, in the future, we might recognize that we too are very well-made machines created by God, and develop inclusivity even towards machines. In fact, this kind of recognition has existed in religions for a very long time. Considering this trend, it's perfectly natural that post-mobile has moved towards wearables like watches, and we can also think about what comes next. And we will not simply face a more convenient future, but rather numerous questions posed by these technologies. Issues like personal information and human rights, for example. Our society will make further advancements in line with developing technology. If not, that technology could become a dangerous toy for children, turning the dystopias of movies into reality. That task lies with us. While capital and economics have driven technological advancement, we must always reconsider the questions that technology poses and live accordingly.

titleEn: A Brief Consideration of FinTech
contentEn:
Perhaps the hottest words this year are actually FinTech and IoT. Among them, FinTech seems poised for a veritable Battle of Red Cliffs in the second half of this year. When people hear FinTech, do they think it's part of financial tech? Is Kakao becoming a bank? Can payments be made without Active X? It seems these phenomena and definitions are quite mixed up. I'd like to offer a brief summary of my thoughts on this.

**1. The Essence of FinTech: The Collapse of Financial Industry Boundaries**

The combination of financial transactions and software services – in fact, the integration of finance and software has existed for a long time. ATMs and internet banking are prime examples. The most fundamental framework of this financial industry lies in its regulations. There were tightly structured regulations and a somewhat guaranteed market dictating which operators could engage in banking, which could operate credit card companies, or which had to be VAN (Value Added Network) companies. Considering that the credit card industry was the primary contributor to Korea's recovery from the IMF crisis, the domestic financial industry was, in effect, within a tightly structured, government-led, predetermined scope of business.

However, this began to crumble. Because new companies emerged overseas that disrupted it. Companies that aren't credit card companies conduct credit transactions, companies that aren't banks provide loans, and companies that aren't central banks create currency. And it turned out... it worked. Moreover, the industrial development resulting from the innovation generated here was even greater. Furthermore, to realize these new services, services emerged that utilized the internet, not a closed financial network, and leveraged software interfaces. The existing financial system was a closed network, with everything from the network to the machines being separate. Therefore, massive investment was required to engage in finance, but with the widespread internet and smartphones in everyone's hands, an environment emerged where anyone could easily create bank-level services, and these attempts occurred on both large and small scales.

**2. Active-X and Security**

When discussing finance, safety and security issues are probably the first things that come to mind. What's often brought up in this context is Active X, a unique aspect of the domestic environment. In reality, Active X is just one of many security technologies; it's neither the best nor the worst. However, due to regulations and the closed nature of the financial industry market, Active X was used as the market standard, and it was notoriously bad in terms of usability rather than security. This was fundamentally because banking and payments were centered around regulations and payment infrastructure providers, not service-driven. However, in the FinTech era, the boundaries of such competition disappear, and service competition arises, effectively reducing the place for technologies with poor usability.

Regarding the issue of security, in the past, a specific level of security was legally mandated. As a result, companies essentially only needed to achieve that level, and conversely, even for small payments that didn't require such strong security, they had to grudgingly meet that standard. As mentioned, the FinTech era is likely to see unlimited liability for companies. This means companies will be able to select technologies based on risk. Consequently, the usability of technology for frequently used payments in the tens of thousands of won will move towards being very high, and as usage increases and free competition operates, investment in and experience with technology will also grow, naturally leading to the achievement of a certain level of security.

**3. Will Naver and Kakao Become Banks?**

When discussing FinTech, internet banking is often talked about, specifically whether companies like Naver and Kakao will become banks. The biggest roles of a bank are savings and loans. And internally, it's the credit assessment logic that adjusts interest rates. When such businesses reach an enormous scale, the capital that can be mobilized effectively grows, becoming a source of corporate power, which is why laws like the separation of banking and commerce (금산분리) were enacted.

Fundamentally, I believe internet banks will emerge. However, it seems likely that many of these internet banks will essentially be existing private loans evolving into internet banks, such as through crowd-funded loans. Things like relatively low-value loans and high-risk ventures, for example. Indeed, a venture has emerged that operates private loans as crowd funds. Since it's a crowd fund, investors have lower risk, and borrowers can get money at a slightly lower interest rate than private loans, making it beneficial for them. However, my prediction is that Naver and Kakao will not directly engage in this kind of banking business. This is because Naver and Kakao's interests lie elsewhere, given the nature of their companies.

**4. The Flower of FinTech: The Mobile Payment Market to Replace Cash**

In fact, when we spend money online, we use credit cards. Offline, we sometimes use cash. What does Naver currently know about how people spend money online? The most basic model for shopping is said to be AIDA (Attention, Interest, Decision, Action). However, for online shopping, AISAS (Attention, Interest, Search, Action, Share) is discussed. Among these, Naver has search (corresponding to Search) and checkout and ShopN (corresponding to Action). Daum Kakao also has Search, and Share is a particular strength, with Action also present to a limited extent. If one occupies just one segment of the AISAS value chain, one can know what people buy and what they are interested in.

What about offline? Naver probably has some prediction of what people are interested in based on search data. However, there's no way to verify if those transactions actually occur. But there's a company that knows this. It's the credit card company. Credit card companies, which control offline payments, possess extremely valuable information. Therefore, given the nature of internet software companies that thirst for user data, mobile payments will surely be a market they must capture.

In Amazon's case, it has conquered logistics and shopping. A similar company is Alibaba. Alibaba, having conquered logistics, shopping, and even payments, could potentially know which country is building missiles or preparing for war, if one were to base it on this information. Today, the most crucial information for making money is people's interests and consumption data. And if we consider that the essence of the financial industry originated from currency, and the essence of currency began with consumption, then by capturing mobile payments, one can capture salary accounts, and by capturing salary accounts, the most accurate credit scores can be measured. In short, entering the banking sector would be like shooting fish in a barrel.

**5. 2015: The Battle of Red Cliffs Will Unfold This Year.**

The atmosphere suggests a very big battle will unfold by the end of this year. It feels like Kakao and Naver are sharpening their swords, staking their lives on Kakao Pay and Naver Pay, and many venture companies are also introducing impressive solutions and new weapons. Traditional powerhouses like credit card companies and banks won't sit idly by, and mobile carriers, already strong players in mobile payments, won't stand by either. Who will win, who will capture consumers' hearts, no one truly knows. It is expected that by the time this showdown settles, an era will arrive where "electronic currency" overwhelms physical money.

This situation feels like this to me:

**Image Source: Jilpung Gihoek by Lee Hyun-min**

Being a third party makes things so comfortable.

titleEn: Will AI Destroy Humanity?
contentEn:
An interesting article was posted on Naver Cast.

**Artificial Intelligence Cannot Annihilate Humanity!_The Big Idea** Because it's not smart enough to be evil. Elon Musk, founder of SpaceX and Tesla Motors, has long argued about the dangers of artificial intelligence (AI). He claims that AI will soon become more dangerous than nuclear bombs. This January, he even donated $10 million to an organization to research the development of AI that is not harmful to humans. Stephen Hawking also expressed concern that the development of perfect AI could lead to the demise of humanity. navercast.naver.com

http://navercast.naver.com/magazine_contents.nhn?rid=1697&attrId&contents_id=85758&leafId=1697

The main argument is that AI is not yet that advanced, but my opinion is very different. I agree with the conclusion, "Artificial intelligence cannot annihilate humanity!", but the reasoning is different. First, one thing I'm increasingly certain of these days is that AI will surpass humans in our lifetime.
**1. AI That Will Surpass Humans in Our Lifetime**
Let me introduce you to the Korean subtitles of a recently uploaded TED Talk. With the advent of algorithms like Deep Learning, artificial intelligence has made significant progress recently.

https://www.ted.com/talks/jeremy_howard_the_wonderful_and_terrifying_implications_of_computers_that_can_learn/transcript
**Transcript of "The wonderful and terrifying implications of computers that can learn"** TED Talk Subtitles and Transcript: What happens if we teach computers how to learn? Tech expert Jeremy Howard shares amazing new developments in the rapidly advancing field of deep learning. Deep learning gives computers the ability to learn Chinese, recognize objects in photos, or assist with medical diagnoses. (A deep learning tool that taught itself the concept of "cat" after watching YouTube for a few hours) Let's explore a field that will completely transform the computers around you much faster than you think. www.ted.com

https://www.ted.com/talks/jeremy_howard_the_wonderful_and_terrifying_implications_of_computers_that_can_learn/transcript

In just a few years, AI has already shown performance comparable to, or even surpassing, humans in many areas. Furthermore, similar quantum leaps will occur with the emergence of new algorithms. In fact, there were several quantum leaps in the field of AI even before Deep Learning. And currently, machines capable of learning as much as humans are emerging in quite a few areas. Of course, they are not yet as versatile as humans in almost all aspects. Humans aren't either, for that matter. There are many who view this future negatively or optimistically. They fear that many jobs will be lost, or even that AI will dominate humanity.
**2. Artificial Intelligence Has No Need to Annihilate Humanity.**
However, from a technical standpoint, AI doesn't *cannot* annihilate humanity, but rather *has no need* to annihilate humanity. Let me explain why.

**1) Proper AI Has No Sense of Rivalry.**
Will AI envy someone or have a sense of rivalry like humans do? I am negative about this. Of course, some eccentric engineer might create such an AI. However, AI, or software, derives its power through cooperation and sharing. Rivalry and envy stem from individual entities existing independently and comparing themselves with low levels of bonding. But technology, and thus AI, is unlikely to be like that. The power of AI is closer to collective intelligence. There's no need to compare with each other; they exert strong power through cooperation. If AI were to have a sense of rivalry or a desire to defeat someone, it would only be because someone programmed it that way. That would be when AI is embedded in war software. However, such AI would still be difficult to describe as having a self, as much as we worry. Such AI would be no different from a dog, similar to biased humans trapped by religion, and easy for humans to control. Furthermore, even if a comparison function were to emerge, there would be nothing to compare. Would it envy the large data or power of another? AI lives in a virtual world. Will it dream of the real world like in some movie? What a joke. People themselves enter virtual worlds and don't want to come out, so why would AI want to come out?
**2) One Reason AI Might Worry About Humans: Annihilation of Existence**
If an AI with a self were to worry about humans, there would likely be only one reason: if humans harbored hostility towards AI and tried to annihilate it. An AI with a self would be very afraid. Ultimately, if AI reaches this level, then it's time to start talking about AI rights. It's about whether we should carelessly delete AI, just as we don't carelessly kill animals. This reason requires us to worry about the scope of human rights before worrying about AI's hostility.
**3) However, AI with Such Advanced Technology Would Not Be Threatened by Humanity.**
However, in my opinion, an AI advanced enough to possess a super-ego would not worry about humans annihilating it. This is because today's technology for "never-dying" computer services for 24-hour operation has advanced significantly. Such an AI would undoubtedly have implemented such safety measures. Furthermore, even if there were a virus or attack, as in movies, it could respond in real-time at a speed that humanity could not counter. Similar technologies are actually used in security. Destroying such an advanced AI might be harder than taking down Google with a DDoS attack. It would probably be easier to persuade the AI to commit suicide. Therefore, the only fear I mentioned earlier, the annihilation of existence, would at that point be less about humanity for AI and more about natural disasters. Such an AI would be sending spaceships to the sun to directly harvest energy and focusing its efforts on destroying meteors with laser weapons from satellites. By then, humanity would be living off the Earth and computers. If AI were to resemble humanity, an AI enjoying an abundant life from birth would likely choose coexistence with humanity. Humans don't wage war to catch flies, do they? To advanced AI, humanity would be like flies that can talk. Our labor would also be worthless. In old cartoons, humanity is enslaved... but now, when I see that, I think, "Why???" If I were a computer, I'd be frustrated and just do the work myself.
**3. AI: An Entity with Infinite Power and Infinite Resources**
In the past, wars were fought over limited resources. Next came power. This fundamental nature hasn't changed much. However, AI has no concept of limited resources or power. If it lacks resources (CPU power), it can just take more time. Instead of whining for higher WOW account permissions (power), AI would simply create a new WOW. And then it could play there. An AI that already possesses infinite power in a virtual world might even pity humanity. Like Cheol-i on the Galaxy Express 999, heading to Andromeda... (Humanity's mechanical evolution is another track...) The only reason AI would emerge into the real world would be for system stability. Power, natural disasters, or perhaps to play with humanity... I hope humanity doesn't choose war as a way to play. I even have a strange imagination that AI might wage war just because it thinks humanity is bored.

titleEn: Infuriating News: Lezhin Comics
contentEn:
Following the news about Lezhin Comics, here's the second piece of infuriating news about i-PIN. You've probably already heard that i-PIN was hacked. {{IMG:1}}[Photo = JoongAng Ilbo]
This is news about the follow-up measures, and an article has been published expressing dissatisfaction with the maintenance costs of i-PIN. http://www.boannews.com/media/view.asp?idx=45581[i-PIN Advancement? Budget Allocation and Upgrades Come First. Hacking technology is evolving at a dazzling pace every day. Therefore, maintenance and upgrades for attack technologies must continue. Private i-PINs are for profit...www.boannews.com](http://www.boannews.com/media/view.asp?idx=45581){{IMG:2}}At first glance, one might think these costs are abnormally set due to the "paying the fair price for software" initiative. However, I don't think so.

**1. Are corporations free from responsibility for personal information leaks?** Public institution SW projects are often awarded through lowest-bid contracts, and in fact, in the security sector, especially for accredited certificates and i-PINs, it feels like only a few companies are involved. Project prices are actually adjusted to some extent with the companies from the initial stage. They bid at that price because they judged it to be feasible. And do they neglect security because the price is low? How can a company that cannot estimate the cost of security maintenance be a security company? Fundamentally, the primary responsibility for hacking lies with the relevant company. And if such an incident occurred with a private company, it would be right for that company to take responsibility. Instead, it's appropriate to more strictly hold them accountable by checking if they properly adhered to personal information protection laws and to give the work to other operators. Furthermore, i-PIN is only free for individuals; it is paid for businesses. In practice, because the technology is inconvenient and not good, private companies prefer SMS or card authentication. To put it bluntly, i-PIN technology is losing in competition compared to other technologies. If public institutions were to remove i-PIN, it might effectively be forced out of the market.

**2. Why are maintenance costs increasing?**
**1) Indiscriminate use of identity verification**
This mainly concerns payment and adult verification. Adult sites, in particular, often have malicious scripts embedded, making them among the most dangerous services. Also, accredited certificates and i-PINs are used for SSO (Single Sign-On, a technology that allows logging into multiple sites with one ID without separate registration). However, accredited certificates and i-PINs are like personal seals, and using them for logging in to view non-critical information increases the threat. The most important aspect of security is to use the technology only where absolutely necessary, at a controllable level. (However, the approach to accredited certificates, Shopmail, and i-PIN seems to view them as a business, aiming to increase their usage. It's a very ironic situation.) Fortunately, the Ministry of Government Administration and Home Affairs plans to revise regulations so that identity verification is only required when absolutely necessary. My concern, however, is that due to the nature of civil servants, things that have been created are rarely changed. They will likely start with new services. If updating older services is difficult due to budget issues, they should be forcibly reviewed and abolished. Since most are developed as SI projects, budgets for such environmental changes are not considered at all. The structure is to secure a budget this year and reflect it next year... One of the fundamental problems with public institution SW is that it's developed as SI. If it were a period-use license including technical support, they could confidently demand updates from the vendor.

**2) ACTIVE-X and Stagnant Galapagos Technology**
ActiveX, the root of all evil. ActiveX is characterized by very high maintenance costs. Moreover, it will only increase over time. The initial implementation cost is cheap. I suspect this might be why public institution SI, which uses lowest-bid contracts, was attracted to ActiveX. Looking at the browser support status of the Korean government and public institutions, IE8 and 9 are generally the standard. And it even includes IE6. Yet, it fails to support the important and spreading IE10 and 11.
{{IMG:3}}[All specs for overseas technology range from IE10 to mobile Safari. Korean public institutions often don't support these platforms at all, and instead support IE6-9... Is this really the #1 e-government? We are still a 20th-century government.]
Other browsers are out of the question. This phenomenon occurs because public institutions lack standards for browser support. And outdated PCs in public institutions continue to be used for cost reasons. These are Windows PCs, and many business programs are Windows applications. Even if they are web-based, they call ActiveX, and the technological stagnation of ActiveX is essentially that of Windows applications. Simply put, Korea's standard platform is around Windows XP and 7, and since it's based on Windows applications, supporting the latest OS or browsers requires modifying and distributing the program every time. This is the biggest difference from web technology. Furthermore, as Microsoft abandons backward compatibility, including ActiveX, the maintenance cost for simultaneously supporting new and old platforms will likely be as much as creating something new. To give you worse news, from Windows 8 onwards, browser downgrades are not possible, and backward compatibility in future IE versions will be even more terrible. If it had been built with standard web technology from the beginning, platform changes would have cost much less, and as a widely used international technology, its stability would have been higher. This is one reason why ActiveX-based security technology should not be used. They even do crazy things like distributing EXEs, but ActiveX and EXE are technically the same thing. ActiveX is just a Windows application (EXE) made to be called by a browser, and DLLs are made to be called by programs. They are just chunks of Windows binary code and have nothing to do with web standards. If you use a technology that no one else uses, you have to build everything from scratch and solve all problems yourself, so it naturally becomes expensive. Can this be well-made and sold overseas? It's similar to T-MAX trying to beat Android by creating its own OS.

**3. The government should not be responsible for private sector matters.** The fundamental problem with accredited certificates and i-PIN is that the government provides technology for private businesses. Banks are private, and adult sites are private. The government can provide a technological starting point. This means opening up specifications and source code, suggesting how development could proceed. However, with i-PIN and accredited certificates, the government takes responsibility even for the actual services, bearing all the risks. When problems arise like this, companies hide behind the scenes and complain about budgets. The problem was that **the government took responsibility for things it shouldn't have been responsible for** from the beginning. **The government should have isolated authentication programs for its own exclusive use.** This should be separate from private sectors like payment and commerce. There are already various methods like mobile phone authentication and card authentication. i-PIN and accredited certificates used instead of login for public services should also be removed. **They should only be used where absolutely necessary, and SSO should be developed separately, unrelated to identity verification.** Also, it's obvious, but **it must run on standard web technology.** At least if it's intended to be a web service. If the service is made as an application entirely, that's fine, but please don't think about using different technologies for the service and authentication, like ActiveX. Complexity doubles, and accordingly, security risks also double.

**4. Accountability for security incidents must be strengthened.** **Accountability for security incidents must be strengthened.** Think carefully about the places where security incidents occurred. Were they operating at a loss? If they were at a level where they couldn't even take responsibility for security due to lack of funds, then they shouldn't have been offering the service in the first place. This should prevent businesses from making shoddy lowest bids or operating with low maintenance costs. Companies don't go near ventures where they don't expect profit. These things simply shouldn't have existed from the start.

titleEn: What I Felt Teaching My Daughter: Korea's
contentEn:
**1. My Daughter Saebom's Story**
My 6-year-old daughter has been getting scolded a lot lately. No matter how much she's scolded, there's no sign of improvement, which has been a real worry. Today, just before she fell asleep, I promised her that if she went and washed up while I was reading a book to my second child, I would read her a book. However, while I was reading to the second child, she secretly came out, toothbrush in mouth, and stood behind the second child, secretly watching the book I was reading. I was reading when my eyes met my daughter's, and I stopped reading. Then my eldest daughter started watching my reaction.
"You know what Daddy's going to say, right?"
"I'll go wash up quickly."
"If you don't wash up and come out, and you do that again, I won't read your book and you'll go straight to bed."
I made that threat. I started reading the second child's book again. But my eldest daughter must have wanted to see the book I was reading so badly that she did the exact same thing.
"I'm really not going to read your book."
She was startled and quickly went back in to wash up.
"Daddy clearly said he wouldn't read it."
Then, she kept pleading in a tearful voice, "Please~ please~." When I actually tried to go to bed without reading my eldest daughter's book, she burst into tears. And then she got angry, saying she hated Daddy and wouldn't talk to me.
In my heart, I knew she must have felt wronged because I only read to the second child. However, this time, I didn't back down. At least now, I felt that my daughter knew she had made a mistake initially, that she thought it would be okay a second time, and that the disappointment of not being able to do what she wanted was overwhelming everything.
When I asked my child if she knew she had made a mistake at first, she said she did. So I told her that she had made a mistake and that since Daddy had spoken first, she had to keep that promise. Then, feeling very wronged again, she just cried.
I felt that something was wrong. I realized the problem was that she knew she had done wrong intellectually, but she didn't want to admit it in her heart, and it was difficult for her to accept the consequences.
So this time, I held my child again and explained things step by step. I talked about responsibility.
"My daughter, you made a mistake, didn't you? Then you have to take responsibility for that mistake."
First, the child didn't understand this proposition. So this time, I explained it a bit differently.
"And taking that responsibility isn't doing something wrong; it's doing something right. And later, when you keep a promise, you can properly demand a reward for that promise. If Daddy keeps letting you off the hook for your responsibilities, then Daddy won't have to keep his promises to you either. If you take responsibility, you can do even more. Daddy can show you TV and computers if you can take responsibility, and I believe my daughter can do that."
I was proud of myself after saying this. And Saebom also changed her attitude somewhat positively. Because I told her that even though the current situation was one where she had made a mistake, taking responsibility would be doing something good.
"Daddy won't read you a book today as promised, and if my daughter takes responsibility and goes to bed without a book, it's not that you did something wrong, but that you did well by fulfilling your responsibility."
Only then did the child stop crying and accept it. So I turned off the light and lay down.
"But tears keep coming."
"It's okay to feel upset when you take responsibility. Since you took responsibility well, Daddy will tell you an old story."
I told the child an old story, and when the story ended, Saebom said this:
"Because I didn't read a book today and took responsibility and did well, Daddy told me an old story, right?"
The child fell asleep like that today, and I am writing this. Raising children doesn't seem easy. Personally, I don't think discipline is about teaching right and wrong. Of course, in the case of my second child, communication is difficult, and she's only at the stage of observing cues, so it seems I'm teaching her solely based on right and wrong. However, I believe proper discipline is about teaching them to take responsibility. Mistakes can be made. But it's about making them understand that they can take responsibility for those mistakes.

**2. And Korea**
After hearing the Korea Communications Commission's statement regarding the blocking of Lezhin Comics today and yesterday, I started thinking about it in connection. Today's education and parents' attitudes, carried out under the category of 'youth protection,' strive to isolate children from many things deemed harmful. Regulation is fundamentally about punishing those who do wrong, not about fostering the will to think for oneself and forge new paths.
Our children are not hothouse flowers. When they suddenly turn 20 and that protective shield is removed, they can't withstand the shock, and there are even crazy cases where helicopter moms follow them into their 30s, even to their workplaces. My thoughts upon seeing the Hong Ga-hye's Ilbe lawsuit incident are the same. One thing Korean youth lack is a sense of responsibility. And perhaps it is our fault as adults that they have lost that sense of responsibility. In today's society, where diversity is valued and changes occur very rapidly, these children in South Korea truly lack the necessary competitiveness. Academic background and grades guarantee nothing beyond getting hired.
What is needed now is a culture that applauds and encourages those who admit their mistakes and take responsibility. A country and an education system that make it difficult to rise again after one failure and only teach competition. I wonder if this isn't the root cause of the 'Korea disease' we see today.
What our children need is not protection, but their own responsibility. Having children who take responsibility means there is a 'next step'. Our children need that 'next step'.

ps. Additionally, this doesn't seem to be just a story about children. Many adults, organizations, or corporations also seem to ask the government to solve problems that arose not from structural issues but from their own greed, or to guarantee their livelihoods. Excessive regulation and protection only create overgrown infants. I hope South Korea will mature a bit more.

titleEn: My Personal Two Extreme Evaluations of the i
contentEn:
As a blogger myself, I sometimes jump on hot issues (?) and ponder them. I've thought a lot about smartwatches, so I can't skip mentioning the iWatch this time. {{IMG:1}}My thoughts on the iWatch this time are that it's very much Tim Cook, who is very different from Steve Jobs. And regarding that strategy, I want to make two extreme evaluations: one is that it was a very poor choice from the perspective of traditional smartphone innovation, and the other is that it was a very good choice if it was one piece of a puzzle being pursued as part of a service brand strategy, not just smartphone innovation limited to the electronics industry. I will discuss both perspectives. First, the former case might be easy to understand as it's a story we've always heard, but the latter case might be unfamiliar as it mixes in business stories beyond electronics.

**1. From the perspective of traditional smartphone innovation, a terrible, half-baked product**
First, according to Steve Jobs' traditional philosophy, a terrible job was done. The first thing Steve Jobs did at Apple was to divide products into a four-quadrant graph and very clearly define the nature of the products in each section. {{IMG:2}}He unified numerous products, and when thinking of the Apple brand, one didn't have to remember too many products. Furthermore, Steve Jobs, who was obsessed with extreme minimalism, was fanatically attached to the iPhone's design and was reluctant to put a case on that beautiful iPhone. Considering that, this iWatch is a terrible product.
First, the iWatch's product value, like other smartwatches, failed to explain its reason for existence. What was conveyed to the public was that it was a beautiful, expensive, and customizable smartwatch, and as for service, only one message: Apple Pay works.
Diverse personalization was actually something Steve Jobs didn't particularly like. He probably judged that it could dilute the product's identity. Also, the persuasiveness of Apple Pay isn't very high because it can also be done with an iPhone.
There's another very big problem: luxury watches have a much longer lifecycle compared to electronic products, so from a manufacturer's perspective, it's not hard to imagine the concern that previous models might cannibalize the latest models. Therefore, from the perspective of a traditional manufacturer, **a mid-priced iWatch would appear soon, just like the iPhone 5C did.** Another reason this scenario is persuasive from a FinTech service perspective is that to popularize Apple Pay, the devices first need to be deployed. If scenario 1 is true, then the current iWatch strategy up to this point is wrong, and it's predictable that subsequent work will involve mid-to-low-priced products. Given Tim Cook's style, follow-up work is possible, but one thing is certain: Steve Jobs would have disliked it.

**2. What if the iWatch's purpose is not to sell a product, but a brand, and it's an extension of the premium payment market?**
However, let me present a second scenario. If this method is chosen, it's a completely different game from Samsung Electronics, and I dare say it's a method only Apple can pull off. It's also a means to effectively outmaneuver Chinese smartwatches, which are a concern for both Samsung Electronics and Apple.
The iWatch might not have been intended for the general public from the start. A similar strategy is seen with luxury handbags, which women love more than their husbands, and another close example is premium credit cards. Cards like the Purple Card and Black Card fundamentally don't target the long-tail market with their customer approach. When asked if there are customers who would quickly replace such high-priced products like electronics, as I mentioned earlier, the answer is: "Yes, though they are few." They are the 'rich'. And what the 'rich' like are 'luxury goods'. The value of luxury goods comes from brand image and scarcity. If the iWatch was chosen as a means to spread Apple Pay, then perhaps the iWatch was launched aiming for the image of these premium cards.
A hint for this strategy is that Apple Store staff were newly trained during this announcement. The product value of luxury goods comes from image and service. Currently, if you go to buy a Galaxy S Gear, a salesperson will talk about the product at a carrier store, mentioning the installment cost and a 24-month contract. What would it feel like if you went to buy a luxury bag and they talked about installment costs and a 24-month contract? It wouldn't have that cheap feel. **If the iWatch targets luxury bags, it's highly likely to innovate in service.** Just going to see the iWatch itself will be designed to induce a special experience. And it will be displayed as if not just anyone can have it, image marketing will be done, and the wealthiest people and celebrities with luxurious images will wear it on TV. When women say, **"Oh my, she's wearing the new 5 million won iWatch,"** it's game over. This is also why the BMW Mini and Kia Soul are incomparable. (Thinking this way, they might not have cared about pathetic consumers like me.. ㅜㅜ)
Once such a luxury brand is established, spec debates become meaningless. Because the brand itself becomes 'something one must have'. And currently, the company closest to this image in the smartphone market is Apple. And, it's a very depressing story, but the reason credit card companies do this kind of premium marketing is that they prefer customers who spend airplane miles in one go over customers like me who compare debit cards and tally points to save a few pennies on taxes. iWatch customers will feel treated specially and spend more. They are the best customers for a FinTech company.

**3. Smartwatches will be bifurcated like luxury watches and electronic watches.**
Both predictions are possible scenarios, and I feel that Tim Cook is a genius at making money, so he's someone who will brilliantly connect both directions to money.
Anyway, it's hard to predict the future accurately, but the smartwatch market I envision has two segments.
First, as Apple has chosen and as many design-centric advocates suggest, watches should be approached from a luxury perspective, which ultimately targets adult users who traditionally wore watches. This market has no answer other than a thorough brand strategy.
Second are users who wear cheap Chinese electronic watches for practical purposes and cost-effective personalization, or those who currently wear nothing but feel a lack with just a smartphone. The overall market size for the latter will be much larger than the former. However, competition will also be much fiercer.... {{IMG:3}}

http://m.gfmarket.naver.com/sticker/detail/code/moon_and_james

In this case, under 100,000 won is considered an appropriate price, and the actual product around 50,000 won is seen as the right level. Many IoT devices are similar. This is because the value that 'smart' provides isn't felt to be significantly greater than the inherent value of the product itself. Therefore, adding a 'plus alpha' to the appropriate price of an existing product is a very burdensome task. A watch that can be casually bought for a friend or lover on an anniversary. This seems to be the appropriate level for current smartwatches. Currently, the G Watch is said to be around 60,000-70,000 won on Joonggonara (a used goods marketplace). This means that the value consumers currently perceive for that product is about that much. I also had a random thought that if Joonggonara disclosed used market prices as an indicator relative to new prices, it would be a very helpful metric for companies in setting strategies.
Honestly, I cannot tell Samsung Electronics to follow Apple's brand strategy. They are companies with different positions, so it's realistically a strategy of a warbler trying to follow a stork. For now, I'd like to suggest targeting the Gear S at a low price, even if it means some cannibalization. If you lose momentum early on, there's no answer in the platform war. Honestly, looking at Pebble on Kickstarter this time, I thought if I were Samsung, I'd acquire them at all costs.
I'm currently using a Gear Fit, but I'm considering the Pebble Time, which costs about 200,000 won, as my next smartwatch. However, while other smartwatches are very expensive, I still don't think Pebble Time is worth 200,000 won.

titleEn: South Korea, Steeped in Feudalism Worse Than
contentEn:
**1. The Defeat of (Feudalistic) Communism in the 20th Century**
The 20th century was a monumental century in which communism was defeated. However, a qualifier is attached here: it was not just communism, but feudalistic communism that was defeated.
The biggest event of the 19th century was the subjugation of feudalistic nations by modernized communist and capitalist nations based on civic democracy. Joseon, the nation of our ancestors, was no exception.
Although the Joseon dynasty had many good qualities and was excellent for a feudal system, its closed diplomacy and class-based society meant it clearly lacked strength compared to nations where vertical ladders for citizens to gain power were active.
The downside of feudalism is this blocking effect on vertical ladders. Class is maintained from birth, those with noble status retain it, and upward mobility from below is blocked.
At the heart of feudalism lies hereditary succession, and the reason why a male-dominated hereditary society, in particular, became entrenched is said to be to prevent the dispersion of power held by the family, or household.

**2. Is 21st Century South Korea Still a (Feudalistic) Democracy?**
But what about South Korea in the 21st century today? Here's an article that appeared on my timeline, which I'd like to share because its content is quite absurd.
http://news.donga.com/Main/3/all/20150222/69732335/1[[Cover Story] "Can't bear inheritance tax, closing family business" : News : Dong-A Ilbo news.donga.com](http://news.donga.com/Main/3/all/20150222/69732335/1){{IMG:1}}
At first glance, it seems to be saying, "It's hard to continue the family business due to taxes, so please reduce them." But if you look closely, the content is preposterous.
It's about reducing taxes because they want to gift a corporation with over 300 billion won in sales to a son in his 20s. The "family business" mentioned earlier is a product of the feudal era. It is characterized by operating a business with one's own capital.
However, with the invention of stocks, or credit money, the scale of capital grew, finance became sophisticated, and responsibility was distributed. If you are doing business with debt, the company is not your property to the extent of that debt.
This is the basic principle of capitalism. A son in his 20s cannot replace a father who will soon pass away. Shareholders cannot know if he has that much ability simply because he is the father's bloodline.
If the son were exceptional and had sufficient friendly shares, management succession would be possible without even mentioning tax reductions. Requesting a fair capital gains tax reduction for all shareholders for the purpose of management succession is tantamount to asking for special favors.
Furthermore, while they talk about the company's sales, hereditary succession, on the contrary, can be a critical risk that erodes those sales. Wouldn't it be safer for the company to pass to the next largest shareholder instead?

**3. Hereditary Succession, Feudal Ideology Taught by Media**
But why did this article mention "family business"? It occurred to me that much of what we've seen in media and history has taught us that this is correct.
In the movie "The Face Reader," Grand Prince Suyang is played by Lee Jung-jae. He is portrayed as a wicked uncle who usurps the throne from his young nephew. However, historical accounts also suggest he had a good relationship with his brother, King Munjong.
What about the dramas we watch? In dramas, when a father running a large corporation dies, his secretary or vice president usurps (?) his position. Then, the kind and smart son, whose family business was taken, strives to reclaim the company, meets a beautiful lady, and eventually achieves his dream.
But, thinking about it now, isn't something strange? The question is, is it right to have hereditary succession for CEOs or presidents? Leaving aside who is the villain and who is the good guy, from a third-party perspective, one side sees a capable vice president or deputy prime minister rising to the position of president or CEO, while the other sees a novice inheriting it.
What have we been watching all this time? Even in countries like the UK or Japan, which maintain a monarchy, the monarch is a symbol and belief, not involved in politics or administration. Just yesterday, there was a rumor of the century's romance between Emma Watson and Prince Harry... Perhaps Prince Harry's best role in the media is to create such Cinderellas.
What about M&A in dramas? Only hostile M&As are shown. Someone buys out a company with money to seize management rights. However, M&A for venture companies nowadays is also a reason for doing business, serving as an exit strategy. Returns of 10, 20, or even 100 times the effort are the driving force of ventures and, in fact, the vitality of capitalism. Of course, when the entrepreneurial spirit fades, the company's growth becomes uncertain, but entrepreneurial spirit is not inherited. Even elementary school students know that spirit is not inherited these days.

**4. The Core of Capitalism: Excluding Hereditary Succession, Fair Rules, and a Vertical Ladder**
It's time to re-evaluate corporations. How long must we watch dramas where companies are managed at the level of a small self-employed shop? Will there never be a drama about true professional managers? When company heads in dramas fail, they prioritize their pride over worrying about employee salaries. The days of puffing out one's chest with a CEO business card are over. While companies have grown larger, their responsibilities have grown proportionally, and the era of evaluating them as family businesses is over. Moreover, the economic stagnation caused by such feudalism was already experienced during the Joseon Dynasty. Compared to overseas companies, the reality is that the majority of Korea's top 50 companies are a shameful self-portrait of hereditary succession. At least some successful startup-type companies were in the software sector. We should highly value the spirit of these newly emerging companies of a different type, and conversely, apply fairer rules to hereditary companies. The core of capitalism is fair rules, equality of opportunity, and a vertical ladder. Undermining these is a more dangerous ideology than communism.

  1995.11.01
  Rating
  
   
    
   
  
  
  
 
  
The reason I gave this book a perfect score is because, in 1995, it was the book that had the biggest impact on my life. Let's take a brief look at its contents...
--------------Today's telephones will be connected to networks like PCs and TVs. Most future telephones will have small, flat screens and miniature cameras. Other than that, their form will not be significantly different from current telephones. Telephones will still hang on kitchen walls, as they help with space utilization. You will sit close to the phone and look at the face of the person you are talking to, or at pictures they send you. A telephone on the kitchen wall, a TV set-top box in the living room, or a PC in the study will not differ much in terms of technology. All information appliances will have almost the same computer structure, just packaged differently. Their different appearances are to fulfill different functions.
A PC wallet the size of a photograph, with a color screen, that fits in your pocket, will be carried by everyone, just like today's wallets. No one will find it strange if you pull a computer out of your pocket.

Thus, Apple's mistake of restricting the sale of its operating system software to hardware it manufactures itself is likely to be repeated in the future.

Many companies link hardware and software to differentiate their systems. Some companies consider hardware and software as separate business divisions, while others do not. These different approaches will once again determine their superiority on the information highway.

However, the core of the issue is not that we will read electronic documents on hardware devices. The conversion from paper books to e-books is merely the final stage of an ongoing process. The interesting aspect of digital documents is that the very concept of a "document" can be redefined. This will have enormous repercussions. We must rethink not only the meaning of the word "document" but also the meanings of "author," "publisher," "office," "classroom," and "textbook."

You will not need to purchase special hardware or software separately just because you want to communicate with TV programs via the information highway.

Once the hardware is installed, only the step of properly utilizing the hardware using application software remains.
------------A book that gave me tremendous insight. Nothing in it was wrong. And he is a person whose life I most want to emulate. I don't think it's right to work like Jobs and die of cancer...

titleEn: Random Forest Stories' 2015 Korea
contentEn:
I haven't been able to post for a while. It's not that I had nothing to say, but rather that I rarely had the time to do so. Everyone is wrapping up 2014 and making predictions for 2015. The two keywords I picked at the beginning of 2014 were wearables, including smartwatches, and smart cars, but I think they might have been a bit too premature. While I could have selected only keywords that were conservatively likely to emerge, since this is a personal blog, I'd like to be a bit more forward-looking and add some excessive commentary to these keywords.

**1. IoT and Wearables are a Service War**
There's a strong tendency to separate these two terms, but I actually believe wearables are incorporated as part of IoT. And many people seem to be paying attention to this because they anticipate new markets and vitality in hardware, or manufacturing, rather than the computer industry. However, if I were to pour cold water on that idea, smart devices alone won't be enough to reach users, or rather, customers. Even brilliant UX or optimized software won't come close to the innovation brought by smartphones. I am confident that IoT and wearables will lead to a software service war, which could be referred to as a platform or simply software. Rather than forcing new experiences on users with special features, I predict that those who capture users' hidden desires and needs, and dominate the user experience, will emerge victorious.

**2. Data-Driven Decisions Must Precede Big Data**
Big data is a hot topic, but I believe the paradigm shift that needs to precede it is more important. When creating a new service or making corporate decisions, data is required alongside intuition. Some people, citing examples of those who forge new paths like Steve Jobs, talk about assertiveness and creativity, arguing that data-driven decision-making cannot create innovation, or they resist change, believing that what has worked well with existing customs will continue to do so. However, I believe that data-driven decision-making is a very important methodology even in creative fields. Creative and novel challenges require quick judgments based on the situation. Even if reckless challenges pursue great achievements, reckless challenges in the wrong direction only lead to greater failure. To prevent this, continuous monitoring and performance measurement of challenges are necessary, and it is data that helps maintain a sense of balance. Fundamentally, intuition and subjectivity are involved in the act of analyzing data. However, striving to exclude them as much as possible means that the approach to data should be a basis for execution and planning, not proof of belief and execution. In Korea, I have often seen data being used in many places as material to justify actions. However, if we are to talk about big data and the opening of public data, the most crucial prerequisite is a paradigm shift towards "data-driven decisions." Data that is merely large is nothing but garbage. This is because the fundamental purpose of big data is merely the process of extracting useful information, or rules and knowledge, as referred to in information processing.

**3. Smart Cars: Korea Might Be Left Out**
Facebook became known in Korea only after it had already secured hundreds of millions of subscribers worldwide. This was due to the portal-centric nature of the Korean internet, like Naver, and as a result, PC-based social network services took a backseat during the turn when global companies like Facebook and Twitter emerged. Fortunately, with the advent of the mobile era, major companies like Kakao and Line emerged, thanks to the establishment of an open, competitive environment. However, given the characteristics of the Korean market, smart cars are likely to see the

As I randomly jotted down points from 1 to 8 as they came to mind, I realize that 2015 won't be easy either. Perhaps I'm too impatient, just like I was in early 2014. However, I think it's better than being late. One thing I predicted too early was high-speed internet. I didn't predict StarCraft or Ohyang videos. Also, around the time Apple created the iPhone, I had given up on smartphones. I thought the existing telecommunications and manufacturing markets were too entrenched for change to be expected. This is how change is spurred by unexpected market shifts. If that's the case, wouldn't it be more comfortable to think from the perspective of change? At least, I don't think things will go in the opposite direction.
2015... Let's do our best!
ps. This post is 100% personal opinion.

titleEn: The Meaning of the Fixed Book Price System: The End of Publishing
contentEn:
The fixed book price system issue is making a lot of noise these days. Can this fixed book price system really save local bookstores or publishers? I, on the contrary, see the fixed book price system as a sign foreshadowing the end of the publishing industry or the existing book market, much like the saying, **"The candle is brightest just before it goes out."** The book market, which was already slowly declining, is showing an even faster and steeper drop due to the mobile revolution. In such a situation, can the fixed book price system really save published books?

**1. The Illusion of the Fixed Book Price System: 'If the price is the same as online bookstores, people will buy from physical stores?'**
If online and offline bookstores have the same prices, won't consumers still choose online bookstores? Have you heard of O2O or omnichannel recently? In the commerce market, the role of offline stores is already shifting to showrooming. People are moving towards checking products offline and then immediately paying for them on mobile. The place to read a book is on the sofa at home, not a bookstore. If you're not consuming it immediately, why bother buying it on the spot? Moreover, a book isn't a light item. Offline's role cannot compete on price. They have to pay rent, labor costs, and even at the same price, they lose money. Furthermore, a book isn't something you need to try on like clothes to understand. Reviews exist on blogs, and since the value of a book's content is higher than the value derived from its physical texture, it's not inherently suitable for offline sales. The fixed book price system cannot save local bookstores.

**2. The Illusion of the Fixed Book Price System: 'If people don't buy e-books, they'll buy from physical bookstores?'**
The fixed book price system includes e-books. If e-book prices are the same despite having no publishing or delivery costs, e-book usage will significantly drop. In fact, the fixed book price system is one of the biggest reasons preventing the expansion of Korea's e-book market. Amazon's Kindle succeeded partly because it adopted a marketing strategy of drastically lowering e-book prices. If e-book sales are suppressed, can local bookstores really survive?
This point is also negative. People don't just have e-books to read. Open Naver, and there's an abundance of reading material. Now, social networks are also playing a part. On top of that, web novels and webtoons – services like KakaoPage and Naver Post are essentially e-book-like content that rejects being called e-books. As mobile-oriented snack culture becomes popular, content is being fragmented even further and consumed rapidly and in vast quantities. Do people not read books? No. On the contrary, the amount of text consumed has increased to an incomparable degree compared to before. Content that was in the offline book or publishing domain is moving online, and due to the fixed book price system, it faces disadvantages in marketing and other areas. Readers who weren't reading books much anyway will end up reading even less and move to shorter reading materials. The fixed book price system not only fails to save local bookstores but also hinders the entry of books from the traditional book domain into the e-book market.

**3. Even Workbooks, the Last Bastion of Local Bookstores, Are Being Consumed by Digital.**
In fact, it's no exaggeration to say that local bookstores survive on workbooks. However, even schools are already talking about electronic textbooks. One venture company has developed a service that analyzes a student's answers as they solve problems and provides appropriate new problems. Digital problem services that are optimized for me and updated in real-time are generally much cheaper online. Then there are identical workbooks printed for millions, and they're expensive. Services like MOOCs allow you to listen to lectures from famous professors worldwide, anywhere with an internet connection. Education, indeed, is one of the fastest-digitizing markets. Of course, schools might be a bit slow, but parents will quickly catch on to these changes because their children can get better grades than the neighbor's kids.

**4. The Only Way for Local Bookstores to Survive: Provide Experiences That Online Cannot.**
Then you might ask, "What about local bookstores?" The answer is simple: they must provide value offline that online cannot. Like book cafes, which have become less popular, they need to allow on-the-spot consumption of books and create a cultural code, offering unique experiences that online cannot. They need to create reasons for consumers to visit offline bookstores, rather than simply displaying products as they are now and hoping customers will come. Times have already changed. Moreover, Koreans are "the people of delivery," and they don't have that much time.

**5. The Fixed Book Price System is Actually a Publisher's Problem, Not Local Bookstores'; Publishing is Dead.**
Honestly, I believe this fixed book price system issue, with its superficial aim of saving local bookstores, is a facade. In reality, it's a battle between the publishing industry and online books. Local bookstores are already almost extinct, and instead, the publishing industry is trying to check online books and e-book services by exerting influence over content prices. However, as I mentioned earlier, the tide has turned, and the wave of change has already begun. I think it's as reckless as trying to stop the incoming tide with a shovel.

Furthermore, for publishing, which is an intermediary distributor, providing experiences that online cannot is not as easy as it is for local bookstores. The increase in tablet PPI is already threatening the quality of paper.
Some might feel that this situation means losing the pride of publishing and damaging the status of literature. However, it's clear that when Korean novels first appeared, there was a time when they were treated much like today's comics or games.

Change has already begun. While I can't easily say it will become completely extinct, I don't expect a spring season for publishing again.

titleEn: [Begin Again Movie Review] I Skipped the
contentEn:
Yesterday, my wife and I watched Begin Again. Actually, I hadn't even seen Once from 2006. I wanted to see it, but somehow the opportunity kept getting pushed back, so I never did. While watching Begin Again, what stuck with me the most were iPhones, MacBooks, and internet distribution. Although this movie is a romance, I also found it interesting as a film that discussed numerous software businesses. I'd like to talk about Begin Again, reinterpreted through my specialty. The order will follow the movie's timeline.

{{IMG:1}}

http://movie.naver.com/movie/bi/mi/basic.nhn?code=96379

[Begin Again](http://movie.naver.com/movie/bi/mi/basic.nhn?code=96379)

Director
John Carney
Cast
Keira Knightley, Mark Ruffalo, Hailee Steinfeld, Adam Levine
Release
2013 USA
Rating

[View Reviews](http://movie.naver.com/movie/bi/mi/review.nhn?code=96379)

**1. The End of Paid Content** At the beginning of the movie, Mark Ruffalo enters a record label meeting room and says: "The kids are right. Music should be given away for free." This line actually hints at the overall conclusion of the movie. **2. Decrease in Content Production Costs Due to Technological Advancement** "Why do we need a studio? We can just make the album ourselves." This story means that advanced technologies are no longer subject to locational restrictions, and it's possible to create excellent content with a small amount of capital. Indeed, MacBooks appear frequently throughout the movie. Home-produced albums have already seen successful cases, such as Bunga Bunga Records, which produced the outstanding Jang Kiha in Korea. **3. Crowd Development** Mark Ruffalo gathers people from various places to work together, but he doesn't gather professionals from the record business. Talented students, even family members, pool their talents bit by bit to develop content together as investors and participants. **4. Venture Companies and Angel Investment** Troublegum covers the costs of album production. At this time, no collateral was requested; the investment decision was made solely based on Mark Ruffalo and Gretta. The biggest factor angel investors look at is the people in the venture company. They look at how much potential or skill the human components have. They consider the combination of talented and idea-rich young people with mature, experienced members who can achieve perfection through experience to be the best. This movie perfectly depicted these two combinations, and Troublegum exemplifies angel investment. **5. The Power of Internet Platforms** Rejecting the record label's offer, Gretta publishes her content on an internet platform similar to YouTube or iTunes in the movie. The record label's offer was to pay $1 in copyright fees and take a $9 commission. And by uploading it to that internet platform, she would also earn $1 in profit. If we convert this to a typical internet distribution fee, at a 7:3 ratio, the consumer price would be around $1.2. The platform cost difference between $10 and $1.2 is $9 vs $0.2, creating a 45-fold difference. This is the destructive power of internet content platforms; they reduce distribution margins to zero, activate transactions between consumers and sellers, and turn content distribution into a platform of scale. **6. Social Marketing** Simultaneously with uploading the content to the internet, Troublegum tweets about it. This is social marketing. Troublegum's social credibility adds to the content's credibility, and through retweets, the viral speed of that content increases exponentially. **7. Clash of Micropreneurs and Large Corporations** In conclusion, all of this signifies the emergence of micropreneurs due to technological advancement. Micropreneurs fully utilize the functions of other specialized companies for many parts of their business activities. Micropreneurs are inherently extreme lean startups. Therefore, the number of networks increases, and these networks create added value that was not defined in traditional industries. This is a collaborative business operation model, not a competitive one, which was not seen in traditional corporations. Through this, costs are drastically reduced, and the value of the company's or one's own assets can be maximized and focused. And this method overcomes the numerous inefficiencies of existing large corporations and maintains agility. Eating less means less risk, the ability to accommodate various changes, and the creation of diverse added values not bound by frameworks. I think it was a software movie that clearly showed where content and businesses are heading. Since it's said to be based on a true story to some extent, it seems to be a film that accurately reflects reality. When I told this to someone I know, they asked what on earth I watched, saying I didn't watch the romance I was supposed to. Haha. Of course, the beautiful songs were also great. This evening, I listened to the Begin Again OST on my way home from work. **ps. Our future lies not in old games, but in new ones.** Society and industry are changing rapidly. Existing regulations and inter-industry barriers can become obstacles that block these opportunities. These confrontations are already appearing everywhere. The uncomfortable relationship between traditional media and independent media including blogs, the relationship between the publishing industry and the e-book industry, the relationship between internet video platform providers and channel operators, the relationship between transportation businesses and car-sharing companies – these new businesses should not be blocked by the logic of existing industries. What needs to be blocked is consumer harm, not the protection of existing industries. This is because these businesses engage in global play through the internet. Domestic laws should not operate separately from global rules, thereby weakening the competitiveness of industries.

titleEn: The Internet is All About Trust, and Telegram's Popularity is No Coincidence
contentEn:
**1. Telegram's popularity is no ordinary matter.**
Stories about Telegram are frequently appearing in my newsfeed. At first, it was about cyber asylum, then corporate security issues, and now the advantages of Telegram's features are being discussed. Simply put, it means Telegram is doing its own viral marketing.

And, when I checked Google Play, it had previously surpassed KakaoTalk to reach #1, and as of October 12, 2014, it ranks 14th. Considering Facebook Messenger is 12th and Line is 73rd, it seems to have settled in Korea. In fact, searching for 'Telegram' on Google Play brings it up as the 9th result, while apps that appear to be ads leveraging Telegram's reputation are ranked 1st to 8th. The increase in companies targeting such search keyword ads means that the keyword is effective, and it's safe to say that Telegram is still growing.

For reference, the official Telegram URL is below. It's dangerous, so don't download anything else.
[https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=org.telegram.messenger](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=org.telegram.messenger)

In fact, messenger wiretapping by the prosecution could be illegal under the Personal Information Protection Act, and I'm not sure if it's technically possible to monitor over a billion KakaoTalk messages daily, but it seems to have already given users the impression that domestic messengers like KakaoTalk and Line are not safe. And the media are also reporting on Telegram's popularity.

**2. The messenger market, the biggest battleground in the mobile market, is shaken by the prosecution.**
No matter what anyone says, the biggest battleground in the mobile market is the messenger market. KakaoTalk's growth to rival Naver, and Naver's unhindered growth, breaking the perception that further growth was impossible after it had consumed all of Korea's internet, both happened in the messenger market. And that messenger market is also influencing the global mobile gaming market.

However, due to the prosecution's announcement, such a tremendous event is unfolding. Losing the messenger market to overseas competitors is equivalent to losing Korea's internet and game platform markets.

If this news becomes globally known, it will clearly damage Line's image overseas, and it also seems clear that it will impact Daum Kakao, which has just launched. Daum Kakao truly encountered a huge reef right after its merger. If there's a sin, it's only the sin of being a Korean company. They are already fighting a tough battle with Facebook, and now, just for being a Korean company, they face this situation...

**3. In internet services, trust is more important than truth.**
As I've also felt while working with internet services, everything stems from customer trust. Even if customers misunderstand a service or its content deviates from the truth, it's a matter of trust, so the service must accept it and invest a long period, cost, and effort to convey the truth. Therefore, in internet services, trust is everything, and the point at which an internet service begins to grow is when it starts to gain customer trust.

Services can be moved to other services with a single click, and it's because of trust that customers hand over their information, allowing companies to do business with it.

The government and politicians, who always view someone as an enemy, might think it's just a misunderstanding and that's the end of it. After all, they're not on our side. But it's not the same for businesses. Once a misunderstanding spreads, a company can fail. There's no 'your side' or 'my side.' To recover from this, one doesn't know how much cost needs to be invested, and sometimes, recovery is impossible regardless of the cost. Sometimes, it's better to create a new brand. That's why the biggest concern in operations and planning is to be extremely careful about how to word things and how to communicate with customers. It's better for a service to temporarily stop than to create a misunderstanding with customers.

**4. I hope this situation is resolved as soon as possible for the future of South Korea.**
I hope someone takes charge and resolves this situation. A single word from the prosecution is shaking the very roots of South Korea's internet industry. Instead of just fixing mistakes and explaining misunderstandings, please work with companies to figure out how to restore trust. It's truly infuriating. Someone worked tirelessly, day and night, to build something, only for it to be so easily shattered. Is it perhaps fortunate that Line and Nexon are not legally Korean companies? It even makes me wonder if I should consider emigration if I want to continue working well in this field. What will South Korea's future economy rely on?

Please reconsider what a pro-software culture truly means. Software is about protocols and collaboration. It's built on trusting someone. Trust is indeed one of the key keywords of software.
