titleEn: How Accurate Were Forest Story's
contentEn:
I'm going to write about the results of the predictions I made in early 2013. How many points will I get this year? [http://fstory97.blog.me/70155086282](http://fstory97.blog.me/70155086282)

**1. Mobile Sector**
**1) Popularization of the Tablet Era due to Windows 8**
It seems the tablet era will become popularized due to Windows 8. This is expected to happen after the emergence of affordable Windows 8 tablets, similar to netbooks, rather than expensive Surface Pro-type ultrabooks. Personally, I believe MS's survival in the mobile era rests on Surface ARM, which I will cover in a separate post. In January 2012, I predicted that MS would surpass iOS to become a strong player, but currently, I will revise that prediction to say it will be difficult in the smartphone sector. I will also mention this in a separate post.

**2) Expansion of Mobile/Tablet Commerce**
Mobile and tablet commerce, still small compared to PC commerce, is expected to surpass it starting next year. Currently, it's not expanding due to device scarcity, inadequate payment platforms, and a lack of product diversity, but it is expected to see the biggest growth with the popularization of tablets. And, companies offering killer services will emerge as a result.

**3) Mobile Surpassing PC Traffic, Cannibalization Occurring**
Until now, mobile has not eroded PC traffic but has acted as a substitute. However, as mobile growth accelerates and tablets, an extension of mobile, increase, mobile will surpass PC traffic starting this year, leading to cannibalization. Already, during specific periods like presidential elections or the Olympics, there were days when mobile surpassed PC. However, mobile is expected to truly overtake PC in 2013. And this will be a threatening year for companies with PC-based business models.

**4) The Portal Big Three Structure to Become a Platform Big Three Structure**
The existing big three portal structure of Naver-Daum-Nate was valid until this year. However, starting next year, it is highly likely to transition into a big three platform structure led by companies that have successfully navigated the shift to mobile platforms. And the contenders are likely to be Naver-Kakao-Daum. Compared to the portal big three structure, a single dominant player might see its fees somewhat reduced, but Daum Communications' weakness seems likely to be very noticeable. Daum, which held a 30% market share in the PC sector, is likely to fall below 20% in the mobile sector. Ultimately, it seems Daum is facing a painful restructuring. And the competition between Naver and Kakao to become the leader in mobile platforms will be the most significant mobile issue of 2013.

**2. Telecommunications Sector**
**1) LTE Boom, Alternative Technologies Under a Cloud**
Throughout 2012, 3G networks saw only a slight increase, almost stagnating. Mobile carriers' aggressive push is expected to continue in 2013, creating an atmosphere where LTE dominates. Similarly, WiBro is also likely to decline. The expansion of LTE will further narrow WiBro's position. Ultimately, this will cast more doubt on the feasibility of a fourth mobile carrier. I think it will be difficult now. Super Wi-Fi, being slow and a technology that could directly impact LTE's profits, will likely not see participation from mobile carriers. Furthermore, since general Wi-Fi used by businesses and homes already satisfies most needs, there will be no companies or coffee shops willing to install Super Wi-Fi to open their networks to those far away. Super Wi-Fi has technical characteristics that make it difficult to sustain without being approached from a public good perspective, and without government effort, it will struggle to thrive. Given President Park Geun-hye's past statements, the power of telecommunication companies significantly influences this, so I believe the expansion of this technology will be difficult. I desperately wish the 10,000 APs she promised to install were Super Wi-Fi... ㅜㅜ

**2) Household Communication Costs Unlikely to Decrease**
One might optimistically hope for a decrease if President Park Geun-hye's promises of abolishing subscription fees, lowering smartphone prices, and improving distribution systems materialize. However, since she avoided direct mention of rate plans compared to other candidates, it seems difficult to view this optimistically.

**3) Gigawifi (802.11ac) Rollout**
The next-generation network of Gigawifi (802.11ac) is a technology that suits mobile carriers. Its speed is 1.8Gbps, faster than existing wired networks. However, since its range isn't significantly extended, mobile carriers are likely to utilize it as a complement to LTE. Home APs will also be replaced with this.

**4) Net Neutrality: A New Topic**
Mobile carriers' position in the service sector will continue to narrow, and in an effort to check this, the net neutrality debate will accelerate. Mobile carriers will maintain their stance on network quality, while service providers will insist on network transparency. This issue cannot be resolved until the government steps in, but since service quality cannot be held hostage due to fear of user backlash, mobile carriers' profitability issues will continue to worsen amidst the controversy. Furthermore, if a technical alternative for network transparency is decided upon, there is a very high possibility that mobile carriers will be relegated to dump pipes. To solve this, I believe the answer is ultimately for mobile carriers to spin off their service companies. What will be the relationship between SK Planet and SKT?

**3. Service Sector**
**1) Boom in Venture and SI Companies**
Due to President Park Geun-hye's promised ICT strategic industry, more funds will flow into the IT sector. This could lead to a situation with a lot of so-called 'blind money.' Therefore, many venture companies utilizing niche markets are expected to emerge, and SI projects for public institutions will also increase. I wonder if this could lead to a second dot-com bubble.

**2) Shortage of Professional Investors, Bubble Expansion**
As a lot of money flows into IT, the dilemma of which companies to invest in will deepen. Therefore, the need for IT professional investors seems likely to grow significantly. This must be absorbed by existing industry professionals. And since this cannot be cultivated immediately, the risk of investment failure remains very high, making an IT bubble somewhat predictable.

**3) Improvement in Treatment for IT Workers**
Ultimately, as the supply of developers becomes insufficient, not only will there be quantitative IT expansion, but also a growing desire for improved treatment for IT workers. Many IT workers who experienced the previous dot-com bubble are also deeply concerned about this.

**4) Expansion of Sharing and Open Services and Technology Value**
To meet faster business demands, mashup services and open source will gain attention. Furthermore, the spread of Gigawifi and quad-core mobile environments are creating an even more suitable environment for cloud services. These technological changes will also lead to changes in the business domain. Methods for resource sharing, such as the sharing economy and sharing services, seem likely to expand not only to software but also to the material sector. (South Korea still has a strong tendency to do everything on its own.)

**5) Expansion of Services for the Elderly**
What was revealed in the results of this presidential election is the demographic distribution of people in their 50s. This group has a significant information gap, but their smartphone penetration rate is rapidly increasing. In other words, it's a blue ocean. Compared to users who quickly adapt to existing trends and are highly curious about new things, this group requires more careful consideration. The IT sector's concerns about this will deepen, and I predict? No, I hope a hit service emerges from this segment this year.

**6) Big Data Bubble**
The illusion surrounding big data seems to have spread widely in 2012. However, I express some concerns about it. In South Korea, due to market size and a portal-centric structure, there isn't much meaningful big data. Facebook and Twitter users are limited, and the most significant search queries in South Korea are held by portals, which are not open about them. (Personally, I wish Naver would sell this data like Twitter does... I'll cover this in a separate post when I have time.) Therefore, most companies, except for those like Hyundai Card that have already secured big data, find it difficult to acquire meaningful big data themselves. Thus, if limited to domestic context, I feel that expectations for big data are too high.

**7) Weakness in Domestic Gaming Sector, Strengthening of Soundness**
With President Park's strong expression of will, I expect the biggest changes here. The global sector was doing well, so it will likely continue to do well.

**4. Beyond Gaming, Expecting Korean Global Hits**
Finally, based on the environmental background mentioned above, we can expect global hit products. For now, NHN's LINE might reach that level, but in the enriched domestic IT ecosystem, services like Kakao, which succeed independently without relying on the power of large corporations (like Naver), are likely to diversify later. Can we look forward to the enriched IT environment of 2013?

**5. Overall Assessment**
**Average by Sector**
Mobile: 72.5
Telecommunications: 72.5
Service: 48.5
Global: 100

I was too reckless with the service sector ㅜㅜ
Out of 16 items, the average is 63.75, and I'll aim to exceed 70 next year. I realize I should refrain from making reckless predictions, and I'm reminded once again that the service sector has a fast lifecycle and is not easy to predict. I will write next year's predictions again in early 2014.

titleEn: Why I Want to Teach My Daughter Software
contentEn:
It was an incident that happened at my daughter Saebom's first birthday party (doljanchi). In addition to the customary items placed on the table for the doljanchi – money, thread, a microphone, and a pencil – a 'mouse' has recently been added. The doljanchi host decided to remove one item, and with the overwhelming support of the guests, the 'mouse' was voted out. I am a graduate of Soongsil University's Computer Science department, and many of my seniors, juniors, and IT colleagues were present. The host joked that it was the first doljanchi he had ever seen that so despised a 'mouse'. Anyway, even within the IT profession, the evaluation of our work is actually like this: I find it interesting and I'm doing it for now, but if I were to pass it on to my children, I'd wonder? Changing such an environment is indeed a challenge we face, and it's something those of us in the field should do. However, national and global trends have begun to highly value software, and countries and companies are stepping up to cultivate young software talent. After the dot-com boom, there's still resistance due to concerns about the ecosystem being damaged by state-led cultivation of low-quality software talent, but fundamentally, I am in favor of teaching children software. If you ask why software among so many things, I'd like to explain why I want to teach my daughter software and what I want to do with her.

**1. Software doesn't wear out.**
Let's imagine a child and a father building something wonderful with blocks or creating a magnificent piece of art. What are the chances this creation will still exist in 10 years? Especially if they built a working machine, will it still function after all that time? The BASIC program I wrote as a child, starting on 5.25-inch floppies, then 3.5-inch, HDD, CD-ROM, DVD-ROM, and now the cloud, has only seen its storage medium change, but it still exists. And it can still run today. What will my daughter feel in 20 years when she sees the comments her father left?

**2. The Importance of Collaboration**
What I want to teach is not coding. Coding is just like learning how to hold a brush. What I really want to do is create 'something' together with my child. We'll plan, draw image resources, and code to make it run. And I'll divide the tasks with her. Perhaps we might even bring in a few more friends. Building blocks can, of course, provide this kind of experience. However, there is no tool as optimized for collaboration as software. To the extent that just learning management tools for collaboration can be a huge undertaking. Teaching the concept of configuration management, this can teach the fundamentals of collaboration.

**3. Concepts of Complex Logic Sets through the Software Lifecycle**
Everyone thinks software is perfect, but bugs are actually inevitable. What's even more interesting is that initially simple software becomes a patchwork as requirements increase and features multiply. Logic that appears perfect and has been around for a long time all possess these structures. Along with awe for how great the knowledge we've accumulated is, we can teach about the many flaws that arise from its complexity, and how difficult and remarkable it is. We can teach why the adult world is so complex and why even simple things cannot be maintained. (Perhaps she'll become cynical too early.)

**4. Global Mindset through Open Source**
First, there's the issue of teaching English, but I want to use open source and eventually have her participate in it. Even without sending them abroad, even if they're not fluent in English, developers are actually the kind of people who find communication through a line or two of code more comfortable. You can build blocks together, but you can't build them with a friend in Argentina on the other side of the world, can you? In the software world, global experience is possible with just a few clicks.

**5. The Ability to Realize Thoughts**
I know children have many ideas. That's true. However, I want to teach and let them experience what problems arise when concretizing these ideas, and how to focus on and develop ideas more effectively.

**6. Confidence and Joy from Creating Something**
This is the biggest reason I started with software and am still working in this industry. The sense of accomplishment that comes from creating something with my own hands and seeing many people use or enjoy it can build confidence.

Let me reiterate, what I want to teach is not coding. Coding is merely one of the skills for creating software, and actually creating software is a completely different and much larger endeavor. And its true value comes not from 'knowledge' but from 'experience'. I want to teach my child that experience early on.

What purpose and vision do countries and companies truly have in mind when they try to teach children? I believe concrete and good implementation plans can only emerge under a clear vision and purpose. If it's just about teaching one or two languages, video lectures are actually sufficient. And this experience doesn't mean I want them to start a venture or join this industry I'm in. More than anything, it's about having this experience.

The problem is, I haven't actively worked with software as my main profession for quite some time now. lol (I should at least do it as a hobby...)

titleEn: The Government's Role in the Internet World
contentEn:
Before starting this post, I'd like to show you a picture first.{{IMG:1}}It's probably one of the simplest and most famous drawings in the world. It's a drawing that came to mind when I saw a trend indicator graph of a certain website. It's an indicator graph for a service specializing in internet statistics that recorded hundreds of thousands of visitors in its first week of opening in late September, but by November, weekly visitors were below a few thousand, and page views, which exceeded millions in the first week, were only tens of thousands by November.

**1. What happened to the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport's Vworld, which once dominated trending searches?**
Not long ago, Vworld adorned portal trending searches and was praised by the media as a map surpassing "Google Earth." Vworld is a map service created by the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs, a government agency. You might ask, "Why?", when Naver, Daum, and Google already exist. Honestly, I want to ask the same "Why?" about this. The development cost isn't low, and these days, with the business value of maps confirmed by Google, Naver, Tmap, etc., portals and specialized companies are staking their lives on creating good services in this area.

If you search for the service concept, it's "searching for national spatial information." But from a user's perspective, how often would they need to search for national spatial information? How often would they search for nearby restaurants? Overwhelmingly, it would be the latter. It's clear that this model is destined to fail in gaining popularity as a map service.

Perhaps because of that, Vworld by the Ministry of Land, Transport and Maritime Affairs, which boasted a flashy UI featuring 3D, is virtually a dead service. After its initial launch, it succeeded in attracting millions of users, even to the point of servers crashing, due to how much marketing budget, or rather, how many articles they pushed in the media. My thought at the time was, 'They're really putting on a show of administrative performance'. Because it succeeded in attracting user attention, but it seemed like a service with no sustainability whatsoever.

**2. Services cannot succeed with bureaucracy and outsourcing.**
In reality, no company succeeds solely with great ideas and great technology. Those are just seeds; creating a proper business and a useful service is like cutting a diamond. However, the government has no experience cutting diamonds, nor does it intend to. Most government projects rely on those important diamond cutters as outsourced contractors for a certain period. Even if they cut well, they don't get anything in return, and from the government's perspective, which initiated the project, "having done it" is what matters, not success, and in fact, it shouldn't succeed. Because the government is not a business operator.

**3. Flawed planning that forgot important values and focused on visible user interfaces**
What's more absurd is that this site used a technology called Active X. Active X is an application. From a developer's perspective, Active X is used in web services to demand high privileges on the user's local machine or to create a more elaborate UI than web technologies. In this case, the latter was the purpose of use. UI is the element at the closest point of contact with the user. And a project whose purpose was to open data, or in developer terms, the "model," "national spatial information," ended up advertising, in 3D UI developer terms, "the 'view' is cool."

It's like a project to introduce a next-generation fighter jet boasting about the interior design of the cockpit instead of the jet's combat capabilities. If social is trending, they attach SNS-like features to government agency websites; if webtoons are popular, they add webtoons; if Naver looks cool, they try to configure it like a portal – they do all sorts of useless things like this. It even looks childishly flashy, like a college student's startup. The essence of a "service" is its core value. Just slapping on trendy things doesn't make it successful. If the goal is to open national spatial information, they should consider the easiest way to open that information. If it were me, I would have created the national spatial information as an Open API and provided it to portals. (Content added below on 2014-05-27) Because the customers they need to meet are there. A service that creates a website and tells customers to come find it feels quite arrogant. **ex) Daum DNA's Public APISensorQL, which I consider a successful case (Content added on 2014-05-27)** [http://dna.daum.net/tools/pg/sensorql](http://dna.daum.net/tools/pg/sensorql)​

**4. What the government should do is not internet services.**
What the government should do is not internet services. Internet services are a business domain. The very act of a national agency setting user traffic as a KPI for administrative showmanship is akin to that national agency engaging in internet business.

**5. For the sake of the market, the government should not interfere with services.**
In fact, recent developments like Shop Mail, Big Data certifications, and adult authentication for youth-harming content all strongly feel like the government is creating opportunities for specific companies. The government should not interfere with services. The government is the most powerful "authority" in South Korea, even greater than Naver or Samsung Electronics, and for that authority to meddle in internet business is something only a "communist state" would do, it's "market disruption," and it's a violation of fair trade laws in itself. I hope we no longer see the government creating internet services as administrative showmanship or favoring specific companies to the point of inconveniencing the industry.

**6. What the government should do is an invisible platform; a good platform should be lightweight and flexible.**
The government is like the nation's platform. A platform never steps forward. I don't want to see politicians who ruin the quality of services by attaching labels to supported venture companies, stating which agency supported them, thereby messing up the UI, or even appearing at IT events to interrupt speeches by famous international dignitaries just to boast about themselves. A good platform must be minimized, lightweight, and flexible to allow services running on it to operate nimbly. At the very least, it shouldn't be a service plastered with Active X, only running on IE and Windows. I sincerely hope the government becomes one that works nimbly and flexibly behind the scenes. The reason Apple made money with iTunes and was welcomed by developers was because it allowed developers to sell *their* apps, not Apple's. And the companies and people who are rewarded will recognize your hidden efforts.

**ps. 2014-05-27 Adding content regarding Vworld's Open API.**
**At the time this article was written, Vworld had already opened its Open API and developer center. My opinion is not that this part was wrong.** That part was well done; however, the regrettable point is that they only emphasized the service aspect of the 3D map. The media talked so much about the 3D map that even I, a developer, overlooked the truly important Open API. They also launched a mobile app, and surprisingly, it was receiving user tagging in a way typically done by startups. My opinion is that it would be better not to provide such user-facing services.

Additionally, I don't know how many private companies have developed using that API since then. Most of the application cases on that site are related to government agencies, and discussions about it are rarely found in developer communities. In fact, from the perspective of developers or third parties, Vworld's platform is not very attractive. The reason is that a service platform should inherently be like solid ground. However, Vworld, being government-led, is uncertain in terms of business continuity, scalability, and global support, making it unsuitable as a service platform. There's no certainty whether it could respond at the level of Google or major portals if it suddenly became a huge success like Line or Kakao while using that platform. If an internet service experiences an outage for a few days, its growth ends there. Zuckerberg, seeing cases where existing social network services failed during growth, responded with his life on the line during Facebook's growth, and that was precisely why. Responding to such a service is impossible with outsourcing and bureaucratic technical support without partnerships. Service platform providers prioritize partnerships for mutual growth, and therefore, agile response is considered the foremost virtue. However, it's naturally difficult to expect this from government projects where the operating entity and the ordering party are separate. Again, a 3D map is a service platform. The government's role is to stop at the technical platform level.

titleEn: Reflecting on the Value and Changes of Education in Light
contentEn:
**1. Suneung, South Korea's Biggest Event: A Nation of Fierce Competition**
I only realized today was Suneung (CSAT) day after seeing mobile news on my way to work. Suneung, one of South Korea's biggest events, is not just a major occasion for high school seniors and families with children preparing for college entrance exams. Police become busy, company commutes are delayed, and even airplanes are grounded, showing a situation akin to a national emergency for all citizens. Even civil defense drills, which prepare for actual combat, seem less combative compared to Suneung day. Everyone offers words of encouragement for the Suneung. "Do well on the Suneung." "Cheer up." Students who excel in their studies will be nervous, while those who struggle might feel like they're being dragged to a slaughterhouse. And when the results are announced, there will be those who rejoice and those who sigh, perhaps preparing for another year. Was the ancient civil service exam similar to this? It seems not much different from that time when it was considered the only path to success and honor. Good universities have become like a religion, and South Korea, which values connections, has solidified this, and its power remains immense. They even say that Seoul National University and KAIST dominate everything in the IT industry, which is supposedly merit-based, so that says it all.

**2. Let's Reconsider the Value of Education. The Value of Education is Knowledge Transfer.**
Now, let's talk about current education. It's certainly no exaggeration to say that education culminates in the Suneung, but I question whether today's education truly fulfills its role. First, why do we take the Suneung? Why do we have to study? There's even a webtoon based on these questions:

http://comic.naver.com/webtoon/list.nhn?titleId=495498
**Zero-Point Alliance : [http://comic.naver.com/webtoon/list.nhn?titleId=495498](http://comic.naver.com/webtoon/list.nhn?titleId=495498)**
A one-shot battle called Suneung. What awaits us at its end?
Our alliance to find that answer.
Masatokki / joana

In fact, it's difficult to give a clear answer to this, and to be honest, each stakeholder would state a different objective.

"I want to marry a celebrity." (Celebrity fan)
"I need to make a living." (Cram school director)
"Don't we need to hire smart employees?" (Entrepreneur)
"Shouldn't our university and alumni have power?" (University official)
"My son should live comfortably." (Parent)

Indeed, today's education system will elicit different answers from each stakeholder. Education is, in fact, a massive industry, and the nation, corporations, students, and parents will all have different answers.

However, if we talk about the essence of education, it is, in fact, **"knowledge transfer."** As the power of knowledge became power and money, the importance of knowledge transfer, or education, gained value. In other words, the value of education comes from the power of "knowledge." This knowledge can, of course, include character.

**3. Suneung, Composed of Core Subjects (Korean, English, Math): Why Line Up Based on Basic Knowledge?**
As I mentioned above, I said that the power of knowledge is the value of education. Does the Suneung, created to prove this knowledge acquisition, effectively convey this core value? To do well on the Suneung, you still need to excel in Korean, English, and Math. And these are called "basic subjects." But isn't that a bit strange? The idea that doing well on an exam composed of "basic subjects" holds value, in other words, doing well on the Suneung only proves that a child is good at the "basics." To have value, one must add something beyond these basics.

However, I feel that we are staking too much on these basics, and the value of universities entered through these basics is also excessively high. Personally, I believe the difficulty of the Suneung should be eased, and if the Suneung truly consists of "basic" subjects, it should be a criterion for eliminating candidates, not for selecting them. And in fact, in businesses and practical fields, the standards of Korean, English, and Math are used as criteria for eliminating candidates (civil service exams being an exception).

**4. Suneung, It Is Nothing.**
Let me say it again. Suneung is not about whether you do well or poorly. It's okay to not do so well on the Suneung. Not all brilliant individuals who create highly complex things are good at mental arithmetic. Of course, statistically, they might be better than the average person, because an excellent brain also includes memorization skills. But if we look at overall brain ability, an IQ test is more effective than the Suneung. IQ tests were designed for that purpose.

**5. Is University Really Important?**
Now that we've talked about Suneung, let's return to universities. Universities have set departments and curricula. And these curricula are developed based on academics and industry. They say that if you complete this course, you can succeed in that field. I once heard from a professor that our seniors considered getting a job at the Ministry of Communications (post office) to be the highest achievement. This then led to Korea Telecom (wired communication), then more recently to wireless communication companies like mobile carriers, and nowadays, internet companies are also preferred. Industry changes constantly like this. Universities also change their curricula accordingly, but as the pace of industrial change accelerates, the curriculum might even change between when you enroll and when you graduate. This phenomenon is not limited to a single department. More broadly, there are cases where industry needs shift from hardware to software, meaning from electrical engineering to computer software.

This means there's no guarantee that a popular major when you enroll will still be popular when you graduate, or when you reach old age. Therefore, while the university and major are certainly very important, the direction you set now won't be your final goal in life.

**6. Nevertheless, the Value of University Lies in Youth**
So, I'm not saying that Suneung and university have no value at all. There is definitely value in university. It's highly likely that your university life will be a period where you meet new people on campus, find friends who share similar perspectives, try things together, wonder if this path is right or that path is right, wander, worry, and experience trial and error.

Because it is the only period in South Korea that does not teach "competition." In fact, this is another result that indicates flaws in South Korea's education system, but from elementary school through high school, and then after graduating college and getting a job, South Korea has been teaching "competition" for decades, and that is the current reality of South Korea. Of course, some people now say that universities also involve competition. However, I believe the value of university still lies in youth and freedom. And even if you don't go to university, your early twenties should be a period where you can enjoy that. Because young people have just begun their lives.

**7. Education in an Unpredictable Future**
This post started with the intention of discussing changes in the future education system, but the conclusion has veered too much into university and Suneung talk. In fact, the education system will change. And what is certain is that the current Suneung and universities will lose their competitiveness. This is something I can guarantee. The reason is that knowledge changes faster than curricula, and academia will exhibit an organic pattern of frequent convergence and divergence. The College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT) might attempt to structure itself in a way that enhances problem-solving abilities in preparation for such an era, but what is clear is that such problem-solving abilities will not be assessed by exams or taught in cram schools, but will largely depend on more experiential and intuitive aspects. Because computers already excel at memory, and that memory (information) can be easily accessed anywhere, the aspects that will be considered more important for humans will be these experiential, intuitive, and analytical abilities.

Finally, let me tell you. The College Scholastic Ability Test. It is nothing.
It is merely one line on the resume of your life. Regardless of your Suneung results, it's not your Suneung score or university name, but your experiences and the people you meet both inside and outside of university that will make you shine. And someday, you will realize that this very moment was the brightest.
Cheer up.

titleEn: Legend of Dragonia Part 1 Episode 2
contentEn:
A colossal black dragon. It was Elleasal who first shouted at the dragon.
"You, who abandoned your racial duty, were cursed by the Elder to never return to your original form and were banished. What business do you have with me!" As Elleasal shouted, the Dragon of Envy laughed loudly and said.
"Racial duty? Isn't duty something to be upheld *after* the race exists? Are we supposed to abandon the future of our race and pledge loyalty for the sake of that glorious god and Elder? Are you telling us to keep playing along with the gods' games, just 'oracles'? Forget such ideals! We are far superior to humans, so why do we lack self-esteem even compared to them? And the Elder, who feared my power, ultimately couldn't kill me. Look. Even in this state, I've survived, haven't I? Ah. You might not understand. Perhaps the Dragon of Wisdom didn't tell you everything."
Elleasal clenched his fists, trembling, and scrutinized the Dragon of Envy. A large scar on the Dragon of Envy's neck... That was clearly left by Halhas when he killed the Dragon of Envy. Elleasal had clearly seen a tremendous amount of blood gush out and the head fall off at that time.
"I don't want to hear it! What business do you, who were dead, have here? Don't tell me you've joined hands with a dark wizard? You don't seem to be in a position to talk about self-esteem, do you?"
"Yes. It's been a long time, so let's talk slowly... I was even killed because of you, Elleasal, and that guy's father, so it'll be hard for us to find common ground anyway."
"Ugh..." Elleasal seemed slightly agitated by his words.
“Did you think I wouldn't know? That you were the one who taught Halhas the barrier to bind my magic. In fact, your ill-fated connection started with your father. Yes. Perhaps the reason you took on that role was also because of your father, the previous Dragon of Courage."
“Didn't you clearly commit cruel acts against humans without hesitation! You merely received the just punishment for those sins.”
Aaron shouted. Then the Dragon of Envy, with a look of anger, replied.
"Kuhahaha! Cruel acts, you say... How naive you are, son of Halhas. You speak as if your hands are unstained by blood."
The Dragon of Envy laughed in disbelief and replied.
"I merely made them pay the price for invading our land. Wasn't it humans who invaded and disturbed the land we lived on from the very beginning!"
This time, Elleasal shouted. "Discard such forbidden human logic! Our reason for existence is to convey and carry out the will of the gods. Do you think we're called the 'Race of Wisdom' for nothing? It's because we don't engage in foolish wars! Dragons neither dominate nor are dominated by anyone! We only uphold our duties! You have violated our laws and duties!”
"Laws... duties... what's the big deal about them! And not waging war, you say. That's just the Elder's cowardly excuse. Isn't performing the gods' duty a form of war? And what are you looking for the magic of light for right now? Isn't it ultimately to kill someone?"
"How did you know we were looking for the magic of light?"
Elleasal shouted.
"Do you want to know? I met a few dragons and asked about your whereabouts, and they gave me unexpected answers... They even blabbed on about the magic of light, which I hadn't even intended to ask about. But I don't like bigmouths, so I couldn't let them live. It's a disgrace to have such weaklings among our dragon kin. Ah. One of them was a lady who said she was your childhood friend... What was her name again?"
Elleasal cut off the Dragon of Envy's words. "Stop!"
Elleasal's eyes were blazing with fury.
"Now your eyes look a bit better. I've given you plenty of reasons to hate me, so come at me." The Dragon of Envy said with a sneer.
"Ugh... I can never forgive you!” Elleasal had almost completely lost his reason. Soon, Elleasal re-gripped his sword and charged at the Dragon of Envy. Aaron, too, dragged his weary body and followed Elleasal to help.
"The previous Dragon of Courage was very rational... but you're not as good as your father. I must eliminate you all to achieve my goals with Esbaal, so I will fight with all my might."
The Dragon of Envy's eyes suddenly flashed red like a monster's.
‘So he was indeed resurrected by dark magic power...’
Aaron thought, looking at the dragon's eyes. As the Dragon of Envy spread its wings and flapped them, a tremendous wind blew. Elleasal quickly dodged the wind, but Aaron's body wouldn't move as he wished due to his injuries. He had no choice but to take the full force of the wind.
At first, he felt relieved, sensing that the wind was not stronger than his own power. However, he felt dizzy when he sensed the next tremendous shockwave rushing towards him. Aaron's body rolled mercilessly on the ground, tumbling head over heels.
"Ugh... Damn it, it was imbued with magic power.”
However, Aaron stubbornly got back up. His body was already battered and bruised with injuries everywhere.
"I put a bit of power into that, but perhaps that guy's resilience is even stronger than Halhas's."
The Dragon of Envy, who was fighting Elleasal, muttered. Elleasal was also fighting strenuously. Elleasal couldn't easily seize an opportunity to attack and was merely dodging. Elleasal narrowed the distance to attack the dragon's body, dodging the magic power flying from its wings and the flames spewed from its mouth. Eventually, he closed in to a distance where his sword could reach with just one more leap. Just as he dodged another fiery attack and was about to strike, he felt a huge impact on his back. Elleasal was struck by the dragon's tail attacking from behind and sent flying towards the ruins. First of all, he was at a great disadvantage in terms of size and strength. Nor was there a wizard to cast light magic to bind the Dragon of Envy, as in the past wars between dragons and humans. When he got up again, his sword was broken, having hit something. Aaron felt despair. That guy is formidable. He had never seen Elleasal struggle so much before. He felt despair that even with his full strength added, it would be a difficult opponent to defeat. Then, Elleasal suddenly began to act strangely. He took off all his armor and clothing. The Dragon of Envy then laughed, making a sound as if amused, and did not attack him. “Hehehe, so you're finally going to transform... It's customary not to attack during a transformation.” Soon, he was completely naked. “Ho~ Quite a good physique for a young man, Elleasal.” Elleasal began to chant a song-like spell. Then a strange radiance began to glow from his body. Before long, his body grew larger and began to change form. Aaron watched the scene with astonished eyes. His body was gradually taking on the form of a dragon. It was a blue dragon, though a bit smaller than the Dragon of Envy. He transformed completely into a dragon, revealing his colossal form. “I really didn't want to show this form to Aaron... I don't like fighting this way, it's not very stylish...” Elleasal muttered. “Heh. Do you think you can defeat me like that?” “No

The dragon, with Elasall clinging to it, rose slightly, but soon crashed back to the ground with a loud roar. “Let go! You fiend!” The Dragon of Wrath roared, spewing fire and magic at Elasall with all its might. However, Elasall did not let go, even as he took the full brunt of the flames and magic. Due to the immense flames and magic, Elasall was almost charred black, making it difficult to believe he was still alive, and a vast amount of blood flowed, staining the ground red. But he still held onto the tail of the Dragon of Wrath, which he had bitten, until the very end.

At that moment, Elasall's message was conveyed into Aaron's mind.
- Aaron, you must find the spell of light even alone. This is my last will. We must ensure that the Dragon of Wrath or Bedrava never appear again. For the sake of the people, for our dragon race, for this world, it is something only you can do. The past nine years I spent with you were truly joyful. Goodbye~ My eternal little friend, who has now grown up -

Aaron, startled by these last words, rushed towards Elasall. “No! Master!” However, before Aaron could reach him, he was instead blown away by an immense gust of wind and light. Elasall had cast a self-annihilation spell and sent his final message to Aaron. “Master!”

As Aaron was blown away amidst the tremendous dust storm, memories of his past with Elasall flooded his mind. The sight of him smiling at Danna and himself, discovering his lost self against the backdrop of a dim dawn, teaching him about true courage while pointing at a flower blooming on a rock, teaching swordsmanship to his young self, splashing water and playing on the first day they visited Lishia's house, the battles they fought back-to-back, his grumbling about Aaron's bad sleeping habits. Elasall's various expressions were etched into Aaron's consciousness, and memories with him flashed by. He had been another father to Aaron, just as Danna had been another mother.

But his Master was fading away into the distance of his consciousness. Aaron was losing yet another person among those closest to him. ‘No. Master. Don't go. Please. Don't all leave me alone. You said I could protect my loved ones if I found the power of light. Wait until then.’

However, Elasall's final expression was a gentle smile, stroking young Aaron's head. And then, even that image gradually faded away. ‘What is this power of light... I only ever lose precious people. Is this the fate of a hero? Damn this cursed destiny... If there's a god, just die! There's no way such a fate could be fun. Giving me this kind of destiny, what in the world does this 'god' want from me?’

titleEn: Legend of Dragonia Part 1 Episode
contentEn:
Mount Suria grew steeper the closer they got to the summit. Aaron and Isaac had no idea how much longer it would have taken if they hadn't been riding on Bedrava's shoulders. Aaron thought it was incredibly fortunate that they had met Bedrava.

Even Bedrava found the rough path strenuous, and steam began to rise from his shoulders. After climbing for a long time, the summit gradually came into view. However, just as they thought they were almost at the top, a fog began to roll in. Soon, the fog grew so thick that even nearby objects were obscured, and Bedrava muttered in a low voice.

"It's Limmon. He knows we're here for his flower."

Then, something sparkled in the fog. It was a flower. Even in the limited visibility of the thick fog, a white flower proudly displayed its beautiful form, peeking out from the snow-covered ground.

Upon seeing the flower, Isaac jumped off Bedrava's shoulder without a moment's hesitation and dashed towards it.

"Wait a minute!"

Bedrava thudded after Isaac, and because Bedrava had moved so suddenly, Aaron also fell from his shoulder and tumbled into the snow.

The moment Isaac took a step to reach for the flower, his foot plunged down. Although the ground was clearly visible before him, his body was sucked into the snow as if he had stepped into thin air.

Only then did the flower in the fog vanish, and before Isaac's eyes appeared a bottomless cliff.

"Aargh!"

Just as Isaac

titleEn: Google Nexus 7: Blogger Day with Unclear Intentions
contentEn:
Last Wednesday, I attended the Nexus 7 blog day. As I'm not a full-time blogger, going out once a month is a big deal for me. Moreover, with a family trip scheduled for the very next day, I attended the event bracing myself for my wife's scolding. The reason I pushed myself so hard was simply because it was "Google."

In fact, I once predicted the domestic growth of tablets a long time ago, but compared to overseas markets, it's closer to a complete failure. I have a few thoughts on the reasons for this, but what does Google, the birthplace of Android tablets, think? What changes have occurred at Google, which is even running TV commercials in Korea for the first time in a while? I expected this event to answer these various questions.

**1. Product Introduction**

I won't talk about the buffet-style meal, which was close to fast food, or the T-shirt I received as a souvenir. Of course, the souvenir was much appreciated, but I didn't attend the event just for a souvenir and a meal.

{{IMG:1}}

http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=7028930500

[ASUS Google New Nexus 7 16GB](http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=7028930500)

Brand
ASUS
1.5GHz, Qualcomm Snapdragon 600 Quad-Core, 2GB, 7-inch, 16GB internal storage, USB x 1, approx. 0.29kg...
Rating

[View Reviews](http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=7028930500&tc=6)

**1) It's better. - That's it.**

Longer-lasting battery, Full HD sharp screen, light and simple design, powerful performance. {{IMG:2}} This was the kind of introduction that followed. Listening to it, I honestly felt like I was wasting my time. If it were a small or medium-sized company, I would applaud them for creating such a powerful device. However, this presentation was from Google. Moreover, as a new product, it's naturally expected to have better performance than its predecessor. In fact, tablets have always seen good devices released. The iPad did, and the Galaxy Tab and Galaxy Note did. But the domestic market hasn't changed. It seemed unlikely that the Nexus 7 would serve as a catalyst for the tablet market. I even thought that the Biscuit Tab, priced under 200,000 won, was a more groundbreaking and strategic device in that regard.

**2) Is it really cheap?****{{IMG:3}}**

Unfortunately, Google's Nexus 7 is not a very cheap tablet. Calling it a "value king" is only true overseas; when you factor in exchange rates and so on, it ends up being a device over 300,000 won, with the top-tier model exceeding 450,000 won. Compared to devices that tried to hit $199 and $299 overseas to be considered good value, the price in Korea seems to have been calculated without any thought beyond currency conversion. If they aimed for the same effect in Korea, the Nexus 7 should have been priced at 299,000 won.

**2. Start Your Day with Nexus 7 (Google)?**

**What kind of company is Google, and what can it possibly do?**

It even came up as a quiz question at the Google event: how many Google services are featured in the TV commercial? IT bloggers like me (and most attendees at the event) could easily answer this. But for the average user, how do the numerous Google services embedded in that commercial come across? Frankly, I give that Google commercial, which they ran for the first time in a while, a very low score. The reason is that Google's domestic service market share is still below 10%, and most users don't even know what Google's services are beyond 'Android, YouTube, and Search'.

While it might have been a successful ad overseas, I questioned what purpose it served for Google, a brand with weak recognition in Korea, to simply list a string of services. I think it would have been more important to first highlight the brand and its core services.

**3. The Nature of Nexus 7 as Seen in its Default Menu**

**- The Nexus 7 is a media device!****{{IMG:4}}**

Although I've been listing negative points, if we talk about Google's identity visible in the Nexus 7, YouTube, Google Play, Chrome, and Mail are prominently displayed. This signifies it as a communication tool and a media playback device. Also, beyond apps, Google Play's sales categories, which were the subject of two quiz questions, include movies/books, and the top-selling book is said to be "The Old Man and the Sea" for 1,000 won.

In other words, the Nexus 7's identity is not a device you cling to from the start of the day until the end, but rather one you use to watch movies, read books, or browse the internet while lounging on the sofa. And in fact, that's precisely the tablet's position. A device you carry all day long is the Galaxy S, or rather, a smartphone. If you carry the Nexus 7 all day, the Nexus 5's position becomes ambiguous.

**4. Google's Still Weak Brand and Domestic Content Services**

I believe Google's influence as a content service provider in Korea is negligible. The distribution of apps on Google Play, which Google touts as a strength, is already being shaken up by Kakao. Portals dominate the top spots.

As you know, music services are dominated by mobile carriers, IPTV reigns supreme for movie services, and books barely make a dent. During the quiz, there was a question: "How many copies of 'The Old Man and the Sea,' which is number one, have been sold?" The answer was positive, but the fact that "The Old Man and the Sea" is number one itself implies that it's not selling as much as one might think. If you look at domestic e-book sales sites, the top spots are occupied by RoFanMu (Romance, Fantasy, Martial Arts) and adult content. The reason is that the public wants light and titillating content. While recommended content and the low price of 1,000 won seem to have pushed "The Old Man and the Sea" to the top, it doesn't signify actual sustained engagement.

Where would you go on the Korean internet to find "expected job interview questions" as introduced in the ad? "Google Search?" Sorry, but students know that a cafe called **"Chwieop Ppogaegi"** (Job Breaking) dominates job information. This means Google is a minor player as a content business in Korea in many respects. And honestly, I thought this Nexus 7 announcement, like Amazon Kindle's, might signify an attempt to do something in connection with countermeasures. However, there was no such movement.

**5. If I Had to Pick Something Innovative, It's the Profile System**

Finally, like Windows, profiles are available for family members to set up their own environments. **{{IMG:5}}** **[ It's hard to see, but the blue button at the top is admin, the rest are family members ]** This was introduced as a main feature of the Nexus 7, but it seems highly likely to be adopted in standard Android OS later. I asked about this, but the assistant couldn't answer because they didn't know... ㅡㅡ; The problem, however, is that when the admin enables unknown file execution, all other family profiles also enable unknown file execution. Generally, security vulnerabilities arise from this feature, so more detailed control is needed, rather than just app exposure per profile.

**6. Google's Nexus 7, One of Them Among Domestic Android Tablets**

Summarizing the above, the position of Google's Nexus 7 in Korea can be roughly predicted. It will simply be one of many Android tablets, and while it's expected to gain some popularity due to "Nex-pride," considering the much faster release cycles of the Galaxy Tab and Note, as well as mobile carriers' antics and devices flooding the used market, the Nexus 7 is unlikely to dominate the market.

**7. Does Google Intend to Lead Change in the Korean Tablet Market?**

A few days ago, I visited Nami Island and was surprised to see many foreigners taking photos with tablets. Most of them had iPads and Galaxies. Koreans, on the other hand, were still taking photos with smartphones. I'm curious to see who will play the role of a catalyst for tablets in Korea. If I have time later, I might briefly discuss why the tablet market isn't thriving in Korea.

What's certain is that small and medium-sized businesses lack the capacity to solve this, and Samsung and LG are already selling Android phones and Windows tablet PCs well, so they have no particular reason to push Android tablets. I wonder how Google will tackle the domestic market, or if it even has the will to do so.

titleEn: [App Review/Analysis] Peoplegate: With Good People
contentEn:
**1. The Service Best Suited for Mobile: Social Networks**
What is the most successful app since the advent of mobile? You might think of TCGs, maps, or local commerce. However, the most successful app, without a doubt, is social networking. Social networks best leverage the communication properties of mobile, and mobile's always-on connectivity has explosively increased social network traffic. While KakaoTalk and Line can be classified as messenger services, they are fundamentally social networking apps with an inherent social graph. You can easily understand this by looking at KakaoPage and Line Home, which feature timelines similar to traditional social networks like Facebook. The fact that Facebook and Twitter, strong players in PC-based social networking, grew even larger with mobile also clearly demonstrates this.

**2. Vertical Social Networks Defining Identity**
However, human relationships are formed with diverse needs. Throughout our lives, we form relationships under specific conditions: romantic relationships, club memberships, work relationships. Social networks are effective in strengthening all these relationships. But offline, in certain gatherings, people play specific roles, and expressing all of these within a single social network tends to be confusing for both the viewer and the user. Therefore, in actual social networks, people operate with a specific identity they desire, which can determine the nature of the social network service regardless of the planner's intention. KakaoPage, which became a parenting forum, or Google Plus, where geeks gathered in Korea, are examples of such services. This is sometimes determined by the app's characteristics or its market position.
Conversely, there are cases where a specific role is defined from the planning stage to aim for success, and these are called vertical SNS. Here, what needs to be discussed is very clear. Between, an SNS for couples, or LinkedIn, for professional networking, fall into this category. And Peoplegate, which I will introduce today, is also one of them. {{IMG:1}} **[ Not just friends, but kind friends ]** {{IMG:2}}**[ Welcome these kinds of friends! ]**

**3. Peoplegate: A Vertical SNS with the Clear Purpose of Talent Donation**
To first praise Peoplegate, it is a social network with the very clear purpose of talent donation. It's the concept of sharing what you're good at to do something meaningful and fun together.
When you start the app, you can set your talents like tags and write a brief resume like LinkedIn.
Furthermore, as vertical social networks target clear niche markets, their market size is limited. To overcome this, it's good to go global. The ability to toggle an overseas option for this purpose was also an interesting approach.

**3. Disadvantage: Initial Entry Barrier is Too High**
However, what I felt while testing this app was that the initial entry barrier was too high. It's not easy to get users to install an app, but it's even harder to get them to stay after installing it. Attracting users and making them return determines the success of an app.
**1) Unable to find acquaintances based on phone numbers**
First, what stood out was the inability to find friends based on phone numbers. {{IMG:3}}**[ It's not because I'm an outcast that I don't have friends. ]**{{IMG:4}}**[ Playing alone ]** The scenario of "My friend is doing such a good deed? Should I try it too?" doesn't happen. Facebook pushes known faces from the initial signup via email, and KakaoTalk via phone number, but with Peoplegate, you end up talking to yourself at first. It's perfect for introverted people to just delete it.
Securing a social graph through all available means like Facebook, Line, Kakao, and phone numbers is an absolutely essential feature for a late-comer social network.
**2) Need for basic sticker provision**
Stickers also seem to need an initial allowance. It's not even sold for a fee, yet initial users can't use stickers, which also unintentionally raises the initial entry barrier. It's sad enough not to have friends, but not being able to use stickers too...

**4. Need for Feature Improvements for Talent Donation**
**1) Difficult to find friends with specific talents**
Perhaps because it's not active, even with a clear purpose, it's hard to find friends for a specific purpose initially. When searching for "app development," I could find people with that talent, but when I clicked on their chat rooms, their timelines only showed old posts, indicating no continuously active users. {{IMG:5}} **[ Searched for app development, but most accounts were inactive... ]**
It's difficult to know how much and in what way a user can truly donate their talent, and you can't just approach a stranger blindly.
Therefore, specific information settings for talent exchange seem necessary. At least information like available times and locations should be included. And of course, it should be searchable by that information. {{IMG:6}}**[ Setting a talent is one thing, but having the intention to provide it is another ]**
**2) Project Room Needed**
Talent donation often involves talents coming together to plan a single project, but it seems that if people want to collaborate through Peoplegate, they have to use other private SNS like Band. Therefore, a feature centered around groups (projects) rather than individuals seems necessary. And for a platform to succeed, creating success stories using the platform is paramount. It seems necessary to discover and highlight such success stories through these project rooms. {{IMG:7}} **[ Despite being a talent donation vertical, only usage patterns similar to Kakao Story are seen ]**
There are also services like Tumblbug that are entirely project-centric instead of social networks, which might be good to refer to.

**4. Hope for Peoplegate to Become a Global Korean Social Network Dreaming of a Warmer World**
Recently, Korean social networks like Kakao, Line, and Band are making strong global inroads. It's very encouraging that Korean services are succeeding globally, moving beyond just being an IT infrastructure powerhouse. In the case of Peoplegate, since it's a service that capitalizes on people's spare time, it seems like a truly challenging app in Korea, except for the student demographic. I even wonder if it might be better suited for Western countries where volunteer culture is common. I hope Peoplegate refines itself well and transforms into a global service, not just a Korean one. {{IMG:8}}**[ The problem is, even when I open it, finding overseas friends still seems difficult ]** I also have something I'd like to try together – should I find app developers through Peoplegate? (I barely have time for development now.) Meeting good people is always a joy.

Peoplegate link below.. [http://nstore.naver.com/appstore/web/detail.nhn?productNo=474258](http://nstore.naver.com/appstore/web/detail.nhn?productNo=474258) **ps. This post is an analysis and review based on a friend's recommendation, without any separate sponsorship.**

titleEn: I Think I Was Victimized by Go-Animation'
contentEn:
It's not yet certain if this is a scam, but in case others have experienced similar issues, I'm sharing this online first as it appears to be a fraud case, so they can check.
Mediation requested at [http://www.spayment.org/](http://www.spayment.org/mypage)
**Incident Summary ****1) August 17, 2013, 18:02 PM: SMS received for an unsolicited payment** ----- Content --(Go Animation) Super Jackpot Event 16,500 won payment complete Inquiry 050-5300-9998

Since there was no information about 'Go Animation' when searching online, I suspected smishing and did not call the number.

**2) September 13, 2013, 14:30 PM: Received August mobile payment details from KT**
Confirmed one unused transaction and requested KT to inquire about the company.
14:41 PM: Received the company's phone number from KT (1544-5553)

**3) Company Unreachable*** 1544-5533 busy ** Online ****Searching 1544-5553 revealed numerous posts about "InfoHub" auto-payment scams... *** 050-5300-9998 busy* No information about Go Animation found online

**4) Request for confirmation to KT**
KT said they would request the company to contact the customer within 3 days, and advised visiting the police station in case of fraud ㅡoㅡ

* Upon searching, I found an article about billions in damages from auto-payments affecting 130,000 people in Korea on August 28, 2013 [http://www.nocutnews.co.kr/Show.asp?IDX=2598152](http://www.nocutnews.co.kr/Show.asp?IDX=2598152)

**5) However, given the high possibility of damage, I first searched for ways to report it**
Found a method to request mediation at [http://www.spayment.org/](http://www.spayment.org/mypage)** KT, surprisingly, did not inform me about such a mediation request method. {{IMG:1}}**

** More than anything, I think it's important to identify the vulnerabilities in SMS micro-payments, and if these vulnerabilities are exposed, then users who were unaware should be found and compensated. It seems like elderly people would be helpless victims. By the way, it's only been 3 months since I changed my KT phone, could my personal information have been leaked? ㅡoㅡ To make an SMS payment, one needs to know the phone number, resident registration number, and telecom provider. Of course, there are only three telecom providers, so... let's assume that.**

**I will share updates on subsequent actions.**

titleEn: The Legend of Dragonia Part 1 Episode
contentEn:
**Dragonian Year 22, Nahaliel**
Aaron stood quietly in a forest clearing, eyes closed. Dina watched him from a short distance away, as a spell quietly flowed from Aaron's lips. Aaron opened his eyes, stretched his arms forward, and shouted.
"Uriel!"
With Aaron's shout, large flames erupted in front of where he stood. Aaron's face lit up, and Dina waved her staff, summoning a small cloud to extinguish the fire.
"Wow~ You're doing well now, Aaron."
Dina praised Aaron.
"Hehe. It's all thanks to your excellent teaching, Teacher."
Aaron said this and then collapsed on the spot. Magic, while requiring a certain constitution, was more physically demanding than he had thought. Magic allowed for long-range and area attacks, but for Aaron, it consumed more stamina than using a sword or sword energy.
The blue sky of the forest entered Aaron's vision as he lay down. After a moment, as Aaron's heavy breathing gradually calmed, he sat up. Dina watched him with a smile. When Aaron stood up, Dina drew a circle on the ground with her staff, then drew unknown patterns and letters within it.
"Aaron, this is Uriel's magic circle. If you draw a magic circle, you'll be able to use it more easily. With a sword or staff... But it seems you might not be able to handle advanced magic. Magic is more about constitution than skill or knowledge. However, with your swordsmanship backing you up, you should be fine against most enemies with that level of magic. But remember, Aaron. The power of magic is not to be used carelessly. Humans borrow the power of the Creator God using ancient language, so if used incorrectly, you could incur the wrath of the gods or be controlled by that power."
"Don't worry about that. I'm more comfortable with a sword than magic."
"Who said that? These days, mages use magic everywhere, and it's a big problem. Especially since you're young and skilled, it's even more concerning."
Having learned magic from Dina for a year, Aaron had now surpassed the level of a magic swordsman and had somehow reached the level of an intermediate mage.
"Mom. When will it end? I'm bored. Can't I play with Aaron?"
It was a voice from a tree next to the clearing. Lishia, hanging from a branch, had a very displeased expression.
"Alright. That's enough for today."
Dina clapped her hands and said.
"Thank you for your hard work, Teacher."
Aaron bowed in greeting, and Lishia, excited, leaped down from the tree.
"Aaron, let's go to the forest."
Lishia skipped into the forest again, and Aaron followed her. By then, Elleasal had also joined Dina, and he watched Aaron's shadow disappear as he chased after Lishia.
In Elleasal's eyes, sixteen-year-old Aaron seemed remarkably grown, almost surprisingly so. Aaron's physique had already grown considerably, to the point of experiencing growing pains, and his voice had already broken.
In contrast, twelve-year-old Lishia still looked very much like a child, but Aaron was a good friend to her nonetheless. His gestures, almost unfitting for his size, seemed to be tracing the lost memories of his childhood.
"How is Aaron?"
Elleasal asked Dina about Aaron's condition.
"He's just like his father. Even more so as he grows."
Dina replied as if stating the obvious, then continued.
"It reminds me of Halhas and Bidia. They were such a loving couple... Our adventures were fun too, weren't they?"
Elleasal replied with a serious expression.
"Fun? It's only a good memory now that it's over. Do you know how many times we almost lost our lives? Now, those children are the protagonists."
Dina laughed, as if finding Elleasal amusing.
"Hoho, is that so? Anyway, it's hilarious."
"What's so funny? Doesn't Aaron's challenging personality remind you of Halhas? By the way, I hope he doesn't inherit Halhas's recklessness..."
"Well, I wonder if he hasn't? They say blood is thicker than water. He even does magic just like Halhas. Like father, like son, I suppose... He seems to have an exceptional talent for fire magic, especially magic used with a sword. Besides that, as a swordsman, he shows skill in defensive and offensive magic commonly used in combat, no less than his father. But what's funny is that, just like his father, his healing magic and practical magic are terrible. Conversely, Lishia is good at trivial magic like using fire for cooking, binding things, opening things, and healing magic, but her offensive and defensive magic used in combat are terrible. Both I and her father are above average in combat magic, you know. Lishia is destined to be a mage who helps people in the village. How can the two of them be such complete opposites?"
Then, Elleasal suddenly asked Dina with a serious expression.
"What? Aaron can't use healing magic at all? Is he only at Halhas's level?"
"Yes, it's true. Halhas's level? Halhas's level is amazing for a human. Besides, he's not a mage, he's a magic swordsman. You're a dragon, so you say things like that. Isn't this all thanks to a good teacher?"
Dina smiled, pleased. Elleasal, however, became a little troubled. The elder had told him that the child with the power of light should be proficient in all magic. Elleasal thought for a moment, then spoke to Dina.
"Dina, I have something to tell you. It's about our dragon race."
Elleasal quietly recounted the prophecy and legend about Aaron that he had heard from the elder.
"Is that true? That child is the Warrior of Light..."
"It's true."
Dina's face darkened. Her painful past concerning light and dark magic flashed through her mind.
"Poor boy... such a harsh fate for that young child... All I can do is teach Aaron magic well so he can protect himself. It will take about another year to teach Aaron everything I know. What do you plan to do after that?"
"Next, I plan to visit the elder."
"From the southern lands of Nahaliel to the northernmost Dragon Lands... It's a long journey indeed."
Dina replied with a worried expression.
"Please take good care of Aaron."

titleEn: A Government Agency in an IT Powerhouse That Und
contentEn:
**1. Unbelievable News: NIS's Massive Internet Public Opinion Manipulation**
Today, I saw some astonishing news.

News was reported that evidence of the National Intelligence Service's (NIS) massive internet public opinion manipulation has been uncovered and confirmed. Not only domestic portals but also global social networks like Twitter were targeted, with millions of retweets involved. Honestly, I had somewhat anticipated suspicions, but I never expected an official announcement of this scale.

In fact, large services like portals and Twitter are always exposed to various forms of abuse and are constantly responding to them. This wasn't new. However, what makes this incident shocking is the fact that it wasn't a small viral marketing firm from China or the Philippines, but a powerful government agency of a nation – specifically, an intelligence agency – that abused these services under clear political objectives. I'd like to discuss how shocking and embarrassing this is, and what significant implications it has for global internet service companies.

**2. The 21st Century Evolution of the Internet, the 20th Century's Greatest Invention: Web 2.0**
Until recently, one of the hottest topics was Web 2.0. Web 2.0 signified a more decentralized, socialized, organic model equipped with collective intelligence. Beyond this collective intelligence, big data, which analyzes massive user comments and social network buzz, has recently gained prominence. In short, big data can actually be seen as a subset of Web 2.0's collective intelligence. Global companies are all interested in research on this, and the most representative global companies using it as a weapon are Twitter and Facebook. And, though the concept might be slightly different, Google's search engine PageRank and Naver's search engine also use big data analysis based on user actions as a weapon.

**3. The Incident That Turned Collective Intelligence and Big Data into Garbage**
However, the background behind the emergence of such hot technologies is the expectation that artificial buzz or abuse can be somewhat filtered out and buried within big data, because a sufficiently large number of users are producing a lot of data. This is precisely one of the properties of statistics: very large datasets have the effect of eliminating noise. Facebook likes and Twitter retweets often form the basis of such data. In fact, during the last presidential election, large portals like Naver even created dedicated service pages by analyzing big data from social networks.

However, this NIS comment and Twitter manipulation incident is a tremendous event that completely overturns this very assumption. In particular, Twitter, which focuses on propagation rather than friend-based connections like Facebook, revealed its vulnerability in this situation.

**4. A South Korean State Agency Hacked the Nation's Largest Portal and Global Internet Services.**
This incident means the NIS hacked Twitter, Facebook, and Naver. Generally, hacking refers to disabling a service or stealing/altering service data. The NIS's abuse in this case has similarities to a DDoS attack. A DDoS attack typically involves overwhelming a specific server with connections from numerous distributed servers, making it inaccessible, but fundamentally, it occurs because the system cannot distinguish between malicious distributed access traffic and normal traffic. In that the NIS used distributed servers to flood comments for a specific purpose, thereby obscuring or corrupting the conclusions of big data (public opinion indicators of the service), it is similar to data alteration, or hacking.

**5. Likely to Be Recorded as the Most Shameful Incident in Internet History**
I consider this incident to be the most shameful in South Korean internet history. And, due to this incident, global internet service companies must have been jolted awake. It has also lit a strong warning light in the big data market, which was previously considered hot. I wonder how international media, Twitter's Dick Costolo, Google's Eric Schmidt, and Facebook's Zuckerberg will view this incident. They might now consider a South Korean government agency to be a more powerful and malicious hacking organization than hackers from the Philippines and China.

The bigger problem is that many people in Korea might consider this a cyber war for a good cause. Is committing evil for a good cause truly a good deed? Perhaps for those who believe politics is the most important thing in the world, the IT industry is just a peripheral matter, and this is nothing. As if the future livelihood of South Korea can be sacrificed as much as needed for the sake of maintaining power for the next five years.

There's just one thing I truly want to ask of South Korean leaders. If you believe everything can be sacrificed for the ideal you pursue, then after achieving that ideal, nothing will be left. Is a leader who thinks it's okay for the entire nation to die for an ideal... truly a righteous leader? You may not fully understand what you have broken, but you have committed a shameful act that will be remembered throughout global internet history, something even China (officially) has not done.

contentEn:
I had always considered it a principle to write at least one IT-related story a week, and in fact, I had a topic in mind, but after seeing my social network timeline, I decided to write this post. Many people posted that they were really looking forward to the meteor shower but couldn't see it. As someone who once had a romantic fascination with stars and chased them, I'd like to talk a bit about stars.

**1. Meteor showers don't fall like rain; they appear as if lightly streaking across the sky.**

**[From Gunslinger Girl: Pretty, but actual meteor showers don't look like this]** If you can't see it on mobile, use the URL below (no Korean subtitles, though)
**[http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g6pEHh18naU&feature=player_detailpage](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g6pEHh18naU&feature=player_detailpage)﻿** 
 
  In illustrations and photos, there are depictions of meteor showers falling like rain, but in reality, meteors are observed for a very short time, so short that it feels like a trick designed to make people believe that wishes made while seeing a meteor come true.
 This is because meteors are said to move at speeds of 12 km to 72 km per second. The meteors I saw felt like they lasted less than 0.3 seconds, which is faster than the neural transmission speed required for visual information to reach the brain and for a decision to be made based on that thought. So, scientifically, it's absolutely impossible to make a wish. ㅡoㅡ
 If you assume hundreds of such meteors fall in an hour, the actual observation time is only a few seconds. Therefore, it's highly unlikely that multiple meteors would be captured simultaneously in a photo. Instead, they appear intermittently, streaking across the sky.
 
**2. The observation location is important for seeing meteors well.**
 In fact, city rooftops are not suitable for observing stars. City skies are as bright as day even at night, drastically reducing the number of observable stars. Consequently, the number of observable meteors also decreases. The number of meteor observations reported in newspapers is not based on urban areas. Therefore, you are bound to observe far fewer. If there's a large building or a bright bridge in the expected location of the meteor shower's constellation, it's best to temper your expectations.
 
**3. Meteors are not only visible during meteor shower periods.**
 Also, meteors are said not to be visible only during meteor shower periods. One or two might be visible every few hours, but because the probability of seeing a bright meteor is lower compared to meteor shower observation periods, it's not easy to observe them. This means that those who enjoy watching the night sky can observe meteors even outside of meteor shower periods.
 
**4. My Meteor Shower Observation Experience**
 I have seen a meteor shower. I can barely remember how many years ago it was, but during my university days, I went to an astronomy village on a specific date. Looking up at the sky there, where many more stars were visible than in the city, my friends and I gasped as we saw meteors intermittently falling from the direction of the Leo constellation. The meteors didn't have long tails like comets, as we might imagine, but the experience of them streaking across the sky in an instant was simply amazing.
 And in the remaining time, we saw more familiar constellations.
 
{{IMG:1}}
My first astronomical journey log: [http://fstory97.blog.me/70005304463](http://fstory97.blog.me/70005304463)

 
When my children are a bit older, I will definitely travel to the astronomy village again. Both of the friends who traveled with me at the time actually ended up working in space-related fields. (Stars are a drug. Me too, someday?)
http://me2.do/5i5LNH67﻿﻿
 
**5. Let's turn off the lights and look up at the sky.**
 These days, there's a lot of noise about electricity, reserve power, and so on, and I wish there would be a period where we all turn off the lights and gaze at the beautiful sky. There's a global lights-out event called Earth Hour, and I wonder if it's a much-needed time for South Korea, which is so thirsty for growth and competition.
 ps. In fact, I've only seen a meteor once that was like a painting, slowly falling overhead with a long tail. It was so picturesque, and because I saw it alone, I'm still confused whether I truly saw it or if I imagined it later. Sometimes in my dreams, I see a beautiful sky and then lose it while looking for my camera.
