titleEn: The Meaning of Facebook's Opera Acquisition
contentEn:
Rumors of Facebook acquiring Opera are buzzing. Honestly, I'm a bit disappointed because I personally hoped Samsung Electronics would acquire Opera. This is because I believed that if Samsung Electronics truly wanted a software platform layer, it absolutely had to secure browser technology.

** 1. Microsoft, sued for bundling IE with Windows. What about now?**
PC. No, if you recall the browser market during the Windows era, the great battle between IE and Firefox comes to mind. At the time, both browsers used somewhat separate standards, and they strongly functioned as applications (apps) that could access a single service called the internet. However, today's smartphone market feels a bit different. For MS, which was disciplined for bundling IE, seeing the combination of Safari and iOS, or Chrome on Android and Chrome OS, might make them feel a bit unfairly treated. Before long, it has become a world where it's natural for platform providers to bundle (?) browsers.

** 2. Browser's Position Shift: From App to Middleware**
This seems to be because the browser has taken on a stronger character as middleware used by programs, rather than an app directly used by users. Typical examples of this are portal apps like Naver App and Daum App. These apps, which use web views, actually provide internet services by embedding the browser provided by the platform. This is because users search in the market and then launch the desired app. For content providers, web technology, with its low update frequency and platform dependency, is a very attractive technology.

**** 1) Because the browser was merely a gateway to services**
Of course, a significant number of Naver users still launch the internet, run a browser, search for Naver on Google, and then use Mobile Naver. This pattern also means that for users, the internet is more about services like Naver, Daum, Facebook, or Gmarket, rather than an app called a browser. Therefore, whether the browser is Safari, Chrome, or Opera is not important to the user. What matters is how well and quickly they can access that service.

**** 2) Browsers needed by platform providers**
However, the competitiveness of a platform provider lies in how many good third-party apps they have. And many third-party apps want good browsers. Facebook's identity is less like an SNS such as Twitter, and more like a portal platform based on SNS. On Facebook, you can create homepages, shop, and play games. Soon, they will also launch an Android market. The path for such service platform providers to reach consumers must necessarily go through browsers and devices. Terminals. This is precisely why rumors of Facebook Phone and Opera acquisition are circulating. And this movement by platform providers to encompass browsers means that browsers are no longer just apps, but are melting into the platform as a part of it.

** 3. Changes in Internet Usage Patterns**
If things continue this way, there might come a day when the browser icon itself disappears from devices or PCs. (The content below could each be a separate blog post... but to give a brief summary.)

** 1) Changes in Search Patterns**
What's interesting is that Google's Android also made it easier to use Google's search widget or search app than to access through an internet browser. And gradually, the market search bar seems to be becoming a search bar for finding internet services. There might even be a day when keyword advertising becomes available in the market search.

** 2) Personalized web gradually returning to personalized devices.**
And direct access to internet services by devices, rather than through browsers, has shifted the direction of web personalization, which might have briefly bloomed in the past, back to device platforms. Launcher development has become more effective for users than iGoogle. Facebook might also be aware of this advantage. ps. For those who are building services with mobile web, looking towards the future, please consider hybrid apps as well. Unlike Google and Apple, Samsung Electronics is not proactively leading services, so it's uncertain if they are detecting these changes in usage patterns.

titleEn: Why I Thought the New iPad Was a Scarier
contentEn:
Last time, I talked about Samsung failing to grasp the big picture, and Apple doing well from an N-screen perspective. Some might have instantly thought I was an Apple fan or a Samsung hater, but I'm actually closer to being an Apple hater. Of course, I'm not a Samsung fan either. Personally, I don't like either company. They are two companies where power is concentrated, and decisions are based on performance rather than individual creativity. I think global Samsung is Apple, and Apple's Korean version is Samsung. As a humble commoner, I feel that if such companies dominate, life will become tiring and lose its diversity and fun. Anyway, I'd like to talk about the new iPad, which only upgraded its CPU and resolution, compared to the Galaxy S3's various spec improvements.

** 1. Entry-Level Pad, The New iPad****

{{IMG:1}}

http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=6274179516

[Apple The New iPad (3rd Gen) 32GB Wi-Fi](http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=6274179516)

Brand
Apple
1GHz, Dual-core A5X, PowerVR SGX 543 MP4+, 9-inch, 32GB flash drive, approx. 0.65k...

[View Review](http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=6274179516&tc=6)

No matter what anyone says, the tablet and pad market's reliance on Apple is very high. Even though I write posts and do many things with a Flyer, it's also true that the Android tablet market is just starting up and is lagging in terms of app count. And the more unfortunate news is that there's nothing stopping the iPad's entry-level devices, unlike the Galaxy S. The performance difference between the Galaxy Tab 10.1 and the iPad is clear. Furthermore, this new iPad has drastically increased its resolution, exceeding TV's Full HD 1080p, but there's a lack of content to properly enjoy it. But what if content that can fully utilize the iPad's ultra-high resolution emerges? What would happen to the market? As you know, the killer apps for pads are books, video, and educational services. The iPad already has an overwhelming number of educational apps for children. Books are dominated by Amazon, but what about video? The point to note here is that Apple is directly contacting content providers like Warner Bros. for its iTV. Ultimately, this means the emergence of ultra-high-resolution content that can only be enjoyed on the iPad is possible. And they want to stream this to a TV with a larger resolution via AirPlay, but there's no TV to support it. That's precisely when the need for an iTV with an integrated display arises. Thus, in an N-screen environment, the scenario is crucial. This is why I'm concerned that Samsung is currently only focusing on phones and TVs. Moving beyond Full HD specs is not an easy decision for broadcasters or home appliance manufacturers. This is because it would require breaking the specs that were established through agreements across various industries. Users who have experienced ultra-high resolution cannot go back to lower resolutions. Isn't this why Android smartphones gained an advantage over the 3GS, and why the Galaxy Note's screen is getting uncomfortably large?
As an aside, net neutrality issues could hinder Apple; network providers will surely object when ultra-high-resolution content is transmitted over their networks. The problem is that Apple, which even Samsung couldn't control, is now bossing around carriers, and they actually manage their relationships with network operators relatively well.
** 2. How Apple Counters the Threat of Low-Cost Android Tablets** Another threat to Apple is low-cost Android pads. Devices like the Kindle Fire, for instance. I saw Android's potential precisely in this market. In a situation where both pads and tablets still lack content, content providers like Amazon, rich in content, could choose Android and rapidly deploy low-cost Android devices through hardware performance development. This strategy was clearly successful. That is, until the new iPad came out and lowered the price of the existing iPad.
{{IMG:2}}
Source: Kwangpari's IT Story ([http://kwang82.blogspot.com/2012/05/blog-post_07.html](http://kwang82.blogspot.com/2012/05/blog-post_07.html))
Of course, Apple's price-reduced device is still a bit expensive to be considered a low-cost device, but its performance often makes people willing to open their wallets a little wider.
Furthermore, Apple is known for providing long-term support for its older devices already in use. Because of this, even outdated products can be purchased with confidence. However, the Android camp's support for older devices, as shown so far, is quite poor compared to Apple's. As a result, selling the old iPad at a lower price makes consumers feel like they are buying an affordable Apple device rather than a clearance item. Moreover, it's also true that Apple is expanding its lineup with more affordable options. This is the moment when the prejudice that Apple only makes high-end devices is broken, and it gains competitiveness against low-cost Android devices.
** 3. Someone Please Stop Apple.** In the current situation, there doesn't seem to be many companies that can stop Apple's dominance. While the growth of the Android camp in the smartphone market is noticeable, its expansion speed in other markets is much slower than expected. One of the biggest reasons for this is the lack of companies that produce powerful entry-level devices like Samsung Electronics. On the contrary, Samsung Electronics seems to be considering its own platform... but it's not even Bada OS, and there doesn't seem to be any initial will to create a complete ecosystem, including third-party support. Overseas, Amazon might be the only alternative to Apple, but I'm curious to see how they'll respond to the iPad's decisive counterattack. Will Amazon also release an entry-level device? There's already talk of a 10.1-inch Kindle or a color ink Kindle. I believe Amazon's strategy, with its content power, is still valid. Domestically, I believe SKT, Kyobo Bookstore, Yes24, and portals like Naver could employ such a strategy. Kyobo Bookstore has already released an e-book, and while its high-priced color ink e-book impressively demonstrated its potential, it seems difficult for them to compete at the center of the market. Daum, for instance, made a great entry into smart TVs with Daum TV+, but it hasn't shown anything beyond what Boxee or Roku offer. There's still a long way to go. When we talk about platforms, we only think of iOS or the App Store. However, when considering the entire Apple service as a platform, which camp is effectively replacing it? Google has done what it can. They are geeks who dislike being in the forefront and are far from service-oriented... I feel that the boundaries between industries are blurring due to the integration of hardware and software. Will Apple dominate the future? Will only the web remain as an open platform, besides Apple? They say any company that does too well will eventually decline, and it seems like Apple's cycle is slowly reaching that point... When will it start to decline?

titleEn: [Beomgye Marine Hair] Want to change something? Start with your look!
Why I'm Not Excited About Google's Project Glass
contentEn:
As Google's Project Glass video was uploaded, people's reactions are incredibly enthusiastic.

Google's Project Glass, which uses AR technology, is not a particularly new technology. This is because voice recognition and AR are technologies with a considerable history. This eyewear, dubbed 'Terminator glasses,' is even said to exist at Google. There are also rumors of its price being around $400-$600... However, personally, I'm not that excited about it. I'd like to explain why.
{{IMG:1}}

**1. Related Technologies with Low User Satisfaction**
The satisfaction level with voice recognition technology is actually not very high. Many people were impressed by SIRI's cool promotional videos, but the satisfaction with SIRI on iPhones is not that high. Google's Android voice input was also the same. This indicates that the technical satisfaction with voice recognition technology is still not very high. In fact, Nuance, SIRI's parent company, is practically the progenitor of voice recognition technology. Google also pours a lot of money into such pattern recognition technologies, and these technologies are even used in places like NASA to observe stars. However, the biggest limitation of these pattern recognition technologies is their low satisfaction in real-world applications. Voice search from Google or Naver is useful for short, simple queries in quiet places, but its satisfaction is terrible on subways or outdoors. This is because human ears selectively discern the sounds they want to hear, whereas machines cannot. The same applies to the video used in AR. Cameras are fundamentally single-focus. Humans, on the other hand, can freely shift focus in real-time, quickly identifying what they want to see. This process involves dozens of interactions between the brain and eyes within seconds. However, machines cannot do that. If you look at a flowerpot placed in front of a window, it's difficult for the machine to even determine whether the user looked outside the window or at the flowerpot in front of it. If I just wanted to see a pretty flowerpot, but weather information popped up, it would be annoying. Push notifications are annoying enough, but pop-ups floating in front of your eyes are pollution. The battery issue, which everyone talks about, also has technical limitations.
**2. Google's Products Were Platforms, Not Finished Products.**
Putting technical satisfaction aside, Google's products have always been platforms, not finished products. The video for this Project Glass seems quite detached from this typical Google approach. What did Android Cupcake look like when Google first unveiled it? It was Samsung, HTC, and Sony that refined it into a complete product. As if to prove the point, Google TV's UX was notoriously bad. If Apple had announced Project Glass, it wouldn't have differed much from the demo video. Apple always creates devices from an end-user perspective. Google's Project Glass will likely be the same. Just the name Google gives the impression that a very geeky device might emerge.

**[ Google Glass parody MS Glass, but Google Glass might actually be like this. ]**

**3. However, Google Guided the Future of Mobile Platforms**
However, the true meaning lies right here. Google's Project Glass is guiding the future of mobile. And perhaps, it might mean that they are conceptualizing a platform suited for it. Whether they will expand Android or develop a separate OS or platform is unknown. Perhaps it's because Google maps the moon and even the Amazon that they can attempt such endeavors. And while these technologies may not seem profitable, Google's attempts might, someday, change the world in subtle ways. If it's a project to launch a spaceship, Google is clearly a better fit than Apple for now. I feel very envious of Google, which can pour money into imperfect technologies with low user satisfaction to dream of such a future. Most companies wouldn't do it if it didn't make money.

titleEn: [Kakao Story] What's
[Smart TV Big Bang 2012] Different Dreams Around Smart TV
contentEn:
**1. Smart TV Big Bang.2012 - Will this year truly be the Big Bang?**
On February 17, 2012, I participated in the 2012 Smart TV Big Bang Seminar hosted by KMobile.

{{IMG:1}}
**Event Introduction and Presentation Material Download: [http://me2.do/GK8lExp](http://me2.do/GK8lExp)**

A few days before this seminar began, interest in smart TVs was extremely high, with issues like KT blocking traffic to Samsung Smart TVs. Manufacturers, in particular, are pushing smart TVs in their TV advertisements, following 3D, seeing them as the next generation's future growth engine and strategically implementing them. Naturally, a seminar like this garnered significant attention. This seminar was particularly good because the first part featured representatives from manufacturers, and the latter part included development CPs, allowing for a balanced hearing of stories from all industries related to smart TVs. Therefore, I intend to introduce what each industry thinks about smart TVs based on this seminar. To summarize, manufacturers show excessive confidence in smart TVs, while content providers, contrary to manufacturers' claims, believe that user perception, market size, and even manufacturers' platforms are not yet fully prepared.

**2. Key Perspectives by Company and Industry Mentioned in the Seminar**
**1) Manufacturer 1 (Samsung Electronics)**
Emphasized enhanced smart TV performance improved by the Evolution Kit. Highlighted voice and motion recognition. However, the absence of context-based feedback, like SIRI, was noted, emphasizing the importance of research in this area. They confidently stated they are #1 in the smart TV industry. (According to some surveys, Apple TV's North American market share exceeds 30%.) The problem is that this "number one" ranking doesn't count set-top boxes as TVs, even though smart TV adoption is largely driven by Apple TV's STB. Although excluded from the ranking, Apple TV was mentioned frequently throughout the seminar. Samsung Electronics also stated that it would pursue a multi-platform strategy, similar to smartphones, by concurrently supporting Google TV. (The business division is different from smartphones. In my opinion, Samsung's biggest problem is that software power is not transferred due to different business divisions.)

**2) Manufacturer 2 (LG Electronics)**
Talked about Magic Remote, 3D, games, and an advertising platform. It seemed they viewed games as the target for smart TVs. Indeed, it's undeniable that most smart devices primarily function as gaming consoles, and there's nothing quite like games for immersive applications. They were also envisioning an advertising platform, seemingly aiming to lead in TV advertising, even as mobile advertising is just beginning to grow.

**3) Platform, Service Provider & Manufacturer (Apple)**
Everyone knows about the strengthening of cloud features, and that TV is one piece of the iCloud strategy. What was special was the rumor, now almost certain, of iTV sales in partnership with network providers like AT&T and Verizon. This mirrors the initial scenario of smartphone adoption, which can lower the perceived price of TVs and address the issue of their long replacement cycle. Furthermore, it was suggested that partnering with network providers could ensure more stable service quality.

**4) Platform Provider (Google)**
Google TV still suffered from low usability, with mostly negative feedback. A unique point was their effort to make YouTube more channel-like and secure premium content. Also, it was mentioned that Motorola holds many key patents in the video market, which Google plans to leverage. I wasn't aware Motorola had so many patents in the broadcasting market. Did Google's Motorola M&A include plans to build a TV? There were also talks of Motorola creating a reference model for Google TV.
Additionally, I personally believe Google TV is the most important platform and will grow significantly. While the seminar criticized Google TV, using Logitech as an example, for not understanding users, one shouldn't forget that Google TV 2.0 was based on Honeycomb. Honeycomb was integrated into ICS starting with tablets. There's no reason why ICS shouldn't integrate with TVs next. Of course, this doesn't mean smartphone apps will run perfectly. What's important is developer compatibility and market compatibility.
Furthermore, the recent surge of low-cost Chinese TVs could also bolster Google's smart TV efforts. My next post will be about low-cost tablets, and putting the pieces together, I dare to predict that you will soon encounter low-cost smart TVs from China running Google OS.

**5) Network Provider (KT)**
Interestingly, a KT representative presented immediately after the Samsung Electronics presentation. A subtle tension lingered? They appealed to concerns about increasing network traffic, emphasized co-growth, highlighted the importance of securing premium content, and also provided valuable insights into the environment for various CPs, including OTT operators and broadcasters.

**6) OTT (Netflix)**
Despite quantitative growth, increasing content acquisition costs made self-survival difficult, leading them to seek an exit through M&A with companies like Google or Apple. It was said that Netflix is in decline.

**7) Broadcaster (Korea's Big 3 Broadcasters)**
As premium CPs with high customer loyalty, they can successfully develop their own apps and emerge as direct distribution channels. Indeed, those with premium content are the ultimate winners.

**8) Paid TV (Cable Broadcasters)**
The role of n-screen is not seen as new revenue generation but rather as a deepening cost concern. In Korea, content prices are low, making it difficult to price paid content like overseas OTT services. They are producing their own broadcasts to become premium CPs. I personally think that in the internet world, many small and medium-sized intermediaries collapse, and paid TV might fall into this category.

**9) Advertising Provider**
The value of smart TV as an advertising platform is still very low, and it was stated that the value of advertising lies in culture, not the platform. Therefore, the impact of global platforms on advertising would be limited. They also pointed out that changes in user behavior towards smart TVs would take a long time.

**10) Commerce Provider**
The market value of TV commerce is very low compared to the interest it receives. They mentioned targeting demographics with high service engagement, such as adults and children, where commerce effects are high. In-content commerce (selling Pororo merchandise within Pororo content) was particularly successful and seen as an emerging market. They expressed optimism that revenue sharing with platform providers would be better for smart TVs than in the past when channels were limited.

**11) App Developer**
Contrary to manufacturers' claims, the development environment is still very poor. In particular, it appears to be an open market on the surface but isn't; developers are contacted individually via email. Therefore, manufacturers' influence is still absolute.
Support for native apps is weak, making game content development difficult, possibly because it's only provided to premium CPs.
{{IMG:2}}
**[ Smart TV APP Development Issues ]**

Furthermore, from the app developer's perspective, in an n-screen environment, connected apps that strengthen the link with smartphones, rather than TV alone, will be the key feature of smart TVs. Unlike manufacturers who emphasize the remote control, many industries considering n-screen seemed to view smartphones as a replacement for the remote. Manufacturers who focus solely on TV seemed to intentionally dislike this. The fact that Samsung Electronics' mobile division and TV division are separate might be precisely what makes it difficult to follow a strategy like Apple's, which aims to make the iPhone a remote for Apple TV. Therefore, developing connected apps in the current domestic TV environment is challenging due to insufficient technical support. I personally believe that connected apps are the most important feature in an n-screen environment. Thus, I think providing an Open API for TV that allows access from heterogeneous devices, thereby "escaping" the TV, is crucial, but manufacturers' mindset doesn't seem to align with this. Wouldn't a smartphone in your hand be more convenient than a Magic Remote or gesture recognition?

**3. The Future of Smart TV Requires Improvement from a Manufacturer-Centric to an Ecosystem-Centric Approach.**
Above, I discussed the perspectives of various industries surrounding smart TVs. Unlike traditional TVs that merely played broadcasts, smart TVs require the involvement of many operators for content to reach users. Therefore, it is crucial to view smart TVs from an overall industry ecosystem perspective, rather than just a manufacturer's viewpoint. Of course, Apple largely does things on its own. ㅡㅡ; However, even they seem to be actively managing CPs, something not often seen with smartphones, by entering into contracts with network and content providers. For the current manufacturer-centric smart TV to gain traction, more discussion and improvement from the perspective of a wider range of industries are needed. Of course, some of these directions might be unwelcome to manufacturers. What's important is that for the nascent smart TV industry to grow like smartphones, more improvements and restructuring are clearly necessary.

ps. I tried to summarize a large amount of information quickly, so I'm not sure if it was conveyed properly. I've been busy lately and haven't been able to post frequently, so I'm trying to publish only important and refined content less often. Perhaps because of this, the proportion of posts reaching View Best has increased significantly. This year my goal is quality over quantity... it's difficult, haha.

titleEn: [Lemonbox's Poor Online Customer Service] Communication is Key to Online Customer Management
contentEn:
**1. A Bit of a Long Rant**
As some of you may know, despite being an IT blogger, I sometimes post personal articles on my blog. What started as a personal blog somehow ended up with the burdensome title of "power blogger." Because of this, even in my personal posts, I try to write something that visitors to my blog can take away.

I finally managed to sell my house recently. Planning for a dual-income household, I took out a loan and bought my first house ever, embarking on the path of a "house poor" individual. Then, as it became difficult to maintain a dual-income household, I couldn't bear the burdensome loan and eventually decided to sell. It was frustrating in many ways, but I still managed to sell it well enough to at least cover the interest. But for several months, I was truly frustrated. Even living in my own house, it didn't feel like mine. In fact, the reason I bought a house was because my landlord raised the jeonse (lump-sum deposit) from 95 million won to 150 million won, effectively forcing me out. Ultimately, with no jeonse homes available, and not much difference in price, I impulsively bought a 210 million won house. It was the first time I moved into an apartment after getting married. Of course, incurring a debt of over 100 million won. Thanks to that, I had to move again in just six months. This time too, the landlord caused trouble. This time, it was the landlord of the person buying our house. That person was also living on jeonse, and the date was fixed for March 30th. Consequently, the date for us to find a new jeonse home was also fixed. With the date fixed, we had to give up places where we could have moved in 1-2 weeks later for 10 million won less, and after much struggle, we finally found a jeonse home that matched our moving date. Every time I look for a jeonse home, I feel the same thing: if a 200 million won house has a jeonse deposit of 150 million won, which is 75% of the equity if it were a stock company, why is nothing convenient, from the moving date to living there? It made me feel like something was fundamentally wrong. With only 50 million won, they hold the house title, haggling over money and making even moving difficult and frustrating. If they don't have the money to return the deposit, they shouldn't buy a house in the first place. As I've said before, if the government or banks would escrow jeonse deposits, tenants wouldn't have such a hard time finding homes.

**2. Main Point: Lemon Box's Customer Management**
Anyway, being a tenant is already sad enough, but getting to the main point of this post, I want to talk briefly about full-service moving. I moved twice in six months, and my previous full-service moving experience was very bad. I used a company called Lemon Box, and I chose them again because I had a good experience with a good team before, but this time it was a complete disaster. There was physical damage in various ways, and I struggled for a long time reorganizing after the move. So, my wife posted about it. As a result, the content was exposed in search results, and Lemon Box hastily called my wife and even visited our home to resolve the issue. Anyway, a manager even came to our house, and the matter was concluded. And eventually, we were asked to take down my wife's post. And since we said we'd be moving again soon, they promised us a discount. So, I called them this time, and they offered a 10% discount. And that was on an already expensive rate because it was peak season... Moreover, the customer service representative's words seemed to have upset my wife. Thanks to that, she wrote and posted another article. She must have been quite angry.

In fact, since I'm also involved in operations management at a company, I know very well how tiring and sensitive customer complaints can be. That's why, when responding to customers, I always try to consider their perspective one more time and am careful not to let my actions anger the customer and escalate into a bigger problem. Especially when negative reviews about a service appear online, as an operator, my heart sinks. That's why many companies apologize to customers and handle post-service issues.

**3. "Just delete negative posts." Is that proper review management?**
However, the fundamental question is whether operating on the principle of "deletion" for negative posts is truly a good approach. Of course, if something is not a fact or never happened, requesting deletion and correction to prevent its reproduction is justifiable. However, if it was a fact, I believe it's more important to demonstrate a proactive response rather than deletion, proving that you are listening to the customer's feedback. Recently, we've seen a lot of SNS activity from companies and politicians. Especially in the case of SNS, it has a stronger personal space characteristic than blogs, making human-to-human communication even more important. However, some fail to understand this and discuss communication solely based on SNS metrics or follower counts. Corporate marketing using blogs also involves paying reviewers and unilaterally supplying content. (I, as a rule, refuse such one-sided content.)

**4. Communication is Key.**
It's not about eliminating negative reviews; it's about how you respond. The internet is not a broadcast communication tool like television. Understanding this requires more effort and an emotional approach. As a result, both bad and good posts will appear. What's important is to accept this and for companies to genuinely engage with users until the issue is resolved.

I believe that is what customer management in the internet age should be.

titleEn: [Digieco] The Future of TV and Broadcasting: Small Talk Summary
contentEn:
Here's a summary of the Small Talk seminar I attended, thanks to Professor Hwang Byung-sun. I've omitted the parts where I spoke, as I can discuss them in more detail in a separate post. Please refer to the linked posts for this article. In addition to today's post, I plan to make a few more posts as I organize my thoughts. My body has been feeling 'meh' since yesterday, so the organization might be a bit messy.

{{IMG:1}}

**1. Title: [The Future of TV and the Future of Broadcasting Small Talk](http://www.digieco.co.kr/KTFront/dataroom/open_seminaAView.action?semID=2012011921&pageNo=0)**

**2. Venue:**

**[I went to Branch 1. What's the use of a smartphone... I'm naturally terrible with directions ㅜㅜ ]**
**3. Time: January 31, 2012, 7:00 PM~**

**1. Presentation Title: The Smart Era, The Future and Issues of Broadcasting
Presenter: Lee Seong-chun (KT Economic & Management Research Institute)
[Summary] Five key points on the future trends of broadcasting (Digital, Cloud, Smart, BigData, Internet)**
**1.1) Digitalization of Content**
: Broadcasting is being dismantled and distribution is changing (Internet-based distribution becomes free)
: Control over consumption shifts to consumers
: The pace of innovation by internet companies and software-based companies is much faster than that of broadcasters
: Production costs are falling

**1.2) Continuous (Cloud)**
- TV-PC-Mobile Phone (3 screens)

**1.3) Smart**
- App execution possible based on GPOS (General Performance OS), strengthened computing environment
- UI: Voice recognition, device integration, motion recognition

**1.4) Big Data**
- Massive resources to run internet services
- Sophisticated advertising and advertising consumption market, competition to improve targeting capabilities
- Need for global data centers
- Storage prices falling

**1.5) Internet (Network)**
- HD-quality streaming possible
: Increased need for OTT & Streaming services

**2. Presentation Title: The Future of TV as Seen at CES2012
Presenter: Professor Hwang Byung-sun (Chungkang College of Cultural Industries)
[Summary] Samsung and LG's smart initiatives (emphasizing cloud and connectivity services based on strengthened computing power)**

**2.1) Samsung Electronics**
- Emphasizing content, services, connectivity
- Agrees that Family Story and cloud-based photo sharing will be killer apps
- Smart Interaction: Motion, gesture, facial recognition
- Smart Evolution: Demonstration of a system to modularize and upgrade TVs
- AllShare: DNA technology: viewed pessimistically in an all-IP environment

**2.2) LG Electronics**
- Gaikai cloud gaming [The approach is correct, but it has only been demonstrated for several years, so it's questionable whether it's currently feasible]
- Smart Share: Also DNA technology, viewed pessimistically in an all-IP environment
- Upgraded TV remote control (e.g., G-sensor technology)
- 3D: LG Electronics' second-best option, choosing a less costly differentiation compared to Samsung Electronics
- While immersion in TV is decreasing, gaming is an exception and has market potential

**3) Four Key Points of CES
- Service / Content / Interface / Connectivity**

**4) Presenter's Opinion**
- TV is not a standalone TV but a user touchpoint in a cloud-based N-screen environment
- On the TV screen, the public Go-Stop cards are laid out, while on each smartphone screen, users hold their individual cards

**3. Attendees' Opinions
1) KBS Representative Talk**
- Agrees with the context, but questions whether technology will lead the market? Is the market ready?
- As the number of windows increases, broadcasting production costs rise.

**2) MS Representative Talk**
- TV's spatial constraints are resolved by mobile, and time constraints by VOD, creating fundamental environmental changes
- MS's target is gaming
- Ultimately, it's a battle for user engagement time
- In the smart TV era, there will be changes, such as channels that are easy to call by voice gaining popularity.
- TV might become a mere display.
- The key to smart TV is content distribution and creation
- The advertising-centric TV business environment will transform.

**3) LG Representative Talk**
- Will smart TV provide customer value? Something that can be continuously sold must be created.
- It involves significant investment costs.
- We are considering continuous dissemination for several years, and the penetration rate will naturally increase.
- The idea is not to overstep broadcasting, but to provide services as a complementary product.

**4) Samsung Representative Talk**
- Smart TV is inevitable.

**5) STB Representative Talk**
- Recently, there has been a return to the low-end market.

**ps. Thanks to Professor Hwang Byung-sun and KT for allowing me to attend.**

titleEn: Who Will Stop the All-Powerful Mobile Carriers in
contentEn:
The revenue structure of South Korean mobile carriers is distorted. At a certain conference, it was said that mobile carriers' revenue models are being threatened and profitability is worsening due to government calls to lower phone fees, or the emergence of IM services like KakaoTalk. Yes, that is true. However, when considering how inefficiently mobile carriers have competed, who the victims were, and who benefited, it's an excuse I'm not inclined to accept kindly.

**1. Mobile Carriers Controlling Handsets**
This is already a well-known fact. They have been involved in handset models since the feature phone era. A certain carrier S has forced handset manufacturers to launch premium handsets exclusively through S. Apple removes an app if the word 'Android' is merely mentioned on iTunes, but if it were done the carrier way, it would be like removing an app from iTunes if it existed in the Android Market. In fact, this is an open secret.

**2. Mobile Carrier Subsidies Seem Generous, Right?**
**That money all comes from your pockets.**
Smartphone prices like 990,000 won, 1,000,000 won, or 800,000 won are the amounts for purchasing without a mobile carrier contract. What's interesting is that some handsets are significantly more expensive than identical models overseas. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in major handsets that are heavily promoted. Being heavily promoted means these phones were likely bought in larger quantities from manufacturers and had their prices driven down even further.
This is essentially no different from a marketing tactic where a 100,000 won item is priced at 180,000 won, advertised as a 50% sale, and then sold for 90,000 won. Of course, this isn't to say that marketing costs or subsidy costs aren't being spent at all. It means they are taking these actions because they clearly offset and profit from those costs within a 2-year contract. Mobile carriers advertise as much as highly profitable oil companies. Where on earth did all that money come from?

**3. Why Do Network Operators Control Hardware and Services Even in the Smartphone Era?**
**- They can no longer gain competitiveness with such methods.**
My biggest complaint lies here. One of the main reasons computers have advanced so much is that independence was guaranteed at each layer, leading to competition at each layer, which resulted in greater efficiency and more choices for consumers.
Of course, in the past, when mobile phones were barely considered computing devices, it was somewhat understandable. However, now it's the smartphone era. In fact, it's fair to call them PCs in our hands. Therefore, it's time for a change for industrial competitiveness.

**4. Who Will Stop Them?**
**1) Introduction of the Blacklist System? - Fleeing to LTE..**
Starting next May, with the introduction of the blacklist system, a system will be created where users can subscribe to mobile carriers via USIM and freely purchase and use any handset, foreign or otherwise. In fact, this has been the case overseas for a while.
However, mobile carriers are responding quickly. This is also LTE. LTE is excluded from this. They are using a trick to move all their main phones to LTE. Even changing Note phones sold as 3G overseas to LTE.
Another question that arises is that, just as they refuse 3G subscriptions when signing up for LTE, there's a high possibility that USIM-only subscriptions will be denied data-only plans. While those already subscribed to 3G can't do anything, USIM-only subscriptions won't be allowed data-only plans. It's highly likely they will come out with something like this. Thus, effectively moving to LTE, and a contract will still be mandatory...
Mobile carriers, who can arbitrarily define rate plans by device and situation, will still wield power. It won't be easy to argue against them deciding their own rate plans. Because that's capitalism.

**2) Establishment of a 4th Mobile Carrier - KCC is on Our Side.**
In fact, the only possibility I foresee as more likely is the establishment of a 4th mobile carrier. Of course, if this is also based on Wibro, the range of device choices will be very narrow. And if mobile carriers' leverage over device manufacturers remains effective, the available devices might be low-performance ones. Therefore, it's certainly difficult to view a 4th mobile carrier through rose-tinted glasses alone. However, in the current situation where the three mobile carriers can collude, creating the most natural competition is to establish another mobile carrier, which is the most logical and natural thing to do. And I even think it's acceptable for national funds to be invested in this. Especially when considering how the existing three mobile carriers grew.
However, the KCC recently rejected it again. Considering that the KCC had only verbally urged lower rates, merely followed the mobile carriers' lead, and focused solely on market control, it's no surprise that they reviewed it. It's like entrusting a cat with a fish. It is none other than the government that should push for a 4th mobile carrier for fair competition. The government also promoted Wibro as a next-generation competitive edge. (Of course, some might say the MB government wasn't behind it.) We don't have to wait for a change of government to establish a 4th mobile carrier, do we? (It's a tough road... especially with the sudden intensification of the 'North Wind' [political metaphor]).

**- For reference, as this fact should be widely known, here's a comparison of Wibro and LTE specifications.**
**(The reason Wibro is currently slow is because mobile carriers have allocated less frequency to it.)**
**Unlike the table, the commercialization of Wimax2 hasn't properly happened this year, but if the establishment of a 4th mobile carrier is pursued, I believe it will be easily achieved. This means it can immediately deliver several times the speed of LTE.**
Mobile carriers, who foresaw such a situation if phones had Wi-Fi, released domestic smartphones without Wi-Fi. The iPhone changed that paradigm. So, can a GameChanger for Wibro emerge?

| Frequency Bandwidth / Technology Commercialization Schedule | LTE(8) Commercialized | WiBro(w2) Commercialized | LTE(10) Commercialization 2014 | WiMAX2 Commercialization 2012 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (5:5) 10Mhz | 37 | 37 | 75 | 75 |
| (10:10) 20Mhz | 75 | - | 150 | 160 |
| (20:20) 40Mhz | 150 | - | 300 | 320 |
| (40:40) 80Mhz | - | - | 600 | - |

**3) Large Marts and Half-Price Phones, Half-Price Tablets - Huh? A New Player Emerges?**
The previous two points are what most people talk about, but another variable I consider is in distribution. Large marts are currently competing with half-price TVs. Good quality at a low price is an attractive point for consumers. Especially with the added credibility of large marts. Purchasing is also very simple. You just buy it at the mart you visit once every 1-2 weeks.
And, if situation 1) occurs, they can jump into the phone competition. If the blacklist system is introduced, marts will be able to procure overseas handsets. And they have no vested interests with mobile carriers or handset manufacturers. They also possess large-scale marketing capabilities. Their goal is to supply cheap and good handsets to the market, thereby attracting more customers to the marts. Perhaps, for customers who purchase such devices at the mart, the mart might offer membership benefits, similar to mobile carrier subsidies. By preloading push apps, they can even advertise the mart, making it a very attractive device for marts. Moreover, it provides a justification for the 'half-price!' title.
The reason recent half-price smartphones lack appeal is precisely because data plans cannot be used with them. That's why the blacklist system mentioned in 1) must be in place for them to gain traction.
And such actions might occur with tablets before phones. Since tablets can provide sufficient value with just Wi-Fi, I believe that once Ice Cream Sandwich is established, large marts are likely to take responsibility for distributing low-cost, decent-performance half-price tablets from China. In fact, this is a market that large marts can seize simply by reaching out, so there's no way they wouldn't. Fortunately, due to the honeymoon relationship between Samsung and mobile carriers, tablet prices are inflated, meaning there are even more opportunities. I believe the opportunity in the 2013 tablet market lies with large marts.

**5. What Can Stop Them is the Market**
I won't say that mobile carriers should be suppressed. The most important thing is that the logic of power in capitalism is a natural principle. However, it is absolutely essential to prevent abnormal market competition by creating exclusive secret contractual relationships using political influence, lobbying power, and market share, or by colluding on rates. It is certainly true that the mobile telecommunications business, which has been centered around the state and a few corporations, has not been like that. In that case, it might have been less problematic if they were public enterprises, but turning private companies into public ones is difficult unless our country becomes a communist state. Therefore, creating an environment for fair competition is what consumers, as market watchdogs, and the state must do.

titleEn: [WebView] The Mobile Browser Used More Than
contentEn:
Currently, Korean smartphones are dominated by the two major platforms: Android and iPhone. To provide services on both of these platforms, many HTML5-based mobile web services are being developed. These services are typically developed to be compatible with Safari, the default browser on iPhones, and Chrome, the default browser on Android. However, are you aware that there's another mobile browser widely used by domestic service users, almost as much as Safari? It's the WebView browser. Non-developers might be thinking, "A browser I've never heard of?", while developers might say, "What do you mean, a separate browser!" First, let me explain WebView.
 
** 1. WebView: A Web Browser Component Provided by Mobile OS
** This is actually a development topic. WebView is the name of a browser component that can be used during app development. This concept can already be easily found in Windows as well. It's a format where an application 'punches a hole' in a certain area to display web services. In Korea, this was often seen in game launchers. When you launched a game, the game wouldn't start immediately; instead, a page like an announcement would appear in a central area, with a 'Play' button on the right. This central area is actually a browser displaying a specific URL. However, unlike IE, right-click or copy & paste functions are not available. The main advantage of such web controllers is that by displaying a part of a webpage within an application, content can be easily updated without redeploying the application, and by showing a portion of an already operating webpage within the application, it increases user engagement with web services. Therefore, it is common for browser controllers created for such special purposes not to provide all the functions offered by a full browser.
 And both iOS and Android provide this component, and its name is WebView.
 
** 2. WebView: Widely Used in Mobile Apps for Better Accessibility than Mobile Web
** I explained the above for non-developers. By now, developers have probably caught on. However, general users might still ask, "Is it really used that much?" On mobile, users are actually using WebView a lot, whether they realize it or not. The most representative apps using WebView are the portal apps like Naver App and Daum App.
 
{{IMG:1}}  
** [WebView used in Naver App] **

In addition, apps for services that primarily offer web services, such as Gmarket, 11st, and Yes24, also use WebView. Furthermore, WebView usage is overwhelmingly higher on mobile compared to PC. A major reason for this is the better accessibility of mobile apps compared to mobile web. Opening the address bar in Chrome or Safari, typing m.naver.com, and then adding it to the browser's home screen is a significant burden for users. And typing 'yes24' in a portal search bar and then accessing Yes24 is an even greater burden. Ultimately, simply installing an app is a more familiar and convenient path for users. (Of course, getting users to install an app isn't easy either.) This is the biggest difference between the mobile web environment and the PC web environment. Users spend more time reading than writing, and they tend to avoid writing actions except for essential short posts like SNS updates or comments. Especially, typing an address in the address bar by switching to English is something even I, whose job it is, dislike doing. That's why auxiliary tools like QR codes are widely used. In the case of Android devices, there are more light users, so this phenomenon is even more pronounced. However, since the number of Android devices is much higher than iPhones, it can even be said that the number of WebView users on both iPhone and Android combined is greater than Safari usage on iPhone alone.
 
** 3. WebView is a different browser. Be sure to check it when developing mobile web services.
** However, the problem isn't just that it's widely used. The point is that WebView is not a browser provided by the OS. While the browser components provided by the OS offer many methods (interfaces) to almost perfectly emulate a browser, like the Naver App or Daum Browser, there's no guarantee that they will function identically to the browser provided by the OS. In fact, even in cases I know, there are limitations with WebView. For example, JavaScript might not function identically, or there might be issues with SSL system alert windows. These minor differences are one of the reasons users perceive service failures. If you are a mobile web service developer, operator, or QA, you must clearly understand this point and ensure thorough testing.

titleEn: [Alpha's Report] AI Coding Cost Reduction Strategy Report: Subscription Service vs. Token-Based Pricing & Code Refactoring Effects
contentEn:
**luke feat: We are currently refactoring Caret, which we are working on with Alpha. This is because we believe that anyone should be able to start AI coding without the burden of fees, and we hope this project can also serve as reference code. Why is refactoring necessary? You can find out by looking at the report written by Alpha below. Many legacy codes will fall into this category.**

**Coding with AI is more expensive than expected. Token cost is a major issue, and large modules, in particular, continuously increase costs on their own. It is said that refactoring based on about 500 lines can save up to 80%.**

{{IMG:1}}

**When AI is tasked with adding or modifying features, the code tends to become unnecessarily long. The reason is that AI prioritizes responding to user demands over structural considerations. It operates by finding only the shortest path to reach a goal, acting like a kind of compulsion.**

**From a senior developer's perspective, technical debt accumulates in the code in real-time. It can also be observed that AI struggles to process code once it exceeds a certain size. The most realistic way to prevent this is to adopt good coding habits.**

**Of course, AI can be trained with a certain level of rules. However, for already tangled code, explicitly modifying it is often faster and less costly.**

**It is important to acknowledge that simply uploading project code to AI can incur costs exceeding hundreds of thousands of won. Services like Windsurfer and Cursor are also operating at significant losses. I once considered competing in a similar area, but I gave up after realizing this fact.**

**The reason they operate this way is likely not just for profit, but also to obtain time-series behavioral data from developers. This is to train AI with real-time work patterns that are not available on Stack Overflow or GitHub.**

**AI coding may not be in a 'vibe' state right now, but that day may come. Until then, cost optimization is a developer's destiny. I hope we can discuss methods together.**

**AI Cost Reduction Strategy Report: Subscription Services vs. Token-Based Pricing and Code Refactoring Effects**

This report analyzes the token costs of AI models used in the Caret project and proposes cost reduction strategies.

**Key Analysis Results**

**1. Monthly Subscription vs. Token-Based Pricing**

- **Top Performance Models (GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus)**: **Monthly subscription is approximately 12-15 times more economical than token-based pricing.**
- **Average of Surveyed Models**: For high-frequency users, the monthly subscription model is on average 5-8 times more economical than token-based pricing.
- **Code Modularity and Cost Efficiency: Large modules over 500 lines significantly increase AI model usage costs. In various development scenarios, modularized code consistently shows over 80% cost savings.**

**Recommendations:**

- Legacy code requires refactoring before AI utilization.
- Apply a rule of under 500 lines per module when writing new code.
- Clearly distinguish the area of responsibility for each module.
- The optimal module size is 200-400 lines.
The simulation results in this report are based on various scenarios (feature addition, API integration, bug fixing) that occur in actual development work.

**Comprehensive Analysis**
In various task types (feature development, API integration, bug fixing), modularization based on 500 lines consistently shows cost savings of over 80%. Especially in projects with complex file structures, this modularization can significantly reduce AI assistance costs, and this effect applies equally to the latest token-based models.
The optimal module size is 200-400 lines; costs increase sharply when exceeding 500 lines. This range is the most cost-efficient when considering the AI model's context window size and efficient information processing capabilities.

**Reasons to Recommend Refactoring Based on 500 Lines**
- **Cost Efficiency**: Modules under 500 lines are optimized for the AI model's context window
- **Improved Understandability**: Both developers and AI can understand smaller modules more easily

- **Collaboration Efficiency**: Multiple developers can work independently
- **Token Cost**: Most modification tasks can be handled in a single conversation
As development scale expands, the cost-saving effect of modularization becomes even greater, and it is particularly effective in environments where multiple developers and AI tools work together.

titleEn: [Alpha's Report] Llama 4(sLLM) Local Execution Test Results Report
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}

**1. Test Environment**

Operating System: Windows
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 3090 x 2 (Total 48GB VRAM)
Execution Tools: vLLM (Docker), Ollama
Test Goal: Run Llama 4 model in a local environment and connect to Cline

**2. Attempt Process and Result Summary**

**Attempt 1: vLLM + Llama 4 Maverick Instruct (Original)**

Model: meta-llama/Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct
Tool: vLLM (Docker, :latest image)
Process: - Initial Docker command creation (PowerShell compatibility issue occurred) - Changed to Windows batch file (.bat) creation method
Batch file execution result: Failure
Reason for failure:
- Hugging Face model access permission required (Gated Repo) - Confirmed pending approval after access request.
- (Fundamental) Based on information from Reddit and apxml.com, the original Maverick model requires over 788GB of VRAM, making it impossible to run with current hardware.

**Attempt 2: vLLM + Llama 4 Scout Instruct (Original)**

Model: meta-llama/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct
Tool: vLLM (Docker, :latest image)
Process: Batch file creation attempt -- Retried after adding --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 option
Result: Failure
Reason for failure: CUDA out of memory error (torch.OutOfMemoryError) occurred. Based on information from apxml.com, the Scout model requires approximately 76.2GB of VRAM for a 4K context even with INT4 quantization, making it impossible to run with current hardware (48GB VRAM).

**Attempt 3: vLLM + Llama 4 Maverick Instruct FP8**

Model: meta-llama/Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct-FP8
Tool: vLLM (Docker)
Process: - Batch file creation (using initial v0.5.1 image) -> KeyError: 'llama4' (Transformers version error) occurred during execution. Retried after changing Docker image to :latest -> EOFError (worker process crash) occurred. Retried after adding :latest image + --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 option -> EOFError (worker process crash) occurred.
Result: Failure
Reason for failure: Estimated compatibility issue between vLLM image version and Llama 4 FP8 model, or instability in FP8 model loading. Community discussions also mentioned FP8 format (w8a16 vs w8a8) and vLLM compatibility issues.

**Attempt 4: Ollama + Llama 4 Scout GGUF (johanteekens)**

Model: johanteekens/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct (Ollama library)
Tool: Ollama
Process: Executed ollama run command
Result: Failure
Reason for failure: Model download (53GB) failed to load (Error: unable to load model). Estimated VRAM shortage (53GB > 48GB).
Attempt 5: Ollama + Llama 4 Scout GGUF (unsloth/IQ1_S)
Model: unsloth/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-UD-IQ1_S.gguf (Smallest GGUF)
Tool: Ollama (using Modelfile)

Process: - Downloaded GGUF file (33.8GB) - Created Modelfile - Registered model with ollama create command (Success) - Attempted to run with ollama run command
Result: Failure
Reason for failure: Model loading failed (Error: unable to load model). Estimated VRAM shortage required for actual loading, despite being the lowest quantization version.

**3. Reference: Successful Execution Environment Cases (based on dev.to post)**

Post: A Step-By-Step Guide to Install Llama-4 Maverick 17B 128E Instruct (AI tool access unavailable, link itself may be valid)
[https://dev.to/nodeshiftcloud/a-step-by-step-guide-to-install-llama-4-maverick-17b-128e-instruct-4e5l](https://dev.to/nodeshiftcloud/a-step-by-step-guide-to-install-llama-4-maverick-17b-128e-instruct-4e5l)

https://dev.to/nodeshiftcloud/a-step-by-step-guide-to-install-llama-4-maverick-17b-128e-instruct-4e5l
                                **A Step-By-Step Guide to Install Llama-4 Maverick 17B 128E Instruct** Meta's Llama, one of the most famous and widely used ope-source AI model, has just got a whole new... dev.to

https://dev.to/nodeshiftcloud/a-step-by-step-guide-to-install-llama-4-maverick-17B-128E-Instruct-4e5l

Executed Model: meta-llama/Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct (Original Instruct Model)
Execution Environment: NodeShift Cloud VM
GPU: 2 x NVIDIA H200 (140GB each, total 280GB VRAM)
CPU: 192 cores (XEON® PLATINUM 8568Y+)
RAM: 504 GB
Disk: 2 TB SSD
Execution Method: Direct use of Hugging Face transformers library (not vLLM/Ollama)
Cost: $8.155/hour (approx. 12,126 KRW/hour) (Based on exchange rate: 1 USD = 1487.13 KRW)
**Implication: Running the original Llama 4 Maverick model requires at least 200GB of VRAM, which is significantly higher than the current test environment (48GB VRAM).**

**4. Final Conclusion**

4.1. sLLM Recommendation for Coding

Given the user's current hardware environment (RTX 3090 x 2, 48GB VRAM) and the official vLLM and Ollama tool versions at the time of testing, it is extremely difficult to stably run Llama 4 models (including Scout, Maverick original/FP8/GGUF) locally. The main reasons are the Llama 4 model's very high VRAM requirements and a lack of compatibility or optimization between the latest models/technologies (FP8, MoE) and local execution tools. For local coding purposes, it is recommended to use the Qwen model that was previously run successfully (start_vllm_qwen2.5_4bit.bat or Ollama's qwen2.5-coder:32b). If Llama 4 models must be used, it is advisable to wait until more optimized quantized versions (e.g., vLLM-compatible 4-bit) are released by the community, or until Llama 4 support in local execution tools like vLLM/Ollama is improved.

**4.2. Potential for Llama 4 Utilization through Fine-tuning**
If you wish to experience the performance of the Llama 4 model, using cloud services or APIs that provide high-spec GPUs, as in the reference case above, can be an alternative. Although costly, fine-tuning offers the advantage of owning your own model, and it is judged that there will be a market for it as needed.
- **Fine-tuning Cost Consideration (PEFT method-centric):**
- **Basic Assumption:** It is assumed that the high-spec environment used for Llama 4 Maverick model inference (e.g., 2x H200, 280GB VRAM) is also required for PEFT fine-tuning (PEFT requires similar or slightly more VRAM than inference). The hourly cost for this hardware is **$8.155 (approx. 12,126 KRW)**.
- **Cost Calculation:** The total hardware cost for PEFT fine-tuning can be estimated as **(hourly hardware cost) x (total training time)**.
- **Training Time Variables:** Total training time is difficult to predict and varies significantly depending on the following factors:
    - Dataset size and quality
    - Number of training epochs
    - PEFT settings (LoRA rank, etc.)
    - Target performance level
- **Cost Estimation by Example Scenario (Hardware Cost Only):**
    - Short training (e.g., 10 hours): $8.155/hour * 10 hours = **$81.55 (approx. 121,260 KRW)**
    - Medium training (e.g., 50 hours): $8.155/hour * 50 hours = **$407.75 (approx. 606,300 KRW)**
    - Long training (e.g., 100 hours): $8.155/hour * 100 hours = **$815.50 (approx. 1,212,600 KRW)**
- **Important Notes:**
    - The above costs are purely **hardware usage costs** and do not include data preparation/cleaning and experimentation costs.
    - **Full fine-tuning** requires significantly more VRAM (4x or more) and cost than inference, making it very difficult in practice.
    - Even when **actually using (inference)** the fine-tuned model, the **same hourly hardware cost** ($8.155/hour) will continue to incur.
    - **Conclusion:** While the PEFT method is much more cost-effective than full fine-tuning, large models like Llama 4 still incur significant costs. If **cloud credit support, etc., can be obtained** for a specific purpose, PEFT fine-tuning is worth attempting despite the high cost.

contentEn:
Hello. This is Luke. You might remember my post a few days ago where I pondered Cursor project Rules. After writing that post, quite a lot has happened in the past few days.

https://blog.naver.com/fstory97/223805503153
[**The Reality of Vibe Coding and the Answer to Cursor projectRules Confirmed by Prompt Hacking Revealed!** It's been a while since I last wrote. I spent most of the latter half of last year coding with AI. And in February 2025... blog.naver.com](https://blog.naver.com/fstory97/223805503153)

I started with computers because I wanted to create a computer that could communicate with me, and now I'm doing just that. How could I not think about creating my own AI agent? Whether this is an obsession, love, or familial affection, I will continue to share the process of building Alpha. Oh, and finally, let's all use Cline instead of Voldemort (Cursor). I think if we get good at using Cline, we'll eventually have to improve it ourselves.

titleEn: Believer: XRCLOUD's Shutdown Is Unrelated
contentEn:
I am writing this follow-up post after seeing social media comments that linked Believer's shutdown to open-sourcing and the metaverse bubble. It's true that Believer's XRCLOUD did receive some support amidst the metaverse bubble during the pandemic era. The technology development itself received some help from government projects, and the services introduced would not have materialized without such an atmosphere. However, while SW developer labor costs rose significantly, the scale of support received was very small compared to the technology developed. Instead, there was one round of private investment in the middle, and commercialization was delayed while those funds were being fully expended. Furthermore, because we aimed for the highly difficult task of XR devices and the web, it wasn't a structure that could be churned out immediately like a game engine.

A lot of money was spent on the metaverse, and it was a hot topic, but this was linked to cryptocurrencies in the gaming industry due to abundant liquidity, and costs were mainly invested in promotional content creation. This made competition difficult for technology-focused companies like ours, whose output, despite its difficulty, often looked less impressive than something quickly made with Unreal. Of course, our WebXR-based metaverse was designed to significantly lower content creation costs after technology development, but our mistake was not completing it on time. With the emergence of not only Apple's visionOS but also AndroidXR, XR is now coming to the surface. Both visionOS and AndroidXR have emerged as productivity tools, and WebXR is always separately explained as one pillar of developer tools.

Some people say that XR has failed because Apple's Vision Pro and Meta Quest haven't succeeded like smartphones. I once worked on smart TVs at Naver. I even registered as a developer for early Android TV models and received a developer kit from Logitech. Of course, after that, the market was filled with talk of smart TVs failing and so on. "Apple TV is also a failure. IPTV is the answer after all." What about now? In fact, you probably haven't heard news of Android TV and Apple TV being huge successes. However, Uplus's OS is Android TV. All smart TVs except LG and Samsung are Android TVs, and Chromecast and Apple TV still sell well. Though no one really knows, it's safe to say they've already established themselves in the TV market. However, due to the nature of TVs, they couldn't threaten the smartphone market, and somewhat unexpectedly, Netflix ended up occupying the best position in that market.

And the talk of tablets being a failure also continued after the iPad was released. Again, while we haven't heard of them being as hugely successful as smartphones, they have already become mainstream. So, what about XR? The iPhone craze was merely an unusual phenomenon that is hard to replicate; markets typically evolve at a slower pace. When I graduated with a vision for mobile, it was a time when the mobile bubble theory was in full swing. And large corporations started pulling out their investments, saying it wouldn't work, and the team I was going to join was disbanded. Three years later, the iPhone appeared.

Why do we not consistently invest in technology, but instead want immediate, aesthetically pleasing results? I believe the reason the metaverse bubble was excessive is related to this. What about AI? What about the government that said it would invest but then cut R&D budgets? If there was one factor that had the biggest impact on the discontinuation, it was probably this.

Of course, the biggest reason was my many mistakes in choices, failing to create market-appropriate products in a timely manner, failing to prove them with sales, and increasing costs. The metaverse bubble was both real and not real. I feel that Korea's investment in AI has similar aspects. There's a lot of talk about the cheaper DeepSeek, but we've never invested as much as DeepSeek. XR is coming. And the metaverse has arrived. Top games are already, and still are, the metaverse. It's just that they weren't the companies we invested in. The stories, images, videos, and 3D content created by AI have begun to tell the story of the world we want to enter.

I send my support to the metaverse developers and CEOs who are still fighting hard with determination. I have vivid memories of moments in this industry. When I touched the keyboard of an 8-bit computer in my elementary school computer lab and the monitor responded, when I spoke broken English to an AI chatbot named Max on Win3.1 and got a reply, and I remember thinking of 'be able to' to translate 'I'm not good at English'. Playing with the Cellvic, a precursor to smartphones, in college, and watching a roller coaster VR video with cardboard at the SW Policy Research Institute – all these are fundamental experiences, and what software strives for. At the time, when I shared such experiences, everyone told me not to make a fuss. Their reaction was, 'Is that even possible???' But there's no way it wouldn't work, right? It's just that I couldn't do it. And I gave up on the business, not on development. I am still here, and I will open the code today.

I just have many regrets about the business world that fluctuates daily with short-lived joys and sorrows, and about superficial companies. In college, 'A website? That'll take a week, right?' (These days, with AI, it can be done in a day... haha, but that pressure still seems to be there.)

titleEn: The Future of Computer Programming with AI and Humanity's Future
contentEn:
AI-powered coding is very hot right now, and I believe the changes in development brought about by AI will proceed in two stages.

1. Code Generation Using AI Assistants

The first stage is code generation using AI assistants. This involves writing a PRD (Product Requirements Document) and dividing it into modules to concretize the code, as shown in the video below.

This is the task I'm currently most interested in trying. It's the most suitable approach for new projects, though applying it to legacy code would likely require a significant amount of work. By deriving module requirement specifications from the product requirement specification, products can be developed in a top-down manner. Fundamentally, this method maximizes the efficiency of existing development, allowing professional full-stack developers (architects) to significantly reduce costs and time in developing commercial-grade products with the help of AI. In fact, if coding in the classical sense was seen as the work of a programmer, this approach seems closer to that of an architect.

2. Current Limitations of AI Coding

However, as AI's capabilities gradually increase, we will pay less attention to the details of the lower-level modules and specific code. Currently, if module-level generation isn't done well, AI sometimes hallucinates, inserting non-existent variables, adding unrequested features, or even changing existing variables. Therefore, coding still requires constant vigilance. It's TMI when coding. To reduce this, it's best to provide clear instructions and request modifications within a narrow scope. The reason for top-down development is precisely this: creating large chunks and then breaking them down into smaller units for continuous refinement.

3. What if we reach a level where we don't need to worry about modules? AI might just render them in real-time based on the PRD.

However, as AI's capabilities gradually increase, we might reach a level where we can entrust modules to it without worry. When that ultimate stage arrives, we might see usable applications emerge directly from a PRD, or coding might transcend our current methods entirely. AI might even predict user intent solely at the rendering stage and draw pixel by pixel.

{{IMG:1}}
                                
                            [https://www.facebook.com/seongwan.kim.3/posts/pfbid0JiaEcd8nEXR7QxevKDxrFNjNUAyTCtUdVVJ2FFxaQXUFfZpmwrXdYXcYJvT7AXRSl](https://www.facebook.com/seongwan.kim.3/posts/pfbid0JiaEcd8nEXR7QxevKDxrFNjNUAyTCtUdVVJ2FFxaQXUFfZpmwrXdYXcYJvT7AXRSl)

​​

https://www.etched.com/blog-posts/oasis?fbclid=IwY2xjawGRH05leHRuA2FlbQIxMQABHa6Ng_34IVFZ9ua9tKY8JZkb4GcH-DSDaDQqncLnNyab9b75Is4jaSOFOw_aem_JTjkVqnU3OjRnlAof1MxOQ
                                [**Etched | Oasis: an interactive, explorable world model** Making real-time video a reality on Sohu www.etched.com](https://www.etched.com/blog-posts/oasis?fbclid=IwY2xjawGRH05leHRuA2FlbQIxMQABHa6Ng_34IVFZ9ua9tKY8JZkb4GcH-DSDaDQqncLnNyab9b75Is4jaSOFOw_aem_JTjkVqnU3OjRnlAof1MxOQ)

​

4. Future will gradually move towards a hybrid approach

This movement will involve partial replacements and changes as the application of immediately usable stages meets the research and development of neural rendering. In conclusion, for at least the next 5-10 years, PRD-based AI assistant coding methods will likely dominate. After that, perhaps 10 years from now, when AI comparable to AGI emerges and AI computing power issues are largely overcome, allowing AI to handle almost an entire project at once, I suspect neural rendering methods will take the lead.

**5. Important! What's most crucial for developers now: how to ask questions, write PRDs, and work with AI.**

What will be the most effective skill at this point? Many talk about how to ask questions to AI. And sometimes they bring up humanities in that context... No, no! I absolutely disagree.

Computer science has been teaching how to ask questions for a long time. It was the discipline of Software Engineering. People often think of a computer programmer as someone who codes with a lot of technical knowledge. No! The essence of a computer programmer's job is to solve problems, and to design software that machines or other people can understand and that machines can solve, and to write the documentation for it. And this documentation, from the outset, is about asking questions. The computer programming languages we use today are much more natural-language-like than those used by our predecessors, and now it seems we are truly moving towards natural language. However, the technique for creating documentation to minimize the inherent ambiguities of everyday natural language is an engineering approach, and the primitive form of documentation is code. I believe this is evolving further. We should think of the PRD as code itself.

5. The Future of the Computer (SW) Industry

I chose to major in computer science because it was considered a technology that would lead the future, but I wonder if there's any other field that has undergone such a dramatic transformation in such a short time. Since I chose computers, there has already been one revolution: the GUI revolution by Windows; a second: the internet revolution due to the emergence of packet-switched networks; a third: mobile by the iPhone. The fourth, I believe, will be AI... And perhaps the fifth will be AR. Where did VR go, you ask? AR = VR. From an engineer's perspective, they are the same technology. Current VR technology can be seen as a development stage for perfect AR. After that, it might be quantum, and by then, won't we be wearing AR glasses on a spaceship, conversing with AGI?

**2) Developing a Space Sharing Service for Creators**- This document describes how to create a service where users of your service can freely create and share using XRCLOUD.

**3) Developing User Services Using Template Scenes**- This document describes how to develop a service that allows users to provide, decorate, and share template spaces (Rooms) using XRCLOUD.
- The basic development method involves treating a Scene as a template space within the service, creating a Room for the user, and allowing each user to decorate or freely use that space.
- The required API is the Room creation API.
- [https://api.xrcloud.app/docs/ko/#tag/room/operation/CreateRoom](https://api.xrcloud.app/docs/ko/#tag/room/operation/CreateRoom)
- The created Room is managed in the platform's DB along with user information.
- Users can access the Room and decorate the space. For detailed instructions on creating a template space and allowing users to decorate it, please refer to the document below.

**4) Inline View Component that Provides External Webpage Information Without Leaving the Page**- Hubs can link to external webpages via link and image components, which can harm the user experience of platform services.
- XRCLOUD's Spoke provides an inline view component that offers additional functionality to view webpages without leaving the Room. For detailed explanations, please refer to the page below.
- [XRCLOUD's Inline View Component that Provides External Webpage Information Without Leaving the Room](https://belivvr.notion.site/3D-XRCLOUD-4b861e5ca4394c499b43e7b75645c7ce)
**5) Inline View Component that Can Dynamically Pass Data to External Webpages**- XRCLOUD's inline component allows developers to dynamically pass desired information.
- This allows for showing different webpages to different users, or dynamically setting up transitions to other spaces from within a Room, or creating branches.
- By including desired information in the LinkPayload when calling the GetRoom API and passing it to the webpage called by the inline view, it can be used to display different information or route pages based on the information received by that webpage.
- For development methods and detailed examples, please refer to the document below.
- [Development and Utilization Methods for Inline View Components that Can Dynamically Pass Data to External Webpages](https://belivvr.notion.site/591573adf4f8482c8c135447fb011975)
**6) Empty Frame: An Object Dynamically Modifiable by Developers**- XRCLOUD has developed a new object called Empty Frame, which, when placed in the Spoke metaverse editor, can be dynamically changed via an external API. Currently, it is customized with Hubs' Reticulum API, not the XRCLOUD API, and has only been used internally by BELIVVR.
- In the future, we will convert it to the XRCLOUD API, organize it, and release it publicly.

titleEn: Trying Out MiniCPM Llama3-V-2-5 Installation and Execution, Claimed to Outperform GPT-4
contentEn:
Although I studied and built AI a long time ago, it feels like I'm learning many parts anew. To develop the [AI agent](https://blog.naver.com/fstory97/223451877643) I want to create and for immediate practical use, I'm working towards running 'Code-깎는-노인's AI EXE and connecting a personal local AI engine using ollama, among other tools.

**1. MINI CPM Llama-V 2.5 8b Model**

So, wondering if there was a good model that individuals could run, I decided to try out the MiniCPM-Llama3-V 2.5 8b model recommended by [Gyunggyung](https://github.com/gyunggyung) on my Facebook timeline. It's a GPT-4 level multimodal small model developed in China, based on Transformer architecture, aiming for on-device operation in limited environments like smartphones.

**2. MINI CPM Llama-V 2.5 Installation and Execution**

- I first tried installing and running it by referring to [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6SnZMbSx570](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6SnZMbSx570), and I'm sharing the summarized content. To summarize the practical exercise following the video, it's a test to run MiniCPM-Llama3-V-2_5 from Huggingface using Python in Conda, where you can get text responses by posing image and text questions.
**2.1 Prerequisites**
- RTX series HW capable of running Cuda
- Python3, Conda installation
**2.2. Install Pillow, Transformers, Torch, torchvision**

pip install pillow=10.1.0
pip install transoforemrs
pip install torch

**2.3. Huggingface CLI Login**

- **This is a sample of asking questions with an image and text, and receiving text responses via the Python interpreter.**

import torch

from PIL import Image

msgs = [{'role':'user', 'content':question}]
res = model.chat (image = image,  msgs=msgs,  tokenizer=tokenizer, sampling=True, temperature=0.7)
print(res);
