                                {{IMG:26}}
                            
                                
                                        [**Onar** 14-27 Taebongdumil-ro 406beon-gil, Gapyeong-eup, Gapyeong-gun, Gyeonggi-do](https://blog.naver.com/PostView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=223834004873&redirect=Dlog&widgetTypeCall=true&noTrackingCode=true&directAccess=false#)
                                
                    [Reservation](https://blog.naver.com/PostView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=223834004873&redirect=Dlog&widgetTypeCall=true&noTrackingCode=true&directAccess=false#)

It was a pool villa that I went to through a friend's recommendation. I think it's my first time at a pool villa since my honeymoon.

http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70015729611
                                [**A once-in-a-lifetime trip to Krabi!** My first overseas trip and honeymoon destination was Krabi, Thailand. At a wedding expo, I was recommended by Gaya Travel Agency... blog.naver.com](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70015729611)

I was worried because it was cloudy and rainy during the week two weeks ago, but it was sunny on the weekend. The fine dust even cleared up, making it perfect for going out with the kids. The view upon arrival was like this. The modern building in the upper right is Onar Pool Villa.

1. Pool Villa Overview

{{IMG:27}}
                                
                            Onar Pool Villa distant view

Looking a little closer... it's a truly modern detached house. You see two doors, right? The leftmost one is the swimming pool connected to the villa, and the middle door is the entrance.

{{IMG:28}}
                                
                            Onar Pool Villa private house

But we arrived a little early. They were still filling the pool. ㅜㅜ Fortunately, there was also a wonderful outdoor pool, so our kids immediately took to that. My son and daughter were so eager to get in. My heart pounded when they got close without life jackets. I sternly warned them to be careful and then hurriedly put on their life jackets from our luggage.

2. Outdoor Swimming Pool

{{IMG:29}}
                                
                            Onar outdoor pool, kids wanting to go in

Looking from a little further away, the pool looks like this.

{{IMG:30}}
                                
                            Onar outdoor pool, distant view

The water depth was roughly waist-high. There were two parasols, outdoor chairs, and even a large tube available, so you could really just show up and play.

{{IMG:31}}
                                
                            Onar Pension, outdoor pool, parasols

Our luggage is under that parasol. They put our luggage in the refrigerator of another building right next door, so we could even eat cool fruit.

{{IMG:32}}
                                
                            Beach tube

The tube was so large that I could ride it with my child. If you tell the owner about the tubes you brought, he'll inflate them with a compressor. Even a large boat can be inflated quickly. My second child, Igyeom, was scared of the water at first because he remembered falling into the sea with his mom last year while playing, but after riding on his mom's belly, he later asked to play more.

{{IMG:33}}
                                
                            Igyeom (second child) happily on mom's belly

There are many photos with even happier expressions, but I'm reluctant to reveal my children's faces these days, so I won't share them.

{{IMG:34}}
                                
                            Panorama photo

3. Indoor Pool with Spa at the Pool Villa

After playing outside, the water was all filled, so we came inside the pool villa. What a sight when we came in! Our family could use this spacious pool all to ourselves. Haha.

{{IMG:35}}
                                
                            Onar Pension private indoor pool

{{IMG:36}}
                                
                            Onar Pension, Spa

What you see above the pool is a spa. In fact, if you just swim, your body can get a bit cold, so you can fill the spa with water, warm up, and then go back into the pool repeatedly. It's large enough for about 3 adults. There is an air conditioner, but it wasn't the middle of summer, so we didn't turn it on. There are also a table and chairs next to the pool where you can eat, and it connects directly to the barbecue area. It seemed like you could grill meat in the barbecue area and eat it right at that table and chairs. We grilled meat in the barbecue area and brought it inside to eat, so we didn't use that spot.

{{IMG:37}}
                                
                            Onar Pension private indoor pool 2

And the reason we didn't really need to use that table was that if you open the sliding door right next to the pool, it connects directly to the interior of the pension.

4. Sunbeds and Lounge

When you open the sliding door, two beautiful sunbeds are placed there. From the sunbeds, you can see the beautiful sky and your children playing in the pool.

{{IMG:38}}
                                
                            Sky viewed from the sunbeds

{{IMG:39}}
                                
                            Pool viewed from the pension

And to the right, there's a space like a lounge. It looked like a charming place to have tea. If you look at the kitchen photo later, there's also a coffee maker.

{{IMG:40}}
                                
                            Lounge with a beautiful painting

5. Master Bedroom

Next to the reception room is the master bedroom, the largest room. There are a total of 2 rooms. In addition to the bathroom in the living room, each room also has its own bathroom, making a total of 3 bathrooms. Naturally, all of them come with shower booths. The pool villa can accommodate a basic number of guests, up to a maximum of 6 people. In other words, it can accommodate up to 3 couples. You might wonder how that works with only two rooms? I'll explain that later.

{{IMG:41}}
                                
                            Master bedroom next to the middle living room

{{IMG:42}}
                                
                            Two large beds.

A large master bedroom that seems big enough for a large family to lie down in, with two large beds. Our family brought my mother-in-law, and we stayed in this room while she stayed in the adjacent room.

{{IMG:43}}
                                
                            And a TV and dressing table

You can also access the pool from the master bedroom. The door visible next to it leads directly to the pool.

6. Small Room

When I got home, I realized I didn't take any photos of the small room where my mother-in-law stayed. ㅜㅜ It also has a large bed of similar size, a big LCD TV, and a spacious bathroom/shower booth attached. While not as large as the master bedroom, it's as clean as a large room in a typical two-person pension.

7. Living Room

The living room has a generously sized sofa... it was wider and more comfortable than our sofa at home. We used that table for...

{{IMG:44}}
                                
                            Onar Pool Villa Living Room

Ta-da! This is what we travel for, isn't it?

{{IMG:45}}

The carpet, which our kids rolled around on because it was so soft, might be difficult to clean, so be careful... Fortunately, a vacuum cleaner is provided, so I vacuumed the carpet once before we left. I mentioned 3 couples earlier, and you might have found it strange that there are only 2 rooms, right? The secret lies in these stairs next to the bathroom.

{{IMG:46}}
                                
                            Loft stairs

Climbing those stairs reveals a beautiful loft space. It's designed so that the top isn't easily visible from below, which seems to offer privacy, and there's also a small table. While you can't stand up straight, it's a sufficient space when sitting, so it doesn't feel particularly low.

{{IMG:47}}

8. Kitchen

A good kitchen is important for good eating. First, the kitchen shelves are stocked with coffee mats and various convenience items.

{{IMG:48}}

A spacious double-door refrigerator, water purifier, toaster, and a full set of microwave oven!

{{IMG:49}}

Plenty of cups of various sizes on the shelf,

{{IMG:50}}

Plenty of faucets, and a 2-burner induction cooktop.

{{IMG:51}}
                                
                            Dining table

My wife said she wished she had a kitchen like this ㅜㅜ How many pyeong (Korean unit of area) would an apartment need to have a kitchen like this?

{{IMG:52}}
                                
                            Kitchen view

9. Charming Entrance

Next to the kitchen is this beautiful entrance. It doesn't lead directly outside; there's a turn and an inner door.

{{IMG:53}}
                                
                            Entrance

10. BBQ

A pension wouldn't be complete without a BBQ. I diligently grilled and brought the food inside. The kids had been playing in the water, so I couldn't eat outside in case they got cold.

{{IMG:54}}
                                
                            BBQ area

The view from the BBQ area is also wide open.

{{IMG:55}}
                                
                            View from the BBQ area

11. And a Charming Night View

Perhaps because it's summer, the days have gotten longer. A panoramic view of the pool villa pension taken from outside. It looks very peaceful.

{{IMG:56}}

And, the evening view of the reception room.

{{IMG:57}}

And, there's even a piano! ^^ Since it's a private villa, you can play to your heart's content. My wife, who loves it because it's an acoustic piano, unlike the digital one at home, says it feels great. (Even though our digital piano at home wasn't cheap... ㅜㅜ The charm of an acoustic is different, after all).

{{IMG:58}}

I enjoyed the relaxed feeling that you can't experience in an apartment. I had a great time eating and playing after a long while. Even if it feels a bit expensive, the reason to go to a pool villa seems to be for the sense of relaxation. While there's a certain charm to visiting crowded places in summer, when you're jostled by people, you can't tell if you went to relax or to suffer. Moreover, if you have young children, there are countless things to worry about. The distance isn't too far, so it might be good to go and relax. I wonder if I'll ever be able to live in a house like this when I get older?

12. Modern and Special Other Spa Pensions and Glamping Sites

In addition to the pool villa, there are other modern and wonderful spa pensions and glamping sites where you can enjoy a camping atmosphere. They also offer pickup service, so check out the link below.

[**Onar** gp-valley.co.kr](http://gp-valley.co.kr/)

{{IMG:59}}
                                    

https://blog.naver.com/PostView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=223834004873&redirect=Dlog&widgetTypeCall=true&noTrackingCode=true&directAccess=false#

                                
                            Click the photo to go to the pension page.

**PS. This post received a complimentary stay from Onar Pension, received no other compensation, and visited through a friend's recommendation.**

titleEn: VR All-Purpose Era is Coming: Sports, Education, Military, Industry, and Office
contentEn:
This post is a draft written at the request of the Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA). A refined edited version was published in KOCCA's K-Content May/June 2016 issue, titled "Stimulating the Five Senses: Immersive Content," with a more detailed article [Zoom 3 The World Expands, Worlds Multiply](http://sitehomebos.kocca.kr/k_content/vol19/vol19_08.pdf).

http://www.kocca.kr/cop/createcont/view.do?menuNo=200903&nttNo=29
                                [**K-Content < Periodicals < Content Knowledge < Korea Creative Content Agency** www.kocca.kr](http://www.kocca.kr/cop/createcont/view.do?menuNo=200903&nttNo=29)

1.  The 2018 PyeongChang Olympics is a VR Olympics

The 2012 London Olympics was a very fast and vivid Olympics for us. People received real-time news about the London Olympics through smartphones, a new medium, and with the start of UHD broadcasting, they could see the scene more clearly. And, in May 2016, the Ministry of Science, ICT and Future Planning included new ICT technologies in the 2018 PyeongChang Winter Olympics.

{{IMG:1}}

                            .[K-ICT PyeongChang Winter Olympics Realization Strategy, Source: Ministry of Science, ICT and Future Planning]

This is none other than VR (Virtual Reality), which is a hot topic these days. How can virtual reality be applied to sports where people actually sweat? VR technology makes you feel as if you've entered another world through a head-mounted display (HMD). If the London Olympics allowed spectators to watch games through a clearer and larger window, the PyeongChang Winter Olympics might offer an experience of being directly at the scene, wearing a virtual reality device like Gear VR. Technically, this involves shooting with a 360-degree camera and then viewing it through a virtual reality device. Moreover, it's not only the best seat to watch the game, but you'll also be able to turn your head and look for attractive people in the stands. The service model of sports is changing from the traditional one-way broadcasting concept to providing an on-site experience. Additionally, a better aspect than being at the venue is that you can watch comfortably from your sofa at home, and since it's virtual reality, you can also receive additional information like commentary and scores, just as you would on a TV screen. However, for now, VR technology is starting with games and 360-degree videos rather than live broadcasts, because various technical issues still exist. Various problems exist, such as motion latency that can cause dizziness in VR devices, or limitations in communication speed for transmitting high-resolution 360-degree videos. The 2018 PyeongChang Olympics is also a testing ground for 5G networks, making it a perfect environment for VR, which requires large-volume data transmission. Thus, the immediate advent of more complete and mature VR technology will enable many more things beyond games and 360-degree videos, such as live sports broadcasts.

2.  Cheaper and More Pleasant VR Tourism

What about tourism? In 2018, the same year as the PyeongChang Olympics, Russia will host the World Cup, a global football festival. If you go to Russia, watching the World Cup would be great, but you'd probably also want to visit the Kremlin Palace. However, during your trip, chances are you might experience unpleasant service, local rip-off prices, or get exhausted in crowded places.

{{IMG:2}}

                            [Ideal vs. Reality of Tourist Attractions, Source: Tencent News (騰訊新聞)]

But what if you could experience this with VR? Perhaps that experience would be much more wonderful than reality. You could tour closer than reality, in the most magnificent places, and listen to explanations in Korean from a friendly guide. Moreover, the best part about such VR tourism is that it's very cheap.

3.  Living, Moving, and Safe VR Educational Content

Furthermore, once you enter the virtual reality world of Moscow, you might have a unique experience that you could never have in the real world. You could even visit the magnificent coronation ceremony of Empress Catherine in old Moscow. You would not only transcend space but also time, arriving in the year 1762. Such new experiences have high potential for use in education. Google already launched its Expedition Pioneer program, an educational program using Google's VR device Cardboard, starting in September 2015. Within just two months of the program, it provided an environment for 100,000 students to experience over 100 regions around the world, including the Great Wall of China, through virtual reality, rapidly increasing interest in VR-based education.

{{IMG:3}}

                            [Classroom scene using Cardboard, Source: Google]

Attempts to utilize various digital technologies in education have continuously existed. Children already use word processors to write homework and search the internet. Presentations are made using PowerPoint. However, while paper has changed to word processors, books to the internet, and presentations to PowerPoint, the experience provided by education hasn't significantly changed. However, VR is highly valuable because it innovates that experience. The experience of putting VR devices on children can bring effects beyond reading books and watching videos. It provides higher immersion than video and offers game-like feedback. If VR input devices like Oculus Touch are used, science experiments could be conducted even more safely. There would be no fear of getting burned by an alcohol lamp, and perhaps even a small nuclear reactor could be built. You could visit volcanoes, space, or the South Pole and underwater. Even if the cost issue for field trips to volcanoes or space were resolved, no parents would send their children for safety reasons, but with VR, it's different. Images over text, videos over images, and VR over videos. Finally, with VR technology, educational content has begun to come alive.

4.  Industrial and Military Applications of VR

Furthermore, areas where safety is even more crucial are the industrial and military sectors. In reality, many accidents occur, and the damage and impact when an accident happens are very significant. It can lead to loss of life or very large financial incidents. Drones or robots equipped with 360-degree cameras could be controlled through VR technology. You could work in dangerous environments without being physically there, and without fear of being shot.

{{IMG:4}}

                            [Norwegian Army's experiment securing virtual vision with VR, ZDnet]

Also, work often involves multiple people collaborating, not just one. VR technology can effectively facilitate collaboration, even with people on the other side of the world. Until now, collaboration meant talking with a video camera on, or limited interaction with remote collaboration software like Google Docs. Or, in the medical field, it required very specific environments like remote surgery. However, VR technology allows scanning each other's bodies with 3D cameras, enabling multiple people to converse and work together with virtual tools in a virtual room.

{{IMG:5}}

                            [Microsoft Holoportation, Source: Microsoft Research]

In March 2016, Microsoft unveiled a technology called Holoportation, which turned this imagination into reality. Just like in movies, you can see a distant person in 3D as if they were right next to you. Being together also means being able to do something together. Through such technology, we might be freed from the discomfort of cramped business class seats.

5.  The Meaning of VR

The value VR will offer us in the future is not merely a means for games and videos. Virtual reality technology breaks down the barriers of physical distance and time, which are limitations of the real world. And this technology will be much cheaper than real-world experiences, offering more information and more wonderful experiences. This will change many aspects of our lives and provide new value. Of course, I don't believe VR technology will completely replace reality. It must provide experiences for more senses, not just sight, which is represented by HMDs. Furthermore, it will need to overcome numerous technical limitations. VR has only just begun to show its industrial value and will quickly start to reveal its full potential. And, in the process, I also expect VR to help us discover the value of experiences that VR cannot provide in the real world.

titleEn: The Real Smart Thermometer for Kids, Thermocare is Good for Newborns
contentEn:
I had almost forgotten about it due to the reward crowdfunding, but the item has arrived.

{{IMG:1}}
                                
                            Who are you?

What could it be?

http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/220559178208
                                [**[Thermocare] A smarter and safer thermometer than the Braun thermometer** 1. Do you know the Braun thermometer? A thermometer that every home with a child has, the Braun thermometer... blog.naver.com](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/220559178208)

1. A smart thermometer in my hands

The smart thermometer I participated in crowdfunding for last December has arrived.

{{IMG:2}}

{{IMG:3}}

2. First impression: It's pretty.

My first impression is that it's pretty. It's much prettier than the bulky Braun thermometer I have at home. It's designed to fit well in a woman's hand, and the grip feels good. It uses two standard AA batteries, so they're easy to replace, and there are three buttons in total. While a smart thermometer is typically used in conjunction with a smartphone, it works perfectly fine on its own and its basic functions are surprisingly robust.

3. Measurement is easy and fast.

Measurement method: Point it at the child's forehead or temple area and press the middle button. Above all, I was surprised by how incredibly fast the measurement speed is. The button flashed briefly, and then it displayed the temperature. Since it's a non-contact thermometer, there were slight differences depending on where it was measured, but not to a significant degree. It felt like I could take 5 or more measurements in the time it takes to take about 2 measurements with a standard in-ear Braun thermometer.

4. Easy to measure at night.

Children often get fevers at night, and my role then was to shine a phone light. It required a two-person team: my wife measuring and me illuminating. If the strong phone screen light even slightly shone on the child's face, I'd usually get scolded. However, a feature of Thermocare is that it's easy to measure at night. This is because it displays with an LED. Watch the video below. (It's normal not to see much; the flashing light at the end is the measurement result.) Let's not disturb a child's deep sleep. They say it hinders growth... which is a very important issue for me.

{{IMG:4}}

5. Surprisingly useful object temperature measurement

After moving recently, a slight inconvenience arose: my apartment uses an individual boiler, and if I turn on the bathwater, it gets excessively hot. Pressing the top-left button changes the icon from a person to a box. The box indicates object temperature measurement mode.

{{IMG:5}}
                                
                            Press lightly

{{IMG:6}}
                                
                            Into object measurement mode like this

{{IMG:7}}
                                
                            Bathwater starts running, lukewarm temperature

It's a bit cool. A bit too cold for kids to bathe in.

{{IMG:8}}
                                

https://blog.naver.com/PostView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=223833999385&redirect=Dlog&widgetTypeCall=true&noTrackingCode=true&directAccess=false#

{{IMG:9}}
                                
                            It's gotten a bit warmer. A good temperature for bathing.

{{IMG:10}}
                                

https://blog.naver.com/PostView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=223833999385&redirect=Dlog&widgetTypeCall=true&noTrackingCode=true&directAccess=false#

{{IMG:11}}
                                
                            Ugh... I knew it was hot, but it's over 55 degrees Celsius.

It was hot even with rubber gloves on when washing dishes, so there was a reason. It's also possible to measure baby bottle temperatures as an example. When measuring object temperatures, it's best to align the measurement sensor with the object you want to measure. Since it's non-contact, if you don't pay attention, you might measure a completely wrong spot. Also, the measurement temperature range is 10 to 70 degrees Celsius, so it's inaccurate for industrial uses like measuring a blast furnace or a refrigerator. Please keep this in mind.

6. Smartphone integration

As a smart thermometer, smartphone integration is a given. By connecting via Bluetooth, you can do this... and add family members for individual measurements.

{{IMG:12}}

You can delete incorrect measurements. The 27.8-degree reading was just an air measurement. Temperatures outside the normal range seem to be indicated with a different color... Huh? A new discovery: the app also displays temperature and humidity. Haha, since the appropriate humidity varies with temperature, this information seems very useful. Additionally, it provides various health and hospital information, allowing for immediate response based on the child's condition. Currently, the app is in its early version and feels a bit unstable, but they plan to improve it quickly, so it's worth looking forward to. Apple HealthKit is currently being integrated, and Samsung S Health and Google Fit will be supported sequentially.

7. A smarter AI smart thermometer

Even with just this much, it seems to be worth buying, but even better news I heard from M-Tree Care, who is developing Thermocare, is that the service will become even smarter in the future by utilizing artificial intelligence.

{{IMG:13}}
                                
                            Source: 4th ICT-A.I Forum, Reliability Study on Pediatric Febrile Patient Response Using Thermocare Smart Thermometer and IBM Watson

No joke, they are creating an AI thermometer using IBM's AI Watson, which has beaten humans in quiz shows and performs cancer diagnoses beyond the level of doctors. Wow. Even though a thermometer might seem like nothing, as a medical device, it requires high reliability and undergoes numerous verifications. And it aims for more effective treatment and care based on data. While it will start as a simple temperature measurement device, I expect it to evolve into a service that acts like an AI family doctor in the future. And the fact that this is possible just by a software upgrade to a device purchased once, isn't that great? Instead of having to buy a new device every time a new feature comes out, I support the Thermocare thermometer that will automatically evolve into a better service. Moreover, in a situation where high-quality, low-cost devices from China are flooding the market, it seems like a good IoT device that competes on quality, capability, and reliability.

8. General sale not yet. Special limited sale scheduled for June 13th on 11th Street.

Ah... Lastly, many people ask about where to buy it, but it's not available yet. The general sale price will be 69,900 won through 11th Street on June 13th. As a little extra buying tip, it will be sold for 55,900 won for a limited quantity of 500 units, so those planning to buy should take advantage of this. If you're planning to buy a Braun thermometer or any other thermometer, I recommend holding off for a bit. **P.S. This post has not received any separate compensation, and the product was purchased directly through crowdfunding.**

titleEn: The Conflict Between Men and Women Might Be More
contentEn:
Even amidst a hectic day at work today, I found myself at the center of a misogyny debate on Facebook. After several discussions, I came to realize that this issue might not be so simple. Even as I write this, I'm cautious, and although I've failed to organize my thoughts perfectly, I'd like to share some of my thoughts.

### 1. The Gangnam Station Murder Case and My 'Kim Yeosa' Remark

Regarding whether the current situation surrounding the Gangnam Station murder case is excessive, I agree that it is not. I believe this incident serves as a trigger, offering a good opportunity to innovate and address underlying societal problems. Change and innovation are not born from lukewarm responses. Even when a ship carrying hundreds of students sinks, the path to innovation still feels long. The controversy on Facebook today stemmed from a comment I made, using 'Kim Yeosa' as a theme, under a post expressing anger at people who don't use their car turn signals. First, to offer a slight excuse, my comment was not intended to demean women. However, it seems many women did not perceive it that way. So, after the controversy, I thought about it more deeply. Initially, the controversy around the comment revolved around an attempt to argue that women have lower visuospatial abilities, which is reflected in societal perceptions. However, the counter-argument veered off in a strange direction, claiming it was unscientific, and an argument ensued. But upon reflection, this argument was misguided from the start. The perception of a word cannot be the same for the speaker and the listener. The two issues are distinct: (women's argument) that a listener can feel offended regardless of the speaker's intent, and (men's argument) what the speaker's actual intent was. This is because both individuals made judgments based on their own confirmation biases in their brains and only expressed their own perspectives. In fact, in the brain, what the truth is isn't that important. If there is only one truth, it is the fact that everything must be doubted. Therefore, it is necessary to consider both the speaker's and the listener's perspectives, regardless of the intention, and consequently, it is right for the person who ended up in the position of causing offense to apologize and be cautious, which is why I apologized and resolved to be more careful with such remarks.

Within the brain, a single word is defined based on countless experiences. It's similar to how AlphaGo learns Go moves. In my case, when I first encountered the 'Kim Yeosa' issue in an old online community, most members were male, and the first thing that came to mind was the scooter ajumma episode from 'You're Under Arrest!'. It was a cliché of a pushy, brazen, and typically bothersome middle-aged woman. Some young women might also agree that such a cliché exists for older women. In fact, it's a cliché that frequently appears in media, even if the specific term 'Kim Yeosa' isn't used. Even if not all older women are like that, and even if it actually captures one facet of our mothers, I believe that even simple issues we categorize as male vs. female can be rather complex, requiring consideration of culture and the spirit of the times. Perhaps the reason the 'Kim Yeosa' remark is offensive is that it aligns with the character of a brazen and helpless woman, a character that I dislike? Conversely, if I were to think of it from a male perspective, the fact that I might be associated with the 'gaejeossi' (obnoxious middle-aged man) or 'kkondae' (condescending elder) character would not feel good.

### 2. Are Men and Women Truly Biologically Equal? Or Are You and I Equal?

Today, science has shattered many preconceptions. It has proven that Black people and women are not biologically inferior to men. However, on the other hand, it has also begun to uncover their differences. And it has revealed that traits are not only influenced by biological factors but also by a complex interplay of environmental factors. The recent development of precision medicine utilizing AI aims to identify differences by considering genes, environment, and individual habits, rather than group-based medical care, and to provide suitable services accordingly. The most fundamental hypothesis here is not that all individuals are the same, but that they are, in fact, all different. Disease is not the result of a single cause, but a complex interplay of various factors. Furthermore, how groups operate is even more complex. This is what is known as a complex system. Individuals are also, in fact, composed of intelligence built from conflicting experiences, and there are even theories that emotions are products of intelligence. Since groups are made up of such individuals, they are naturally even more complex.

To confess, I probably possess elements of a 'gaejeossi'. I won't deny it. The Japanese manga and anime I mentioned earlier often contain what could be called a 'gaejeossi' perspective. However, I don't believe such elements are exclusive to anime or manga created as commercial media products. I also consider EDPS (a slang term for lewd jokes among computer science students), which was common among male students I didn't particularly like at the time, to be such an element. What's interesting is that explicit sexual objectification and sexual abuse content exist in subcultures for both men and women. Of course, I oppose its use as a means to justify sexual violence, like Ilbe or Megal, and I consider it abnormal. Ultimately, the scientifically confirmed fact is only that the actual groups we know are not clear-cut, and complex parameters influence each other. Therefore, it might not be possible to extract a single factor to explain communities like Megal and Ilbe, or the interpretations of the far-right represented by Trump and Abe, and perhaps opposing organizations or individuals are influencing each other through numerous butterfly effects?

### 3. In the End, There Is No Conclusion. Don't We Need to Objectify It More?

You might have expected a grand conclusion in my writing. However, there is no conclusion. I haven't been able to organize my thoughts either. The only confirmed fact is that such groups exist and are fighting. And that everyone, just like me, is not free from such prejudices. This exists not only in issues between men and women but also in religion, politics, or within companies and families. I hope that the recent advancements in software development might offer some answers to this. Some say what we need now is empathy, and while empathy is certainly the most effective skill in conflict, I also believe that empathy itself might be the result of certain factors. Therefore, wouldn't a simpler or more fundamental approach be to bring empathy out of the realm of non-science and into the realm of science, and to find models that mediate and advance conflict resolution?

Of course, I also fight with my wife... planners fight with developers... elders fight with children... that's how everyone lives. The fortunate thing is that humanity doesn't live in a dog-eat-dog world where losing a fight means being devoured by the opponent. I think the time has come to understand the brain, humanity's greatest skill. Perhaps that will be one of the moments when humanity passes a singularity, successfully understanding itself. If I were having this conversation with my friend over drinks, he would probably say this: "Shut up and drink. That's why you never had a girlfriend. Be grateful to your sister-in-law." I wonder if some perverted engineering students like me would fail a Turing test if liberal arts female students administered it. Lol. Women are great, and in fact, I think the first ones to be replaced by computers might actually be men who are solely engrossed in such logical thinking.

To cool your head, I'll leave you with the opening of 'You're Under Arrest!' (逮捕しちゃうぞ). It's a manga that not only gave me the image of 'Kim Yeosa' but also instilled in me a romantic ideal of small cars.

titleEn: Google AI Dreams of 'Taking Over Everyday Life' for Humanity
contentEn:
This column was published in the May issue of Shindonga.
Original article: [http://shindonga.donga.com/Library/3/22/13/533477/1](http://shindonga.donga.com/Library/3/22/13/533477/1){{IMG:1}} For those in the IT industry, Google is not an unfamiliar name. With a market capitalization more than three times that of Samsung Electronics, Google is a top IT company that competes with Apple for the world's No. 1 and 2 spots. Despite being such a formidable company, its presence in Korea is relatively faint. This is because domestic portal companies like Naver and Daum have historically dominated internet search in Korea.

Google's 'significant' presence in Korea emerged in 2010 when Samsung Electronics launched its Galaxy smartphones. The 'green robot' used by domestic mobile carriers in their Galaxy marketing at the time is the mascot for Android, Google's smartphone operating system (OS).

A smartphone OS is the 'brain' of a smartphone. Just as Microsoft (MS) Windows is installed on PCs and laptops, Google's Android software is installed when you buy a Samsung Electronics or LG Electronics smartphone. According to the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA), as of the second half of last year, Android OS held an 86% share of domestic smartphones, while Apple's iOS held 14%. With over 40 million smartphone users in Korea, approximately 34 million are Google's 'customers'. The company that created the formidable artificial intelligence that defeated Lee Se-dol 9P is close to us.

#### The 'Superman' of the Real World

To understand Google, let's first think of Naver. Like Naver, Google also makes money through internet search. Whether on Naver or Google, if you search for 'airline tickets,' a list of companies selling airline tickets appears in the search results. Some of these are advertisements (usually located at the top). These companies pay Naver and Google to gain the right to be displayed prominently. Google's advertising revenue in the fourth quarter of last year was $19.078 billion (approximately 22 trillion won). During the same period, Naver's advertising revenue was 646.9 billion won, which is only about 1/30th of Google's.

Google, with over 70% market share in the global internet search market, receives 3.5 trillion search queries per day. In the movie 'Superman,' there's a scene where Superman hears the voices of people all over the world from Earth's atmosphere. Google is effectively doing something similar in reality.

The original internet map service, like Naver Maps and Daum Maps, is Google Maps (map.google.com). Google Maps shows almost every place on Earth, even reaching Antarctica. YouTube, where Psy's 'Gangnam Style' surpassed 200 million views, Gmail, used by over a billion people, and the mobile-dominant app store Google Play are also services provided by Google. Like Microsoft, it also creates office programs for documents and other tasks, as well as PC operating systems.

Thus, everything online can be done through Google. While the Korean mobile market is dominated by Kakao (which acquired Daum), splitting it between Naver and Kakao, Google has seized control of both PC and mobile across the global market. With the advent of mobile, the boundaries between online and offline have long disappeared, so it's no exaggeration to say that Google is synonymous with 'the daily life of people worldwide'.

titleEn: The Age of Deep Learning: Can Computers Understand Us Now
contentEn:
Now that Google's deep learning AlphaGo has swept through, Facebook has again released AI bots, declaring it the era of bots instead of apps. It seems AI is indeed making a lot of noise.

Image does not exist.

**1. The Past and Limitations of AI**
However, AI that plays Go or AI conversational bots are not new. From a service perspective, not a technical one, AI that plays Go is closer to a sophisticated NPC game machine. Conversational bots like Max in the PC era and SimSimi in the mobile era have already appeared in Korea.

Image does not exist.

[ Source : [http://goo.gl/h7Cxqe](http://goo.gl/h7Cxqe) ]
However, the reason these could not become truly meaningful services was the difficulty in creating human-level AI. Simple speech recognition or individual context recognition each developed separately. Computing resources were limited, and there were individual situations where if one thing didn't work, another would have problems. Although the situation has improved with the development of computing technology, humans still process an enormous amount of unstructured data in real-time, including visual, auditory, contextual information, and past experiences, making AlphaGo's 160,000 game records seem trivial. Furthermore, experiences etched into genes through tens of millions of years of evolution, combined with decades of life experiences, amount to an enormous volume if converted into data. Unlike the public's misunderstanding that AI in computer science means creating a human with a computer, its true meaning lies in a machine solving problems it couldn't solve before, like a human, by finding approximate values for a specific purpose. Among these, conversation is a very high-difficulty problem, actually more difficult than Go. Ordinary people like us cannot beat a machine that defeats Lee Sedol at Go, but we can argue better than AlphaGo. This is because conversation is actually one of the most advanced brain functions, and we only know of one machine that has just passed the Turing test in an unconventional way. Clearly, it seems we are passing a certain point.

**2. So, who can do it well?**
So, who can do it well? Will an AI startup with geniuses suddenly pop out an amazing search engine like Wolfram Alpha? Geniuses always surpass the thoughts of ordinary people, but in my humble opinion, only companies with massive amounts of user data can excel at AI bots. Even if there are thousands of supercomputers, they are useless without data to train them. Furthermore, the training data must have at least minimal tagging or related information suitable for training. In social network services, this could be relationships between people, or links embedded in tweets. In the case of search services, it's queries and the results clicked by users. To discuss and develop AI services, the major premise is that a platform capable of collecting user data must exist. Or at least, collect and release it for research purposes. I believe this is why government-led initiatives, simply pouring money, cannot solve the problem.

**3. What about South Korea?**
Fortunately, in Korea's case, I think the situation is a bit better. Because there are Naver and Kakao, which created Line, as platform companies leading user data. However, it's difficult to be optimistic due to the fact that 70% of the world uses Google, Facebook, and WhatsApp. It's hard to expect to become a global company by analyzing only Korean. AI is not just a technology; its final product is data created by society, AI software technology, and computer hardware. I believe the difficulty order is society, software, hardware. This is why I believe AI needs to be viewed with a longer breath. An approach like suddenly building some hardware and expecting results in a few years can quickly extinguish the nascent spark of AI. I hope people don't have high expectations for Facebook's bots either. Personally, I don't think it will be much different from Line's "official accounts" that used to answer weather or fortune-telling questions conversationally.

Image does not exist.

**[Source : [http://hotdog-life.tistory.com/249]**](http://hotdog-life.tistory.com/249%5D)
However, as a platform company, their know-how might be a structure that allows more third parties to achieve more free and advanced development. Could they be thinking of an AI platform company? In fact, IBM is already attempting this, calling it the "cognitive era." And it's important not to forget that massive resources have been invested in this for a long time, and these companies are no longer hardware companies but software and (B2B) service companies.

titleEn: NAVER's Divine Move: NAVER Pay Check Card
contentEn:
Today, I was originally going to add more to the VR story, but Naver has brought out something incredible, so I'd like to talk about that instead. It's a check card. A smart check card? No. It's just a plastic card.

[**Naver Pay Check Card Pre-application** Apply now for double benefits! 0 annual fee, no previous month's spending requirement, 2% accumulation anytime, anywhere campaign.naver.com](https://campaign.naver.com/x2/)

**1. What is O2O for Giant Online Companies? Thirsty for Offline Data.**

When it comes to O2O, the hot company these days is Kakao. This is because they are conducting O2O business centered around on-demand services that allow users to instantly find and receive various offline services online. In fact, O2O is less of a technical term and more of a business trend. It refers to the trend of offline commerce companies expanding online, and online commerce companies expanding offline, leading to convergence. The O2O story, which began with Uber, is now spreading to taxis and hair salons. But why do online companies venture into offline markets? Especially large corporations (?) like Kakao, entering fragmented network markets like taxi drivers and hair salons. And, the moment they enter this market, co-existence issues are bound to erupt. It's a market that poses a considerable burden for large companies. The answer is data. I've also worked at a certain portal, and from the perspective of tracking (confining) almost all user behavior online, what I'm curious about is offline user data. Is the restaurant review this user posted truly accurate data? Is it a place many people actually visit? Do they really go to that restaurant after seeing this blog post? Things like that. From an online company's perspective, a user exists only as a URL, a query, and an account. There's no way to track their actions offline. But then, mobile suddenly appeared. Although mobile is an online information device, people carry it outdoors. They take photos while eating, and even play music while exercising. Plus, payments! Naturally, for online companies, it's akin to the blind gaining sight. The data that offline businesses have been accumulating haphazardly is simply money for online companies that feed on data. Therefore, neither Kakao nor Naver, nor eBay, Amazon, Google, or Facebook can afford to ignore O2O.

**2. Naver's O2O History is Surprisingly Long.**

Everyone only thinks of Kakao, but Naver also did O2O. ㅜㅜ The QR code service that Naver and Daum are still offering was actually one of the intermediary technologies connecting online and offline, and NFC is a technology in that extension. Real estate services that backed down due to co-existence issues... Wingspoon, and the business-oriented Me2day, which thought of applying Cyworld's brand mini-hompy to offline businesses, later created 24시 (24 hours) and coupon services. Naver's O2O history is quite seasoned. While one might evaluate this as a lack of skill, it can also be seen as having internalized knowledge from failures. Among these, online payment initially started with Naver Pay's predecessor, Checkout. Checkout solved the trust issues between various online merchants by acting as a PG for PGs. Thanks to this, small SOHO businesses were able to use Naver's reliable payment infrastructure. And expanding this to offline was probably a natural progression, a picture they had already envisioned long ago.

**3. The Challenge of Korean FinTech and Payment Systems: Card Benefits and Convenience**

You might wonder why I'm talking about FinTech while discussing O2O, but at the intersection of O2O and FinTech lies payment systems like Kakao Pay, Payco, and Naver Pay. However, there was a challenge in the Korean market for this sector. I don't quite remember which year it was. Back when NFC integration into Android was certain and rumors were swirling about iPhones, a certain bank unofficially gathered bloggers and some so-called experts and asked if a business model where iPhones would integrate NFC, possibly in collaboration with their bank, would be viable. The so-called early adopters gathered, but they all responded, "It probably won't work." The reason was that card payments in Korea are excessively convenient. They happen instantly, the benefits are monstrous, consumers feel minimal inequality regarding fees, and there's income tax deduction, plus the premium image that Korean cards possess... The common opinion was that even the mighty iPhone couldn't overcome this situation. This problem remains valid even now, with NFC integration becoming common in smartwatches and smartphones. The biggest enemy of smartphone FinTech is the plastic card.

**4. But then, the Naver Pay Check Card Appeared.**

However, today, an item appeared that aims to directly solve this problem. It's the Naver Pay Check Card. Currently, the accumulation rate for check cards is around 0.1-0.5%. General credit cards are around 1-2%. But the Naver Pay Check Card guarantees 1%, and 2% this year... And, unlike the era of NFC rumors, what has changed is that the income tax deduction rate for check cards has become better than for credit cards. In fact, because of this, card companies are currently concerned about decreasing profits. Naver's long-standing concern, as mentioned earlier, is also about knowing what people are doing offline. From the customer's perspective, they're collecting points through Naver Pay, but from Naver's perspective, they can now know what you're doing offline too. Finally, it means that if you have an AK47 in your Naver game inventory, it can be scientifically proven that your probability of buying a gun offline and killing innocent citizens increases. The correlation between Kakao's heart delivery count and hallucinogen purchases could also be revealed. Of course, like Amazon, they might even commit the atrocity of determining a girl's pregnancy and tipping off her father.

**5. Will the Relationship with Card Companies Be Okay?**

What surprised me with the appearance of this product, in fact, is how Naver managed to launch such a groundbreaking check card with a card company. From the card company's perspective, an increase in check cards could directly lead to a decrease in credit cards, and Naver possessing offline payment information might somewhat diminish the card company's most crucial role as a marketing platform. Should this be seen purely as Naver's business acumen?

http://m.ekn.kr/section_view.html?no=207944
[**Era of 100 Million Check Cards... Card Companies Trapped in a Negative Margin Swamp** m.ekn.kr](http://m.ekn.kr/section_view.html?no=207944)

Anyway, while Kakao was embroiled in absurd debates about whether it's a large corporation or not (by that logic, Yello Mobile would also be a large corporation), and internet banks were floundering in a swamp of regulations, Naver quietly and powerfully delivered a blow from behind. Naver continues to be smart and good at business. Of course, Kakao and various other companies are also capturing the O2O market from different positions, so it's difficult to perfectly predict whose victory it will be. For now, I've pre-ordered the Naver Pay Check Card.

titleEn: What Can Korea Do with Open Source AlphaGo?
contentEn:
With Lee Sedol's first win, the atmosphere has shifted again. However, misunderstandings about AlphaGo still seem prevalent. It brings tears to my eyes to see expressions like AlphaGo's 'mistake' or 'bug' still being spread by major media outlets. Even people in software development, who haven't looked into AI, seem to misunderstand it as a rule-based program. Anyway, I hope these perceptions gradually improve, and with the news that Google has open-sourced AlphaGo, I'd like to briefly discuss what we can do with it.

**Oh, you didn't know? AlphaGo has been open-sourced.**
****I made a mistake and am correcting it. The source below is not Google's source. It is an open-source project attempting to replicate AlphaGo based on the paper. Currently, global companies like Google, Facebook, and MS are releasing open-source or open APIs to advance AI, but AlphaGo's source code has not been publicly released. ****
****Correction: However, since the paper has been published, we can independently create our own versions or participate in the project below. (The content below is uploaded without further modification, so please read it with this in mind.)**

https://github.com/Rochester-NRT/AlphaGo
                                **Rochester-NRT/AlphaGo** AlphaGo - A replication of DeepMind's 2016 Nature publication, "Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search," details of which can be found on their website. github.com

https://github.com/Rochester-NRT/AlphaGo

The meaning of open source is that anyone can actually look into how AlphaGo was made, or how it "thinks." You can even participate in AlphaGo's improvement, whether you're Korean or a foreigner. I checked today, and people are diligently making commits up to this very day.

{{IMG:1}}

It doesn't seem like the entire project is uploaded yet. So, let's talk about how we can use this valuable opportunity that Google has given us.
**1. Cornerstone for the Development of Korean AI**
Open source means that Koreans can participate as much as they want. Currently, AlphaGo's open source is entirely in English. It would be good to translate it. Through this, actual AI research can also be conducted. While there aren't many AI researchers, Korea's Go population is said to be 10 million. If even 1/1000 of them showed interest in AI, that would be 10,000 AI developers! (Unlikely, of course.) Anyway, I hope the interest in AI sparked by the match between AlphaGo and Lee Sedol will soon lead to increased competitiveness in AI. Then, the day will come when the public also realizes that talk of AlphaGo's mistakes or bugs is nonsense.

{{IMG:2}}

[https://github.com/Rochester-NRT/AlphaGo/graphs/contributors](https://github.com/Rochester-NRT/AlphaGo/graphs/contributors) Let's get some Koreans onto that contributor list.
**2. Cornerstone for the Development of Korean Go**
People keep framing it as AI vs. humans, anthropomorphizing AI, and saying things like, "That's an AI move humans can't understand!" But if you look at the AI's source code and how it actually operates, humans *can* understand it. You can extract all the calculated results: what probability is expected when a certain move is made, and how the opponent is expected to react. Of course, this is limited to developers. Fortunately, the source code has been opened. Of course, it seems the data and models haven't been released, so it might be difficult to perfectly replicate it. But more importantly, if we collect data, run it, and conduct research, we might be able to discover new moves through AI. By looking at that data, we can confirm "why" the AI made those decisions. AI can answer "why" it made a decision, but it doesn't actually know the "meaning" behind it. That is within the realm of human capability. This is essentially what data scientists and big data analysts do. The research process in today's scientific community consists of these kinds of procedures. For example, feeding vast amounts of data into computers, discovering exceptional situations and investigating them intensively, or inputting hypotheses and finding similar data to prove theories. The discovery of exceptional situations by AI is extremely helpful in creating new moves and strategies. AI can analyze data, but it cannot create data-driven insights. Utilizing this is ultimately up to humans. In other words, if research on Go using AI is conducted, the Korean Go community can develop by leaps and bounds. This is typically the identity of what is now called "Computational X" in academia.

**3. Not "Humans vs. AI," but ****"Humans with AI"**
Let's forget about the Terminator for a while. Not only is it difficult to create such a scenario, but from AI's perspective, humans are cumbersome and inconvenient animals. There's no value in dominating them. Rather, AI's value lies with humans. We need to think more proactively about how to utilize AI. However, (traditional biological) humans might head towards a world where they self-extinguish. Let's postpone judging whether this is a dystopia or a utopia. Endless abundance brought by AI will make humans question the value of biological humanity. A more beautiful lover, a kinder boss, a wiser politician – these might be brought forth by AI. But here's the thing: AI is humanity's child. The main difference is that it wasn't born from a painful labor. Whether they will be filial or unfilial, I don't know, but what's clear is that from Earth's perspective, or rather, the universe's perspective, humans and AI are not separate entities, but descendants of humanity. I believe we will either live alongside AI in the future, or our descendants might become AI. There are many animations that deal with this. We are creatures with nostalgia. However, from a distant perspective, this might not be very meaningful. We have already forgotten the nostalgia of letters and the joy of meeting friends after walking long distances. I don't think giving up biological nostalgia will be very difficult. It might sound like a very distant story, but like AlphaGo, it could suddenly appear among us at any time. What's important is for us to understand AI, and to understand ourselves. As I mentioned in a previous post, our strength is not productivity. Nor is our strength analysis. And we have come to a time when we must consider how to pass this on to the AI that will be our descendants.

{{IMG:3}}

**"There are many kinds of humans. The definition of a human in any given era is quite ambiguous. If you are one who sings, understands loyalty, and dreams of the starry sky, then perhaps you can now be called human? You are the one who has inherited what we lost and forgot, more strongly than anyone else. So, go forth with your head held high. And if you ever meet someone on your travels, tell them proudly: 'I am a descendant of Earth's humanity.'" - From *Expelled from Paradise***

titleEn: Even if Lee Se-dol Loses, Humanity
contentEn:
이세돌 9-dan lost. Everyone seems to think something big has collapsed, but I'll explain a few reasons why that doesn't have to be the case.

1. It's natural for humans to lose to computers in "games".

Go is a game. A game is a brain game that involves reasoning within a set of rules. Computers, naturally, are designed to mimic human brain activity. The easiest of these was memory, followed by computation, and then the slightly more difficult task of reasoning. Predicting and inferring how to win a game is now almost exclusively the domain of computers, especially with the advancement of data analysis technology. The majority of stock trading is already done by computers, and astronomers also use computers to assist with calculations in their research. It's now common to find hidden patterns that people haven't noticed in big data and to create models. What did AlphaGo discover from 160,000 game records? It's completely different from the human learning process.

2. Lee Se-dol and AlphaGo are not yet on equal terms. The human brain is still great.

Do you really think Lee Se-dol and AlphaGo are on perfectly equal terms? Let's consider what Lee Se-dol, or rather, the human brain, does while playing Go. It looks at the Go board, scans the image of the board, analyzes the white and black stones to create a 19x19 matrix (which is as difficult as playing Go itself), makes inferences in the brain, and then, when commanded to place a stone, picks up and places the stone. Not only that, but while doing this, it breathes and simultaneously manages all autonomic functions. In contrast, AlphaGo only performed inference; a human placed the stones for it, and a human also handled the recognition. It also didn't consume electricity for breathing or smelling. The amount of information a human processes moment by moment is incomparable to AlphaGo. A slightly bothersome phrase during the Go broadcast is "it doesn't waver." A human wavers due to the influence of a wide variety of information. AlphaGo already has much information blocked from the input stage. It also doesn't think about other things. While playing Go, Lee Se-dol might think, "What if I lose? Oh, I'm hungry... My butt is itchy?" and indulge in such flights of fancy. For AlphaGo to implement this, it would need more CPU and RAM than for Go itself.

Computers have only caught up with a very small part of humanity, in specific tasks. We don't lament that a hammer drives nails better than our fist. We don't lament that a computer remembers better than us. We still do many things, and especially, the human brain is still greater than computers. Of course, with the current pace of computer development, it's said that computers will soon reach a complexity similar to humans. The problem is that research into the information to teach them and the algorithms for teaching methods must continue. Go enthusiasts who enjoy the intellectual pastime of Go should just continue what they're doing. **AlphaGo may be good at Go, but it cannot find the meaning of life there. (Why not check out a webtoon?)**

[**Oh Min-hyuk Short Stories - Hwajum** Hwajum comic.naver.com](http://comic.naver.com/webtoon/detail.nhn?titleId=667010&no=1)

{{IMG:1}}

3. But why a 'dumb' AlphaGo is scary

However, AlphaGo is still scary. The reason is that most of you get paid for performing specific intellectual tasks when you work. You're essentially getting paid for a very small part, a specific activity, of your brain. In fact, 99% of the human brain is already great, but a 1% difference creates the gap between the "880,000 won generation" and those earning hundreds of millions of won annually. And that 1% can be modeled by computers. Let's imagine Lee Se-dol 9-dan's annual salary is 100 million won, and a Google engineer's annual salary is 200 million won, with 20 engineers involved. For 4 billion won, you could create a 100 million won Lee Se-dol. The problem is that this "Lee Se-dol" could be put online for millions of people to play against, like Hangame. Can you imagine its value? That's precisely why AI is scary, even if it doesn't necessarily resemble a human. We already ask Naver and Google for most of our knowledge searches. We no longer ask our fathers and mothers first.

titleEn: VR: The Present and Future of Next-Gen PCs and TVs
contentEn:
Recently, interest in VR has become incredibly hot. However, despite that interest, it's a stretch to say that the actual market has opened up. For the first time in a while, I'd like to talk about the VR market from my perspective.

**1. VR is the next-generation PC and TV, AR is the next-generation mobile.**
First, the meaning of VR, as I see it, is the next-generation PC and TV. PCs are representative productivity devices, and TVs are representative entertainment devices. The commonality between these two devices is the limitation of the physical size of their displays. VR's biggest advantage is that it eliminates this physical size limitation. To explain it with an analogy from past experience, if a PC is a newspaper, then VR is the internet – that should make it easy to understand. Once a newspaper was published, it was difficult to change, and the value of the small space for headlines was overwhelmingly expensive. Then, with the advent of the internet, banners on Naver's main page changed according to the user's group, in real-time, or even by region. When I joined Naver in 2006, to borrow Naver's expression, the Naver main page, which opened 800 million times a day, was how many tens of thousands of times larger than a soccer field? Anyway, they used the expression that it had an enormous amount of space. However, this was a story limited to the size of the monitor. What if you change this to 3D? VR, which adds 360-degree space and depth, not just a 27-inch monitor, changes the meaning of space. In the case of AR, it provides an enhanced real-life experience, so it's essentially mobile. Of course, AR is a market that will grow even larger in the future, and if it covers 100% of the space, AR would soon mean VR, so it seems fair to say that AR includes VR. However, just as mobile followed PC, this is expected to happen sequentially.

**2. PC and Mobile started with games and evolved into general-purpose tools, what about VR?**
Games seem to hold significant meaning in the digital environment. Most platforms I remember experienced explosive growth thanks to games. The MSX I wanted to buy to play cartridge games, Wing Commander which popularized AT computers, StarCraft which connected the entire nation to the internet, Angry Birds which made people buy smartphones, and even Anipang which showed that KakaoTalk could make money. And now, once again, there's talk of games in VR.

{{IMG:1}}

**[VR device Amusphere from the anime Sword Art Online]**

As always, there are attempts to port famous past games to push them as brands, and there are also considerations for games optimized for the new environment. Based on past experience, while the former method can attract attention, it is likely the latter that will elevate the platform. And digital devices, which spread from hardcore users through games, are reborn as general-purpose devices with the emergence of killer apps. For PCs, it was word processors; for mobile, it was maps; what will it be for VR?

**3. Has the technology truly matured?**
Has the technology truly matured? If someone asks me, I would still say no. Of course, I don't know if MS's HoloLens or Google's Magic Leap will suddenly drop to a level as if they tortured a UFO. In the smartphone era, which was once Pocket PC, the iPhone played a somewhat similar role. But what's clear is that the current perceived experience feels like the era when touch phones were appearing just before the iPhone's debut. Therefore, the content market might be a bit too early right now, platform diffusion should be prioritized, and technological maturity is still needed. As always, the first versions created by developers are likely to be terrible. The iPhone matured with the 3G, and the Galaxy from its second iteration. If you buy the first one, you become a guinea pig. Of course, if you're an early adopter or looking to seize an opportunity in this field, you should naturally consider purchasing it. What's clear is that it's only a matter of time; it will happen someday.

**4. However, technical issues might not be as problematic as thought.**
One of the common criticisms regarding technological immaturity is that it causes dizziness. I also felt dizzy after using it for a long time. But here's the thing. It was more tolerable than when I first encountered Wolfenstein 3D. When I first played Wolfenstein 3D, I endured motion sickness to play it.

{{IMG:2}}

**[Wolfenstein 3D, a landmark in FPS, Source: Namuwiki]**

Because... it's fun! And after a while, the motion sickness decreased. This is because motion sickness is essentially a rejection reaction to a cognitive dissonance in the brain, and it might not be a big problem once the brain adapts. The human brain learns 3D perception through acquired experience. When a congenitally blind person gains sight, they cannot distinguish between an apple in a photo and a real apple. In other words, the aversion our brains, trained in the real world, feel in VR can lessen as we become accustomed to VR. Major Motoko Kusanagi, the protagonist of Ghost in the Shell, is depicted as having undergone full-body cyberization (changing her body to a machine) as an infant, which allows her to exhibit exceptional ability in handling her full-body prosthesis (robot body and mind). However, it seems to be the reality that there is still more widespread suspicion that VR might cause side effects in children. Recently, when I went to Hyundai Department Store, the staff at the Gear experience zone prevented my daughter and son from trying it. (Even though they are already familiar with Cardboard and Cocomong 3D eye... ㅜㅜ) Personally, I don't think VR will cause significant harm to children. This is because the human brain is more adaptable than we think. And while it might seem confusing, the brain doesn't get confused by similar but different information; rather, the learning effect is strengthened. Just as the number 1 and the English letter I being similar doesn't negatively affect the brain. However, I am more concerned about the talk that electromagnetic waves from various devices pose a risk of DNA damage, and I believe that if appropriate content emerges, technical issues will be covered. Since when did game graphics become the entirety of a game?

**5. Who will seize hegemony in the VR ecosystem?**
Ultimately, the concern for all companies and governments will be: how to seize hegemony in the VR ecosystem? Should we create content? Or a platform? Does content just come for free if you only build a platform? What about devices? These efforts will occur simultaneously across all layers of CPND. Generally, it starts with Device, grows through Contents, and then the one who captures the Platform ultimately gains hegemony. And currently, Google and Facebook seem to be leading in this market. This is because various VR videos are already being distributed through YouTube and Facebook.

However, the remaining question is whether VR videos will be the killer content for VR. We might need to abandon existing formats more. According to the history of platforms so far, the killer content for a new platform was always something that maximized the platform's distinctiveness while providing essential value. What could that be for VR? It seems likely that various experiments will be conducted until we find out.

titleEn: Common Misconceptions About Evolution and the Bible
contentEn:
Personally, I am a Christian. However, I believe that the Earth's history is 4.5 billion years old. In other words, it means I find it difficult to agree that Adam and Eve were the first humans. Moving back and forth between science and Christianity, I've found some relatively objective facts to create a link, and I believe it's more accurate to say that ancient history falls under the realm of science, not theology. However, as a standard for our lives, theology, or rather, the realm of religion, greatly helps to center us, and I understand the strange 'error' of believing that Jesus is my savior and my guide. That's okay. As *Sapiens*, which I recently read, stated, the advantage of the human brain is that it understands (and believes in) errors and even turns them into strengths. First, I'll briefly write about some misunderstandings regarding evolution.

**1. Evolution does not explain the origin of life.**
I, too, once attacked evolution on the point that the origin of life cannot be probabilistically explained by evolutionary theory. For that to be the case, microorganisms that emerged 3 billion years ago are too complex. However, returning properly to science, and to borrow the words of Darwin, the founder of evolutionary theory, evolution is not a discipline that explains the origin of life. It is simply a discipline that studies why life has become so diverse. Even if you believe that God created life, it poses no problem for evolutionary theory.

**2. Evolution only adapts to the environment; it does not progress.**
Evolution does not progress. Progress is rather a biblical interpretation. This hierarchical picture, with angels and demons under God, humans under them, and animals under humans, does not apply to evolutionary theory. Evolutionary theory is simply like a formula. In a formula, there's no reason why 7 should be more respected than 3. Paramecia and humans are merely the final nodes in the differentiation of life. Apes are not our ancestors but our cousins, and even the bananas we eat are distant relatives of humanity.

**3. Evolution is the environment, or Earth's history, and it is ongoing.**
Therefore, evolution is not just about digging up fossils; it is evidence of Earth's history. The Earth's atmosphere and ocean composition changed as a result of external environmental factors like meteorites, supernova explosions, or major tectonic shifts, consequently leading to different ecosystems. Evolution is not the will or direction of an organism but the result of environmental change. And we are currently truly conducting that experiment on Earth. The consensus among scholars is that global warming is creating changes as rapid as the cataclysmic periods Earth has experienced throughout its history, and we are witnessing these results in the oceans and mountains. We are contemplating what impact this will have on us, and it's not a firestorm from the sky, but rather, in the short term, coastlines are changing, economic paradigms are shifting, and if it continues to an extreme, we face the realistic problem that we might change our own atmosphere and oceans to the point of extinction.

**4. Evolution, or genetic interpretation, is being applied and faces social issues.**
While you might think evolution has nothing to do with us, the interpretation of genetic codes has undergone dramatic changes today. Genome analysis can be done directly on internet sites for just a few hundred dollars, not just in research labs, and it even predicts what diseases you might get and to what extent. This world is facing ethical issues, such as the possibility that future marriage partners might be chosen based on genome analysis codes rather than religion.

Next, let's return to the Bible.

**1. The early Bible was transmitted orally, not in writing.**
The point is that the early Bible was transmitted orally, not in writing. We tend to interpret it literally, but the early parts of the Old Testament were transcribed from oral traditions. While it's understandable that people go to great lengths to ensure every single letter of the Bible is accurate, understanding the context of the early parts literally is virtually impossible. Some theologians even argue that the context and themes of the orally transmitted parts differ from those of the transcribed parts.

**2. The Bible is humanity's ancient history, and some parts do not align with today's standards.**
The Old Testament of the Bible does not recognize women's rights (they were not even counted, or if raped, they were married off to the perpetrator for money) and does not adhere to the Geneva Conventions (children and women in conquered territories were killed). Because of this, Christians are seen as accepting discrimination and tabooing non-Christians, while non-Christians view Christians as exclusive. However, this is ancient history. In other words, it reveals the characteristics of tribal society and nationalism. In fact, if you look at Korea's ancient history, it's not much different. From our perspective, it was a northern expedition or a southern expedition. From the opponent's perspective, they were barbarians, and the war was incredibly cruel. In fact, war should not be glorified. No war has ever been humane. It is dangerous to accept these values from the Bible today. At that time, Israel did not know that Eskimos existed, nor did they possess weapons of mass destruction like today. Instead, remember what Jesus said to Peter, who had a sword.

**3. The Bible revolutionized this ancient history and bound the world together.**
Although Christianity is often called exclusive, it was actually the Bible that negated previous rules and bound the world together. Perhaps Jesus' statement that he came to fulfill the law is in this context. From Napoleon to Gandhi and Che Guevara, it's hard to find examples of great conquerors and revolutionaries who were not influenced by the Bible. It is also a representative religion that proclaimed the equality of all people before God and fostered freedom and the pioneering spirit. If I had to name the greatest book that changed the world, I would unhesitatingly choose the Bible. The spirit and teachings of Jesus are not solely the heritage of Christians, and Christians should further uphold them.

I want to look at things scientifically and judge them like a Christian. Because I believe that is the balancing point that corrects blind faith in both science and theology.

titleEn: A Toy That's Not a Toy: China's RK3126 Kids Tablet
contentEn:
1. Children and Digital Devices

Children want to imitate adults' behavior. Especially these days, children are very interested in the small, shiny devices in their parents' hands. These devices react when touched, show fun cartoons, read books, and allow video calls. Yes, as you might guess, it's a smartphone. And when I'm working in front of the computer, my children always come next to me and want to press the keyboard and mouse. Thanks to this, I often give them unused mice or keyboards as toys. Many parents are reluctant to expose their children to digital devices at a young age. In fact, it is said that excessive and indiscriminate exposure to stimulation is not good for children with weak self-control. However, conversely, with the emergence of keywords like "software-centric society" and the emphasis on software education as digital literacy (digital reading and writing) these days, there's a concern that complete isolation from digital devices might actually cause them to fall behind. In my case, I believe it's good to show appropriate content at an appropriate level and provide experiences, as long as it's done with a parent. Of course, when it's time to stop, children sometimes throw tantrums and demand more, but such behavior is not exclusive to digital devices. When playing with LEGOs or reading a book before bed, children's reactions are similar, though the degree may vary. (Especially when they're sleepy, children are hard to control.) However, parents' level of concern is different. It's the worry about addiction. Why is the label "addiction" attached only to certain media or devices when they show the same reactions? As someone who works with software, I feel a bit dissatisfied. Anyway, rather than focusing on whether it's an addiction or not, I want to look at it from the perspective of how these excessively(?) attractive devices can be used more beneficially for children. In fact, I've loved computers since I was young and studied math and English with digital devices earlier than others. My parents kept seeing it negatively, which made me more determined, so I organized study materials and wrote a diary on the computer. (I can't even remember where that 5.25-inch floppy disk diary went. ㅜㅜ I wish the internet existed back then...)

2. Let's search on AliExpress.

In Korea, Samsung has a kids' tablet, but its price is comparable to a high-end Chinese smartphone. Other toy tablets were truly just toys.
