1) Setting > Language > Change to Korean
2) Wifi settings
3) Google Play login
4) Search for Keyboard and install a Korean keyboard

{{IMG:11}}

https://blog.naver.com/PostView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=223833997665&redirect=Dlog&widgetTypeCall=true&noTrackingCode=true&directAccess=false#

Keyboard connected perfectly to OTG, and charging is fine via either micro USB or adapter. Since a separate adapter is used, charging is possible even when using a keyboard with OTG. When set up like that, it looks like a PC. Performance is about this much... 1224 points on Quadrant, lower performance than the Samsung Nexus S released in 2010...

{{IMG:12}}
                                    

https://blog.naver.com/PostView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=223833997665&redirect=Dlog&widgetTypeCall=true&noTrackingCode=true&directAccess=false#

AnTuTu scores around 14,000 points. You can consider it about 1/4 the performance of a latest smartphone, so don't expect too much.

4. Default Apps and Launcher (Home Screen)

The default home screen allows user registration for children, and parents can arrange apps into four categories: Game, Book, Video, Study. It seems to have usage time settings, but I didn't worry about it much since I'll be supervising them. The default apps are surprisingly robust, and perhaps because they are well-tested, they are quite good. I particularly liked things like phonics. In my case, I hid all the games first. Considering the 8GB capacity was a bit insufficient, I went into App Management in settings and disabled all apps I wouldn't use (mostly game apps). If default apps are enabled, Google Play automatically updates them, increasing their size. When my daughter and son learn multiplication, I might install or reactivate the games.

5. Other Apps I Use and Have Arranged

Among the default apps, I selected and arranged 8 game apps that I thought were suitable for children. These are games like card matching and such.

{{IMG:13}}
                                    

https://blog.naver.com/PostView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=223833997665&redirect=Dlog&widgetTypeCall=true&noTrackingCode=true&directAccess=false#

For BOOKs, I tested RidiBooks, and even the voice reading worked well. I also installed the Britannica Encyclopedia, which I received during an event on Naver App Store.

{{IMG:14}}
                                    

https://blog.naver.com/PostView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=223833997665&redirect=Dlog&widgetTypeCall=true&noTrackingCode=true&directAccess=false#

For VIDEO, I confirmed that Juniver and Hobi run well, and the children's YouTube, which is a default app, is good so I kept it. The rest are the default Android apps for Photos, Gallery, and Video.

{{IMG:15}}
                                    

https://blog.naver.com/PostView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=223833997665&redirect=Dlog&widgetTypeCall=true&noTrackingCode=true&directAccess=false#

Next is Study. I confirmed that the default apps, Khan Academy, Lightbot, and ScratchJR (for SW education) all run well. Additionally, I purchased and installed Kkam-bu's Hangeul Play. And since I needed an English dictionary, I installed Naver Dictionary. Apps with a green background and primary colors are default apps.

{{IMG:16}}
                                    

https://blog.naver.com/PostView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=223833997665&redirect=Dlog&widgetTypeCall=true&noTrackingCode=true&directAccess=false#

6. A Few Drawbacks and Overall Review

One regrettable thing was that the 'Open Knowledge Door' app didn't work. ㅜㅜ Also, unusually, apps cannot be moved to the SD card. The SD card can only be used for storing videos and photos to display. I wonder if this is a 512MB memory issue. I have Kyowon's 'Open Knowledge Door' books at home, and these days, when you scan such books, videos or content with additional information are played. It's a world where you can't just sell books anymore. To give an overall review, I thought it was **unbelievably powerful for a 70,000 won toy**. The price makes these drawbacks seem like nothing, and it even made me feel apologetic for having such expectations. When I was young, I practiced typing on a laminated printed keyboard... I feel a sense of how much times have changed. And I wonder what Korean manufacturers should really be doing...

titleEn: [Mobile Car Wash O2O Service] Yper
contentEn:
I've introduced Yper service on my homepage a few times, and now I've had the chance to experience it myself, so I'd like to share it with you. Yper is a leading O2O company in Korea, introduced overseas, and has swept various awards, making other startups envious. Simply put, O2O refers to services where you use online platforms like smartphones to receive services that were traditionally offline, or part of daily life, at your desired location. Yper falls into this category because they come to your location to pick up your car.{{IMG:1}} A characteristic of O2O services is that while you apply for and access them online, the actual service takes place offline. This often leads to limitations in service areas. Yper's only drawback was that its service was limited to the Gangnam area, where its partner companies are concentrated. It's great news that it's recently expanded to Pangyo. After praising Yper's service, I was given the opportunity to try it myself, so I'm writing this review of my experience.

They meticulously checked the car's condition in case of any disputes.{{IMG:11}} And the handover receipt. It also includes insurance, so I felt at ease. This happens very quickly, and here's a tip: most parking lots in Gangnam offer free exit within 30 minutes.
{{IMG:12}}
After the meeting, I received a call, and the car was coming...{{IMG:13}} It should have arrived... but when I used it, the map function was still lacking. News broke yesterday that they signed an MOU with a location specialist, so I believe they will now provide location tracking like Kakao Taxi.
And ta-da! The new car arrived.{{IMG:14}} Ta-da! The new car arrived. Looking at its condition, it was quite meticulously done.
And here's a tip: if you adjust the car return time to when your work ends, you can save on parking fees. Save on parking fees while getting your car washed during work in Gangnam.
And after driving the car for a few days, I noticed that even though it's an outdoor apartment parking lot and cars get dirty easily, the shine lasted quite a long time. I realized, "This is the beauty of a hand car wash." Seeing my sparkling car among other dirty ones gives me a strange sense of satisfaction.
Since it's coming to Pangyo soon, I should use it occasionally, even if not every time.

titleEn: I Wish We'd Focus on the Essence of Education, Not State-Authored Textbooks
contentEn:
The discussion about state-authored textbooks continues endlessly. Recently, however, I read an article that questioned the very essence of "Korean history." Reading it made my head spin. It felt like the pieces of everything I had learned were finally falling into place.
http://m.mediatoday.co.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=30564[“Goguryeo History is Neither Korean History Nor Chinese History” This interview was published on September 1st in SNUNOW (www.snunow.com), Seoul National University's internet news. Reprinted with the author's permission. [Editor's Note] StarCraft ...m.mediatoday.co.kr](http://m.mediatoday.co.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=30564){{IMG:1}}
The history subjects we learn are broadly divided into two: world history and national history. However, when we learn science, we learn the history of science; when we learn math, the history of math; when we learn music, the history of music; and when we learn art, the history of art, at least lightly. When I connected these things, I wondered, "Why didn't I think of that before?" In other words, it's not that we haven't learned it. The 1996 College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT) I saw was a shock itself. There was a passage about land in the national history section. This type of problem, which I had never seen before, flustered me. As a result, the CSAT taken in 1996 recorded the lowest scores in the history of the CSAT. At the time, students and parents were furious at these new types of problems that rendered countless efforts of high school seniors useless. Consequently, the difficulty of the 1997 CSAT was lowered.

But looking back, when I worked as a planner in a company, all the problems I encountered were full of these kinds of issues. Wanting to enter a new field, looking at overseas cases and wondering how to apply them to domestic situations, identifying our problems, and figuring out how to improve them. I connected disparate facts, analyzed them, created alternatives, and implemented those alternatives. Many of these endeavors sometimes led to success and sometimes to failure, but there was no absolute success or absolute failure. Success had to be refined, and failure had to be learned from. No knowledge was independent; everything influenced each other, and in fact, there were no boundaries. There were only different results from different perspectives. And the work of organizing those perspectives and coordinating different opinions – that was precisely the problem-solving process. As someone from a software engineering background, I was quite familiar with handling numbers (data), and since our work was in the internet, or rather, the software field, it seemed to be a strong advantage as a specialist that it was very easy to integrate.

Discussions about SW education, when delved into in detail, are integrated into SW utilization covered in practical arts and physical computing in technology subjects. Furthermore, SW naturally originated from mathematics. It seems that establishing its place by defining common ground with existing subjects is not an easy task. In programming terms, it's like having legacy code and adding new features, isn't it? Moreover, due to the computing resources used by legacy code, resources for implementing new features are severely lacking. Many new systems or initiatives in Korea find it difficult to apply new things within existing frameworks, which is quite similar to this situation.

In this case, in programming, there are two methods. First is the method most preferred by programmers: creating something new. This involves building anew based on the essential requirements that are superficially apparent, without analyzing existing details. It's also easy to apply the latest techniques, and there's no need to worry about existing history. However, if that's not possible, the structure of the existing code is changed. Simply put, it's undertaking innovation. I believe innovation isn't about coming up with something cool and new, but about breaking down outdated practices. It's a very difficult task. It's hard to know what problems will arise when modifying code, and in fact, you have to fix it assuming problems will occur. The stabilization period is quite long, and if not careful, it can truly fail.

However, there are cases where both the first and second methods are difficult: when there is no authority to modify existing code, or when the existing code is too complex to know what problems might arise if modified. Not having modification authority simply means using an external library. In this case, assuming problems will occur, additional code is haphazardly attached, and it's not clean. In terms of work speed, it's actually very good because you can use the existing code as is and quickly add additional features. However, it's not stable, and it's inefficient when implementing additional features due to the legacy.

So, our current education system continues to choose the third option. It's applying short-term remedies. It seems to be because there's no authority to modify the legacy when adding something new, and there's no overarching philosophy that permeates the education system.

I'm just rambling on today as thoughts come to mind, but this isn't just a problem with national history. What should be the goal of the core subjects of Korean, English, and Math in education? Discriminatory power for university admissions? I once saw an article stating that Korea's functional illiteracy rate is among the lowest in the world.
http://ideas0419.com/457[The Sad Portrait of South Korea: Functional Illiteracy Rate Among the Lowest in OECD A recent past survey result is once again gaining attention on social media. It is the fact that South Korea's functional illiteracy rate is among the lowest among OECD countries. High...ideas0419.com](http://ideas0419.com/457)
To be precise, it refers to reading comprehension. If students just memorize passages for exams, what need is there for reading comprehension? What Korean language education should aim for is reading comprehension, writing skills, and presentation skills. Listening well to others' writing and speech, and expressing oneself well – that is the fundamental value Korean language education should possess. Spelling and grammar, I believe, are perhaps secondary issues. Furthermore, literature is also intertwined with Korean language, but personally, I think it's closer to art than to the Korean language subject itself.

Literature, art, and music are fields that express emotions. In other words, they are functions of the right brain. What can encompass technology and SW is not technology, but engineering.

If I were to redefine things as they come to mind, it would be something like this: Korean Language (listening, speaking, writing), Mathematics, Natural Sciences (Biology/Chemistry/Space/Physics), Engineering (SW, Technology), Arts (Fine Arts, Literature, Music, Media Art), Industry (Economics, Finance, Marketing, Entrepreneurship), History (History of Technology/Science, History of Philosophy/Ideology/Religion, History of Nations/Wars/Politics), Foreign Languages (English/Chinese). As a side note, the advantage of SW is that it can divide a single piece of information into multiple dimensions or classify it through tagging. In fact, I believe that is the original essence of information (academics).

I recently heard talk of removing calculus education from mathematics. I oppose this. It's not because I'm against reducing children's study hours; I agree with reducing study hours. However, if one knows that calculus is used in almost all engineering and sciences, one would even argue that the grade level at which it's taught should be lowered. The important thing is not spending time teaching concepts, but the problem lies in teaching how to solve difficult problems. We need to broaden the level of abstraction in learning. If we understand how all knowledge intertwines, we will know what to study more deeply to solve a particular problem. If we are making things insanely difficult just to rank students and testing how few mistakes they make, then we have lost the essence of education.

Currently, that is the fundamental question of our education. I agree with the premise that SW fosters problem-solving abilities. However, I don't believe that memorizing what's taught in SW and doing well on exams can cultivate problem-solving abilities. SW is an empirical discipline. One must fail and experience enough to develop problem-solving skills. It's not a discipline where scores are counted by the number of correct answers, but one where overcoming mistakes is counted as a score.

In fact... this is the concept of differentiation (acceleration).

I've just rambled on today as thoughts came to mind. For future talent, perhaps we need to break the mold of subjects and engage in a grand discourse on education simultaneously.

titleEn: Problem-Solving Skills Over Knowledge, How to Teach
contentEn:
평생 교육에 대해 큰 고민 없이 살았는데, SW교육이 시작되는 시점부터 많은 고민을 하기 시작했고, 최근에 국정교과서 이슈까지 다다르고 보니 한국의 가장 뜨거운 문제이자 가장 좋은 희망을 이야기할 수 있는 것이 교육이라는 생각이 든다. 특히 이번 국정교과서의 이슈는 매우 매우 아쉬운 생각이 든다. 그 이유는 교육의 가장 중요한 부분들의 논란이 제외된채로 정치적 논란만 커지고 있기 때문이다.

**1. 학생들에게 필요한건 지식보다는 문제해결 능력**
지금 국정 교과서에서 논의 되는 것은 "무엇"을 가르칠지에 대한 이야기가 주로 논의 되고 있다. 그것이 빨갈지 파랄지... 그러나, 개인적으로 나는 이게 문제의 핵심이 아니라고 생각한다. 아이들에게 천동설을 가르칠지, 혹은 지동설을 가르칠지를 고민하고 있다고 치자. 오늘날 사람들은 모두 지동설이 사실이란 것을 다 알고 있으니 왜 천동설을 가르치느냐라고 반문할지 모른다. 하지만, 우리의 교육은 사실 천동설을 가르치고 있다. 다만 과학의 역사에서 가르친다. 천동설이 어떻게 지동설로 바뀌어왔는지를 가르친다. 사실 여기서 핵심은 지동설을 가르치기 위해서라기보다는 지동설에 다다르기까지 사람들이 어떤 고민을 어떻게 합리적으로 했느냐를 가르치는 것이 그 핵심이라고 생각한다. 여기서 한가지 가정을 해보자. 말을 배우는 시점에 모든 사전 정보없이 맹목적으로 아이에게 지동설을 가르친다. 두번째는 오늘날 우리의 교육방식인 언어를 배우고, 햇님 달님이 뜬다라는 표현을 학습해서 무의식적으로 천동설을 학습한 이후, 지동설에 다다르기까지의 모든 정보를 교육하고 지동설을 아이에게 가르치지 않는다고 가정해보자. 지동설을 알려주지 않고, 모든 행성과 별은 지구를 중심으로 돈다고 가르친 후, 갈릴레이가 했던 것처럼 이오(목성의 위성)이 목성을 돌고 있다고 추론할 수 있는 모든 정보를 제공한다. 또한 일식과 월식의 정보등 천동설로 설명이 안되는 수많은 데이터로 아이를 멘붕에 빠뜨려 보자. 어느쪽이 아이에게 더 많은 생각을 하게 할까? 그리고 어느쪽이 더 올바른 교육일까? 첫번째 아이는 아주쉽게 지동설의 정답을 마킹할수 있을것이다. 두번째 아이는 아주 괴상하고 틀린 해답들을 찾아낼지 모른다. 물론 그것이 사실이 아닐지라도 말이다. 우리가 교육에 관해 논의하고 있는 것 중 하나가, 바로 지식, 어떤걸 가르칠지에 대해 지금 너무 맹목적으로 집중하고 있다고 생각이 들지 않는가? 빨갛고 파란게 선악의 문제가 아니다. 아이에게 필요한건 어떻게 빨간색과 파란색이 다름을 구분할 수 있느냐 이다. 지식은 정의(Justice)가 아니라 정의(Define)에 가깝다고 생각한다. 그 본질은 지식(Data)가 아니라 생각하는 능력(Algorithm과 Process)이다. 사람의 뇌를 묘사한 Computer의 능력을 Storage의 크기보다는 Computing파워에 중점을 두지 않는가? 핵심을 잊지 않았으면 한다.

**2. 무얼 가르칠지 보다는 어떻게 가르칠지?**
원하는 인재가 What보다는 How라면, 가르치는 방법도 동일하게 What이 아니라 How를 고민해야 한다. 지식 중심이 아닌 경험 중심의 교육으로 이전되야 한다. 평가모델또한 시험과 검정의 문제가 아니라 경험과 경험을 공유하고 가치를 더하는 형태로 이전되야 한다. 일방적인 교육방식과 시험에 의한 줄세우기가 아닌 오히려 보다 인간적이고 관계중심적인 교육이 필요하다. 이를 위해서는 우리에게 필요한건 아이들이 틀려도 괜찮은 시간을 주는 것이 중요하다. 틀린것을 바로 잡아보지 않는 아이가 문제해결을 할 가능성은 없다. 오늘날 많은 사회인들에게 듣는 말인데 요즘 아이들 똑똑하고 학력도 좋고 영어도 잘하는데 도통 하나부터 열까지 가르쳐야 한다든지. 일을 못한다는 평가가 있다. 앞서 말했듯이 시험점수를 잘 맞기 위한 요령들을 익히고 그것이 최고라고 교육 받았다면 사실 너무도 당연한 결과다. 이런 아이들은 틀리는게 너무 두렵다. 이점은 바뀌어야 한다. 사회나와서 틀리면 회사가 망하거나, 가족이 굶어야 한다. 따라서 완벽함과 치밀함을 갖춰야 한다. 그러나 학교에서는 틀리면 바로 잡아가면 된다. 그것이 교육이다. 사회에서는 교육을 할만한 여유도 없을 뿐더러 그 대가가 너무 혹독하다. 그런데 학교에서 조차 틀리는 것을 허용하지 않는다면, 틀림으로서 배우는 것들은 어디서 배운단 말인가? 우리의 교육은 틀리는 아이들에게 너그러워질 필요가 있으며, 기다려 줌이 필요하다. 수학 교육이 망해가는 이유도 바로 여기에 있다고 생각하며, SW교육도 이것을 갖추지 못한다면 사실 수학교육을 따라갈 수 있다. 수학은 기존의 것을 전부 이해하지 않으면 다음단계로 나가가기 어렵다. 중간에 잠깐 정신차려서 해당 부분만 쏠랑 점수를 빼먹을 수 있는 암기 과목이 아니다. 차근차근 지식을 쌓아 높은곳에 도달하는 학문이다. 그런데 한국의 교육의 경우 진도에서 나가 떨어진 학생들을 구원할 별도의 방법을 마련하고 있지 않다. 그 아이들은 패배자 취급하며 벌을 주어 더 열심히 해서 따라오기를 종용한다. 최근 73억을 투자받은 스타트업인 '노리'의 경우 이를 해결하기 위해 수학지식을 잘게 쪼개어 모듈화하고 관계화 하여 학습하는 모델을 만들었다. 그 외에 플립드 러닝, 국내에서는 거꾸로교실이라고 불리우는 학습방식도 온라인을 통해서는 개념 학습을 동영상으로 진행하고, 오프라인 수업시간에는 체험활동과 조별활동을 한다. 이러한 학습방식도 시험이 목적이 아니고 활동이 목적이며, 필요한 지식은 온라인을 통해 언제 어디서든 다시 접근이 가능기 때문에 학습의 효과가 높다. 우리에게 지금 필요한 것은 무얼 가르칠지가 아니라, 이제는 어떻게 가르칠지 이다. 한자교육을 하자. SW교육을 하자. 역사교육을 하자. 같은데에는 이유가 있다. 사실 뭐 더 배우자는데 특별히 반대할 이유는 없다. 그러나 중요한 것은 입시 위주의 현 교육은 무얼 얼마나 아느냐, 아니 실수를 얼마나 안하냐의 교육이다. 이러한 프레임워크에서는 올바른 교육이 설자리가 없다.

**3. 공부와 교육을 혁신해야 나라와 미래가 산다.**
공부의 신이라는 페이스북계정에 올라온 이미지. 사실 이게 현실이다.
{{IMG:1}}
와.. 정말 이정도 노력하면 다 공부잘하지. 라고 생각할지도 모르겠으나 10번씩 보고 달달 외워 실수 안하는 것을 측정하는 것이 우리 교육이라면 매우 잘못됬다. 정보를 오류없이 기억하는 것은 사실 인류의 뇌는 매우 형편없는 기계다. 뇌(생물)는 진화론적으로 편향되었고 오류투성이다. 그리고, 사실 그렇기 때문에 창조적인 결과가 나온다. 그런데 이런 어처구니 없는 것을 기준으로 우리는 우수한 학생을 선발하고 있다는 것이니 정말 문제가 있는것 아닌가? 국정교과서 중요하다. 지식을 획일화 하는것은 기본적으로 반대이다. 아마 '과학'근처에 있는 분들이라면 누구나 나와 같이 생각할것이라고 생각한다. 차라리 난 그 대안으로 위키를 추천하겠다. 올바른 지식이란 소수에 의해 집필되어 똑같이 나가는 지식은 올바를 수 없다. 지식은 합의의 결과 뿐만 아니라 합의의 과정도 포함해야 한다. 그런점에서 위키에는 토론의 내용이 함께 공개된다는 점이나 다양한 관점들을 계속 기술 할 수 있다는 점이 좋다. 다만 국정교과서 논란의 문제는 그 반대측역시 교육에 대한 인식이 크게 벗어나있지 않다는 점이 안타까울 따름이다. 그래서 교육혁신을 위해 필요한 에너지가 소모적인데 사용되고 있는 듯하다. 우리가 비판해야 하는것은 바로 그 점이다. 국정교과서에 대한 관심이 SW교육을 비롯한 교육혁신에 대한 욕구로 까지 번졌으면 좋겠다. 우리는 좌우에 고민하고 있을때, 아이들은 비명을 지르고 있다.

titleEn: Is South Korean Real Estate a Bubble? An Analysis with
contentEn:
While discussing real estate in a certain post, I found some interesting statistics. [How much have Gangnam house prices risen, and you say Korean housing prices aren't in a bubble? 잡상 (雜想) is literally a post written as thoughts come to mind, so please don't read it too seriously. ★★★Real house prices in Korea/Germany/Japan since 1986...blog.naver.com](http://blog.naver.com/hong8706/220398025486){{IMG:1}}
Although I was blocked from that post, I'll take comfort in having learned about a good indicator. My comment on the discussion post didn't really have deep analysis, so please take it only as a reference. I'd like to take a closer look at the indicators referenced in that discussion post and share my interpretation. The reason for sharing is that I hope you'll correct me if my interpretation is wrong, and I'd appreciate it if you share any better insights you discover. First, in the discussion post, the conclusion was drawn that Korean house prices are cheap compared to overseas, based only on the 'Price in real time' indicator... I will now present my interpretation after examining the entire set of indicators. While statistics are as objective as possible, they actually contain many pitfalls. The method of data collection or one's own preconceptions can creep in. I want to state upfront that this point cannot be excluded.

[http://goo.gl/n8YyV](http://goo.gl/n8YyV)
http://www.economist.com/blogs/dailychart/2011/11/global-house-prices
Location, location, location
Audio and Video content on Economist.com requires a browser that can handle iFrames. THE Economist tracks the health of housing i...www.economist.com

http://www.economist.com/blogs/dailychart/2011/11/global-house-prices

**1. House-price index**
The period was set from 1994 to 2015. The reason is to observe Korea's IMF crisis around 1997, the turning point of the 2008 subprime mortgage crisis, and the present.
{{IMG:2}}
Korean real estate... it's killer. A graph similar to China's, with its brilliant economic development. Looking only at this graph, one would think they should have invested in real estate. KOSPI was around 1100 in 1994 and now fluctuates around 2000, so KOSPI's return rate is good. However, upon closer inspection, a sharp drop is visible immediately after the 1998 IMF crisis, followed by a long period of stagnation. Therefore, the myth of real estate invincibility is actually false. Also, when the 2008 US subprime mortgage crisis erupted, the US economy crashed. But it has almost recovered. When it crashes, it goes up. That's normal. There's no need to worry too much about a complete collapse, as long as debt isn't excessive and real estate is driven by actual demand. Just get past that valley. It would have been good to have European or global indicators, but France shows a similar indicator. China is out of the discussion due to its dazzling economic development... Japan shows a typical graph of long-term stagnation, but real estate prices are stabilizing. This seems to imply that the impact of real estate prices on the economy has relatively decreased. You might argue that this is low economic growth due to a real estate slump, but I don't agree with that for now. We can't know that from this indicator, so let's move on for now. Germany... what a strange indicator. It's completely different from other countries' indicators. It seems to be evidence that the real estate market is a local market. Therefore, it doesn't seem like a useful indicator for reference. By the same logic, you might ask, 'Is there any reason for Korean real estate to follow the US or Japan?' There is a reason. Japan is structurally similar, and Korea is an export-dependent nation. Considering that, in the current situation of high dependence on China, China's economic adjustment could be even more dangerous than America's.

**2. Price in real terms**
{{IMG:3}}
The myth of Korean real estate invincibility is false. This indicator makes it clear. During the IMF crisis, it plummeted to 75% of its level. What's interesting is that this indicator also shows that the Lee Myung-bak administration failed to revive the real estate market. And in the discussion post, it was argued using this indicator that real estate is not in a bubble... that argument seems insufficient. This graph is a relative variation graph based on the starting year. It's designed to show trends and gaps, so saying it's low just because it's below this point is absurd. There was an adjustment during the 1998 IMF crisis, but what's noticeable is that it did not experience the 2008 global real estate adjustment. Personally, I believe the reasons it didn't experience an adjustment in 2008 were the rise of China, the foreign exchange reserves accumulated during the IMF crisis, and defense through household loan increase policies. However, this graph alone cannot confirm that, and interpretations may vary, so let's move on.

**3. Price against average income**
{{IMG:4}}
**According to this indicator, Korean real estate prices seem to be maintained at less than 75% of their pre-IMF level. Furthermore, this graph could actually be used as evidence that Korean housing prices are not relatively high. The problem is how income was measured. If it was based on GDP, given the worsening polarization, that graph might not be accurate. In reality, housing affordability per capita might have significantly decreased. This is purely speculation. It would depend on how income was calculated. If anyone knows, please share... (I'm too lazy to look it up further...)**

**4. Price against rents**
{{IMG:5}}
I'm not sure if this 'rent' includes 'jeonse' (a unique Korean deposit system). Looking at the graph, it's presumed to only include monthly rent, but I'm not certain. (This is because jeonse is a system unique to Korea, and the skyrocketing jeonse prices are a widely acknowledged fact, but it's not represented here.)

**5. Percentage change**
{{IMG:6}}
Finally, the ultimate result of real estate fluctuations. It has slightly decreased since '94. However, there doesn't seem to be much insight to gain from this. It's hard to tell if the decrease is good or bad. In Germany's case, it decreased, but the economy seems to have improved. Japan is also indicated as having plummeted terribly, but did its economy worsen by exactly that much? That's also a question mark. Korea's economy has improved. Although it has declined a bit recently. While there may be issues with distribution, it's clear that the nation's overall wealth has increased. Because people are starting to recognize this, questions like 'Is growth always the answer?' also seem to have increased recently.
With statistics, you should only take what you can get. Also, you should always be suspicious. As powerful as they are, if used incorrectly, they can be poison. On the one hand, I'm so envious that such a variety of statistics are available at an international level in the real estate sector. ㅜㅜ There should be more for software too...
ps. Personally, I am lukewarm about excessive activation of capital markets like real estate. This is because such markets stifle other business activities that require dynamism. When I see cases of promising software companies with technology and sales being ruined by financial games and then the perpetrators fleeing, it really makes me want to curse them out.

titleEn: Our Approach to Embracing AI
contentEn:
본 칼럼은 스마트초이스의 의뢰로 작성된 칼럼입니다.
**Original: Our Stance on Embracing Artificial Intelligence (2015-05-29)**
[http://www.smartchoice.or.kr/smc/smartreport/smarttalkview.do?sm_Seq=3918](http://www.smartchoice.or.kr/smc/smartreport/smarttalkview.do?sm_Seq=3918)

Just a few years ago, artificial intelligence was a vague entity to be realized in the distant future, an imaginary being seen only in sci-fi novels. A few years ago, I asked a professor specializing in pattern recognition, a sub-field of AI, this question:

"Will AI, as natural as those in cartoons and at a level where human rights must be discussed, emerge during our lifetime?"

The answer to this question was negative. Some scholars discussing AI predicted that human-level AI would appear within a decade or so, citing the complexity of the brain, but many scholars probably still responded with "Well, I don't know."

However, the technological changes that have poured out in recent years, and the stories in various films reflecting them, almost certainly indicate that AI is no longer an imaginary being, and that a significant level of AI will emerge at least during our lifetime. And, considering the pace of technological development, there is also the frightening prediction that AI, once it reaches our level, will easily surpass us in a very short time. Tesla's Elon Musk even said that AI could bring about a dystopia, while Google's Larry Page and Ray Kurzweil, conversely, were optimistic about the future.

Even without talking about such distant AI, computers are already recognizing cats, learning Chinese, writing articles, classifying photos, and diagnosing cancer at a level similar to humans.

**The Wonderful and Terrifying Potential of Computers That Can Learn** What happens when we teach computers to learn? Technology expert Jeremy Howard shares surprising new developments in the rapidly advancing field of deep learning. Deep learning gives computers the ability to learn Chinese, recognize objects in photos, or assist with medical diagnoses. (A deep learning tool that taught itself the concept of "cat" after watching YouTube for a few hours.) Let's explore a field that will completely transform the computers around you much faster than you think. www.ted.com

https://www.ted.com/talks/jeremy_howard_the_wonderful_and_terrifying_implications_of_computers_that_can_learn?language=ko

It's not about some great AI that will dominate us or lead us to heaven in the distant future, but rather, we need to reconsider whether we are ready to accept even the current level of AI. Let me tell you a few things about the short-term future that this AI will bring.

**1. Jobless Growth, a Society of Extreme Productivity Increase**

Computers are incomparably fast compared to humans. Specific jobs replaced by such AI will experience an extreme increase in productivity. As a result, a lot of money will be earned, and many inefficiencies caused by human labor will be eliminated. In other words, a few companies with this technology will achieve global success, while companies without the technology will be left behind. In the process, white-collar workers in those fields will lose their jobs. According to a research team at Oxford University in the UK, 47% of 702 jobs in the US are expected to disappear.

This problem implies extreme unemployment and the concentration of wealth in specific software companies like Google that possess AI technology. From a societal perspective, this is a social change brought about by AI. It's like the re-enactment of simple blue-collar laborers being replaced by machines in the industrial society. As a result, in developed countries, even blue-collar jobs that involve excessively simple labor no longer exist. It's like the disappearance of jobs like putting eyes on dolls or sealing envelopes. Ultimately, this issue involves how to solve the unemployment problem, along with the question of whether the concentration of wealth in companies that have earned large sums through the introduction of technology should be seen as a natural outcome of capitalism.

Currently, the answer to this is not clear. In Amazon's case, by reinvesting the money earned through technology back into technology, it contributes to increasing jobs for highly skilled workers. There could also be social systems, namely wealth redistribution through taxes. While making money is the reason for a company's existence, an astronomical amount of money concentrated in one company would make that company ponder how to spend such vast sums. The fundamental value of a company is not in hoarding money like a bank, but in the continuous circulation and growth of money. In the short term, in the US, a virtuous cycle of M&A and technology investment seems to be taking place. However, in South Korea, M&A is not common, and there is no guarantee that AI technology at the US level can be secured, so it is unclear whether AI technology will bring benefits to the nation or lead to massive capital outflow. If only a few companies that expensively adopt and use foreign technology see increased profits, and unemployment only worsens, it could become an even more terrible situation. The development of technology must be accompanied by discussions on wealth redistribution and social safety nets. Otherwise, AI might not be a friend that provides leisure to the public, but a devil that only takes away their jobs.

**2. Can We Follow AI's Decisions?**

In traditional machinery, the role of computers was largely about control. Many parts were automated in inevitable and clear-cut areas. However, tasks that were unclear and could incur responsibility were generally performed by humans. For example, diagnosing cancer and deciding on surgery is the role of a doctor.

Nevertheless, many medical accidents did occur, and legal and cultural frameworks have supported alternatives to address them. But what would happen if even these areas were decided by AI? IBM's Watson already shows an average diagnostic accuracy comparable to that of professional doctors and is pursuing business based on this. "Average," you might think, so most people would still prefer a responsible human doctor. But what if it showed 99% accuracy, surpassing the average human or even the best specialists? It would probably be logical and common sense to trust Watson's word and proceed with surgery. However, what if, by bad luck, an accident occurred in that 1%? Who should be held responsible? Or could that accident even be accepted? Autonomous cars present a similar problem. Even if autonomous cars are much safer than human-driven cars, people are not yet ready to accept accidents caused by machines. Both the average public perception and institutional frameworks are not yet prepared to accept such AI.

{{IMG:1}}

However, what is clear is that in a capitalist society, companies will eventually yield to these very clear numbers and seize great opportunities. For instance, the company providing the AI might offer insurance for accidents caused by AI. While AI cannot be held responsible, the company that profits from AI can be held accountable. And companies doing business with AI will crunch the numbers and progressively enter areas of business where they can bear the responsibility. Ultimately, it will be an era where AI's decisions are naturally accepted in many areas.

**3. AI Human Rights, and Society**

We are probably not yet at the stage for such discussions. However, it might happen someday. It's unclear which will come first: software created by humans discussing human rights, or an electronic brain that has directly scanned and modeled a human brain discussing human rights. In the former case, machines evolve into humans; in the latter, humans evolve into machines. This could even be called a new stage of evolution. Recently, movies and animations with such themes have been increasing, likely due to the visible achievements AI is demonstrating.

Technology is changing society. Saying we are in a software-centric society is, in fact, an early discussion of these very topics. We need to consider whether we are prepared for this and what we should discuss. It won't be solved by prematurely concluding that it will bring bad results and rejecting it. This is because it is already at an inevitable level, just as the anti-mechanization movements during the Industrial Revolution failed. AI is predicted to reach a singularity that surpasses humans. Perhaps that point in time will be the singularity of our human society, of humanity itself.

titleEn: Reflecting on 1 Year of the Mobile
contentEn:
**1. Effects of the Terminal Distribution Act: Who is telling a trustworthy story?**
The Terminal Distribution Act (단통법) was implemented in October 2014. Since then, there have been opinions from netizens that all citizens are now forced to buy phones at higher prices, and subsequent news articles show quite a few conflicting opinions. Personally, I tend to disregard the opinions of netizens. Based on my experience of frequently using methods to buy phones cheaply before the Terminal Distribution Act, only a very small fraction of people were able to buy them at low prices back then. From my experience of catching subsidies that appeared on weekends or "buses" (spot deals) that popped up at night, not many people could take advantage of them. It was a structure where significant benefits went only to a very small number of people who were familiar with the internet. To be honest, I made good use of such benefits and helped people around me as well.

However, having worked in internet services, I know very well that I am not a typical user. Moreover, even if it's a minority of users, if their sense of deprivation is severe, things can get very noisy. Since the implementation of the Terminal Distribution Act took away the benefits of a noisy minority of netizens, their opinions are difficult to trust. Then, can we trust the media? I don't think that's easy either. The biggest advertisers for the media are mobile carriers and manufacturers. As advertisers are entities they must be more mindful of than the government, they tend to express opinions with very different tones depending on whose tune they are dancing to.

Therefore, I believe that only objective figures and information that is tangibly felt by people around us can be trusted.

**2. I fundamentally agree with the purpose of the Terminal Distribution Act's introduction.**
First, I agree with the purpose of introducing the Terminal Distribution Act. Although it may seem like an excessive, somewhat socialist intervention, intervention is necessary in a market dominated by only three large corporations, where there are no alternative choices, and where evidence of collusion has been found multiple times over a long period, leading to numerous disciplinary actions against mobile carriers. Furthermore, excessive marketing and device distribution stores, which seem to be on every other block, are somewhat unrealistic. Isn't it strange that there are more smartphone stores than Chinese restaurants for a device we replace every two years? Therefore, consumers are clearly contributing to excessive spending. If the goal is to save small business owners, I'd rather order fried chicken one more time.

{{IMG:1}}

**[ ▲ The beautiful Republic of Korea, overflowing with philanthropists who will give you a smartphone for free ]**

**3. Let's re-examine only the trustworthy information.**
In January 2015, mobile carriers' ARPU (Average Revenue Per User) surged, and a quick search of articles on this attributes the cause to decreased marketing costs and an increase in high-paying subscribers. In other words, the goal of reducing marketing costs, which was the intent of the Terminal Distribution Act, was achieved, but it failed to lighten the burden on the public's wallets. Recent ARPU articles show a decrease in ARPU in May 2015, and some articles suggest this is due to the effects of the Terminal Distribution Act. Whether it's a success or a failure, there are a few things that everyone generally accepts as truth.

**1) Mobile carriers' marketing costs have decreased.**
First, a decrease in marketing costs. Marketing costs are money. Creating advertisements costs a surprisingly large amount of money, and executing them also incurs significant expenses. And the source of that money is the consumer.

**2) Low-cost phones have become more active.**
Second, the activation of low-cost phones. The Terminal Distribution Act is cited as the reason for this, and there are claims that Pantech and LG faced difficulties because of it. If one attributes the difficulties of Pantech and LG to the Terminal Distribution Act, based on my past experience in making mobile phones, I think it's an absurd claim. This is because both Pantech and LG are companies with very high overseas sales ratios. Whether low-cost or high-cost, they could have made a profit by creating well-made products with a technological gap. However, customer value has shifted from hardware to software, and their struggle against the high quality of low-cost Chinese products is not unique to the Korean market. Apple's success, on the other hand, is due to China not being able to produce iOS phones, allowing Apple to avoid direct competition and maintain unique differentiation. However, Korean companies developing Android phones directly compete with China, and with the standardization of hardware, they have to compete on price, which inevitably makes the fight with China very difficult. For similar reasons, even the number one company, Samsung, is not in a great situation. Even with the very well-made Galaxy Edge series, it's difficult to achieve the glory of the past with hardware differentiation alone.

**3) Rate plans have become predictable and simpler.**
Third, predictable and simplified data-centric rate plans. Before, you had to wait and agonize over when to buy a smartphone and search for information, but now you can buy one at a fair price anytime. This means that instead of timing and guesswork, you can now focus on the actual product and the mobile carrier's service when making a choice. There's a reason a bottle of soju is made to yield seven and a half glasses; rate plans were designed to be this intricate and complex, and the more complex they are, the more disadvantageous they are to the consumer. When factors like subsidies are added, the complexity increases even further. Moreover, for seniors who only make voice calls and use KakaoTalk, when replacing their phones, they no longer need to pay for 6GB or more of data that they won't even use for three months. They can now switch to a very affordable plan with enough data for KakaoTalk and internet use without much trouble. Looking at the expenditure over three months, it was actually over 200,000 won, which was comparable to the price of a cheap device these days. I actually replaced my parents' smartphones through an MVNO, and both received FHD quad-core smartphones with plans in the early 30,000 won range. Through this, they enjoy video calls and leave comments on their grandchildren's photos on KakaoStory.

**4. Can you really buy expensive, latest-model phones cheaply? Is that expensive phone truly worth that much money to you right now?**

                
                    Image does not exist.
                
             **[ You've already lost ]**
Are you dissatisfied because you can't buy the latest phones cheaply due to the Terminal Distribution Act? I want to ask if you truly need that phone. The younger generation is called the "880,000 won generation." What the 880,000 won generation absolutely needs to pay for is communication fees. Regardless of whether it's expensive or cheap, mobile communication is now like electricity and water. Should we raise everyone's communication fees and cause hardship to these people and to parents who only make voice calls, just so a few can buy expensive phones cheaply? Are those low-cost phones still so bad that you can't even run games on them like before? On the contrary, I'm truly glad that data communication fees have become more realistic. When the iPhone 3GS first came out, the "i-plan" was the first usable data plan. Since then, as LTE got faster, rate plans also skyrocketed, but after the Terminal Distribution Act, data fees decreased and stabilized. Now that the Terminal Distribution Act has stabilized, I imagine those who are unhappy are the manufacturers and mobile carriers who forcibly sold expensive smartphones with marketing costs, the advertising market that created their ads, and perhaps mobile carrier sales outlets. There were certainly too many of them for too long.

**After the Terminal Distribution Act, things are simply returning to their proper place. We were enchanted by the magic of the iPhone, but now it's time to return to reality. Jobs is dead, and the smartphone party is over. Now, the opponents we must fight are Tim Cook and Xiaomi.**

titleEn: Predicting the Future of Mobile Search Envisioned by KakaoTalk
contentEn:
KakaoTalk recently launched its search business. I had predicted a long time ago that Kakao would inevitably enter the search business someday. However, mobile search is not as easy as PC search. This is because the mobile search ad market is not as optimistic compared to PC ads. It's an environment where users find it very inconvenient to input queries, and the screen is also very small, so search ads are not a particularly good market compared to PCs. However, what's clear is that the proportion of users' mobile usage time is increasing compared to PC usage, and even in the living room, more users are lightly acquiring information via tablets rather than sitting in front of a PC. Therefore, it's clear that the existing PC search market has reached its limits. So, how will KakaoTalk approach search in the future? Let's talk about that briefly.

**1. Shop Search Directly in Chat Window, Card View-Based Section Search**
Currently, KakaoTalk allows immediate search by pressing the '#' button in the chat window. What's also interesting is that it displays search results in a card view, allowing you to swipe to see results for each section. The third main menu item, 'Channel,' maintains the traditional portal-style scrolling method, but the '#' search shows a much cleaner format. Which one is the correct answer, I don't know yet. However, KakaoTalk can analyze data from these two types of search results to see which is more suitable for mobile users, or if it varies by usage pattern. The ability to share search results means that one person's search result can be disseminated to many. Therefore, it could also mean having a higher impact than typical search results. Moreover, KakaoTalk, with an reach rate of over 96%, can be said to be the search window that the entire nation spends the most time looking at on mobile.

So far, this is all common knowledge. However, let's talk about something a little different. This is about the O2O lineup that KakaoTalk is recently building. Of course, please note that the content below is a fictional scenario I've envisioned, not an official announcement from Daum Kakao.

**2. My Predicted Kakao O2O Search Model**
Daum Kakao recently acquired Kim Gisa for 62 billion won. They are also aggressively pushing Kakao Taxi, and Kakao Pay seems poised for a major showdown with Naver Pay in offline payments this year.

As for O2O examples, in the case of Lineable, a lost child prevention bracelet I introduced before, it uses crowd GPS based on installed apps. Also, if you install the CU convenience store app recently, a popup appears informing you of various benefits every time you enter a CU store. Recently, everything from laundry, car wash, to mobile phone battery charging... almost all aspects of daily life are gradually moving online based on apps, delivering services right where I am. The characteristic of these businesses is that they are based on location and apps. What all companies wishing to engage in O2O business desire most is for their app to be installed on every user's device. What does this mean? In the past PC era, when starting a business, companies would create a homepage and register their businesses with search engines like Naver, allowing users to access services through search. That was the very foundation of the search business. However, what about the mobile era? Do we have to register mobile web pages again? If we use mobile web, can we receive beacon services? It's impossible to solve this with just the web, which is the traditional search ad model.

This point means that the mobile search market could be different, and this is where KakaoTalk's search opportunity lies. KakaoTalk can become both a search platform and an app platform for all companies wishing to engage in O2O business.

For example, let's say I type 'hand car wash' from my current location. Currently, car washes offering hand car wash services are marked on the map. But what if Yper, which I introduced before, is available in the service area?

http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/220408564204
**[Delivery Car Wash Yper] Don't worry about hand car wash when you're busy** 1. Why O2O? Now there's no business unrelated to software. Until recently, all startups seemed to be doing social networks, but recently O2O has been strong. O2O service... blog.naver.com

http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/220408564204

Instead of a webpage, an app might appear in the search results, and it might even indicate how much or when I can receive the service in my current area. If you click on that search result, the most common scenario would be to install the app, log in via Kakao ID, and receive the service. Going a step further, additional app installation might not even be necessary. What if, on the mobile web, you allow location information access and push notification permissions for the Yper service via Kakao ID? Without additional app installation, Yper can know the customer's location information, location information and pushes needed by the app can be handled through KakaoTalk, and the rest can be serviced 100% via mobile web. This could be the answer to the app installation problem for all O2O businesses. If crowd GPS, like Lineable, is used based on KakaoTalk, almost every place where people are present would be covered, leading to a truly lost-child-free world.

http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/220132879345
**[Lost Child Prevention Bracelet Lineable] Innovation is solving problems, not specs** 1. Innovation is solving problems and changing our lives, not specs. I'm tired of talking about innovation again. Samsung and Apple were debating whether it was innovation or not, and now I'm... blog.naver.com

http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/220132879345

Even without urging customers to install the CU app, CU could deliver beacon services to them. And eventually, it could naturally connect with search advertising. Naver, a direct competitor to KakaoTalk, has a similar Naver Simple ID, but the reach of the Naver app is very low compared to KakaoTalk, and its social login utilization is also lower than KakaoTalk's. Furthermore, Naver has not yet established its O2O business lineup, so if such a market unfolds, it doesn't seem like a very favorable situation for them. Therefore, currently, if the O2O search market expands, Kakao would be in a much more advantageous position.

**3. So When Will Kakao Search Be Considered a Success?**
When did Naver enter its period of success? I believe it was when TV commercials started saying, 'Type OOO into the Naver search bar.' All advertisers placed ads on Naver and urged users to type something into that search bar. Kakao Search will be similar. However, its location won't be TV, but rather offline stores. After saying, 'Search for OO on KakaoTalk,' it will provide additional coupons or value to users who make payments or share it with friends through this. Thus, I believe the point when advertisers start advertising themselves is when search advertising will succeed. Will we see messages like 'Search for OO on KakaoTalk' or NFC tags encouraging Kakao search while walking around? Won't there be some resolution around this time next year? I wonder if we can anticipate a fierce counterattack from Daum Kakao.

titleEn: [KakaoTalk Shop Search] Mobile Search Showdown
contentEn:
**1. My predictions for Kakao's future. How accurate were they?**Among the businesses Kakao operates, which of the following elements are they currently engaged in?1) Launching free services for user lock-in: PWE (Personalization Tool) service2) Offline coupon market: Expanding into the local coupon (social commerce) market3) Digital content and game market: Kakao Content Store4) E-commerce market: Kakao Social Shopping5) Media market: Curation and news service6) Community market: Kak카오-style Knowledge-in and Agit revamp7) Advertising market: The ultimate revenue model, search advertising

In fact, it's no exaggeration to say that with the merger with Daum, they are doing almost all of these things.

Why am I stating the obvious? These seven items are not from an article written this year, but a list of businesses I predicted Kakao would pursue around 2012. Didn't I get them quite right?

http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70149360673
                                **What will Kakao become? Current and Future Revenue Models** 1. Kakao, which has created hit products, is it making a living? KakaoTalk's recent hit product, well-known for KakaoTalk, is Anipang. This is due to the penetration rate and social graph that the Kakao platform possesses... blog.naver.com

http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70149360673

Among them, they recently launched #Search and brought news into KakaoTalk, effectively starting a search portal business. This is essentially the final scenario I had anticipated.

Looking at Daum Kakao's recent actions, it can be summarized in one phrase: a firm determination to fight Naver with a mobile-first strategy. With this conviction, they are gradually streamlining old Daum services and focusing their efforts on mobile. Some may complain about the termination of good Daum services, but I see it differently. Even for a company with a lot of money, its core personnel are limited. Launching many businesses means spreading the front too wide, making it difficult to focus on a single venture. Moreover, what if the opponent is Naver? I was someone who had always asserted that Daum could never beat Naver. The biggest reason for this was Daum Communications' failure in selection and concentration. Naver, whether successful or not, showed a consistent focus on one thing. Me2day, which they pushed heavily at one point, demonstrated this, and years of consistent investment in Japan eventually led to the massive success of Line. Naver's greatest strength is its persistence and focus on businesses it believes it must win. In contrast, Daum tended to match Naver's lineup rather than concentrating on services with potential. However, it was clear that Daum was not comparable to Naver in terms of scale or capital. As a result, it was difficult to win even one battle, and Daver was easily defeated piecemeal by Naver. By ceding mail and cafe services, Daum effectively became a perennial second-place player.

However, after merging with Kakao, Daum has recently shown a distinctly different approach, centered around Chairman Kim Beom-su. They are consistently moving towards a single direction. Of course, there may be failures along the way, but having a single objective is clearly a different approach. I'd like to share the objective I perceive and Daum Kakao's "Next."

**2. #Search and News can shake up the Korean search market.**#Search, which will change the landscape of mobile search, currently sees Naver still as the number one in mobile search. However, it's also true that Naver shows a much weaker performance compared to PC, and the reason is Google. In South Korea, where Android accounts for over 90%, Google is the default search engine. And Google's number one search term is Naver. -o- This means people search for Naver on Google and then go to Naver to search. But what's clear is that users have now distinctly started to feel Google's presence, and as a result, Google's search has gained a market share incomparable to its PC counterpart.
However, the undisputed mobile powerhouse in Korea is KakaoTalk. Would you believe it has more users than Google Play? It also secures the most user time. And now, a portal has entered KakaoTalk's main menu. It's clear that this will have a more powerful influence than Google's pre-load.
Furthermore, looking at recent trends in news consumption, internet dependency has overwhelmingly increased. The reason is the desire for breaking news. Traditional TV, newspapers, etc., with their morning and evening editions, provide news consumption twice a day, which is unsatisfactory for users who are glued to their smartphones 24/7. People wanted to know the number of confirmed MERS cases in real-time with visualized images and consumed breaking news. And this news spread to local cafes and friends.
Most of the shocking news I heard spread fastest via text messages, Facebook, or KakaoTalk. Things like, "Did you hear about ***?" Currently, perhaps taking a breather, Daum's popular search terms are not attached to KakaoTalk. One of the most influential things on mobile is this popular search term service. Of course, even without it, the influence of already curated content cannot be ignored. The destructive power of Naver's main page and Daum's main page was like a god in the blogger sphere. Ultimately, content producers who want to create content that fits this will eagerly jump in. Where PVs gather, quality content gathers. When quality content gathers, search also improves.
Of course, Naver's search quality is currently far superior. However, search is strongly driven by issues and habits, so they cannot be complacent. Moreover, what's scary about KakaoTalk is that most users are logged in users. It also has social information. This means it has far more means than Naver to know what kind of search results a user with a particular taste would be more interested in.

**3. The future of mobile search: O2O search**Another variable for Daum Kakao that I didn't predict in 2012 was O2O. At the time, I only thought of it as a local coupon service. It was a time when it was difficult to imagine local commerce as a profitable direction. But now I can clearly say that the answer lies in O2O companies that innovate services based on online connections, rather than simply moving offline services online. Representative services of this kind are companies like Uber, and in Korea, services like Kakao Taxi. These models transplant all behavioral patterns of daily life online and innovate the service method itself based on information. Such models have the potential to arise from everything we do and experience offline. From waking up in the morning until going to bed, even without looking at a smartphone due to IoT. And this will innovate existing PC-based search services. If PC was query-centric search, mobile will be situation-centric search. An early attempt similar to this was Naver or Daum apps providing nearby bus stop information, but now, beacon-based systems will recommend optimal information of interest and induce search. You'll start seeing advertisements everywhere saying, "Try typing #** in KakaoTalk," just as you used to see TV ads saying, "Try typing ** in Naver's search bar." And it won't just end with search results; it will connect with various O2O services. Mobile search will be at the heart of breaking down the boundaries between offline and online. In the future, it will aim for AI agent models like Siri or Google Now, but currently, the gap in technological level is still considerable, so in the transitional period, service-centric O2O search, solved by people and processes, seems to have a significant advantage.

**4. A true mobile search showdown**This is what I believe to be KakaoTalk's future and potential that I hadn't considered. Naver started to rise when it attracted people by saying, "Ask ** on Knowledge-in." After that, businesses themselves solidified the market by saying, "Type ** in Naver's search bar." However, this model is not working well on mobile currently. KakaoTalk, I believe, is currently closest to a solution for this. Of course, Naver won't stand still either. Its large advertising pool, the expansion of offline commerce centered on Checkout, and the fintech battle are also as interesting as the Battle of Red Cliffs. However, Naver has a slight advantage in that even if it struggles a bit domestically, it can apply Kakao's proven model to Japan and capture a larger market than at home. It already had a similar experience with games once.

I feel that KakaoTalk is truly sharpening its sword recently. In contrast, I also worry that most of Naver's top talent might be focused on Japan or overseas expansion. There is no eternal number one. I look forward to the upcoming competition even more.

P.S. Some people consider Daum Cloud's service termination a mistake, but I think it was a good decision. Daum Cloud and N Drive are file-based PC services. Google's success with Google Photos over G Drive illustrates this shift in times. I wouldn't be surprised if KakaoStory benchmarks Google Photos soon.

titleEn: Children Who Play Are More Likely to Succeed Than Children Who
contentEn:
**This post is a column contributed to TheGear.**
**Original: [http://thegear.co.kr/8520](http://thegear.co.kr/8520)**

{{IMG:1}}From 'The Simpsons' cartoon

A future society where studying becomes poison and playing leads to success might soon arrive. I'm not talking about idol trainees. Of course, in South Korea, where the "Cinderella Law" (= **[Refer to Shutdown Law](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EB%8C%80%ED%95%9C%EB%AF%BC%EA%B5%AD%EC%9D%98_%EC%85%A7%EB%8B%A4%EC%9A%B4_%EC%A0%9C%EB%8F%84)**) was created because games disrupt children's sleep, yet self-study at night is encouraged, this premise is absolutely unacceptable.
However, such a future is actually coming. While I worry that my child might fall behind, if we just look at recent trends, a frightening thought arises: how much academic competition is turning into a low-probability game for success.

### **The Collapse of the Value of Studying Has Begun.**

**{{IMG:2}}**
During our school days, everyone grew up hearing "Study hard." Studying was a game where teachers wrote something on the blackboard, and children who memorized it and answered many questions correctly got high scores. These scores led to good universities and good jobs, which actually guaranteed a reasonable level of success. Thus, we have empirically taught our children that studying is necessary to not fall behind in the world and to succeed. However, these traditional learning methods and ideal talent profiles are now facing a major crisis.

What is the competitiveness of the studying we teach?
The first is "differentiation of knowledge," the most fundamental purpose of studying. Knowing what others don't know and deepening what one already knows is the core competitiveness.
The second is 'diligence.' In our school days, everyone studies math, which is hardly necessary for daily life. Children often ask, "Where do we use math? Did you use it, Mom?" The model answer to this is diligence. The attitude of studying, the habit of sitting at a desk, is a competitive advantage, and it helps cultivate diligence.
Indeed, many elite employees at large corporations diligently arrive on time, work steadily, and even work overtime before leaving. In summary, the reason for learning math was to work overtime!
However, these two competitive advantages are gradually disappearing. This is due to software, IT, and technology.

**1) Collapse of the Value of "Knowledge Differentiation"**
{{IMG:3}}

Having a Ph.D. certifies that one has learned more and can do more than others. This is because it's difficult to store knowledge in one's head, and a "knowledge monopoly" creates added value in a knowledge society. However, with the advent of computers, storing and copying knowledge has become easier. For example, even if one cannot store as much in their head as a doctor, if a doctor's knowledge is digitized, anyone can put medical information on their smartphone.
What remains then is the monopoly of knowledge, but the recent 'sharing economy' is collapsing even this. The sharing economy doesn't just mean lending an empty house to someone, like Airbnb. When the concept of the sharing economy shifts from hardware to software, like 'knowledge,' its value is maximized to an astonishing degree. This is called the 'public good nature of software.' The easiest example is open source. Open source refers to the movement of sharing computer software for free and collaboratively improving it, or the software created through this movement. Currently, commonly used open-source examples include Android smartphones, and broadly speaking, internet services like Naver and Facebook were also built using open source.
When in school, everyone learns mathematical formulas and uses them in necessary fields. Of course, one doesn't pay to use equations. However, a long time ago, these equations were like secrets known only to a few mathematicians. Open source is like those equations, once known only to a few mathematicians, being made public. People easily use commercial software and achieve more. Mark Zuckerberg was able to create global services like Facebook at a young age thanks to commercial software.
Open source is also behind the recent boom in software startups. This is an example of how disclosure, rather than monopoly, of knowledge creates more added value. This movement has also spread to hardware, leading to the creation of open-source hardware. However, the open hardware movement is not about sharing hardware itself, but about sharing manufacturing secrets—that is, knowledge and software—and is essentially a type of open-source software movement.
Reference link: [http://navercast.naver.com/contents.nhn?rid=122&contents_id=56137](http://navercast.naver.com/contents.nhn?rid=122&contents_id=56137)

"If I have seen further than others, it is by standing upon the shoulders of giants," is a famous quote by the scientist and mathematician Newton. Just as Newton did, the disclosure of knowledge, rather than its monopoly, will create more innovation. Furthermore, the validity period of value derived from knowledge monopoly will become increasingly shorter, making it likely more difficult to create wealth through it.

**2) Collapse of the Value of Diligence**

{{IMG:4}}

The value of diligence is also collapsing. Diligence is essentially about increasing the quantity of labor. When creating the same value in the same amount of time, the higher the diligence, the higher an individual's value. In short, it's not wrong to say that the value of labor is the value of sweat. The same applies to knowledge workers. The fundamental belief that human labor creates a certain value has been the driving force behind our industrial society.
However, this fundamental belief is now breaking down. Because of machines.
Machines are clearly more diligent than humans. Therefore, the productivity of machines in physical labor is already beyond doubt. But what about knowledge workers, like doctors, whom machines find difficult to imitate?
IBM's 'Watson,' a computer famous for winning a quiz show in the US, is already producing results similar to the intellectual labor of an average human. Watson has recently been operating as 'Dr. Watson.' Watson diagnoses patients' illnesses just like a doctor. Its level is already that of an average doctor. Since it reached the level of an average doctor in just a few years, it's predictable that it will easily surpass that average soon.
However, one might still argue that human labor is sacred and creates unique value. Yet, the world is currently experiencing an oversupply of capital and goods. While there is a problem of wealth distribution, production is in surplus, and due to technological advancements, the amount of labor input is drastically decreasing. This means the world is already performing more labor than it needs.
"Diligence," that is, the value provided by labor, is rapidly decreasing. This has led to social problems such as an increase in temporary workers, corporations becoming richer, and people becoming poorer. However, this is also a problem that arises during a transitional period. In the further future, another characteristic of technology, "value increase due to openness," will also become very high.

If you've read this far, those who only pushed their children to study might be feeling a sense of crisis. You might ask, "Then which academy should I send my children to?"
No. The point is to stop sending them to academies.

### **The Increasing Value of Playing**

{{IMG:5}}

Economic value stems from human needs. According to psychologist Maslow, once the 5th stage physiological needs and 4th stage safety needs are met, the 3rd stage and beyond transition to intellectual needs such as belonging, love, esteem, and self-actualization. Applying this to industry, stages 4 and 5 are similar to physical value. For example, "manufacturing" industries like Samsung Electronics fall into this category. However, as mentioned earlier, the added value of needs in stages 4 and 5 is rapidly decreasing due to technological development. Considering that these industries have relied on "knowledge differentiation" and "diligence," their competitiveness is bound to continuously decline.
So, what industries can create added value based on intellectual needs beyond stage 3? In my personal opinion, they are the internet software industry, which aids information acquisition and relationships, and entertainment industries like gaming. However, the talent profile required by these industries is not one that diligently applies differentiated knowledge learned in school. One must be sensitive to people and the world and have a good understanding of what people enjoy. This kind of learning cannot be acquired by sitting at a desk. Rather, it's an attribute gained from cultural activities like consuming mass media or playing with friends, getting up from the desk.

This is not just my speculation. This phenomenon is already occurring throughout society. The expansion of the entertainment industry and the success of games, SNS, etc., are evidence of this. Those who succeed in these fields are more sensitive to changes around them, possess the ability to elicit empathy, and have the skill to commercialize these aspects. Of course, the role of learning has not completely disappeared. However, because the differentiation of knowledge has decreased and the pace of social change is rapid, it is difficult to keep up unless one feels it with their body, not just their mind. So-called creative talent can only emerge from play rather than learning.

### **Playing is Important. But Playing Well is Not Easy.**

So what should we do now?
If you ask, "Should we gather children and make them compete to see who plays best?", then you've misunderstood again. Competition is a type of material that makes play enjoyable, but by only emphasizing competition, children's empathy has disappeared, and their creativity has been buried.

Play is the joy of brain activity. Young children enjoy trying out what they've imagined and seeing the results. That's the core of play. Through play, they imitate parents and enjoy riding a box even without a sports car. No one ever taught them. In fact, humans are designed to play well from birth. What's important is to secure time for play. It's crucial to observe children with time and leisure, not competition or learning.

Now I need to talk about what parents worry about most: games. Many typical parents view games as an object of addiction, not as play. However, games and webtoons (comics) are also growing as a form of popular culture, stimulating imagination, and are the most active areas for the creation of secondary works (new creations made by users or readers). It's more appropriate to accept them as a type of play transformed by technology rather than treating them as an addiction. Furthermore, if children only play games, before considering the possibility of game addiction, one should examine whether it's due to excessive study hours leaving them with little free time. This is because games and webtoons are low-cost play alternatives that can be accessed in a short amount of time, simply by turning on a smartphone or computer.

In the industrial era, we demanded excessive knowledge and, as a result, took play away from children. However, the future brings a different era, one that demands creativity, often called a software-centric society. We need to take the time and leisure to consider with our children how to play better for their competitiveness. It is truly ironic to prepare for a future society where the paradigm is completely shifting, using the study methods of the industrial era.
