titleEn: Galaxy Gear: Predictions and What It Needs
contentEn:
With recent interest in smartwatches, interest in the Galaxy Gear is currently very high. Looking at some of the revealed specs, I'd like to share my cautious predictions about the Galaxy Gear, along with one path it should avoid.

**1. Since the Galaxy Gear does not use LTE, widespread success will be difficult.**
Looking at comments on news about the Galaxy Gear, many people are concerned, with many predicting that their wrists will get hot. And regarding the price, many bring up carrier subsidies, but for this to be possible, it must be equipped with LTE. It's a clear fact that no smart device has successfully achieved widespread adoption in Korea without LTE.

**2. The Galaxy Gear will not be a smart device, but an 'app-cessory'.**
However, I have a very negative view regarding an LTE-enabled Galaxy Gear, and indeed, the known product specifications do not include LTE. There isn't even Wi-Fi.

Also, I've used smartwatches a few times briefly, and the biggest issue was battery life. It's very inconvenient if a watch dies in less than 24 hours. The biggest battery consumers in a smartwatch are the display and Bluetooth.

The best way to solve this is Bluetooth 4.0. While Bluetooth 3.0 focused on speed improvements, 4.0 was entirely improved with power consumption in mind. Although the speed will be around 1Mbps, which is even slower than 3G, battery life will dramatically increase.

What the Galaxy Gear must have is battery life, and ultimately, the Galaxy Gear's choice will be Bluetooth 4.0 to save battery. **This will consequently hinder app usability and internet usage. Therefore, given these technical characteristics, it is correct to view the Galaxy Gear not as a dedicated smart device like a smartphone or smart tablet, but as a supplementary 'app-cessory'.**

**3. What the Galaxy Gear Should NOT Do**
**1) Unless it intends to follow in the footsteps of Windows 8, TouchWiz is an absolute no-go.**
The Galaxy S, in other words, a smartphone, is essentially a computer disguised as a phone. Those who play various 3D games on it would not deny this. However, the Galaxy Gear should not become a computer. It should strictly be an 'app-cessory' that works organically with a computer, meaning a Galaxy S or Tab.

If TouchWiz, which customizes the home screen, is built-in, then the Galaxy Gear ceases to be an 'app-cessory'. Instead, it becomes an overly burdensome device. There was also a concept where you unfold the Galaxy Gear and use it like a phone... The moment I saw that, I was reminded of Windows 8 Smart PCs. A device that belongs to neither category.

**2) Google's standard Android for smartphones is also a no-go.**
This might sound strange to those dreaming of the latest Android version, but this is also a no-go for the same reason. If it has a strange structure like Android, with a notification bar at the top and pop-up push windows, there won't even be space to touch on such a low-resolution screen. Trying to go into Google Play and install KakaoTalk on such a resolution would only infuriate people.

In the concept video, when you unfold the Galaxy Gear worn on the wrist, icons are arranged in three columns, just like a regular smartphone... It's too inconvenient to use. I hope it's just a concept.

Ultimately, it's likely either a newly created branch version of Android, or they are creating a new Android for watches, similar to Google TV, in close cooperation with Google. Given Samsung, the latter is more probable.

**4. What the Galaxy Gear SHOULD Do**
**1) As a connected device, provide an organic user experience.**
I believe the Galaxy Gear will have two primary strong purposes. It will serve as an extended controller for other devices, and a notification device for push alarms sent from other devices. A prime example of the former function would be call functionality, while the latter would be something like a KakaoTalk push relay. If it takes on the role of a controller, it's expected that the manufacturer's strengths could leverage the appeal of its hardware. Just as the Galaxy Note adopted Wacom's technology, if it incorporates muscle recognition features like MYO, I think it could become a killer feature for the Galaxy Gear.

It must sufficiently demonstrate examples of attractive experiences to users for them to make a purchase, and its appeal as a platform, which I'll discuss later, will also increase.

**2) Role as a Platform**
The extended controller and push alarm notifications should not merely end with a connection to the Galaxy S phone. It should also apply to 3rd Party apps installed on the Galaxy S phone. Users should be able to install an app on the Galaxy Gear to control Naver Music installed on their Galaxy S phone, or view KakaoTalk pushes within a KakaoTalk app installed on the Galaxy Gear.

If it's limited to a few Samsung services, the scope of the Galaxy Gear's movement will become very narrow. And most importantly, as a device more closely integrated with the user than a smartphone, it is a platform that all 3rd parties can pay close attention to.

**5. Above all, I hope it turns out well...**
As the saying goes, 'seeing is believing', though I've rambled on like this, I hope it turns out well. For Samsung, which has mostly dedicated its capabilities to faithfully creating the Google Android experience, this might perhaps be a new challenge.

titleEn: Not an SF Blockbuster, but What Snow
contentEn:
Instead of talking about IT, as I'm supposed to, I thought I'd talk about movies for a change. The reason I have to talk about this is because I don't know how many years it's been since I went to see a movie alone. It feels like it's been about 10 years. The movie that drew me to the cinema was Bong Joon-ho's *Snowpiercer*. It's an SF setting that everyone watches and I love, and it was made by a Korean, so I had to see it. Anyway, I'd like to talk about it.

**1. But it's not a blockbuster SF.** If you go in expecting a blockbuster scale, you might actually be a bit disappointed. It had a cool premise, but it wasn't an SF film based on meticulous scientific facts. Of course, *Star Wars* is also a stretch to call SF, but back then, it was a great movie that blended imagination with appropriate scientific elements. First of all, *Snowpiercer* felt quite far removed from SF historical accuracy and scientific settings.
**- Too small a train and flimsy historical accuracy** First, the train is too small. SF novels dealing with closed, perfectly balanced spaceship-like settings have existed for a long time. Compared to such scales, where artificial suns exist and spaceships can be several kilometers long, the train is narrow and excessively densely populated. Even assuming various technologies are included to technically cover this, it's a balance that's too easily broken in reality. Moreover, if a massacre occurs in such a confined space, the consequences would be very severe. In the case of the tail-section survivors, not only would they need to have survived in such poor sanitary conditions and possess a very strong immune system, but the moment they moved from the tail section to the front, the front section would become a biohazard zone. Crucially, the 'end of parts' mentioned for the engine suggests they didn't bring any engineers on board. This is what happens when you ignore engineers... The Coca-Cola polar bear, which director Bong Joon-ho mentioned as a symbol of hope at the end, is one of the strongest predators on Earth. Unless there's a colony of penguins over the hill and the polar bear is full, it will lack food, and the two surviving children are screwed.
**2. More important are the symbolism and theme**
**- Any system breaks. The folly of those who are complacent** Spoiler alert, but the train that had been running for 17 years stops too easily. And not by the protagonist, but by nature, an external force. From an SF perspective, even though obstacles blocking the tracks were destroyed in the middle of the movie, it's a stretch to consider a train that requires track maintenance as a perpetual motion machine. It's hard to believe that Wilford, an engineer, didn't anticipate maintenance needs. (This train-obsessed engineer didn't study the tracks.) Everyone on the train believed it would last forever, but that wasn't actually the case. Some reviews say it symbolized the cyclical nature of Buddhism, but I see it as based more on Christian thought. It seems cyclical and eternal, and people live complacently within it, but in reality, everything has a beginning and an end. If even Earth and the universe aren't eternal, how could something made by humans be?
**- Those who try to conquer the system and those who try to leave the system** However, if you view it as 'not SF,' the movie becomes quite watchable. The SF imagination was merely a garnish to convey the theme. This story, represented by Curtis and Song Kang-ho—those who move forward within the system and those who try to escape it—is surprisingly simple, yet it's mixed with a lot of symbolism. The girl's name is also 'Yona,' who survived inside the belly of a fish in the Bible. One could compare the forward-moving cars to human history, or to human class structures, but simply put, it signifies a "framework" or "system." Therefore, even as humanity fights over communism, capitalism, conservatism, and progressivism, I wonder if someone isn't heading towards space.

I could also evaluate the detailed situations, but since there's a high chance of spoilers, I'll leave you with a 10-minute space travel video as a meme.

ps. Even if *Snowpiercer* is rated for accompanied minors, please don't bring elementary school kids. It's not an SF movie for them.

titleEn: Legend of Dragonia Part 1 Episode 10
contentEn:
As Aaron was dragged by the mermaids, house-sized conch shells came into view. "What are those? If we boil and eat them, we could eat for a year."
True to a sailor's son, Umma didn't lose his easygoing nature. "You guys are so carefree even in this situation. You can still joke around? Those are our homes..." Elisa asked, seemingly surprised.

"Because being afraid won't change the situation."
Aaron answered her question. At his reply, Elisa's voice trailed off slightly, becoming softer as she spoke.

"Yes. Even though you're young, your courage is truly admirable... Instead, one thing I can tell you is that I can promise there will be no threat to your safety."
Aaron was reassured, certain that Elisa harbored no ill will.
Aaron and Umma passed through the most colorful giant conch shells and arrived before a beautiful, enormous conch they had never seen before. It was almost the size of a small hill, and Aaron and Umma gazed at it, mesmerized. They entered the giant conch. At the entrance, mermaids who appeared to be soldiers guarded the way, and while the exterior was a conch, the interior resembled a human building. The difference was that instead of flat rooms, rooms and paths were chaotically connected up, down, and sideways, suited for mermaids who could swim freely in all directions. Passing through the largest and most ornate tunnel, the decorations and frames hanging everywhere were all rare and precious items.
"Mermaids seem to live better than humans, perhaps."
Aaron muttered. At the final destination, they pushed open a large door and entered a hall.
"Be quiet. You are about to meet the Queen. You must be quiet in the palace."
Elisa shushed the children, cautioning them.
"You expect cooperation after dragging us here as prisoners! Your..."
Aaron yelled out, then lowered his voice and added a respectful suffix. The old mermaid sitting on a high chair at the end of the hall, which caught Aaron's eye, exuded an intimidating and solemn aura just by looking at her. She wasn't particularly large, nor was she frowning, but the charisma emanating from her was that of a queen.
She sat regally, but leaned diagonally with a pillow tucked under one side, as if trying to force herself to sit upright. Her face was clearly strong and charismatic, but it looked excessively pale, and she seemed to be enduring something with great effort.
"Are these the children!"
Her voice also resonated with great solemnity. Elisa was about to answer, but a sturdy merman in armor next to the Queen answered first.
"Yes, Your Majesty."
The Queen scanned Aaron, then spoke in a voice incomparably softer than before.
"He's very young... General, must this be done?"
"But, Your Majesty. You must steel your resolve."
The merman replied again. The Queen then spoke resignedly, and with difficulty, stood up and left her seat.
"There's no help for it... Do as you wish, General."
As the Queen disappeared, the General merman approached with a fearsome expression, striding purposefully, and dragged Aaron away. "Hey? What are you doing! Let go!"
Aaron cried out in panic. "Where are you taking Aaron?"
Umma shouted, but the General paid no attention and dragged Aaron away. The General's strength was immense, and Aaron couldn't resist even once, ending up confined in a small solitary cell. Aaron grew anxious. Before, having a friend by his side had made it a little easier to be brave, but now that he was alone, his anxiety intensified. He desperately wished a teacher were there.
Then, he overheard the guards' conversation.
"What were they thinking, bringing a human child to this solitary cell?"
"Haven't you heard? They say they're going to kill the Child of Light and use their liver to cure the Queen's illness."
'Who is this Child of Light? Are they talking about me?'
Aaron couldn't guess why he was being called the Child of Light, but upon hearing that he was brought there to be killed, the fear he had suppressed surged all at once. His relief, based on the belief that Elisa harbored no ill will, was a misjudgment. Regret washed over him, wishing he had tried to escape somehow even while being dragged to this place. He couldn't tell day from night, but the hunger he felt suggested that a full day had passed. Normally he would have fallen asleep, but an anxious Aaron couldn't sleep at all.
Eventually, he was once again tightly bound by mermaids and dragged out of the cell. The thought of being dragged out to die made him struggle to avoid leaving the solitary cell this time, but it was useless against the strength of several individuals. As the thought of death approaching set in, goosebumps covered his body, and he trembled like an aspen leaf. Aaron cried out in desperation, "Why are you trying to kill me! What is the Child of Light! I don't know anything about that!"
However, there was nothing he could do about his sudden predicament, like a rabbit. He had no sword, nor could he claim to have left his liver outside like a rabbit. He was merely a boy paralyzed by fear. As Aaron was being dragged, he met Elisa, the mermaid, for the first time in the corridor.
"Hey! Ms. Turtle. You tricked me and brought me here to kill me!"
Elisa couldn't meet Aaron's furious gaze. Unlike her vibrant beauty of just a day ago, Elisa looked tired, as if she had been suffering, and hearing Aaron's words, she was terrified and didn't know what to do.
Aaron was dragged past the corridor where Elisa was, and brought before the Queen. Aaron saw mermaids holding sharp, blue blades. The mere thought that he might die by those blades made Aaron gasp for breath. He had felt the threat of death in battles with monsters before, but this was the first time he had faced such a desperate situation. Aaron raised his head and looked at the Queen. Her charismatic face held a hint of a frown and irritation.
"Why are you trying to kill me!" Aaron cried out, his voice trembling with fear.
"Honestly, I don't want to do this. It's a terrible thing." The Queen said in a subdued voice.
"Tch. Don't make me laugh! And where's Umma!"
Aaron was afraid, but at the same time, he was worried about his friend's safety. So, he hid his fear and shouted as if threatening. The Queen looked down at Aaron with pity and spoke.
"You are young, but brave. The other child is fine. However, they probably won't be able to return to the surface. Consider your death your destiny. One day I fell ill and couldn't find a cure. But then, a rumor began to spread among the people that my illness could be cured by magic using the liver of the Child of Light."
"That's absurd... Curing an illness with a person's liver. And a child's at that..."
"Truthfully, I don't believe that rumor either. However, my ministers and many of my people believe that my illness can be cured that way. They say the liver is a symbol of resurrection... If I leave things as they are, they will indiscriminately capture human children, so I have no choice but to follow their words. I am sorry. I am an inadequate queen, unable to control the words and hearts of my people."
Upon hearing the story, Aaron realized the situation was very serious. Knowing that there was no way for a single child to escape once entangled in the politics of a nation, he asked resignedly, "But why am I the Child of Light?"
"You still don't know?" The Queen said, surprised as if it were unexpected.
"This is the first I'm hearing of it."
"If you don't know, it's better for you to live without knowing. But you're going to die anyway."
"What are you talking about? Why would I die!"
The Queen no longer answered. Soon, other mermaids seized Aaron and began to tie his body to something like a torture rack. "Let me go! I said let me go! I don't want to die! I don't want to die!"
Aaron screamed and struggled as if in agony, but in the end, both his arms and legs were bound. A female warrior with a sharp, blue sword approached Aaron. Aaron instinctively tensed his body, but it was useless in his bound state. Aaron raised his head and shouted at the Queen.
"You secretly wish that rumor were true! Is only your life so important, and others' lives mean nothing? You're going to take even a child's life!"
Aaron shouted at the old Queen, at her conscience. "Perhaps..."
The old mermaid smiled bitterly. Aaron sneered at the mermaid and said.
"You'll regret this for the rest of your life! My liver won't be of any use! I guarantee it..."
"Execute him quickly!"
A mermaid next to the Queen shouted. The female warrior's large, blue sword rose high into the sky—no, into the seawater. The moment that sword came down would surely be the end. Aaron squeezed his eyes shut. 'Is this how I die... I haven't even avenged my father and mother... Will my head be cut off and my insides taken out? If so, blood won't flow here... it will just spread... because it's underwater... It will stain this palace, and some of it will probably go outside the palace? And then maybe some of it will float up to the surface of the sea... No, no. It might just mix and disappear... The ocean is vast... there's so much seawater, it will just dissolve in it. Meaninglessly... without even a drop of blood floating to the surface. Just disappear... I'm scared. Where do you go when you die? Will I be able to meet my father and mother?' In Aaron's mind, various imaginations crossed paths in that brief moment.
**You can read subsequent installments a little earlier on Naver Webnovel.**[http://novel.naver.com/challenge/list.nhn?novelId=3231](http://novel.naver.com/challenge/list.nhn?novelId=3231)

titleEn: The Legend of Dragonia Part 1 Episode
contentEn:
The child stood before a lake the color of the sky. The child took off their outer garment. As the two fangs on the child's neck glinted in the sunlight, the child plunged into the blue-glowing lake. It was a terrifyingly cold winter, but the child didn't mind. The child dove repeatedly, then descended to the bottom of the lake and didn't resurface for a long time. After some time passed, a voice calling the child was heard, and the child rose to the surface. The woman who called the child was Danna. Barely past 30, her face suggested she must have been quite beautiful in her youth, but fine wrinkles, seemingly indicative of a hard life, lined it. This woman, neatly dressed, a bit irritable, and speaking in a masculine way, was the only one who could look directly into the child's cold eyes. And she was the child's guardian. There was something in the child's eyes that, in an inexplicable way, intimidated people. "Duma! Come out quickly! Dinner's ready!" The child silently emerged from the water, dried off, and headed towards the bandits' camp.

Though called bandits, they hadn't become bandits because of evil hearts. The irony of this camp was that it was a gathering place for those who couldn't overcome poverty and had left their hometowns – people who, though they sometimes petty-thieved and spoke roughly, were generally simple-hearted. The country's fields and rice paddies had been devastated by long wars, and taxes grew higher day by day. Consequently, the lives of the common people became proportionally harder, and cities also grew corrupt. Many, unable to endure the impoverished life in the cities, chose the forests and mountains.

On the same day, a stranger entered the bandits' camp. Of considerable build, with a long sword strapped to his back, his face, covered by a hood, was obscured by its shadow. Instead, his tattered cloak and shoes indicated his status as a traveler. It was not common for an unknown person to suddenly appear in a bandit camp. The people of the camp gathered to see this stranger. Among them, the leader of the bandits stepped forward and spoke to him. Here, his name was simply a nickname, Aniam (meaning: the groans of the people). As was the case with most people here who possessed some learning and martial skill, no one knew his origin or his real name. "Why have you come here? Are you a spy from the royal palace?" A hint of anger and wariness could be felt in his voice. Thereupon, the man silently removed his hood. He had a handsome face, and a small, seemingly expensive earring in his ear reflected the sunlight. Several people gasped in admiration, surprised by his striking appearance. "My name is Eleazar. I am from the nation of Laodicea." "Then, are you a spy from the nation of Ceres, sent by Laodicea?" Aniam's voice still held deep suspicion, as if he might draw his sword at any moment. "No... I merely said I came from there. I am traveling. I wish to rest here for a few days. In return, I will pay some money." "Hmph~ Traveling during wartime, how carefree. Money? Do you know we are bandits?" "Are you trying to fight me? That would be your loss." Confidence was imbued in his voice. As soon as Aniam gave the signal, several burly men surrounded him. However, the mysterious man was not intimidated in the least. "Wow~ Look at that bulk. Did he just eat and grow big?" Pointing at one of the large men, Eleazar chuckled instead. The large man, feeling insulted, angrily lunged forward. Eleazar dodged the incoming punch and grabbed his arm. What followed was a test of strength; though the large man seemed no match in terms of sheer size, he screamed and clutched his arm. "Such a fuss..." The man named Eleazar clicked his tongue and said. Though his subordinate was defeated, Aniam, instead, spoke with admiration. "Remarkable, you. Why not stay here permanently, instead of just a few days? We also need strong people..." Whether out of respect for the strong, his voice had somehow lost its wariness. "I am bound to no one. Neither to any nation, nor to any individual..." "That's dangerous. You say you won't join us, yet you want to stay here... Are you courageous? Or foolish?" "It could be both, or neither." Aniam laughed heartily, then replied. "Hahaha. I like you, you're truly interesting. I'll tell my subordinates not to bother you. But be careful. Not everyone listens to me, so watch your neck while you sleep." The man offered Aniam one of his earrings. Everyone's eyes widened. In terms of value, it was immense. However, all the traveler wanted was lodging and food. Aniam liked him and personally showed him around. Eleazar, with his cheerful personality, quickly became friendly with the people. No one knew why he had come here. A few people noticed that he, who could have lived luxuriously by selling just that earring, had a strange habit of sometimes falling into deep thought or staring intently at one spot, but they didn't think much of it. Because long wars drive everyone mad... Most people in the camp might have seemed outwardly cheerful and happy, but it was common for everyone to bury their own sorrows and stories, making it a place where a truly ordinary person would seem strange. As night fell, small torchlights illuminated the camp. In the silent forest camp, lit by the winter moon, the incessant sounds were drunken ramblings and sobbing cries. This was such a place.

Eleazar opened his eyes to the noisy morning atmosphere. 'Mornings here start quite early...' He yawned, stretched once, and looked outside. The newly risen morning sun strongly stimulated his eyes, making him squint once. A fresh forest morning, unrelated to the pain of the gathered people. The nature of the wild was always different from that of humans. Aniam, seeing Eleazar, offered a light nod of greeting. The Aniam Eleazar saw again was a man with the demeanor of a leader and a generous heart. Eleazar surveyed the camp. Rather than a band of bandits, it seemed more fitting to call it a village where small farmers lived. Could bandits be so simple-hearted and diligent? In one spot, a small hut was being built high up in a tree, starting early in the morning. He didn't know when they had started working, but people were already busy working from early morning. As Eleazar was about to pass by, something dropped from the tree, followed by a voice from above. "Hey~ You there! Could you pick up a few more just like this?" Looking again, it was a wooden piece, like a joint. Eleazar picked it up and looked around, but there was nothing similar. Instead, Eleazar picked up a piece of firewood much larger than the wooden piece and threw it into the air. His hand seemed to reach for the sword on his back, and in an instant, several pieces of wood fell, shaped exactly like the component. Eleazar sheathed his sword, then picked up the components and threw them to his friend above. "Thanks! I was worried there wouldn't be any down there..." A voice came from above. Eleazar smiled wryly and was about to turn and leave when he heard someone clapping and calling out. "Wow~ What skill!" The voice came from the tree where the hut was being built. Eleazar, surprised, looked up at the tree and saw a woman intently working on something in the hut under construction. Building huts was primarily men's work, so Eleazar, finding a woman there unusual, asked. "What are you doing up there?" "What else? Working." She retorted curtly. The woman, who appeared older, had a somewhat cold and rough tone, but it seemed to be her natural habit, without malice. She lightly jumped down from the tree. "Phew~ Time for a little break." She wiped sweat from her sleeve. "What were you doing up there? All I see here is heavy labor for men..." "Hmph, are you looking down on me because I'm a woman!" "No~ That's not it. I seem to have misspoken." Just then, a person from above shouted. "Danna! Tie this to that very top!" The man from earlier, from above, was holding a rope and pointing to a very high branch. "Watch closely, Mr. Swordsman. Those with things hanging can't do this." She pointed at the rope the man was holding and shouted. "Yulio!" The rope quickly wrapped around the branch the man had pointed to and was tied securely. "You. You're a magician." Only then did she nod and reply. "That's right. Though I can only do a few things..." She sat down on a tree stump. Then, she habitually took out a leaf-tobacco and put it in her mouth. Her smoking figure somehow made observers feel a sense of emptiness. "Why did you come here?" He asked because even a magician with humble skills wouldn't usually have much trouble settling down anywhere. "What good does knowing that do! Did you tell me your story?" Danna retorted curtly. "My apologies. Haha. There's no reason not to. I'm looking for a child about 10 years old." Only then did Danna ask back, with a slightly apologetic tone. "When did you lose him? And your wife?" "Haha~ He's not my son. He's a friend's son." She asked, surprised. "Foolish, you. Are you traveling like this for such a reason? That's a foolish thing to do. To search for a child in this war-torn land? And a friend's child at that... How great a friend must he have been." "Well. I made a promise to a friend." Eleazar replied with a light laugh. Then she said, with an incredulous look. "What a truly good-natured friend. Do you even know how the world works? Alright. Then shall I tell you my story? Because the world I've experienced doesn't seem so easy. But don't tell anyone." "Is it that secretive? Then you don't have to tell me." Thereupon, Danna let out a dry, laugh-tinged sigh and continued. "No. I also want to complain about my lot to someone. And you seem like a good person for it... My intuition is quite accurate, you see. Good people like you are hard to find these days. Who knows? Maybe you'll even..."

"Who would comfort me? If I talk about it here, all I'll hear are complaints that their own lives are more pathetic." She said, smiling like that, and sat down in the shade of a tree. "It won't be interesting to hear..." She made a face for a moment, as if wondering if she should have started the story, then continued. "I lived in the back alleys of the city with my poor wizard father, and a younger brother and sister, each exactly one year apart from me. My mother passed away when I was 10, and my younger brother was very weak and often sick, and he wasn't a great wizard either. He was probably similar to me. You know, binding, unbinding, opening, attaching... that kind of thing... My father drank a lot. He drank even though he knew it was hard to afford my brother's medicine. I hated my mother for dying first, and how much I hated my father..." She paused for a moment.

"Well, I don't think things were bad in my life up to that point. The problem was, one day my father committed suicide. Damn it, he must have been so incapable that was all he could do. He jumped from the church spire in the middle of the city. From the cross at the top of the spire, he cursed God at the top of his lungs for everyone to hear. At first, I was happy. At least the alcohol expenses would stop. But after I took on his heavy burden, I started to understand my father's

titleEn: What We Should Be Wary Of, Through San
contentEn:
**1. "A murder happened at Sanbon Station!"** Recently, "Sanbon Station" appeared on the real-time search trends. {{IMG:1}}
Since I live in Sanbon, I clicked on it, wondering what was going on. It first appeared on Daum, likely because the news originated from Twitter. The news that an incident occurred at 11:09 AM was exposed on search portals' real-time trends in less than an hour. The content stated that a murder had occurred in Sanbon's central commercial district, and soon after, a photo of a blood-stained floor in the dark was uploaded to Naver blogs. Various stories, such as police lines being set up, were posted, but there weren't many detailed accounts of the incident's full story, newspaper news remained silent, and only social networks were noisy. However, it turned out to be a rumor. It was a fight between homeless people where someone was stabbed with a broken bottle, and the incident ultimately concluded as 'attempted murder,' not 'murder.' While attempted murder and murder are similar in that they deal with the subject of killing, the sense of fear conveyed to people is different. And rumors, embellished by that fear, spread through social networks.

**2. "Fukushima Nuclear Power Plant, Japan is now ruined."** Recently, news about the Fukushima nuclear power plant often appears on timelines with very provocative content. Various news circulates, such as "Japan is already finished," "radioactively contaminated fish from Japan are being distributed," and "Japanese diapers can no longer be used." A certain company selling Mamypoko diapers, which my wife had bought, offered a service where they would visit homes directly to check for radiation with a portable detector, and it reportedly became a huge hit. Regarding Fukushima, an initial post that spread on social networks was tracked by another blogger, who revealed that its contents were largely fictitious. Nevertheless, new nuclear plant news from Japan has once again entered the country, making people anxious, and various unconfirmed stories seem to be circulating.

**3. Key Lessons to Extract from Rumors** You might misunderstand my comparison of Sanbon Station and Fukushima as an attempt to defend the Fukushima nuclear power plant, but it is not. Since I can anticipate the comments, let me start with that defense. In the Sanbon Station incident, both murder and attempted murder actually offer us the same lesson. That is, the threat of murder occurred in the Sanbon area. In fact, it wouldn't have been strange if attempted murder had turned into actual murder. Even if the detailed parts and the fear-embellished aspects were fictitious, the "lesson" remains unchanged. Therefore, the definite lesson regarding the Fukushima nuclear power plant is not reactions like "Japan is ruined" or "the ocean is contaminated and scary," but rather that we must monitor whether our nuclear power plants are safe, whether nuclear power itself can truly be trusted, and whether Japan is genuinely handling the situation properly.

**4. The Reliability of Rumors Acquired Through Social Networks, and the Fading of Lessons** The problem is fear and fiction, which can dilute the lesson. Fear and fiction circulating on social networks often dilute even the lesson itself. By quoting unverified information, the persuasiveness of the argument is actually weakened. That's why the more extreme and provocative a rumor is, the more its veracity should be doubted. Because we have already experienced through various incidents how someone can suffer enormous damage due to such fiction. There have even been cases where people committed suicide or companies went bankrupt. What's even more unfortunate is that media loves to sell spiced-up stories, seasoned with this fear and fiction. This is because many media outlets are now doing business based on clicks and page views. A vicious cycle can occur where absurd rumors on the internet gain credibility again by being reported as news or through statements by celebrities. And sometimes, we make wrong decisions driven by this fear.

I'm attaching a good article to read in relation to this. It's an article by Professor Han Sang-ki titled "How Not to Get Hooked by Rumors on Social Media."

If it's an important matter, I think it's worth taking a moment to cool down and consider it.

titleEn: Evolving Tablets: Modern Humans Have Not Yet Appeared
contentEn:
When the iPad was released, there was a lot of fuss as if the tablet era would immediately begin, but it seems the tablet era hasn't fully opened yet. What's noteworthy recently is rather the tabletization of PCs, specifically Windows tablet PCs. However, looking at the broader trend of tablets, it seems difficult for tablets to truly feel like an 'innovation' to users yet. Regarding this, I'd like to compare tablets with smartphones first, and then discuss the current direction of tablets to explore when tablets will become complete.

**1. The End of Smartphone Evolution is the iPhone**

The evolution of smartphones, in fact, ended with the iPhone. It's said that humans didn't evolve from chimpanzees, but rather chimpanzees also evolved in a different direction from humans to become their complete form. From that perspective, all phones we call smartphones today are, in fact, successors to the iPhone. If we compare it to humans, the iPhone can be considered the beginning of modern humanity. However, Windows CE or Symbian, which existed before it, showed direction but were not perfect devices themselves. And that direction was continuously refined, leading to an explosive increase when the iPhone emerged at a certain technological threshold.

And that direction was precisely in network speed and OS versatility. Network speeds only became usable after going through IMT2000's 2G and reaching 3G. This technological advancement led to a decrease in technology costs, giving birth to affordable data plans. The versatility of the OS, which allowed application installation, led from the emergence of WIPI and Brew to Windows CE and Symbian, ultimately resulting in the appearance of iOS. The concept of a smartphone began very early, but it was the iPhone that sparked an explosive reaction from the public, and the iPhone can be called the first ancestor of modern smartphones.

**2. So, what about the tablet's ancestors and direction?**

According to the above (my self-made) assumption, tablets can also be said to be in an evolutionary stage. From MS's Origami Project to the current iPad, Android tablets, and Windows tablet PCs, various products are appearing, and their continuous development shows several patterns.

The obvious ones are network speed, performance, light weight, and battery life. The next is the combination of high resolution and pen input. So, when will tablets reach a threshold like 3G and iOS for smartphones, and what are they heading towards?

It is precisely the tablet's initial fundamental attributes: books and paper. No one would think that smartphones were created to replace books and paper. But what about tablets? I can clearly state that the ultimate replacement for advanced tablets is paper and pen. Therefore, by considering the attributes of paper and pen, we can envision the form of the 'modern human' tablet.

The attributes of paper are outdoor visibility, excellent resolution, lightness, and affordability. These were the attributes that revolutionized printed materials. Therefore, tablets are gradually evolving towards higher resolutions. It's obvious, but while the iPhone 4 has a pixel density of 326 ppi, the 10.1-inch new iPad has 264 ppi. If it were to be raised to the iPhone 4's level, it means the new iPad's resolution still needs to increase further. This implies that even Full HD (1920*1080) resolution is still insufficient for tablet displays, and ultimately, UHD-class resolution of around 4000 pixels horizontally and 2000 pixels vertically (over 500 ppi) for a 10.1-inch class device can be considered the final goal. Smartphones are already being sold with products in the 400 ppi range.

And this phenomenon means that existing LCD monitors used in work environments will have resolutions far exceeding UHD class.

In the case of pens, Wacom pens can be said to be at the forefront of their evolutionary stage. Actual Wacom drawing pads adopt a crisp, paper-like texture rather than the smooth feel of an LCD screen. Ultimately, if the goal is to resemble the properties of pen and paper, then Wacom pen attributes will be adopted. A surface with a texture similar to paper, and angle detection (found in Intuos-class devices) beyond just pressure sensitivity... Perhaps at that point, pen nibs might even be interchangeable for various textures. Reflecting this, Wacom's Cintiq has already started to appear in 13-inch class models.

{{IMG:1}}

http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=6924847322

[Wacom Cintiq 13HD](http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=6924847322)

Brand
Wacom
Tablet, electromagnetic induction method, 299 x 171mm, 5080lpi, 2048 levels, USB+HDMI, pressure-sensitive pen, wireless pen, ...

[View Review](http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=6924847322&tc=6)

However, both the current Ativ and Cintiq have problems: compared to existing USB-connected tablets, they suffer from severe distortion at the screen corners and slow speeds, giving the impression that they are below the level of a Galaxy S1-class smartphone. However, the development of mobile CPUs like Bay Trail is already foreseen, and I believe Wacom's issues will also be resolved someday. Crucially, their prices will also decrease.

**3. Why aren't tablets useful yet, you ask?**

If you ask why tablets aren't useful yet, I can answer simply: The iPhone of the tablet world hasn't appeared yet. Tablets are still evolving and expanding their reach. And someday, just as feature phones were relegated to drawers, a day will come when PCs disappear, and tablets will largely replace the roles of paper and books.

titleEn: The Software Industry, the Driving Force of the
contentEn:
**1. The Value of the Software Industry in the Spotlight of the Creative Economy**
At the core of the creative economy championed by the current government, software success stories are always prominently featured. By becoming a rule-breaker and creating new markets, the creative economy aims to move away from the traditional hardware and sector-specific industry perspectives, adopting a flexible and diverse approach to industry and business. One of the reasons this is possible is that, unlike hardware which is difficult to fix once released, software is organic and easy to modify. Therefore, businesses and industries suited for software are also difficult to define within traditional frameworks.

**2. A Bleak Software Environment Compared to Its Value**
However, the treatment of the software talents, or developers, who are actually driving this industry, has not been so rosy. Even while Korea was promoting itself as an IT powerhouse, the popularity of computer science departments continuously declined, and the treatment of developers did not significantly improve. Now that the importance of "software" has been recognized after observing overseas examples, the quality and treatment of crucial software talents are actually not very good. In this situation, the government's desire to ignite a venture craze among young people is akin to the Chinese Communist Army's human wave tactics, giving them a single pistol and sending them into battle with rosy optimism, as if the enemies were mere natives. Meanwhile, the opponents are already armed with machine guns. While there's no business like volume, and some good results might emerge amidst it, I also worry about the young people being pushed to the front lines. I also hope that the government's actions are not merely a performance to statistically boost employment rates.

While the value of software is rising globally, it cannot be denied that the seniors in the field also bear some responsibility for Korea's current situation. They focused more on sales than technology and did not properly assess the value of software. One of the purposes of M&A by overseas IT companies is to acquire key software talents from small and medium-sized enterprises. However, in Korea, most cases aim for the company itself, meaning service influence, or databases. The reason for this is that both sellers and buyers undervalue technology. There's a strong perception that "it can be developed internally and made the same way anyway."

Furthermore, the developers' lives, known as "Mon-Tue-Wed-Thu-Fri-Fri-Fri" (working all weekend), also create a strong negative perception. The more depressing fact is that overtime pay is not given for weekends, and this has become normalized. Maintenance costs are not paid, and neither buyers nor sellers even expect maintenance. Consequently, high-quality software is not delivered; only what is minimally desired is provided at the lowest price. This is the biggest risk of outsourced development. And this is also why core competency software should not be outsourced. Outsourcing core business, rather than just initial prototypes or exploratory projects, is foolish. However, in South Korea, due to a focus on short-term results, employees who can secure cheap outsourcing deals are highly valued. It's concerning that few people even consider this a vicious cycle. Unless one is a CEO or CTO, there won't be a brave employee to raise this issue. After all, no foolish employee would raise their hand for something that increases costs.

**3. It's Time to Reclaim Our Livelihood**
In any case, compared to the importance of the software industry, the treatment, capabilities, and perception of developers themselves are not very good. During the dot-com bubble, it created a virtuous cycle until the bubble burst, but since then, I suspect it has only created a vicious cycle.

The problem is that the software industry has become even MORE! important. Therefore, the industry has begun to recognize that it's time to mend this broken bowl (livelihood) starting now.

**1) Developers, Let's Reclaim Our Livelihood Ourselves**
Thus, these movements are materializing, centered around OK JSP, operated by CEO Noh Sang-beom. Among them are the launch of a cooperative, the creation of standard contracts, and guidance for freelance developers.

Some people might have a negative preconception, associating "cooperative" with militant labor unions. Some unions are so powerful they could be called "aristocratic unions," contributing to the worsening working conditions even for non-union members. And no developer would want their services or businesses, built with code like their own children, to be ruined by the activities of such a cooperative.

However, I certainly agree that there should at least be a private organization to represent IT developers. And, it is crucial to make business owners who do not even provide minimal working conditions realize that this is wrong. (In fact, business owners who don't even adhere to those minimums are unlikely to succeed anyway. But many people will suffer in the process until they fail.) While it hasn't officially launched yet, such movements are already underway.

**-- OK JSP's Progress as of June 21, 2013 --**

**2) The Government's Continuous Listening and Interest**
As the saying goes, "it takes two hands to clap," and in response to these movements by developers, the government and politicians have also begun to show interest. Examples include the "love calls" sent to the IT sector by Park Geun-hye and Moon Jae-in during the last presidential election, and more recently, Mayor Park Won-soon's 'Cheongchaek' debate (not a typo for 'policy'; 'Cheongchaek' is the correct term for a debate held for listening). (If at least Seoul City's SI environment improves, the ripple effect would be enormous.)

**“Mayor Park Won-soon, Please Listen to IT Developers”**
[http://www.bloter.net/archives/156783](http://www.bloter.net/archives/156783)

**3. The Software Industry is Refactoring to Drive the Creative Economy Forward Again**
Throughout its lifecycle, all code is not a one-time development but must be continuously maintained to adapt to the environment. In fact, once it's open, that's when it truly begins. However, it seems undeniable that our software industry has been steeped in inertia, doing things the way they've always been done.

Now is the time to refactor to suit the changed environment. I believe this is the way to pass on this industry, inherited from our predecessors, in a better form to our juniors. Isn't that the fundamental principle of development? Simply running and operating an inherited framework (code) is sufficient for operators.

titleEn: Rich100: Affordable, Excellent Sound,
contentEn:
This is my second earphone review. To be honest, I'm pretty much an 'average listener' (someone not sensitive to subtle sound differences). I remember being surprised recently when I received a 200,000 won Bluetooth earphone and realized how much sound quality could differ. This time, I received a request to introduce an entry-level earphone released by T-PEOS, a company that makes Hi-Fi earphones. My first impression is this: {{IMG:1}}
**The price is 18,900 won including shipping... If you calculate the 2,500 won shipping fee, the product itself costs 16,400 won.** This is almost the same price as the lowest price for the QuadBeat, the bundled earphone for the Optimus G, which is known as the king of price-to-performance ratio recently. In terms of design, I don't particularly like the LG logo on the QuadBeat, so I'd say this is a decisive victory over the QuadBeat. It also comes in red and black, so there's a wider range of choices. It's said to be nickel-plated, and the shiny metallic trim looks pretty.

I'm not a professional review blogger, so please bear with the photos. They look pretty in person. Ugh. I'll just add some official product photos.{{IMG:2}} The bundled earphones for my Galaxy S2 were too short, which was a problem, but these are long enough. {{IMG:3}}The length up to the split is a whopping 83cm. A generous length. This should be long enough to put in a bag and extend. If it's too long, you can use the included clip. Besides the main unit, it provides a pouch and foam tips to enhance ear fit.

{{IMG:4}} The accessories are really generous for the price. {{IMG:5}}And tangle-free flat-type earphones
The most important aspect of earphones, sound quality, is indeed incomparable to the Galaxy S2 bundled earphones. However, it feels a bit lacking compared to Hi-Fi earphones costing tens of thousands of won. But that said, it feels like a different class altogether compared to regular bundled earphones. I wanted to compare it with the QuadBeat, but I couldn't get one. According to a review by someone on SEEKO, they even said the QuadBeat felt bland in comparison. The earphones I compared it with were the iPhone's earphones, which are known for good sound quality, and they were quite similar in level. (Because I'm an 'average listener'...) I think this is a good earphone for those who feel the sound quality of their bundled earphones is lacking, or for those who want earphones to plug into their computer, without breaking the bank. I also replaced the earphones for my work laptop with these. Of course, it supports hands-free functionality for smartphones. When listening to music, if you use the hands-free button, one press plays/pauses, and two presses skip to the next song. The saying 'you get what you pay for' is now an old saying. For users like me who frequently break earphones, these affordable and good quality earphones are truly the best choice. (Of course, you shouldn't break them.) **ps. This review was sponsored by TPEOS.**

titleEn: What Yahoo's acquisition of Flickr 1TB and Tumblr means
contentEn:
Yahoo, which had seen a decline in public interest, is reportedly showing a forward-looking stance after a change in CEO.

{{IMG:1}}

http://people.search.naver.com/search.naver?where=people&sm=sme_clk&query=%EB%A7%88%EB%A6%AC%EC%82%AC%EB%A9%94%EC%9D%B4%EC%96%B4&os=229064&ie=utf8

[Marissa Mayer](http://people.search.naver.com/search.naver?where=people&sm=sme_clk&query=%EB%A7%88%EB%A6%AC%EC%82%AC%EB%A9%94%EC%9D%B4%EC%96%B4&os=229064&ie=utf8)

Occupation
Businesswoman, Programmer
Born
1975.05.30 (USA)
Education
Stanford University Graduate School
Affiliation
Yahoo

Amidst this, news broke that Flickr increased its free storage to 1 terabyte and Yahoo acquired Tumblr. While the Tumblr founder becoming a billionaire at a young age is a hot topic, I'd like to talk about what Yahoo is trying to achieve above all else.

**1. What Flickr's 1 Terabyte Means**
**" Store all photos as unlimited originals. "**
{{IMG:2}}
Flickr is not very well-known in Korea, but you only need to remember two things. First, it's a service that allows you to upload original-sized images from your digital camera and view them in various sizes as needed. It's most similar to the photo album feature of N Drive. Second, like Twitter, it allows access to or uploading of Flickr images via various Open APIs. And because of these two features, it's a service that allows you to directly upload images taken with a Samsung Galaxy Camera and view them in an LG Electronics digital album. However, there was one hurdle: paid subscription was required to remove storage limits and fully utilize all features. But now, this hurdle has largely been removed, and charging has been changed to apply only to customers who need more than 1 terabyte or wish to remove ads. This means, instead of 'pay if you want full features,' it's 'we'll only charge very rare heavy users.' Therefore, Flickr's increase in free storage is unlikely to significantly help Flickr's revenue.

But why did Yahoo, which was said to be struggling, take such a bold step, sacrificing revenue? The message to users is just one. It means to store all photos as originals, virtually unlimited, on Flickr. This suggests they saw it as more valuable than paid subscriptions. I think this was an excellent choice for Yahoo. Yahoo may have declined, but it still possesses vast amounts of cash. Therefore, a certain amount of revenue loss can be tolerated. However, what cannot be tolerated is an increase in future uncertainty, i.e., a decrease in membership and usage rates. This was an 'investment' precisely for the latter. Moreover, these investment costs gradually decrease, while the value gained from the investment actually increases. This is because hardware and network costs decrease over time, but the value of user data, which cannot be regained, continuously increases.

**2. What the Tumblr Acquisition Means**
**" Share photos and talk about photos. "**

{{IMG:3}}

http://people.search.naver.com/search.naver?where=people&sm=sme_clk&query=%EB%8D%B0%EC%9D%B4%EB%B9%84%EB%93%9C%EC%B9%B4%ED%94%84&os=943811&ie=utf8

[David Karp](http://people.search.naver.com/search.naver?where=people&sm=sme_clk&query=%EB%8D%B0%EC%9D%B4%EB%B9%84%EB%93%9C%EC%B9%B4%ED%94%84&os=943811&ie=utf8)

Occupation
Entrepreneur
Born
1986.07.06 (USA)
Affiliation
Tumblr

[ Karp, a high school dropout who became a billionaire in his 20s, is another example for the government to cite. ]
What then does the Tumblr acquisition mean? It means for users to attach additional information to the data uploaded on Flickr. Who is in the photo, what they think about this photo – all this data is generated through social network communication.

**3. What Yahoo Aims to Create: A Social Network Service Combining Instagram and Twitter**
**" To gain Yahoo's eyes to see the world through a photo-based social network. "**
Ultimately, Flickr and Tumblr signify Yahoo's intention to gain dominance over photos. And the method will likely be a social network service that combines the features of both Instagram and Twitter.

Why such a focus on photos? Because photos are users' memories. Each user becomes Yahoo's eyes and builds memories for the service.

Memory is said to be divided into unconscious and conscious. The realm of the unconscious also means that it contains all memories we don't consciously perceive. Flickr's original images can be interpreted in this sense. I also use a personal 1-terabyte NAS (Network Attached Storage) to store original images. Most of these images are never looked at again. If I do look at them, rather than seeing highlight moments as with old offline photos, I see continuous shots of scenes from that time. I see various expressions of my child in the same place.

In contrast, Tumblr, or for me currently, Facebook, only uploads highlight moments from my photos. And I carefully add comments and converse with others there. If these two are connected, the original data gains information as highlight data and associated data. Highlight data can extract additional context (hidden information) through relationships with other users and comments.

What results will emerge when this meets recognition technology that extracts objects or information from images, and big data technology for processing large volumes of data? Yahoo will gain eyes to see the world through its users.

The surprising experience of how Facebook recommended those friends to me? You might have that experience with Yahoo. It can identify visual information such as places I've visited, clothes I enjoy wearing, and even the expressions I make when I'm with others. This prediction is the same as what I made for Google Project Glass. Ultimately, it means that global internet services are heading towards the same goal.

**4. What Impact Will It Have Domestically?**
While the interpretation of these two services is the main topic of my post, I'm adding my personal predictions on what impact they will have domestically.

**1) Minimal Impact on Domestic Users**
Upon hearing the news of Flickr offering 1 terabyte, I also struggled last night to move all my NAS data to Flickr. In Internet Explorer, after being redirected to the Korean Flickr main page, attempting to log in brings up a page stating that the feature is not supported due to Yahoo Korea's withdrawal. I managed to get in through Chrome in English. The easiest way seems to be accessing English Yahoo, signing up, and then launching Flickr.

Next, to upload numerous folders from my NAS via Windows Explorer, I installed Photo Gallery from Microsoft Windows Essentials 2012, which supports Flickr integration. To integrate with Flickr, I changed Chrome to my default browser and barely succeeded in authentication. Finally, when I tried uploading from Photo Gallery, the speed was terrible. For me, with over 100 gigabytes of photos, uploading won't be easy. Compared to the easy upload shown by N Drive Explorer, it was too difficult and slow. Therefore, I had no choice but to give it a poor score in terms of usability and speed compared to domestic cloud services like N Drive. In the short term, due to Yahoo Korea's withdrawal, it seems unlikely that general light users will easily access Yahoo Flickr. In conclusion, the impact on domestic users can be said to be minimal.

**2) Will Affect Storage Competition Among Domestic Cloud Services**
However, service providers are expected to show different movements. First, the quickest responses are expected from Google, Facebook, and Dropbox. And these companies also have significant influence over domestic light users. And this will naturally affect cloud services from mobile carriers and portals. While it's difficult to predict the timing, I wonder if it will ultimately lead to effects such as a significant increase in N Drive's storage. Just as Gmail's large mailbox competition significantly influenced the increase in mailbox storage for domestic portals.

titleEn: The Difference Between Project Glass and Mobile Platforms
contentEn:
As I had some interest, I was looking into Google Project Glass. More reliable and meaningful than media reports like newspaper articles is actually Google's official developer site material: [https://developers.google.com/glass](https://developers.google.com/glass)
Surprisingly, domestic bloggers don't seem to have much interest. While researching, I found a few points that are quite different from existing mobile apps, and I'd like to introduce them. My English skills are limited, so please point out any errors.

**1. Provide an experience tailored to the lifecycle: Timeline**

Although I haven't seen much, the timeline is at the very beginning of the developer guide. There must be a reason why it's placed at the front, right? This seems to mean that Project Glass always keeps "time" in mind. What stood out most in mobile was immediacy. It was a user scenario that showed what was needed right away with a single touch. Project Glass seems to go a step further, aiming for a timeline-centric UX that automatically displays content according to the user's lifecycle.

**2. Google's way of displaying content: Card UX**

The most basic UI on smartphones is flicking and scrolling. You swipe left and right to select menus and scroll to read long content. However, Project Glass's UI uses the concept of "cards." You can think of cards as the concept of paging in PC web. The part where this "card" concept is already being used on Android smartphones is Google NOW. Google probably sees cards as the future UX for mobile search.

{{IMG:1}}
{{IMG:2}}[Sample card from Google Now (Galaxy S2) ]{{IMG:3}}
[Sample card from Project Glass (Developer Center) ]

**3. Server-based apps, not client-based apps**
The app market created by the iPhone involved development in a PC environment, review on the market or iTunes, and then users downloading and using them from the market. Google Play also followed the same method.

However, Project Glass can be developed from Google's API Console on the web. This also seems to be why it's not called an SDK, but rather Google Mirror API. This is because it adopts a web app-like approach that calls Google's APIs. All apps must use Google's authentication (OAuth 2.0).

You can think of this like Facebook apps or Naver's social apps. Although Google Project Glass uses the Android OS, it's not an app on top of the OS, but rather an app-in-app form that runs on top of the Google Project Glass platform, which is itself on top of the OS. Whereas on Android smartphones, the launcher also functioned like an app, here the launcher is incorporated into the OS domain. This clearly seems to be a more controlled platform than Apple's iPhone.

**4. No ads allowed, no paid apps either.**

Many people were worried that it would become cluttered with ads. There were even parody videos about that. However, Google does not allow ads on Project Glass. It's even stated that collecting user information for targeted advertising is prohibited, and there are no paid apps.

**5. Can it escape being Google's platform for Google?**

Reading the above, the question arises: can Project Glass truly become a platform with 3rd parties like iTunes or Google Play? It's difficult to say for sure without having seen the actual device yet, but so far, it feels like Google's platform for Google. Isn't it more about exploring the possibilities of wearable computing through various experiments rather than making money here?

Furthermore, the iPhone didn't have an App Store from the beginning. The App Store opened after the platform had spread. A prerequisite for such 3rd-party platforms is the size of the platform's user base. And for that, comfortable and differentiated features and success stories are needed. That's why I also think they might be approaching it cautiously for now. Although it's the same method, given that Facebook and Naver Social Apps are generating revenue, I wonder if Google might also change its policy someday if needed. Until then, I think it's an interesting experimental device. And what cannot be overlooked is that the genesis of the PC, created in a garage, was also an interesting experimental device.

ps. It supports JAVA, Python, and PHP. Those interested should take a look. It seems like tutorials can be tried on the web [https://developers.google.com/glass/quickstart/index](https://developers.google.com/glass/quickstart/index)

**Bonus Clip. If Project Glass becomes a reality? SNL humor lol.**

titleEn: [Vega Iron vs. Galaxy S4] Vega is Still Vega
contentEn:
*** This post is a subjective one about the disadvantages I discovered, which are not well-known, after considering purchasing the Vega due to its design and zero-bezel. I have not mentioned the features heavily promoted by the manufacturer or the pros and cons easily found through a search. (My operating principle is to avoid posts that everyone else writes, based on practical IT knowledge. Please don't ask me to revive reviews that everyone does. Reviewing is not my profession, so I don't have time for it. I didn't get the 'power blogger' badge by posting reviews. I didn't ask Naver to give it to me either. Please consider this more of a buzz than a review. The photos were taken with a phone camera. ****Just refer to news and shopping product descriptions.) **** Please keep this in mind as you read.**** If you want to know my thoughts on the pros and cons of IPS and AMOLED, please refer to the post below.** ****** ****
****Many people pointed out the browser comparison screen, so I've revised it based on the Naver app, which is a 3rd Party app. The Naver app is used by over 10 million people as a browser in Korea. ******** ** Today, I touched the Vega and Galaxy S4 for the first time. What I felt was... Vega is just Vega. Even though I was tired of the Galaxy S4's design, Vega's limitations were clearly felt. **
**1. Galaxy S4 vs Vega Iron**
**1) Almost no difference in grip, same size**
There wasn't much difference in grip. There's a difference of a few millimeters, but the perceived difference is very small, to the point where I felt the sizes were almost identical.
{{IMG:1}}
**[ Iron's cool-looking zero bezel ]**
{{IMG:2}} **[ Horizontal difference is negligible. ]
**{{IMG:3}}
**[ Don't even know if there's a thickness difference, especially since the Galaxy S4 is rounded ]**
**2) Iron is heavier than Galaxy**
When you lift both at the same time, there's a surprising weight difference. The heft of an iPhone with its glass screen was felt in the Vega Iron.
**3) Zero Bezel, Screen Size? Enticed by zero bezel, but usable screen area is smaller.**
When I first saw it, the bezel of the Vega Iron felt pretty. However, upon using it, despite having the same LCD size, the usable screen area felt much smaller and frustrating. This was the difference in feeling brought about by the Galaxy S4 using hardware keys and the Vega Iron occupying a certain area of the screen with software keys.
{{IMG:4}} [ The Galaxy S4 shows more than one and a half lines below Naver's main page. ]
{{IMG:5}} [ **When switching to landscape, due to the right SW area, the width is narrow,**** preventing adaptive web from functioning. Both Naver app and Daum app were tested, but ****the same phenomenon occurred.****]****
****[ The SW keys at the bottom have the biggest impact.** **Of course, they can be hidden. ****However, with the Galaxy S4, the physical key area below is also touchable, making that area feel like a touch input, whereas with the Vega Iron, the bezel area below feels like wasted space.] **
Only the bezel is small; the usable area felt much wider on the Galaxy S4. It didn't have the dazzling vastness I felt when I touched the Optimus G Pro. Is this good enough for a 5-inch screen? After touching the Galaxy S4, my eyes were spoiled...
**4) Slow AF**
The AF was noticeably slower than the Galaxy S4. It felt almost slower than the Optimus G Pro, and for me, with a child, slow AF is a fatal flaw.
**2. Conclusion, Vega Iron is still a budget phone.**
The Iron will likely settle as a budget device. If it's the same price as the Optimus G Pro, I'd have no choice but to pick the G Pro. Although it's compared to the Galaxy S4 in advertisements, it felt like a competitor in a different weight class. Pantech has a long way to go...
ps. This post received no ~~ compensation from Samsung or Pantech. The advantage of such an unvarnished review is that there's no sponsor... Personally, I'll rule out the Iron and compare it with the Opti G Pro... The Galaxy S4 has price pressure.
ps. I criticized Vega... and now I'm being called a Samsung fanboy. For the record, I won't be buying the expensive Galaxy S4. First, refer to this post: [http://fstory97.blog.me/70165998608](http://fstory97.blog.me/70165998608) You might call me an LG fanboy too, but if so, here's another post: [http://fstory97.blog.me/70104625600](http://fstory97.blog.me/70104625600) Some even accuse me of being a part-timer, but I don't run this blog to earn a few bucks. I earn enough money outside of blogging. If you ask me how to wisely purchase a smartphone, I recommend the post below: **This is an article contributed to the expert column of Smart Choice ([http://www.smartchoice.or.kr/](http://www.smartchoice.or.kr/)).** [http://fstory97.blog.me/70164184714](http://fstory97.blog.me/70164184714)
* Lastly... I feel a bit sorry for the Pantech officials, not just Samsung fans. I know they worked hard on development, struggling with far fewer resources compared to Samsung. The Vega Iron is a perfectly good phone. However, since it was specifically compared to the Galaxy S4, I decided to make this comparison post. (Even if it stings for the developers, being compared will likely help Pantech's sales.) I merely posted my personal value judgment. In terms of design and price, it seems like a decent choice. But perhaps I had too high expectations, and I feel it still needs a bit more differentiation.
**ps3. Finally, I will close comments for this post. The reason for closing comments is not that I don't want to hear opinions, but because with over 500 comments, I can't find the notifications for new ones. (Finding them became hell after 300 comments.) For additional opinions, please write them on the guestbook, and I will reply.**
