titleEn: A Proposal for the Direction of the Creative Economy Centered
contentEn:
Several months have passed since the launch of the Park Geun-hye administration, which designated ICT as a strategic industry and aimed to make the creative economy a new growth engine. However, no particular direction is visible, except for the plan to create a central ministry called the Ministry of Future Planning, and it still seems there's no concrete picture of what "creative economy" actually means. Perhaps because of this, it seems the Ministry of Future Planning has even launched a policy contest targeting the general public. Amidst all this, I saw a recent article reporting that the "17-year-old 30 billion won millionaire D'Aloisio project" is starting.

Honestly, the moment I saw the article title, I sighed. Reading the content made it even more pathetic. "SW Promotion Policy Including Coding Diffusion to be Announced in May"
I first encountered computers in the third grade of elementary school and started with BASIC on an 8-bit computer. I also remember taking a Fortran class without knowing English or much about it. However, after middle school, I didn't do much coding, except for DOS batch programs. In middle school, I read books by Alvin Toffler and Bill Gates, which set my direction towards computers. I applied to computer science departments for all my university applications and worked as a developer for several years after graduation until recently transitioning to planning.

Perhaps I'm someone who experienced the "coding diffusion" that the Ministry of Future Planning is now aiming for, ahead of time. But looking back, that path wasn't as fantastic as I thought, and I concluded that I couldn't become a Zuckerberg or Bill Gates as a developer.

Even though I learned to code early and was praised for having many ideas in college, I couldn't easily bring myself to start a business. My alma mater in Seoul produces the most computer engineers in the country, and there were quite a few early development members of well-known companies among its alumni. However, very few of them attempted to start businesses, and most of those early development members, except for those who received some stock, rarely participated in the company's ownership or strategy as "developers." My question here is simple: "If people know 'lifestyle coding,' will a Zuckerberg or D'Aloisio emerge?" I would unequivocally answer "No." Of course, there were engineers with such skills at my alma mater. But none of them thought of creating Facebook just because they had coding skills. Many pursued Samsung Electronics' software membership course, and the friend most envied within our Facebook group is not a Samsung employee but a computer science teacher.

**1. Doubt about the effectiveness of teaching software with success as the goal**

However, like the stories of Bill Gates and Zuckerberg, I agree with teaching software development to children. It's not because being able to develop software, or code, will turn them into Zuckerberg or Gates, making them the workforce (growth engine) the country desires. It's because software development helps children understand the principles of information devices they will constantly encounter throughout their lives, just like learning language or art, and it becomes a means for them to express themselves. Just as the skill of professionals improves when the amateur base grows, the quality of software developers might certainly rise. However, I'm not that optimistic. Why are Korean children obsessed with Korean, English, and Math? It's to get into good universities. Why do they want to go to good universities? To get into good companies. What are the best companies in our society? Samsung Electronics? The Financial Supervisory Service? Computers are in textbooks. The problem is that there isn't much desire to work hard at it. If it were included in university admission points, they would work hard, but I'd bet that coding for exams would just lead to something like the Information Processing Engineer certification exam, which has devolved into a civil service exam prep. My concern is that it might just increase the number of bosses who dismiss development as something anyone can do, and thus disregard quality.

**2. The reason young people can start businesses in Silicon Valley is the presence of high-quality senior developers and mentors**

When Zuckerberg first created Facebook, his biggest concern was stable growth. He believed that if the explosively growing service experienced an outage, the success story would end. What he ultimately did was step away from coding himself and recruit talented individuals. Similarly, the reason developers are the most preferred profession in the United States is not just because Steve Jobs, Bill Gates, and Zuckerberg were developers, but also because developers generally have good working conditions, and the salaries of skilled developers are sky-high. But what about the situation in South Korea? Where are the skilled developers now? As I mentioned earlier, they are pursuing software membership courses from university to develop the Galaxy. Therefore, it's not easy for venture companies to create competitive products. Furthermore, can developers even work past their 40s in large corporations? That's also not easy. Around the time they turn thirty and look towards forty, my peers have similar worries. How can we attract these highly paid, house-poor fathers of two children to ventures? The problem of the creative economy must start here.

**3. Look at the soil, not just the fruit**

To bear beautiful fruit, good soil is needed. I wish we would abandon the short-sighted view of only looking at the "creative economy" as a temporary fruit. Creativity cannot be taught by rote. The very word "rote learning" is the opposite of creativity. I understand the government's desire to lead and achieve results, but the venture and internet service industries are where hundreds, even thousands, of companies pursue such goals and fail. For just one blockbuster service that we know of to emerge, countless failed attempts are necessary. Therefore, what's important is valuing failure and providing resources for challenges. Currently, South Korea doesn't even have proper resources for challenges. And those resources come from fertile soil. I'll skip over why this soil has become barren, as it would probably require a much longer essay. Perhaps, if you show a little will and listen to the voices of industry insiders, you'll hear stories about why the soil is barren.

**3.1. The way to create soil, the resources for creation are surplus and people.**

Creation arises from surplus. It happens when unexpected combinations of tasks or knowledge occur beyond predefined work. To explore or execute paths no one has taken, there must be no pressure to stick only to assigned paths. However, Korean society is overflowing with pressure. Students are pressured that if they don't study well, they won't get into university and their lives will fail, preventing them from pursuing other interests. University students focus on grades and specs for employment, and company employees work all-nighters. Such surplus is a luxury. Especially in South Korea, where developers are known for intense work, it's a profession far from creativity. Prohibition of employment in the same industry. Prohibition of side jobs. Inventions during employment belong to the company. In such a situation, can workers truly be creative? With current service schedules, children might forget their fathers' faces—how can there be creativity? Moreover, in South Korea, where people struggle with debt from graduation until their children marry, there isn't much room for such leisure. Surely, it's not about squeezing more time to be creative, is it? In Korea and its industries, where prices are determined by working hours and headcount, this sounds like a story from a distant land. To create fertile soil, surplus must occur, and costs should not be cut to create it. Ultimately, it means increasing the cost invested in people, and this cost must be invested in surplus that doesn't directly lead to production.

**3.2. The government's role is that of a platform operator**

Will launching large-scale projects, selecting skilled contractors, giving them work, and paying them generously improve the soil? It would be better than paying stingily, at least. But where would that increased cost flow in the current subcontracting structure? Let's apply this to an app market like Apple's iTunes. Suppose the government allocates funds for browsers, restaurant reviews, search, and social networks to revitalize iTunes, and announces project bids for market titles. It also sets the scale of eligible bidders and requires only minimum quality. But in the market, a project announced as a 10 billion won, 100-person project, open only to companies with over 100 employees, was actually a 1 billion won, 10-person project. It's natural for large companies with over 100 employees to win this and subcontract it downwards.

Apple didn't define what to do, how much to pay, or the qualifications. The iTunes market's approach was to effectively connect consumers with needs and producers, significantly cutting out intermediate distribution margins. Recently, it even established a policy prohibiting one top app from boosting other apps. This partly means Apple wants to keep the strong publishers' distribution margins (like Kakao or Naver) for itself, but conversely, it also means Apple will maintain an appropriate level while providing more opportunities for small businesses. (Of course, I'm not sure how well this is working. ㅡㅡ)

The government's role must be that of a platform operator. It must honestly admit that a single government (or company) is not smart enough to lead the IT industry. Even smart people in the IT industry cannot predict everything and get everything right. There are simply people who, through immense diversity and competition, were lucky enough to get many things right. Therefore, the government needs to approach this as an ICT industry platform operator. It should connect market needs with producers, provide mesh-up tools to facilitate easy collaboration between businesses, and ensure a healthy flow of collaboration and competition. And it needs to monitor and invest against market diversity being harmed, or concentration leading to unfair competition or collusion.

**3.3. Rather than a Fast Follower Strategy, a highly flexible personalized and future-oriented customized strategy**

The government seems too fixated on the examples of Silicon Valley in the United States. It tries to fast-follow them. The problem is that we and they are fundamentally different, and the path we need to take is too long. And by the time we become identical to them, the ICT market will have been overturned several times. Therefore, a customized strategy that understands the current situation and predicts the future is needed. Thus, when formulating and deciding on policies, I hope that the current situation and future changes are always considered together.

How long will the current mobile-centric market last? Even when our foundation is laid, will the center still be mobile? Flexibility is also very important. Among development methodologies, XP (Extreme Programming) places execution and flexibility at its core. It's a method of acting first, quickly acknowledging and correcting mistakes, and finding the right path. This is a suitable strategy for unpredictable situations. And the ICT environment resembles this. Please abandon the belief that you can decide something at the beginning of your term and stick with it until the end. It's more important to have a thorough process that continuously measures performance, coolly acknowledges mistakes, and allows for corrections at any time. To do so, performance measurement and monitoring are most crucial. Please open your ears wide. Therefore, when creating actual services, measurement tools must be developed alongside them, and the proportion of this cost is quite significant.

**4. A creative economy centered on software is a people-centric economy, not a corporate (group)-centric one.**

Overall, this phenomenon is not just due to ICT itself, but also to the societal changes brought about by ICT. Decentralization is occurring more than centralization, and the value of individuals is being strengthened. Centralized approaches of schools or governments, as in the past, are now likely to lose competitiveness. I predict that by the time of our grandchildren (around 2050?), schools as we know them, with their centralized education, will disappear. What should the Ministry of Education do then? Businesses are already aware of this and are contemplating their survival. It is time for the government to envision a future government and policy framework suitable for this era.

titleEn: Facebook: The Foretold Launcher War Has Begun
contentEn:
News has arrived that Facebook has created a launcher. {{IMG:1}}
A while ago, I briefly talked about Dodol Launcher at NHN's mobile camp, and Daum also seems to be strategically partnering with Buzz Launcher to enter the launcher market. Launchers suddenly became HOT? What's going on? I'd like to talk about that.

**1. Weren't there launchers before?** In fact, I've mentioned launchers twice before on my blog. And those two posts could serve as a starting point to examine the changes in the current launcher market.

**1) Launchers that were gaining attention early on as service providers sought to approach platforms**

This was a post where I seriously discussed launchers. I argued that launchers are the best service for service providers who cannot create an OS to penetrate the platform market.

**2) However, launchers were difficult.**

There was an incident in Korea that poured cold water on the potential of launchers: Daum's removal of its launcher. Around this time, Naver App's market share soared dramatically. I explained the reasons were that services should not be device-dependent, and that launcher services are too difficult.

**2. But what has changed, and why launchers again?** So why have launchers re-emerged? I believe both cases 1) and 2) above have implications. In particular, I also think the reasons why Daum had to abandon its launcher in case 2) have changed somewhat.

**2.1. Decrease in Negative Reasons**
**1) Android's insane market share, device dependency is also okay**
Android's market share in South Korea is truly staggering. Globally, Android is also a winner. Furthermore, emerging markets are booming, and as iOS is rapidly losing ground, Android is becoming the de facto standard. This is why surprised manufacturers are now introducing alternative OSes like Tizen and Firefox. As a result, the factor "services should not be device-dependent," which I discussed in 'Why did Daum App abandon its launcher?', has significantly weakened. Thus, the reasons not to do it have decreased.

**2) Has launcher installation increased? Still no.**
It doesn't seem so. According to Google Play data, Go Launcher has between 50 million and 100 million installations worldwide, and since users install on multiple devices, it had about 6 million unique users in the US as of mid-August 2012. In other words, it seems this aspect hasn't improved.

**2.2. Increase in Importance and Availability of Positive Reasons**
In addition to the fundamental reason of being able to dominate the first screen and user UX, just like on PCs, which I mentioned in my [first post (](http://fstory97.blog.me/70099119358)[The Solution for Korean Portals to Beat Mobile Google, Daum App)](http://fstory97.blog.me/70099119358), additional reasons have emerged.

**1) Emergence of Devices with Sufficient Performance**
Even if launchers wanted to fully utilize user UX, past smartphones had very clear limitations due to device performance. If a launcher became heavy with a flashy UI, other apps would not function properly. However, with quad-core processors becoming commonplace in today's smartphones, there's now spare performance, and the desire for beautiful UIs has increased. This means the era has arrived where we can realize the experimental and wonderful UX that we only dreamed of.

**2) Emergence of Cases Where Apps Become Platforms**
I did talk about apps being able to become platforms in my first post, but at the time, there were no proper examples. But now... Kakao and Line have emerged. Apps have shown how to create a secondary ecosystem on top of the existing ecosystem with 3rd-party apps. Dodol Launcher addressing this with wallpapers and themes is the same case as Kakao addressing it with emoticons, and Facebook will probably benchmark Kakao Games.

**3. The Launcher War Has Just Begun. Launchers Will Get Even Hotter.**
The launcher war has just begun. Frankly, what I found most incomprehensible about Samsung Electronics was the neglect of TouchWiz. While I suspect the relationship with carriers was the most serious reason, now there's an excuse to work on TouchWiz. If carriers see Facebook doing it, there's no reason to stop manufacturers. **It's obvious that manufacturers' and carriers' launchers will also jump into the platform war.** Meanwhile, Google will be smiling comfortably. ^^ It seems the advantages brought by an activated open platform are this powerful. Let's look forward to more beautiful and smarter launchers.

titleEn: The 320 Hacking Inc
contentEn:
** 1. Ignorant South Korea Wandering in Search of the Culprit** Yesterday, there was a nationwide system failure. I won't call it a nationwide hacking incident. While only a few companies were actually hacked, these systems affected other dependent systems, causing the failure. Regarding this, South Korean political newspapers are applying their usual ideological convergence rule, diligently debating whether North Korea was responsible, but none of that matters. What matters is that it was breached, and that led to 'damage' (the failure). Whether it was Whois, a North Korean cyber warrior, an alien Super Saiyan, or even an industrial spy from the US or China, or even the elementary school student next door, the effect and threat are the same. What's important is the fact that our country's internet security is lax. To the media outlets claiming North Korea was responsible, I ask that you absolutely!!! include a demand for the conversion of defense spending into ICT security budgets in your editorials. Please drop any thoughts of just creating animosity for political gain.
** 2. Ignorant South Korea Wandering in Search of a Scapegoat** Secondly, the circumstances of this incident are that malware was distributed through the internal network using a PMS system, and the narrative is now shifting towards a witch hunt against the company that developed this PMS system and the security solutions installed on each PC. While it cannot be said that they bear no responsibility, I want to discuss a more fundamental issue. To make security companies scapegoats would be to ignore the very significant problems in our perception up until now.
** 3. The Real Culprit and Responsible Party is Ignorant South Korea Itself** First, I'll share a screenshot of a conversation I saw on Facebook with someone from a security company.

[> It's long, so I'll fold it. Company, service, and real names have been redacted.](https://blog.naver.com/PostView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=70163324003&redirect=Dlog&widgetTypeCall=true&noTrackingCode=true&directAccess=false#)

[└ Fold](https://blog.naver.com/PostView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=70163324003&redirect=Dlog&widgetTypeCall=true&noTrackingCode=true&directAccess=false#)

 Some might think this is an excuse from a security company, while others might find it understandable.  The current problems I perceive are largely twofold.
**  1) The Security Industry Spreading Solution-Omnipotence and South Korea Believing It**  Fundamentally, even with ironclad security, there's always a possibility of a breach. First and foremost, the people operating the system are the most basic security vulnerability. Humans aren't perfect. And the programs they create aren't perfect either. When a bug is discovered, an attack exploiting the security flaw before it's patched is called a zero-day attack, and there are rumors that it was used in this attack. The problem is that there's no perfect way to solve this.  However, we actually believe there is. And security companies sell solutions claiming they exist. While it's a difference between a salesperson's and a technician's perspective, one excellent system operator is better than one excellent security solution. And the greatest quality an excellent system operator must possess is not trusting solutions. This starting point is wrong. If you buy this solution, you can save the cost of an excellent system operator who would demand a high salary, and you can even tolerate the inconvenience of that demanding system operator tackling everything you do – how much like a dream solution does that sound? And we have the illusion that spending money once will be the end of it, rather than continuously incurring costs for a person. And the purchasing team that bought this excellent solution might even receive an incentive. And the sales teams in the security industry will diligently spread this myth, which helps their revenue. ** 2) The Core of Security is the Process After a Breach** And one of the problems that arose in this incident is the fact that even services not destroyed due to dependencies were halted. What I mentioned earlier is that the core of security assumes that breaches can happen. Making sure that even if breached, daily life is not disrupted, and minimizing damage – that is the core of security. This means that security is not just about purchasing solutions, but about implementing enterprise-level security governance.  Of course, this doesn't mean venture companies also need this. The degree of risk tolerance varies with scale. A solo developer cannot solve this. For such venture companies, applying minimal solutions might be the most cost-effective. While recent cloud and mesh-up services are not a panacea, they are similar in the context of increasing agility. However, for already established companies, it means they have reached a stage where they must turn their attention to security if they don't want to suddenly collapse at some point. And venture companies using mesh-up and cloud services should also consider some form of backup for the worst-case scenario.  Just as South Korea's banking computer networks would have various backup measures to recover even if they were all wiped out.
** 4. The Barn That's Never Fixed Even After Losing the Cow Every Time: South Korean Security** From my perspective, South Korea's security currently seems to gain attention briefly when an incident occurs, only to revert to its original state. As China's industry develops, more hackers will be trained. And as South Korea develops, the fruits of hacking will become more tempting, exposing it to more attacks. South Korea carries the stigma of being a transit point for hackers worldwide. Is this truly an IT powerhouse? Insurance is taken out to prepare for major future accidents. And insurance becomes more meaningful the more you have. And South Korea has more than you might think. Faster, faster, cheaper... I think it's time to change the paradigm. Otherwise, you'll be wiped out in one go, just like this time. In fact, there was news recently about the theft of accredited certificates. Some people say it's fine because accredited certificates are encrypted, but is there any way to be sure whether hackers have decrypted them or not? And if hackers target just one or two people with social engineering techniques and only find out the password for an already obtained accredited certificate, decrypting the certificate is not impossible. There's also this saying: we trust encryption too much, but if there's a hacker who has cracked an encryption method, they wouldn't reveal that fact. Would a thief boast that they have a master key that can open all bank vaults in our house? Ultimately, security is just a matter of probability. South Korea, isn't it time to fix the barn?

titleEn: SMSC 2013 Smart Marketing Strategy Conference
contentEn:
**Title: SMSC 2013 Smart Marketing Strategy Conference**[http://www.inews24.com/smsc/2013](http://www.inews24.com/smsc/2013)
**Subtitle: The Future of Social Mobile Platforms**
**Venue: Korea Science and Technology Center**

**Date: March 5, 2013, 9:30~17:30**
**Organizer: iNews24 Co., Ltd.**

Sharing a review of the event/training I attended the day before yesterday. Some commonly covered or well-known content has been omitted, and I've added some personal notes in bold.
**Session 1. Changes in the Global Mobile Platform Market**
 1) Potential Success Factors for Apple, Google, and MS Platforms
   - Apple: First Mover / iTunes music leverage effect / Securing competitiveness for continuous competition
   - Google: Fast Follow / Open source, strategy to marginalize other platforms with a duopoly strategy against Apple / Allied forces strategy (devices, manufacturers, mobile carriers)
   - MS: Over 10 million VB developers worldwide / Office, business laptop demand / Direct release of low-cost devices
**   Personal Note: I'm not sure if 10 million VB developers is such a big strength. I understand it's based on C# development, so perhaps including C++ developers would have been better.**
** 2) Mobile Platform Issues by Industry Sector**
   - Mobile Carriers: Competition with device manufacturers and market / Lack of killer apps to replace voice calls / Success of their own app stores
   - OS Developers: Competition with Apple / OS market share / Securing 3rd Party developers
   - Device Manufacturers: Competition with Apple / Binary choice between Android and Windows Mobile / Launching their own app stores
   - Developers: Limitations beyond a certain scale / Platform selection and focus / Cross-platform efficiency (HTML5, etc.)
** 3) Expected Changes in Mobile Platforms from 2013 Onwards**
   2009~2012: Apple vs Android
   2013~     : Multimedia Sector [Apple (weak) vs Android (strong)]
               Business Sector [Android vs Windows]
**   Personal Note (Summary): Up until 2012, in the war between Apple and Android, Android caught up with Apple through a fast-follow strategy and gained the upper hand in market share. From 2013, the competition in mobile platforms, expanded into the business sector, is expected to be a battle between Android and Windows.**
 - Apple's market share is expected to drop to 10-20%, with Google and MS splitting the remainder.
 - Service platforms built on top of major platforms, like Line and Kakao, will emerge to lead or disrupt the market.
** 4) Q&A**
   - Will Tizen with HTML5 take off?
         => Negative view. Few businesses other than Samsung are interested (even Intel isn't very active), and Samsung's investment is not as large as expected (about 1 billion KRW in each of 80 countries).
   - How about the Kakao platform?
        => There's a worrying trend of reverting to a vertical platform like MCP.
**   Personal Note (Summary): In the case of the Kakao platform, while I agree it has the characteristics of a vertical platform, I believe it has a complementary relationship with the overly expansive Google Play (to be posted later).**

**Session 2. KT Mobile Platform Strategy**
**1) KT's Future Platform Strategy**
    - Expansion of CP targets: Local/In-house -> Third-party/Global
    - Expansion of products: KT Sellers -> Real Goods (physical) business partnerships
    - Layer independence: Device/Network dependency -> Independence
    - Change in customer approach: Viral/Benefit-centric -> Interactive personalized services (Big Data, personalization)
**Aside: There was nothing particularly special. In summary, KT's platform aims to break its dependence on its own infrastructure-based businesses, expand into physical goods business platforms, and leverage big data.**

**Session 3. SKT Social & Mobile Platform Strategy**
**1) Characteristics of Platform Business**
    - Winner take it all: Monopoly by the winner
     **Aside: I believe niche markets also exist in platform businesses, so I think it's difficult to define platforms solely by "winner take it all."**

**2) Big Data Trend Environment**
    - Number of devices, internet users, data explosion

**3) SKT's Platform Businesses**
    - SKT Digital Marketing Platform: Social network analysis marketing platform
    - Geo Vision Gallery: Region-based marketing platform
    - Big Data Platform:
     Collection of various source data (mobile devices, SK affiliate information, external data) -> Storage (distributed storage) -> Analysis -> Data provision (OLAP, OpenAPI, Download)
    - NFC Platform: Social, location-based
      **Aside (Summary): SKT aims to build a big data platform based on various data it can secure, and sell it as a B2B marketing tool.**
**The example photo shown analyzed a user's Naver web visit history, which I believe violates net neutrality.**
**{{IMG:1}}**
**Legally, processing data not specific to an individual to create rules might not be an issue, but it seems problematic for a network provider to analyze such packets for commercial purposes without consulting the user and service provider.**
**Technically, this constitutes sniffing. It didn't seem much different from a telephone company wiretapping and using call content for marketing.**
**If such attempts increase, I think service providers should encrypt packets. Big data's most sensitive aspect, which needs to be addressed, is user consent.**

-- Lunch, and came in late --
**Session 4. N-Screen and U+AD Advertising Platform**
**1) N-Screen Advertising Platform Presentation**
   - Geo-targeting, big data, high-efficiency advertising
   - Digital Signage Advertising Platform
     : The effectiveness of digital signage advertising is currently judged only by exposure, leading advertisers to doubt its efficacy.
    **Aside (Summary): I arrived late and couldn't hear everything. It was mainly about advertising platforms using location-based push and digital signage, and how these ads increase efficiency through big data-based user analysis. User consent was emphasized more compared to the SKT presenter.**

**Session 5. Online Marketing Strategy and Cases Using YouTube**
**1) YouTube's Current Status and Changes**
    - Where all hot issues exist (e.g., Gangnam Style)
    - Cross-platform encompassing 3 screens
    - Overwhelming No. 1 as a video platform
    - Evolution from a UGC platform to Web TV
    - Strengthening channel features (subscriptions)
    - Where broadcasts can be accessed before TV (This seems related to the effectiveness of the advertising platform mentioned later.)
 **2) YouTube Users, Content Consumption Habits of Generation C**
    - Curators (users who select and recommend content from too much content)
    - Creation (smartphones lower the barrier to creation)
    - Sharing (viral, spread of SNS)
    - Community (mobile, social)
**3) Reasons to Market on YouTube**
    - Sufficient Pool and targeting possible
     : Global platform
     : 15 million users as of 2012 (seems to refer to domestic Android users)
     : Login-based customer segmentation (device-based wasn't mentioned, but seems possible)
    - Precise ad effect analysis possible at low cost
     : For TV, it's difficult to know the effect after execution; YouTube allows real-time, specific user response tracking, reducing trial and error for expensive TV ad campaigns.
      (This seems to be related to the position of being able to access broadcasts before TV.)
    - Platform where virality is possible across all platforms
 **4) TrueView**
     : Delivering personalized ads via ad skipping
     - Delivers relevant ads to users at the beginning of video viewing, allowing them to skip. By analyzing the relevance between skipped ads and users, it identifies suitable target users.
     **\* Aside (Summary): It largely explained YouTube's evolution into broadcasting and its suitability as an advertising platform. The ability to measure video ad effectiveness at low cost, reducing TV ad trial and error, and targeted advertising using user analysis via ad skipping were key. YouTube has already created a higher-level advertising platform compared to current UGC platforms and simple DA-level video ads. There's nothing more to say than "they're doing well."**

**Session 6. Naver App Store, Total Supporters for Domestic App Developers**
**1) Purpose of Naver App Store**
   - Revenue (not very important), search for information users want, win-win with 3rd Parties (extending the lifecycle of apps that quickly disappear from trends and finding win-win points)
   - Naver's own apps are completely excluded from Naver App Store rankings.
   - Plans to provide a total solution including IAP and marketing tools.
   - Multi-platform store supporting iOS and Android.
**Aside: Note-taking stopped during Session 6 due to battery drain ㅜㅜ. Thanks to that, I bought a Windows Atom tablet, W510, which supposedly lasts 18 hours. (Review to follow later)**

**Session 7. Social/Mobile Platform Status and Outlook**
**Aside: I expected Tizen talk, but they talked about other things, so I don't remember what I heard... Tizen is reportedly difficult to mention due to security issues. ChatON, DLNA function, AllShare, S Cloud were presented.**
**Every time I see a manufacturer's presentation, I feel that while they diligently build service lineups, they lack talent in delivering services to users. I think it's fundamentally wrong to expect users to go to [Settings] to do something.**
**In fact, "Settings" is the least clicked menu among all menus, so the very idea that you have to click Settings to do something is already an error. How many people have ever clicked the Settings on their TV?**

**Session 8. Vertical Photo SNS Expansion Strategy Using 'Cymera'**
**1) Plastic Surgery Camera App Based on Face Recognition and Image Processing**
    - Popular among women
    - Secured 5 million users
   **2) Plans to reduce dependence on Cyworld and expand into an independent SNS app.**
**Aside: It seems more difficult than expected, as it doesn't have an overwhelming advantage over Pudding/Naver Camera/LINE Camera in Korea. First, the problem is the lack of storage space like N Drive and an independent SNS. Apps that create effects or specific types of photo images have low technical hurdles and are easy to abandon. The number of photos taken isn't as important as photos saved on the service for lock-in effect, but Cymera hasn't secured this, so its prospects don't look very bright. SK Comms is a bit frustrating... I wonder if something will come out of SKP... The revamped T Store has improved, though.**

**Session 9. Kakao's Marketing Platform Strategy and Plus Success Cases**
**1) Kakao's Current Status**
   - Mobile-specialized company
   - Holds the largest social graph in Korea
   - No. 1 in mobile user time share
**Aside: There were some subtle remarks, presumably targeting Naver, such as statements inferred from PC UVs. Considering Naver hasn't dominated SNS and messaging, I personally think Naver is doing surprisingly well. Comparing time share between search apps and messaging apps, messaging apps are naturally overwhelming... However, it's undeniable that KakaoTalk is an essential app on mobile.**
   - Ecosystem, win-win company: Plus Friend, Gift하기 (Gifting), Emoticons, Story/Story Platform, KakaoLink, Game하기 (Gaming), KakaoPage
   - Rapid growth, aiming for 100 million this year.
   **2) Plus Friend Upgrade**
   - Interactive user participation possible:
    Existing one-way push-based Plus Friend has been modified to allow interaction through chat window functions, enabling event execution.
   **Aside: LINE had such bots from the beginning, and I predicted in an old post that Kakao would definitely follow this feature... It hit the mark again. Good things seem to be copied by each other.**
   - Increased advertiser freedom with a more dynamic and flexible home screen.
**3) Kakao Story Plus**
   **- Brand Account: Unlimited friends, ability to distribute user stories to the news tab, pricing undecided.**
**Aside: What will sell on Kakao Story, which is becoming a parenting forum? I expect mainly household goods and parenting products. I question whether marketing will work well on a closed SNS like Kakao Story, where privacy needs are high. Game messages are already annoying... Seeing ads on the Story timeline would be really irritating. If it does work, it would be a highly effective advertising platform with high costs and high returns. Rewards must be clear for virality to move, and if virality works, it explodes instantly... Also, I have a slight doubt whether KakaoTalk's Plus Channel and Kakao Story Plus, which use the same social graph, might cannibalize each other.**

**End of intense summary. It was a good conference.**

titleEn: The Ownerless Mobile Carrier Frequency War
contentEn:
**1. New 1.8Ghz Frequency Allocation, Interests of the 3 Mobile Carriers**
I recently came across an article about who will acquire the 1.8Ghz frequency. It stated that if KT secures this frequency, it can gain an advantage in the speed competition. U+ must secure it for international compatibility. SKT, not wanting KT to have a speed advantage, would rather support U+ if they can't get it themselves. And, of course, the 'government' will decide who gets this frequency.

From the perspective of frequency management efficiency, KT, which has adjacent bands, would be the right choice. However, for the sake of balancing competition among the three mobile carriers, U+ could be seen as the right choice.

**2. Frequency is Money. But Who Owns the Frequency?**
In 2011, SKT successfully bid approximately 1 trillion won for the 1.8Ghz frequency band for its LTE business. Of course, this went into the national treasury, right? Frequencies are generally put up for auction, where the company offering the highest price is awarded the frequency.

However, I want to raise a question here: "Whose is the 'frequency' that the government sells to companies for money?" Looking at the perspectives above, all arguments, except for KT's claim that it's needed for better quality service, are about a "business" perspective. Which company will succeed or fail in the mobile telecommunications business... and which can pay more money...

Let's reconsider. Companies operate to make a "profit." The government's and mobile carriers' view of frequency is that of a "golden goose," and they are only presenting arguments about how much money to pay for this goose. And while the "frequency" is an invisible golden goose, in reality, it is the public's "mobile phone fees."

So, who owns the "frequency"? Or rather, who owns the "government" that sells the "frequency"? Naturally, it's the people.

**3. Forget the Balance of the Three Carriers; We Must Examine Who Benefits the Frequency's Owner.**
Recently, during the presidential election, "mobile phone fee reduction" was a hot topic. Yet, they are talking about selling frequencies again. In fact, frequency is the biggest carrot to tame mobile carriers. If the people are the owners of the government, then I hope they adopt a frequency policy for the people.

The focus should be on which mobile carrier creates more beneficial rate plans for the public, and what useful services they can create for the public and industry with this frequency. If the logic is simply, "If we give it to A, B and C will weaken, so we should give it to C," then we cannot move a single step forward from the current mobile carrier "chicken game."

Mobile carriers' annual marketing expenses exceed 5 trillion won. This is enough to buy NHN, and an enormous cost that could give 100,000 won per year to every person in South Korea.

But how much benefit has actually gone back to the customers? And how much money have profitable mobile carriers taken from customers' pockets? Of course, the marketing market might take a hit, but even these simple indicators reveal the problems with mobile carriers.

I believe that giving frequency not to maintain **balance among operators or to the highest-bidding company, but rather to an operator who volunteers to "break the rules" by offering benefits to users, is the way to serve the people, who are the true owners of the frequency.**

And that will ensure a stable foundation for the newly opened highway of wireless internet services, upon which many industries will emerge. It would be a gift to "ICT venture companies" and the "people," which is the very reason for the existence of the "Ministry of Future Planning and Science."

titleEn: What's Next for Kakao Games?
contentEn:
The biggest change in mobile in 2012 was the emergence of the Kakao platform. Moreover, what most definitively cemented Kakao as a platform was the emergence of Kakao Games, epitomized by Anipang and Dragon Flight. How are Kakao Games changing in 2013, and how will they change? Based on the current situation, I'd like to write a 'novel' – my specialty. ^^

**1. The Current State of Kakao Games in 2012**
Kakao Games achieved immense success. While not a global success, the ripple effect of that success was so significant that it even influenced Google Play. Games that took off on Kakao earned more money than several major game developers combined, making it a tremendous success. And Line, which adopted this model directly, also achieved great success.

{{IMG:1}}
[ Source : [http://blog.appannie.com/app-annie-index-january-2013/](http://blog.appannie.com/app-annie-index-january-2013/) ]**In summary, Google Play is the LINE and Kakao version.**

**2. Kakao Games: Red Oceanization of a Single Channel and Big Brother**
However, this success tends to be concentrated on a small number of games. This is because Kakao Games uses a simple list format. This list format allowed a few games to achieve immense success. And many games lined up. Ultimately, since Kakao makes the selection, it somehow reminds me of SKT's old WIPI Market.
{{IMG:2}}
[ Image Source : [http://www.bloter.net/archives/124014](http://www.bloter.net/archives/124014) ]

**3. Evolution into a Market**
I don't think Kakao will continue in that form. It will eventually transform into a market. I wonder if it will take the form of having basic categories like Popular/Recommended/New? Actually, after writing this post, I realized I was late to the party. I checked KakaoTalk today, and it had indeed changed that way. ㅡoㅡ (Ah, I should have written this sooner.)
{{IMG:3}}
**[ It's a market.. ]**

However, there's still no search or review function. If these are added, it will likely become a complete independent market structure. If this happens, Google Play in Korea will become merely an infrastructure concept, providing simple app storage and IAP.

**4. Will KakaoTalk's Game Revenue Increase Further?**
However, will KakaoTalk's game revenue increase further? It's difficult to give a definitive answer. I believe blockbuster success stories like Dragon Flight and Anipang have already reached a significant portion of the game revenue that KakaoTalk can achieve. This is because the value comes from the nature of the platform rather than the game's inherent quality. Therefore, I lean towards the opinion that even if it evolves into a market, KakaoTalk game revenue will not skyrocket. Instead, it's more likely that greater focus in the game sector will lead to higher profits from Google's IAP. I'm not sure if the contract terms for joining KakaoTalk include giving a certain portion of IAP revenue to KakaoTalk. For game developers, this would be a double burden...
{{IMG:4}}[ Source : [http://blog.appannie.com/app-annie-index-january-2013/](http://blog.appannie.com/app-annie-index-january-2013/) ]**You can consider South Korea and Japan as Kakao and Line, respectively..**

Ultimately, it seems that the fact game developers need to refocus on making good games, rather than relying on the power of social platforms, remains unchanged.

**5. KakaoTalk Games' Breakthrough: Global Expansion**
However, what if KakaoTalk's own distribution power grows? KakaoTalk's game revenue will increase. LINE would be a prime example. Perhaps, like Naver App Store, it could offer independent downloads and secure apps that don't use Google's IAP, thus avoiding the 30% revenue share with Google? However, I don't think that will happen. If KakaoTalk's challenge is global expansion, there's a risk that KakaoTalk itself could be removed from Google Play. Therefore, Kakao's growth targeting the global market will inevitably include Google's 30% revenue share. (Google must be happy..) There's also talk that developers were recently pressured to create iPhone games as well, which I believe is a choice made with global markets in mind, to manage app quality and considering the still significant proportion of iPhones.

**To conclude, KakaoTalk will take on an independent market form, but a break with Google Play is difficult, and global growth will ensure the viability of Kakao Games.**

How will Kakao Games have changed by the end of 2013? Will they have transformed into a positive form for both developers and users? Or will they simply recreate the old WIPI Market?

titleEn: Is Naver Webnovel a KakaoPage Killer?
contentEn:
Naver, the powerhouse of webtoons, has launched web novels. {{IMG:1}} [http://novel.naver.com/webnovel/weekday.nhn](http://novel.naver.com/webnovel/weekday.nhn)
For those familiar with existing services like Joara or Munpia, this is likely a familiar service. It was rather strange that Naver, which has a webtoon system for amateur serialization like Best Challenge, hadn't started a genre novel service until now. In fact, as someone affiliated with Naver, I've wished for a very long time that Naver would offer a genre novel service. This was because I believed it was one of the most entertaining content created and consumed by users. But why has Naver started something it hadn't done before, and why now? I'd like to talk about that briefly. This post is purely my personal opinion, contains no information obtained from the company, and I do not know if this service truly adopted such a strategic approach. Please consider it purely an outsider's commentary.

**1. Content Consumed More on Mobile: Genre Novels**
First, genre novels are the most consumed content on mobile. On mobile, lighter, 'killing time' content is effective. Of course, if you move to a more stationary device like a tablet, heavier general books might be more effective than these. However, just as entertainment/variety shows are more popular than documentaries or educational programs on TV, these light and stimulating novels are very popular on mobile. Consequently, the genre name 'light novel,' a subgenre of genre novels, reflects this well.

**Oh, I forgot to explain what genre novels are for those who don't know. They are (male-oriented) fantasy/SF/(female-oriented) romance novels that occupy the largest portion of book rental stores.**

**2. So, what's the connection with KakaoPage?**
You might be wondering why I titled this post 'KakaoPage Killer'. **KakaoPage is said to be a service that allows the creation and distribution of paid content to be consumed on mobile.** So, what content will be most widely distributed here? Articles by famous novelists or bloggers? If they are articles by 'wifeloggers,' they might sell quite well. However, the problem is also that Naver Blog has a lot of high-quality free content. The same goes for news. The fact that Naver distributes news for free makes it difficult for KakaoPage to distribute news for a fee.
Ultimately, excluding these, the largest proportion of document-type content (e-books) sold for a fee consists of genre novels and comics. (Personally, I believe educational content will be significant later, but it doesn't seem mature yet.)
The content KakaoPage can primarily sell is comics and genre novels. The fact that webtoon characters already occupy a significant portion of Kakao's emoticon market also increases this possibility.
However, in the case of comics, Naver's influence is absolute, and the area that was still vacant was precisely this genre novel market. And I suspect Naver has quickly filled this void.

**3. Mobile Genre Novels: Kakao vs. Naver Platform Clash**
**Content Platform Power of Free Webtoons vs. Paid Kakao Mobile Social Power**
In summary, the clash in this market could be a game between Naver, which has transferred the power of its free webtoon market to the web novel market, and Kakao, which aims to transfer its mobile social power, based on paid services, to the web novel market.
First, users are familiar with it, and the completeness of the platform ecosystem favors Naver. While it may not match Kakao in mobile reach, Naver Webtoon's highly loyal user base and content creator pool are the same for the web novel market. Furthermore, compared to Kakao, which leverages a well-structured paid platform as its competitive edge, Naver is a content competition platform.
Therefore, this suggests that Naver could be overwhelmingly larger in terms of volume.
From a platform strategy perspective, Kakao is a closed platform that filters content quality for participants, whereas Naver is a completely open two-sided market platform.
**more. First, Kakao lacks five virtues. If it wishes for development in this field, it must increase the volume of the amateur market. Of course, under the current government, which dislikes games, comics and web novels might also face difficulties..**

**4. Naver Web Novel's Big Challenge: Paid Platform**
However, Naver does not yet have a paid content sales model. I wonder if this could be solved based on N Store's e-book store? Some webtoons are already available for free in the e-book store. It's a bit regrettable that there's no paid model. Wouldn't it be better to allow completed webtoons to transition to a paid model?
As I also work on N Store-related matters, the immaturity of the paid model in Korea is a very regrettable situation. In the midst of this, I also wonder if the emergence of web novels might inadvertently hinder the paid model. There are people who level up to become book authors on Joara or Munpia, but it seems this will gradually become more difficult.
Shouldn't 'Naver Webtoon,' which is free, also prepare for the era of 'Mobile Naver Apptoon,' which includes paid content?

**5. Naver Web Novel Improvement Suggestions**
First, I thought I couldn't properly evaluate web novels without using them, so I uploaded a web novel I serialized in the past to Naver Web Novel. I first made a name for myself on the internet not as an IT blogger, but as a fantasy novel cyber writer. ^^ Before Naver and Daum became popular, my homepage was in the Yahoo Cyber Writer category. In fact, I still hold the title of IT blogger, but I also feel that my posts, including this one, are still at the level of fantasy novels. (I'm one person who believes imagination is most important in IT)
It was already on my blog, but I closed the category. I've been serializing it on and off for over 10 years... If you're interested, I'd be grateful if you could recommend my novel. ^^ (If the response is good, I might actually finish it.)
{{IMG:2}} The Legend of Dragonia (Scheduled for Mon/Fri serialization) [http://novel.naver.com/challenge/list.nhn?novelId=3231](http://novel.naver.com/challenge/list.nhn?novelId=3231)
After using it, the direct disadvantages I felt were the lack of comments on the work list. And the inability to upload images when uploading a work, especially the latter, is critical. I can't upload maps used in the novel...
And, again, the issue of quality control seems to be the most serious. This is because if a uniform recommendation-count-based algorithm is used, abuse is easy, and sensationalism can easily be prioritized over artistic merit. I also wonder if Naver Webtoon's star rating system wasn't better. As was problematic in Best Challenge in the past, the appearance of crazy people (who glorified elementary school sexual assault...) is possible, so it would be good to consider a report button and a system of pre-screening before publication. I also think that operation will be the most difficult.
Above all, I hope it becomes a communicative platform.

titleEn: [Crema Review] 2. Who
contentEn:
We briefly looked at the features of the previous Crema. This time, rather than a review, I'd like to discuss an essay-like approach, which is what I usually do.

{{IMG:1}}

Reference : [Crema Review] 1. Let's take a closer look at Crema. {{IMG:2}}[http://fstory97.blog.me/70154564054](http://fstory97.blog.me/70154564054)

**1. Who should buy this device?**
**1) Users who want an educational device rather than an entertainment device**
To summarize the previous post, it's a text-centric e-book reader and electronic dictionary with Wi-Fi internet at an affordable price. Compared to a tablet, which might be a comparison target, it's a slightly burdensome Facebook, multimedia (music, video), and gaming machine. To put it more simply, **the former is a cheap and affordable educational device, and the latter is an entertainment device.** Looking at it this way, it becomes clear who needs this device. What kind of device would a tablet be in the eyes of parents who have bought smartphones for their children? The number one graduation gift children want is an iPad, but their reasons for wanting it sound flimsy to parents. Are there any parents who believed their children when they said they bought a computer to study? No parent would want to buy another expensive game console. So, what about Crema? The price is also affordable for a graduation gift. Targeting this audience, they are selling a SKY Edition, which bundles books recommended by SKY universities. This seems like a very good initiative.
{{IMG:3}}
http://me2.do/FYilEv4[http://me2.do/FYilEv4](http://me2.do/FYilEv4)**[ I was briefly tempted, thinking the model was Suzy... Ancient Architecture Department, the real model for Architecture 101? ]**
**2) Users who are tired of heavy physical books, and find smartphones frustrating and distracting**
Secondly, these are people who are sufficiently satisfied with their smartphone's functions but want to read books lightly. A small, flickering LCD screen, and above all, KakaoTalk messages ringing constantly – you picked up your Galaxy Note to read a book, but suddenly found yourself playing Dragon Flight. What's the point of getting first place in Dragon Flight if you can't even buy beef? The essence of reading is to focus and listen to others' stories, but smartphones offer too many distractions. If you're a user who wants self-improvement and already owns a high-end smartphone, considering Crema might be a good idea. Your existing smartphone can solve Crema's drawbacks. Imagine listening to music with a Galaxy and Bluetooth headset while reading a book on Crema. This is at least more realistic than reading a book on an iPad. If you read on an iPad, you'll soon find yourself receiving wings and hearts.

**2. Who should NOT buy this device?**
**It's not recommended if you already own a 7-inch tablet or are a gaming enthusiast.** Your expectations are too high. While it lacks the advantages of a long-lasting battery and eye comfort, all of Crema's functions are available on your existing tablet. You'll ultimately have to choose between the two devices. My case is exactly this; I'm using a Galaxy S2 and HTC Flyer combination. I'd like to switch to a Galaxy Note 2 and Crema combination later, but the HTC Flyer's contract is holding me back. Should I try to transfer the contract?

**3. The path Crema should take**
**1) Demand for lower-priced e-books**
**- The damned fixed book price system, which I don't know who it's for**
My wife's first reaction to e-books was, "Why are they so expensive? There's no physical feel like a real book, no shipping costs, but the price is similar – isn't that just highway robbery?" This is one of the most common user reactions to e-books: "I want to read it, but it's too expensive. How much profit are they making to sell it at this price?" However, there's an industry secret here: the 'fixed book price system.' This system, which limits the discount rate of online bookstores, also applies to e-books, meaning online bookstores cannot drastically lower prices at will. Therefore, to address this demand, I believe a revision of the 'fixed book price system' or a way to circumvent it is needed.
**2) Book n-screen**
**- What if e-books were given to users who purchased physical books?**
So, the idea that came to mind was, what if users who buy physical books were also given the right to use the e-book? When I first received Crema, I felt a sense of betrayal seeing the empty device, knowing I had bought dozens of books from Yes24 over the years. If the method above is used, users would have an n-screen environment where they read physical books at home and carry e-books in their bags. An n-screen doesn't necessarily have to be a TV and a smartphone. Furthermore, e-book users could also gift physical books to friends, which would also boost the desire to purchase physical books. If such a method becomes known, users would likely buy without hesitation, even if it costs about 10% more than buying the physical book alone. Currently, the proportion of physical books is very high, so expanding the e-book usage experience to these users is very important.
**3) Need for additional content suitable for e-ink**
**- Paging-based mobile web/app**
Using Naver as a browser was truly unusable. The same went for Facebook. I felt that web/app content suitable for e-ink was needed. Scroll-based mobile web is not suitable for e-ink devices. Paging-based mobile web/apps are required.
**- Need for news, magazine-type subscription services**
Since I couldn't view Naver, it was difficult to read the news, which is one of a reader's desires. For newspapers, a 1-month subscription fee is over 10,000 won. In 12 months, you'd cover the cost of an e-book. In other words, it means that a subscription-based product linking content and devices could be created. Wouldn't it be possible to distribute free e-books with a 2-year subscription to the XX Daily?
**- Need for comics**
While it goes somewhat against the educational device concept, mobile devices tend to be light and enjoyed for more private content. I assume you already know this, as you're likely selling genre novels.
**- Need for free Bible**
This thought immediately came to mind when I saw the free dictionary app, and I won't elaborate on why the Bible is needed. The Bible has been a bestseller for hundreds of years and is always at the top of the market.
**4) Cheaper with ads, develop a platform (two-sided market) ad model**
Crema's main interface is currently based on 'My Library.' But what if a specific page, like Naver's, were created? And what if a portion of that area were bid out to publishers, and the revenue earned from that was used to further lower the cost of Crema's distribution? Amazon is already doing this, so I won't elaborate further. ^^
**5) Develop Kindle Fire, develop educational color tablets including online lectures (video)**
If Crema's educational concept is expanded, it could extend to color tablets capable of consuming educational video content that YES24 possesses. Again, since Amazon has the Kindle Fire model, complex explanations seem unnecessary.

**4. If you care about the environment and self-improvement, buy an e-book.**
YES24's e-book also feels like a special-purpose tablet, a vertical platform specialized for a single need within the general tablet platform. I also think this vertical platform has successfully met the needs arising from the gaps between existing general-purpose platforms. Most importantly, I like that Crema itself is more of a self-improvement device than a consumption device, and that it's environmentally conscious. If you need to lighten your bookshelf and create some mental space, please consider the lightweight Crema.

titleEn: The NIS Female Employee Scandal: How the
contentEn:
To those who dislike political talk, I apologize, but please press the back key. This is my last political post, though I had intended not to write any more. Last time, I only discussed the technical and circumstantial suspicions surrounding the 3-day confinement? lockdown? period. After seeing the comments on that post, I realized that the Saenuri Party's image strategy was truly excellent. My head is throbbing today. I wasn't going to talk about it since it's a lost game anyway, but I'm frustrated by those who don't know what they were deceived by, so I'm going to organize my thoughts. Because the comments have annoyed me a bit, I'm writing this shorter than usual, so please understand. If you don't like this, just hit the back key and leave; I won't be accepting comments. Those who agree, please quietly click 'like,' and those who disagree, please just shout "fuck" internally, and I'll accept it in spirit. Lastly, I will only discuss how the Saenuri Party won this battle in the NIS female agent incident.

** 1. The progressive side's claim is not about the NIS female agent's election interference, but about the NIS's election interference.**
First, the progressive side's claim is not about what the NIS female agent did. It's about the suspicion that the NIS interfered in the election. Reverend Yoon's remarks in the final episode of 'Naggomsu' also greatly fueled suspicions of NIS involvement. To prove such suspicions, I'm not sure if it would even be possible at the level of a special prosecutor. I will not judge whether this is a political maneuver by the progressive side or something else. However, what is certain is that the progressive argument is not about the female agent's comment-posting as an election law violation, but about the suspicion of NIS involvement. Her alleged comment-posting is merely one aspect of that claim. **Let's be clear about the main point.**

** 2. The progressive side's failure to secure decisive evidence and letting the case drag on was a mistake and ultimately led to their defeat.**
Anyway, the progressive side has not yet secured decisive evidence. Whether it was a 3-day sit-in, lockdown, or confinement, whatever the cause, they failed to obtain evidence. One of the scenarios I wrote in my previous post was, 'Why did they hold out for 3 days?' In reality, given the NIS's capabilities, they might have been able to destroy evidence in less than 3 days. They might have strategically needed those 3 days. The NIS agent might have destroyed everything in just 5 minutes, reported, received the next directive, and then been told with a smile to just bide their time. Of course, this is fiction. The 3-day standoff itself could have been a fake. **The important thing is that the progressive side has reached a point where they can only write fiction because they couldn't secure evidence. Suspicion is just suspicion; it has no legal effect. Here, the progressives have already lost.**

** 3. The conservative side did not miss this (failure to secure evidence) and launched a counterattack, and their strategy, which I suspect, is as follows.** : This is not assuming the NIS is guilty. It's about how the Saenuri Party exploited that situation in the election.
** 1) Narrow the focus from NIS election interference to NIS female agent election interference.**
 -> Make "**NIS female agent**" appear in real-time search rankings instead of "NIS interference." By reducing the incident to a localized issue, people forget that the progressives' current target is the NIS, and thus the current government. Highlighting individual human rights is an excellent way to achieve this. It prevents people from seeing the background and the core issues due to concerns about human rights. Damn... it's really brilliant. I don't know who planned it... but it's commendable.

** 2) Exploit the situation where no evidence was secured to highlight the 'no charges' status during the investigation process.**
 -> As I mentioned last time, the failure to secure decisive evidence ultimately prolongs the investigation. Of course, this is my personal opinion, and it might hurt the police's pride, but **I believe the police's investigative capabilities cannot surpass those of the NIS. The NIS is an intelligence agency. What they do is not an investigation; it's warfare**.

** 3) Highlight the illegality of the progressive side's excessive arbitrary investigation process to obscure the main point of the issue.**
 -> They rammed a car, 70 people swarmed... well, I don't know if that happened. I'm not well-versed in law, so I'm not sure if that's illegal, but it probably seems very minor compared to NIS election interference, though there might be some illegality. **However, the problem is that the existence of this illegality is an independent issue completely unrelated to the veracity of the suspicions raised by the progressive side.** I'm not a spokesperson for the Democratic Party, so stop nitpicking me about that. If you have a complaint, just sue the Democratic Party. It's a completely separate track.

** 4) Frame the NIS election interference case, which has fallen into a labyrinth, as a political maneuver by the progressive side, making people view the clearly illegal 'Sibal-dan' incident as an extension of political maneuvering. And minimize mentions of 'Sibal-dan' as much as possible.**
 -> This is the result of my analysis. I don't know if there were comment-posting agents or not, but **the conservative side invariably brings up the NIS female agent's comments whenever the 'Sibal-dan' is mentioned. Conversely, not to be outdone, the progressive side brings up the 'Sibal-dan' whenever the NIS female agent is mentioned. Damn, the progressives already started losing here.** It's been diluted. What the progressives should have done here, even if suspicious, might have been to coolly say 'Oh, sorry.' It's not easy dealing with the NIS anyway.

** 5) Request cooperation from the media regarding this.**
 -> It seems the media faithfully adhered to the content of point 4). Well... I won't elaborate. They're the ones who usually follow Saenuri Party's official letters and embargoes well... They were criticized for sending an official letter recently too.

** 4. Still don't get it? It's the same incident, but I'll give you an example with a different image.**
It might seem a bit forced, but let me tell you a story about an incident. There were suspicions that intellectually disabled children, unable to express themselves, were being serially sexually assaulted. Some local residents, however, suspected the police officers from the violent crime investigation unit. They found a suspicious point about one of the officers. Driven by a sense of justice, the residents rammed a police car with their own to find out his address. Then, at a moment when rape was suspected, they stormed his house. But he closed the door and wouldn't open it. After 3 days, he opened the door and was taken to the police station. When they opened the door, there was only one intellectually disabled girl who couldn't express herself at all. They took this woman to the police station and the hospital. However, just 2 minutes after the woman arrived at the hospital, the police announced 'no charges' during the investigation. The reason given for the announcement was that there were no traces of semen on her skirt. They said her underwear hadn't even been examined yet. And the violent crime investigation police officers accused these local residents of illegal confinement and human rights violations.

Okay. It's not a perfectly smooth story since I forced it, but did the police officer commit rape here? Or not? Most would probably think he did, given his suspicious behavior. But legally speaking, strictly, it's 'unknown.' And 'no charges' is correct. He might even be able to sue for false accusation. And he might actually not have committed rape. The reason he opened the door after 3 days could have been because the door was broken, and the reason for the 'no charges' announcement in 2 minutes could have been that someone kept bothering them with questions during the investigation. In my opinion, there were so many suspicious points that my remarks were enough to be called a spy? How could even a host of MBN, a cable channel often criticized as conservative, say, 'An 11 PM announcement, that's unusual'? And the 9 PM announcement was so absurd that reporters protested, but they just ignored it... And one more thing, did the residents, burning with a sense of justice, commit an illegal act? Or not? Based on the above, yes, the residents did commit illegal acts. But in that story, do you want to side with the residents? Or with the police? Do you understand now what obscured the main point?

Of course, this story is forced. It's an absurd story. I deliberately used rape and police as provocative examples. But the situation is the same.

** 5. Reflect on why the public harbors such suspicions in the first place.**
This is a separate track from the NIS female agent. I'm talking about why the NIS female agent incident became plausible. Was the police force trustworthy under the Lee Myung-bak administration? And the 'code appointments' that spread through various public institutions, the media, and even the scientific community. Can we guarantee that the NIS wouldn't do the same? Isn't it harder to imagine reasons why the NIS *shouldn't* have done it? With incidents like the DDOS attack, the DDoS tunnel incident, the Sibal-dan incident, and events predicted by 'Naggomsu' turning out to be true, what should we do about the comical situation where 'Naggomsu' is more trusted than the media? Who is more trustworthy: the guy broadcasting, ready to go to jail, or the broadcasting company president comfortably sitting and confronting his employees?

Anyway, the Saenuri Party actually won because of this. You Win! Good for you. Celebrate. And the progressives should reflect on their immaturity. This is the end of political talk! I'll be back to IT topics next week.

titleEn: Lessons for North Korean Missiles from Sputnik
contentEn:
**1. North Korea launched a missile called Unha-3.**
Recently, there has been a lot of noise about North Korea launching a missile. (Hereafter, I will refer to it by its official name, Unha-3. The media seems to intentionally avoid calling it Unha-3 to maximize fear...) There's a feeling that some are trying to exploit this politically, and all newspapers are creating a sense of dread as if the North will immediately build an ICBM and start a world war. Instead of these uniform and unproductive narratives, I want to talk about Unha-3 a bit more objectively. I wished at least one article would discuss this, but no one is. This is why South Korean science is in this state. So, let's begin.

**2. Do you know about Sputnik?**
Not Haruki's novel, but the first artificial satellite launched by the former Soviet Union.
Let me show you part of the Wikipedia content.

**3. Unha-3 is 100kg, so it's ICBM development? Do you know the history of space development?**
However, the Saenuri Party, perhaps due to the presidential election, seems to be almost defining it as an ICBM.

**But, Sputnik 1 was 83kg, and Unha-3 is 100kg.**
Shall I show you something more interesting? This is the spec of Uribyol-1, Korea's first satellite. ([http://me2.do/FYeXzwt](http://me2.do/FYeXzwt))
Uribyol-1 weighs **48.6kg**.
How much does one satellite cost? What reckless fool would launch a several-hundred-kilogram observation satellite into space from the start?

**4. There is no difference between Unha-3 and Naro-ho. And Naro-ho is no different from an ICBM.**
Based on the above, it's impossible to know whether the purpose is ICBM development or not. Fundamentally, launch vehicle technology and ICBM technology are the same, so only Kim Jong-un knows the purpose. Are the National Intelligence Service and the Saenuri Party using mind-reading?

**5. More importantly, the Sputnik Shock, the Unha-3 Shock**
I will refer to Wikipedia content again.

**The possibility of ICBM development definitely exists. And, the US also repeated a very similar history.**

**6. What we can truly learn from the Sputnik Shock**
Let's return to Unha-3 and our situation. Let's rename Sputnik to Unha-3, and Vanguard or Explorer to Naro-ho.

**1) Nuclear war using ICBMs did not happen.**
Nuclear war did not happen. Just because the technology exists doesn't mean it's easy to launch. And, in the case of South Korea, an ICBM is not necessary; even with Daepodong, the entire country can be hit by a nuclear attack.

**2) Vanguard, hastily launched under pressure, exploded.**
This is the most concerning part, but Naro-ho faced immense pressure due to the political burden of having to launch it within the Lee Myung-bak administration, compounded by North Korea's actions. However, space development is not an easy industry, so please maintain the pace. And even if it fails like Vanguard, we can launch Explorer (the second, third Naro-ho) again.

**3) NASA was established.**
We already have it since we have KARI (Korea Aerospace Research Institute). However, the budget NASA uses is enormous. And, techniques like PERT were born for complex project management, which still greatly influences the SW industry. I hope this can lead to massive investment not only in the hardware of the aerospace industry but also in the software industry, along with significant overall investment.

**4) The Internet was developed.**
The Internet was developed for network survivability, fearing ICBM attacks. With the Internet already developed and a spider (grid) network in place, what I want to talk about, following point 3), is the SW industry. This is a common topic, so let's move on.

**5) Basic sciences and science education began to be emphasized.**
It's time to genuinely consider the importance of basic sciences and science education, instead of just talking about preferential treatment for STEM fields or overworking engineers.

**6) Open policies for foreign highly skilled workers began.**
South Korea does not look favorably upon foreign workers. However, human resources are an asset. This is something that definitely needs to be reviewed at a time when the population is decreasing.

**7) Kennedy, who promised to send a man to the moon, was elected.**
Instead of fear, he made the public dream a grand, simple, and beautiful dream. South Korea also wants such a president.
**8) Ultimately, Apollo reached the moon.**
This is the goal we must achieve. China is short-term pursuing this goal, and NASA is currently planning to send a manned spacecraft to Mars.

**7. Why did North Korea launch Unha-3? Actually, it's not important.**
**A hundred times more important than which party to vote for because of this, is launching Naro-ho.**
Whether it's a political show or a show of force to the world. Frankly, it's not important to South Korea.
That worry is for the US or Japan, who are now within range.
**What's more important to us than the reason Unha-3 was launched is that we must launch Naro-ho.**
Perhaps Kim Jong-un genuinely just wanted to beat Naro-ho. Of course, North Korea, where continuous large-scale investment is difficult, may not easily make progress like sending manned spacecraft. What he gained might just be ICBM technology.
Our capabilities are far greater in the future.
We don't need to worry about North Korea's over-technology. They are still far from reaching Alpha Centauri (a condition for civilization's scientific victory). It is most important for us to maintain our pace.

**ps. As a bonus.. I'll recommend an anime.**

titleEn: Piacere Songdo Branch: Free Maternity Photoshoot Experience
contentEn:
**1. Second Child Saedong-i (Fetus's Nickname), Second Maternity Photoshoot**
A while ago, we visited Piacere to take maternity photos for our second child, Saedong-i. It was located in Songdo, not Cheongdam. First, since we live in Sanbon, we took the outer ring expressway, which was quicker than going to Cheongdam, and arrived sooner than expected. Although it's not Seoul, there's a subway, and perhaps because it's an international city, the roads are well-maintained, so it wasn't difficult to get there.

After only preparing breakfast for our first child, Saebom-i, we rushed out, and my wife and I hadn't had a proper meal. While my wife was getting her makeup done, I drove about 3km to Paris Baguette, bought some bread, and we ate. If you plan to visit without eating, it would be a good idea to bring something to eat beforehand. There are no convenience stores or bakeries nearby.

**2. You can take photos with your own camera during free time.**
While my wife was getting her makeup ready, I took photos with Saebom-i...{{IMG:1}}
**[Princess Saebom-i]**
I forgot to bring Saebom-i's shoes... so the outfit doesn't quite match. OTL.
{{IMG:2}}
**[Wow, it's a star...]**
One of the staff members was also named 'Saebom,' so she was especially fond of Saebom-i. ^^

**3. Full-fledged Maternity Photoshoot**
Then, the maternity photoshoot officially began. I also took photos with them.
There were many semi-nude styles, which made my wife a bit uncomfortable, but all I could think was how beautiful the photos turned out...{{IMG:3}}
A couple's photo, taken after what felt like a very long time.{{IMG:4}}
Since Saebom-i was born, it seems we haven't had many photos of just the two of us. One of us always took the pictures, focusing on Saebom-i... It's been a while since we took a photo together, and it has a wedding photo vibe.

And finally, the family photo they took for us.{{IMG:5}}
Everyone burst out laughing at Saebom-i's mischievous face.
Next year, we'll be able to take a photo with four of us, right?

**4. Write a review and receive an additional photo frame.**
In addition to the free maternity photoshoot, if you write a review like this, you'll also receive an extra photo frame. It requires some effort, but for a beautiful frame...

**5. We were so pleased with the experience that we ended up choosing a growth album.**
Because we weren't satisfied with Saebom-i's growth album, which led us to do two photoshoots and spend double the money, my wife and I ultimately decided to sign up for a growth album here. The results of this photoshoot were so pleasing, and the price wasn't bad either.
For those who are pregnant, it might be a good idea to check out Piacere Studio.
It was a great experience, also serving as a family outing.

**P.S. Please note that this post is based on a free trial available to the general public, and no separate fees or advertising costs were received.**
