titleEn: SK Talks About Coexistence. Planet X / Random IT Thoughts / IT Stories
South Korea's ICT Strategy Framework V0.9
contentEn:
Some members of the Facebook group 'Korea IT Alliance' who had time recently gathered for a discussion. To be honest, my expertise isn't that high, so it was a place where I could learn a lot rather than speak. Many discussions took place, from very specific agenda items to abstract but important directions. The summary of this was separately done by someone else, and further discussions ensued about how to proceed. These discussions weren't particularly secret, but since I didn't get the speakers' consent, I can't share them.

**However, what I felt was best about that meeting was directly discussing the large and small problems prevalent across the current IT industry.**

After the meeting, I thought about the scattered topics and the broad scope of IT as an industry, so I came up with a separate framework. I also wonder if the contents discussed at that time could each fit into the framework I created.

Since I created this framework, ^^; I thought it would be okay to release it independently first, so I'm sharing it. This is not a finished version. As it's a diagram I pondered over for a short time, I believe it needs more revisions.

** **

It seems that sub-topics and issues can be added for each component of this framework. And if these topics and issues were compiled into a list of questions for the current presidential candidates and their answers obtained, wouldn't it also serve as a criterion for evaluating the candidates? **If you have any IT strategies, policies, or problems in mind, where do they fit into the framework above? If there's anything that doesn't fit, please let me know. Also, point out anything that seems oddly placed.**

** There is one reason why I am releasing this framework.** This imperfect framework is merely an opening gambit, hoping that more people will contemplate it. **Additionally, please provide good suggestions for parts that need revision in the comments and trackbacks. For a better IT world where juniors say they enjoy working. .Thank you. **

titleEn: [Steve Jobs Storygraphic] The Images Jobs Left Behind
contentEn:
**1. The Person Who Best Understood the Power of Images (Graphics)** Who do you think this silhouette belongs to?{{IMG:1}}

Yes. It's Steve Jobs.

{{IMG:2}}

http://people.search.naver.com/search.naver?where=people&sm=sme_clk&query=%EC%8A%A4%ED%8B%B0%EB%B8%8C%EC%9E%A1%EC%8A%A4&os=174292&ie=utf8

 
  [Steve Jobs](http://people.search.naver.com/search.naver?where=people&sm=sme_clk&query=%EC%8A%A4%ED%8B%B0%EB%B8%8C%EC%9E%A1%EC%8A%A4&os=174292&ie=utf8)
  
  Occupation
  Entrepreneur
  Born
  1955.02.24 (USA)
  Education
  Reed College
  
 

     
The image we have of Steve Jobs can be recognized by his silhouette alone. That image is actually no different from Hong Seok-cheon's, but the trade dress in people's minds for this silhouette is Jobs. I think Steve Jobs was the one who best understood the power of images.
It's been about a year since Steve Jobs passed away, and I received a book that allows you to see him at a glance through images.
 {{IMG:3}}

http://book.naver.com/bookdb/book_detail.php?bid=7017672

 
  [Steve Jobs Story Graphic](http://book.naver.com/bookdb/book_detail.php?bid=7017672)
  
  Authors
  Kim Seok-ki, Kang Jae-min
  Publisher
  Cloudbooks
  Release
  2012.10.05
  Rating
  
   
    
   
  
  
  [View Review](http://book.naver.com/bookdb/review.nhn?bid=7017672)
 
       This book, composed of images that could also be called infographics, refers to them as "story graphics." Did they use this term because the infographics have a continuous story? (As someone not majoring in design, I'll pass on that question...) Anyway, the most unfamiliar aspect of the book, which features various images overlaid on Jobs' silhouette, was that it was a landscape-type book. Moreover, it resembled the 4:3 aspect ratio that Jobs loved during his lifetime.  However, upon opening the book, I understood why it was a landscape-type with a 4:3 ratio. In any case, I'd like to write a short review after reading this book.
**2. A Book Weaving His Legacy of Images into a Story** The images Steve Jobs wanted to embody were artist, genius, pirate, craftsman, and revolutionary. There are also some slightly negative images he left behind, such as workaholic, control freak, tyrant, and perfectionist with a touch of paranoia. Throughout his life, Steve Jobs created various images through what he wanted to be and through his actions. And when all those images combine, they form the Steve Jobs we see. One thing we can certainly acknowledge about him is that he faithfully pursued the image he sought and conveyed it excellently to the public. And through that image, it was easier for everyone to understand him.  Perhaps that's why he's also called a presentation genius. In that sense, this book also felt like a presentation of his entire life through a series of images. I even wonder if, had he been alive and asked to create a book introducing his life, it wouldn't have been a text-listed autobiography, but rather a book like this.
**3. The Power of the Image He Left Behind** I believe his greatest achievement might not be the iPhone or iTunes, but rather these images. Products will soon be forgotten by new ones, but images will endure and be talked about by people. Furthermore, someone will likely pursue this image to become a great entrepreneur or a great programmer. Even if Wozniak is recognized as the ideal person in the true programmer community, Steve Jobs' greater influence is likely the most effective image for drawing people onto the path of becoming a programmer in the first place. Just as The Beatles, not an IT person, created Steve Jobs, it's unknown what great artist or figure Steve Jobs will create in what field next.
**4. What Image Am I Creating in My Life?** And finally, looking at these brilliant and diverse images, the question that came to mind was: What image am I creating, and what image am I pursuing? When I die, even my family won't be able to recognize me just by my silhouette, like Steve Jobs. However, what's clear is that I, too, am living and leaving behind certain images. What image are you, the reader of this post, leaving behind in your life?** A book that allows you to see what he left behind, and things about him, in his style, without spending a lot of time. ****This concludes the review of "Steve Jobs Story Graphic." ****
**** P.S. to Nio. The complete absence of book photos is absolutely not due to my laziness. It's to protect copyright..****

titleEn: Tim Cook's First Year After Jobs: Signs
contentEn:
It's already been a year since Steve Jobs' passing, and Apple is marking that anniversary. There have been articles suggesting that Tim Cook's first year has been fine, given that there hasn't been a significant decline. However, I view Apple's recent actions somewhat differently. I'd like to discuss Apple's recent 모습 (appearance/actions) as I've perceived them, and the mistakes Apple has made as a result. Of course, this is 100% my personal opinion, so there may be those who disagree. I welcome many opinions.

**1. Mistake 1: A Defensive, Not Offensive, Move – Apple Confronting Samsung with Patents**
First, there's the patent war between Samsung and Apple. I believe this is the result of Jobs' firm resolve during his lifetime to stop Android by any means necessary. However, using a weapon of mass destruction like a nuclear bomb brings considerable repercussions. While they succeeded in getting a judgment for a seemingly enormous amount in patent damages, I wonder if they suffered even greater damage to their image. Although some argue it was a crucial ruling as a warning against copycats and for the protection of intellectual property, patents are a double-edged sword. By comparing its own technology to past inventions or competitors, it made people question the illusion of innovation Apple had fostered. In fact, patents are not commendations for innovative companies. As much of innovation actually comes from minor changes, Apple's image of innovation, which appeared to the public as creating something out of nothing, has been significantly diminished. While the reality of innovation is often more about improvement than pure creation, this difference from the image Apple had built for the public has become poison for Apple. Furthermore, by essentially admitting that Samsung could be a threat to Apple, it feels like Samsung, conversely, gained more. Apple's actions, perceived as a defensive measure rather than an innovative one, have, I believe, damaged Apple's image.

**2. Mistake 2: The 16:9 iPhone 5, Which First Caused UI Fragmentation**
The iPhone, which had used a patent shield as a strategic move, ironically began adopting the aspect ratio of the Android camp. While 16:9 isn't exclusive to the Android camp, it has created a situation where Apple has contradicted its own long-standing claim of the 4:3 aspect ratio's superiority. And more significantly than simply following Android's aspect ratio, the bigger change for the iPhone is the emergence of software fragmentation. The iPhone, which chose software fragmentation for hardware satisfaction, feels quite different from its past self. As a result, iPhone developers, like their Android counterparts, are now facing UI fragmentation for the first time. While supporting two or more aspect ratios in software offers the advantage of wider choices, it's clear that it diminishes the ability to focus on a single one. This was commonplace in Android, but it's a new change for iPhone developers.

**3. Mistake 3: Low Software Quality – iOS6 Maps**
The much-talked-about iOS6 Maps was shocking. Of course, iPhone users say you can just install a portal app, but that's not the important point. The question is, would Steve Jobs have launched iOS6 Maps at that level of quality? If it had been a Google service, one might have shrugged it off, as they often keep a 'beta' tag, but this was a significant departure from the craftsmanship expected of Apple.

**4. Perhaps, a Weakening of Apple's Software Capabilities?**
Connecting the 16:9 iPhone 5 and iOS6 Maps mentioned above leads to one conclusion: Compared to hardware advancements, software quality has declined under the Tim Cook regime. Even while saying I disliked Apple, one compliment I never forgot was their software power. They created perfect, well-functioning software that was precisely tailored to the hardware. And that synergy made the iPhone shine. The iPhone 5's camera is excellent, and even though its screen is smaller than the Galaxy's, I believe the hardware product, which effectively covered its past weaknesses, is flawless. However, in Tim Cook's first year, Apple's software has delivered a 'patent shield' and a disastrous map service. The start shown in software, compared to hardware, doesn't seem very good. If this is a signal of weakening software capabilities at Apple, I question whether the Tim Cook regime can sustain Jobs' glory. With the smartphone market already starting to level up and facing attacks from China, among other things, can Apple effectively fend them off with its premium strategy? If what I've thought is reality and not just a groundless fear, then I also think the Tim Cook regime might not last very long. I'm not sure if Apple's situation can be viewed optimistically.

titleEn: [Mobile App Development Log] Beauty Meter: What'
contentEn:
This post is an advertisement heavily mixed with my personal interests. It's a free app, and most importantly, **I made it!!** I had a lot of posts to write while working on this, but I haven't been able to write them yet. I apologize for not being able to present you with a decent post and instead just dropping this ad.
{{IMG:1}}

**Beauty Scouter (BP Scouter)**[http://nstore.naver.com/appstore/web/detail.nhn?productNo=480356](http://nstore.naver.com/appstore/web/detail.nhn?productNo=480356)

**1. Reason for Creation**
One reason I created this app was to make up for the embarrassment of having written many posts about mobile but never having developed or operated an app under my own name. Of course, I've participated as an operator for company apps with over 10 million users, but the position of a personal developer is different, so this time I truly tried it as a personal developer.

**2. Introduction and Features**
The features are simple. It's an app where you take a photo, check your score, see fun messages, and share them with friends.
{{IMG:2}}{{IMG:3}}{{IMG:4}}

**3. Who Made It?**
Team F&B (an acronym for Food & Beverage, meaning 'to make a living,' and also referring to F from 'Forest Story' and B from 'Black Dog').
[http://blog.naver.com/wono77](http://blog.naver.com/wono77)
Also, juniors from Soongsil University's Multimedia Research Club helped with translation and image work for buttons, etc.

**4. How Was It Made?**
**1) Target: Competition and Fun**
First, the target of this item is competition and fun. It's a psychological element similar to looking in a mirror and asking, 'Mirror, mirror, on the wall, who's the fairest of them all?' If you check your score and boldly eliminate competitors by feeding them poisoned apples... you'll be arrested. I tried to emphasize the fun elements a lot. So, the main focus of this app was the comments for each score. I also tried to draw unique and fun illustrations for each score, but I simply didn't have the capacity, so I gave up and just used comments. I just picked up some images lying around on my hard drive and used them. I tried to get some help from my juniors, but it was difficult since we didn't have a professional designer. The buttons were done by the juniors. I drew the main illustration. ㅡㅡ Even the mosaic-blurred face uploaded to Google Play is mine.

**2) How is beauty measured?**
The principle of beauty measurement is based on some scientific evidence. It is said that people perceive beautiful women as having average faces. Therefore, I created several 'beautiful' celebrities as training models. I quantified the similarity between the standard data of these celebrities and the input data, and then converted it to a 100-point scale. Black Dog, who worked with me, handled the engine. I fine-tuned the model training and parameters using a PC batch, and there were indeed issues. ㅡㅡ However, spending too much time on this seemed unrelated to fun, and the release date was dragging on too much, so I boldly gave up at a reasonable level. If the response is good later, the engine might be improved, or a male version could be developed, but if the response is poor, I might boldly give up here? Personally, I want to try my hand at 'technology planning'. It's about supplementing difficult, incomplete technologies with service-oriented elements to make them fun for users. For me, it had a bit of that challenging meaning. Quality is OTL. I don't have much will or time to improve it. Even this seemingly shoddy app took several months due to lack of time...

**3) Global Challenge**
With the thought of expanding the market as much as it's shoddy, I supported four languages: Korean, Chinese, Japanese, and English. It was hard to find a Chinese translator. I paid for part-time work, but I wonder if the ad revenue will cover the part-time wages. In Korea, I'll try various free promotions like blog posts, but overseas, I have no promotional means, so I don't know if I'll get any downloads. I will let you know the results in the future. For those reading this post, please download and click an ad once...

**4) Future Plans**
Open-sourcing the Beauty Scouter and publishing it? Since it's hard to make money with an app anyway, perhaps there's meaning in trying to publish it? Black Dog, who worked with me, is the author of 'Making Pocket Money with Android,' so he might take on the planning and operation of the second volume. There's also a very high chance it could fall through depending on the publisher's will. There were also plans for feature upgrades. The original plan was to see a list of Facebook friends' scores, but it might be supported someday... Currently, the elements that stimulate competition are too weak; it was just about adding sharing. Should I add KakaoTalk sharing as well?

**5. Please Look Forward to the Next App**
Since I have plenty of useless, non-profitable ideas, I'm thinking of a few more simple apps to create. They'll probably be cheap toy-like apps again. ^^ Since the time I can invest is very limited, I can't create a grand app. They say a typhoon is coming these days, so I'm thinking of making a typhoon game... A game where you change the path of a typhoon appearing on a map of Korea, China, and Japan using finger touches, and get points for destroying buildings. NPCs repair or prepare buildings, and you have to skillfully avoid them to destroy the buildings. Or should I make a game where you send it to Japan? ^^; (Would that become an international issue...?) I can't make game apps that require such significant resources. OTL. If the response isn't good, I might get discouraged and not make the next app. Please give me some feedback. I'm begging for warm reviews and ratings. ^^

titleEn: Transitioning the ROK Military to a Volunteer System
contentEn:
While browsing Naver News, I found an interesting article. **"Even if accused of being pro-North, I will implement a volunteer military system in South Korea."** It's the opinion of someone named Kim Doo-kwan. Honestly, I don't even know who he is.

{{IMG:1}}

http://people.search.naver.com/search.naver?where=people&sm=sme_clk&query=%EA%B9%80%EB%91%90%EA%B4%80&os=159598&ie=utf8

[Kim Doo-kwan](http://people.search.naver.com/search.naver?where=people&sm=sme_clk&query=%EA%B9%80%EB%91%90%EA%B4%80&os=159598&ie=utf8)

Occupation: Head of a metropolitan local government, Political appointee
Born: 1959.04.10 (Namhae, Gyeongsangnam-do)
Education: Dong-A University
Affiliation: Democratic United Party

However, thanks to this, I got to think about the topic of national defense that I had considered before, and the current and future national defense of South Korea.
**1. South Korea in 10 years. Can the current conscription system be maintained?** **The conclusion I've reached is that a volunteer military system is naturally the way to go.** Why did I come to this conclusion? It's because of South Korea's demographic structure. How will South Korea have changed in 10 years? The biggest change will be the population problem. As the population declines, it will emerge as a social issue. The biggest problem of population decline will occur among the younger age groups. Furthermore, even if slowly, South Korea will have achieved more economic development than now, and wage rates will have risen. **This means that the cost of human resources will rapidly increase more than that of material resources.** Currently, all South Korean men must serve in the military. However, the biggest cost incurred here is actually the expenditure on human resources. Young people who should be active economic participants in society are fulfilling their national defense duty. Moreover, in a highly educated society, **the duty of national defense performed in the middle of university life also significantly increases educational costs. It's necessary to consider that the current conscription system was established during a time when teaching up to high school was considered good education, and human resource costs were very low.** With increased human resource costs, the maintenance cost of a 600,000-strong military, including social costs, is bound to be much higher than just the salaries of 600,000 soldiers.
**2. The number of soldiers decreases by 1/6? Salary 10 times higher? Does this make sense?** Naver News had an interesting comment. It asked how it's possible to create a 100,000-strong military (1/6 the current size) and give them 10 times the salary. That's just the salary. ^^; Costs like barracks, food expenses, and communication costs used by soldiers can be significantly reduced by increasing human efficiency. Therefore, it's not an impossible figure. **I'm actually more concerned about whether people would even join the military for a mere 1 million won salary.**
**3. Future South Korean national defense needs to be reorganized around material resources.** So, an idea I had in the past was to implement a donation-based exemption system. A donation-based exemption doesn't mean, "Buy one tank worth hundreds of millions of won, and you're exempt." **It's a plan to expand the national defense duty, currently borne only by men, to women as well, and require young people above a certain income level to contribute half of their income for three years to national defense. Young people who cannot pay this would serve in the military and receive a salary equivalent to that of a civil servant (roughly a Grade 9 public official) during their service.** **The duration and obligations for reservists should also be expanded, and a portion of these costs should be borne by corporations. Just as corporate taxes are collected, corporations, as groups protected by the state, should also have duties commensurate with their rights.**
**The idea is to expand duties and reduce burdens.** Actually, thinking about it, this is quite similar to a volunteer military system.
What is absolutely certain is that South Korea's national defense needs to be reorganized around material resources, not human resources. National defense capability doesn't simply mean the number of tanks or people; it signifies total war, including economic power. We need to find the most suitable way to prepare for total war, and the current conscription system's inefficiency will only grow in the future. **The biggest reason for low morale in the military is the sense of deprivation compared to those who are active in civilian life (exempt). To resolve this, compensation greater than what those in civilian life receive is needed, and responsibilities** must be imposed on those in civilian life (exempt). A limited volunteer military system could be the answer here.
**4. Is now the right time to discuss this? We need to start now to barely achieve it in 10 years.** But the question is, is now the right time to discuss this? I hadn't really thought that far, but I felt that discussing it at this point is quite timely. **National defense reform takes decades. The problem is that South Korea will have already changed in 10 years. Therefore, we need to start now to meet the 10-year deadline.** Those who enlist now will unfortunately only see some of the benefits. Changing to a volunteer military system is a very large-scale transformation, so the current conscription system won't change overnight. Perhaps the next president will have done a great job just by properly laying the groundwork. If we start now, it will likely be a long-term plan of over 10 years, with sequential plans in 3-year units. Panzer's idea of paid support personnel, which he evaluated as populism, could also be a starting point. (I also agree that it's not immediately possible. The military doesn't have the capacity for it either.)

**Nevertheless, if we hope for a strong South Korea in the future, shouldn't we start contemplating it slowly from now? Unless we set a direction, or if we only act when social problems arise and are imminent, good implementation plans will never emerge.** This isn't something for pro-North leftists; rather, it seems like a banner that conservatives who desire a strong South Korea should be carrying. Other candidates, regardless of party, should also consider this.

**P.S. This does not mean I politically support candidate Kim Doo-kwan.**

titleEn: Pol-X Smartphone Bluetooth Watch Event
The Significance of Google Nexus 7: A
contentEn:
Following MS's Surface last time, I'd like to talk about the Nexus 7, which created its own tablet. The strategy of the tablet and Windows 8 in Surface {{IMG:1}}
[http://fstory97.blog.me/70141201767](http://fstory97.blog.me/70141201767)
The Nexus 7 is clearly also a model released to stop the iPad's dominance. So, what kind of model is the Nexus 7?

{{IMG:2}}

http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=6491060187

[Google Nexus 7](http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=6491060187)

Brand
Google
nVidia Quad-Core Tegra3, 1GB, 7-inch wide, 8GB internal storage, USB x 1, approx. 0.34kg, And...

[View Review](http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=6491060187&tc=6)

**1. Nexus 7's Goal: Lower iOS Market Share in the Tablet Market.** The Nexus 7 was launched with the goal of lowering iOS's market share in the tablet market. Even when Samsung was excitedly selling its "world's number one smartphone" story to the media, Apple was growing the iPad at a terrifying pace. There were rumors that a significant portion of wireless internet traffic, including Wi-Fi, was coming from iPads. Users don't actually buy devices; they buy services. "What can I do with an iPad?" "What can I do with a Galaxy?" These are the main concerns. Such services are OS-dependent, except for the web. Even the web, which is somewhat less OS-dependent, is controlled by Apple to prevent its influence from spreading to apps. (I'll discuss this separately later.) The traffic generated by iPads is incomparable to that generated by Galaxies, and a larger screen means more content can be delivered and a larger service market can be created. In my personal opinion, Google has no intention of selling hardware for profit for the time being. Apple's power, in fact, comes not from hardware but from software, and the power of software has transferred to hardware. This software is actually the power of the iOS platform. Samsung Electronics' sales limit lies in the fact that the Galaxy S3's biggest rival is the need to replace the S2, but even if the iPhone 5 doesn't replace the 4S, Apple's revenue generated from the iOS ecosystem (platform) is unaffected. This is also why Apple doesn't create a multitude of hardware devices and why it continues to support its hardware to the end. In Samsung Electronics' case, if they continue to support the Galaxy S2 to the end, it's likely to only lower the sales rate of the S3, and there's no utility gained compared to the resources invested. If utility does arise, it belongs to Google, which owns the Android platform. That is the difference between Apple and Samsung, and the goal of Google and Apple.
**2. Why Did Google Create Its Own Hardware Instead of Samsung Electronics?** Why did the Galaxy smartphone turn out to be a good product? The Galaxy became a good product because the interests of Google, the platform company, Samsung Electronics, the manufacturer, and mobile carriers, the network operators, aligned well. But what about the tablet or pad market, which isn't a smartphone? In reality, even a 7-inch tablet doesn't score very well in terms of portability. Furthermore, it's a device that generates significant traffic for network operators. Ultimately, the three interests mentioned earlier don't align as well as they do for smartphones. Also, as a manufacturer that primarily made phones, there was a strong feeling that tablets weren't their original domain, so they likely didn't feel the need to stake their lives on creating a tablet that mobile carriers weren't cooperating well with. It might have felt like, "Our 5-inch smartphones are doing well, so let's take it slow." Therefore, Google is the one feeling anxious. Just when they felt they had barely curbed Apple's dominance in smartphones, the tablet sector was making rapid progress, and Apple was pulling the PC web ecosystem, which was Google's backyard, into apps. Consequently, Google had to create a tablet to secure a viable platform share in the market.
**3. Nexus 7's Strategy** The iPad is good. It's even cool~. Everyone agrees. But if there's a slight hitch, it's the price, portability, and the fact that not everyone can participate in device manufacturing. Although the Nexus 7 was made by Google, anyone can make the same hardware. Furthermore, this market is open not only to mobile phone manufacturers but also to navigation companies, PC companies, and hardware companies from the old Wintel camp. The Nexus 7 is less a reference device for Samsung Electronics' mobile division and more a reference device for the PC division. It's also ironic that MS's Surface appeared at the same time. This market is of little interest to mobile carriers. If the Nexus 7 spreads, far from increasing LTE subscribers, Wi-Fi costs will increase. This movement signifies that Google is fundamentally maintaining its strategy as a service provider with a platform as its weapon. And the strategy Google chose saw potential in the Amazon Kindle. My prediction earlier this year that ICS-based low-cost Wi-Fi tablets would bring about a big change – with the release of the Jelly Bean-based Nexus 7 – doesn't this mean that Google intends to lead this change as well? While my prediction that this year would be the first year of the Android tablet market has been pushed back a bit, the fact that Google has finally released its first reference tablet means that the possibility of my prediction is not yet over.
**4. Nexus 7's Success** In my personal opinion, it won't sell. Especially not in Korea. In Korea, where a brand's distribution capability is more important than the device itself, there are no third parties to strongly push Google's Nexus 7. Rather, I believe success will begin when small and medium-sized enterprise tablets identical to the Nexus 7 appear, or when Samsung and LG devices start to emerge. Although the Nexus 7 was made directly by Google, it still means that Google will not be the one to lead the Android tablet market. The important thing is that future Android tablets, unlike the Galaxy Tab which was previously constrained by mobile carriers' requirements, will at least have the performance and price competitiveness of the Nexus 7. I look forward to next year.

titleEn: [Tip] How to Save on Smartphone Data Charges (
contentEn:
I use two devices: an HTC Flyer tablet and a Galaxy S2. Among these, the HTC Flyer's plan is quite generous at 12,000 won per month, offering 10GB of WiBro and 1GB of 3G, while the Galaxy S2's plan is a 34-plan, using 100MB of data per month. Combined, I'm paying roughly the equivalent of a 55-plan. This is because the HTC plan is so cheap that I use tethering with it. Most of you probably know how to save money with tethering, so I'd like to talk about how to make the most of the 100MB from the 34-plan. The downside of tethering is that you have to set it up every time, so if you use the 100MB data plan wisely, you can use most essential functions without tethering. The feature I'm introducing today is one of my favorites since the Galaxy S2's ICS upgrade.

**1. Let's use the data usage options on ICS or higher. (Menu > Data Usage)**
If you go into Settings, you'll see something like this:
{{IMG:1}}
From here, select Data Usage.
{{IMG:2}}
Before ICS, there was only the 'Data network usage' option. You could only decide whether or not to use 3G data. However, starting with ICS, more detailed features are available.

**1) Set data limit, set usage cycle**
First, you can set a data usage limit and a usage cycle. It provides a warning about usage and completely disables data if you exceed a certain limit. In my case, since my plan only allows up to 100MB, I set a warning at 75MB and a limit at 100MB.

**2) Find the culprit: which app uses the most data.**
{{IMG:3}}
You can see which apps have used the most data. This includes data downloaded in the background, so you can identify the culprit consuming your data.

**3) Restrict background data - Set limits per app**
Background data restriction refers to features that use data in the background even when the user is not actively using them. Most Android push notifications and widgets use this feature. In the case of Facebook, it's not something I necessarily need to receive in real-time, and I usually view it on Wi-Fi or when I choose to, so I will set a background data restriction for it.
{{IMG:4}}
If you select 'Restrict background data',
{{IMG:5}}
Press 'OK'. Now, Facebook push notifications will not work on 3G. Instead, you can save that much data.

**2. Fast speed? Large capacity? What's better is smart usage habits.**
I also use a lot of data, but I wonder if it's really necessary to pay expensive fees for the huge data allowances provided by carriers, especially when using 3G. If you use the methods above well, you can manage even with a 3G 34-plan. For users who only use KakaoTalk, 100MB is more than enough. (Of course, in this case, only use VoiceTalk on Wi-Fi.) After all, Wi-Fi zones are plentiful. I use the 10GB WiBro I currently have generously, even with tethering. However, dead zones are the most annoying. I think what mobile carriers need most is quality, rather than just speed and capacity, at this point. Mobile carriers who want to raise prices probably won't like that, though.

titleEn: [ITX CLOUD] Cloud:
contentEn:
**1. Cloud: The New IT Trend**
Since Apple created the iPhone, the focus of the IT market has shifted to mobile. Mobile is divided into two solutions, apps and web, but the real power of smartphones lies in the network. And this network, in turn, means the internet. Most of the apps we use rely on the internet. KakaoTalk, for example, handles a very large amount of traffic. This new market, a "blue ocean," has opened up due to environmental changes, including the mobile market situation, but recently there's another trend: infrastructure cloud.

**2. Why the Cloud Market Opened**
Users typically think of cloud services like NDrive or iCloud when they hear "cloud." Indeed, that's how public cloud services are generally known. However, "cloud" actually started as a term for B2B (business-to-business market) infrastructure. It's a method of virtualizing assets like servers and networks, leasing them out, and generating profit from it. This became possible because what companies truly want is not the physical server hardware, but the capabilities like networking and computing that a server provides. Companies specializing in such infrastructure virtualize hardware and lease out idle assets to other companies for a fee. This is a win-win model: cloud providers can focus on their core asset, infrastructure, while service providers can lease areas that are not their core assets, gaining financial benefits.

**3. Cloud: A Blessing for Small Startups**
Furthermore, this SW technology called virtualization has made it possible to lease hardware broken down by time and resource. This means you can build a server environment that perfectly fits even the most minute requirements. This change in environment is a great blessing for small startups. **For startups that currently lack funds but hope to grow suddenly someday, cloud computing is a good solution for several reasons.**

**1) The time spent on server setup before creating a service is over.**
When creating an internet service, a lot of time is initially spent on server setup. Moreover, if a company specializes in services, it often lacks much know-how and is unsure if it's doing it right. Cloud computing offers an alternative to this.

**2) The days of high server costs even without visitors are over.**
Servers are built to prepare for peak times and a sudden surge in future visitors. Naturally, this can be a significant burden for startups. Paying high costs for a server that only a few developers access is tough on a startup's budget. The solution to this is also cloud computing. Turn them off when not developing. Set up the minimum specifications required for development, and then, as visitors increase during service operation, you can easily copy to servers with better specifications sequentially.

**3) Fear of sudden growth is also over.**
While sudden growth may seem like a blessing, expanding servers is not an easy task. Quickly deploying servers and distributing traffic is crucial for a company's sustained growth. With cloud computing, if you receive the welcome news of sudden growth, you can open a web browser and respond in a very short time with a few simple clicks. Of course, server costs will increase, but it's also time to seek investors with your visitor numbers. Now, forget about server costs and technicalities; the important thing is how to maintain that growth.

**4) Difficulties in managing security attacks are also over.**
Although I've written "4" as the title, it's not entirely true to say everything is over. There is no silver bullet for security. Even if you use some solutions provided by the cloud, the person in charge must continuously possess knowledge about servers. However, the state of being defenseless due to complete ignorance, as in the past, can be greatly reduced. Leasing very expensive security equipment is also easily possible, and at least you'll have someone to ask when you don't know something. Cloud providers are, after all, experts in this field, more so than service providers.

**4. What Cloud Services Can I Use Right Now?**
**1) Amazon AWS**
In fact, if we talk about the leading player in cloud services, it's Amazon AWS. Recently, the AWS developer site was localized into Korean. The micro-tier is free for one year, so if you're not running an actual service, it's worth trying. However, it's in English, and you'll need to study it a bit, which is good for learning. Since the servers are not in Korea, the perceived speed is lower. (This could be critical.)

**2) KT's uCloud biz**
In Korea, KT is one of the companies most actively pursuing Amazon as a target. It offers various options, and if it's a hugely successful large-scale project in Korea, KT's inexpensive network fees will be helpful.

**3) Hyosung ITX Cloud**
Actually, the reason I published this post was not only because I wanted to talk about cloud computing, but also because I received a small sponsorship from Hyosung ITX. **The advantage of the cloud service provided by Hyosung ITX is that it offers very large traffic for free compared to KT. Additionally, snapshots, which are charged by capacity, are partially free, and load balancers are offered at a much lower price.** For blogs or small to medium-sized websites that are not very large services, ITX's cloud seems to offer benefits. **I plan to upload a more detailed pricing analysis post later.** Before that, I recommend visiting the site. [http://cloud.hyosungitx.com/](http://cloud.hyosungitx.com/)

**5. The Era of "I can't start a startup because I have no money" is Over**
I've explained above why cloud computing is a blessing for startups. You can start a service with pocket money. You can even achieve speeds where you set it up today and start development today. In addition, abundant mashups are another weapon that today's startups can utilize, but I'll talk about that later. The era has come where even students, if they have an idea, can use the cloud to pursue their dreams anytime.

ps. This was a post I had already been thinking of writing, so I thank Hyosung ITX for providing a good impetus.

titleEn: What is Software-Centric Convergence, and Why
contentEn:
** 1. What is convergence (융합), the future of Korea?**
The name of the team I'm part of at my company is the Convergence Service Team. I'm not a convergence expert, and due to the nature of the company, teams change frequently, so I don't know when the name will change or when I'll move to another team. However, currently, I'm working on supporting devices that can have various views beyond the web, which is the company's main focus, and related services. These devices could be TVs or mobile phones. When thinking about convergence, what was most talked about in the past was the integration of cameras into mobile phones. Conversely, the term 'divergence' also exists. Many people ponder what to combine and what to separate. And sometimes, they think that's the end of convergence. But is that really the end?

** 2. Let's actually do convergence. Is it that simple? That's why SW is needed!**
However, let's imagine doing convergence not just by talking about it, but by actually creating products. What completely different industries would need to do when coming together is to define specifications for interfacing with each other. That could even be about how many pins there are. Early convergence in the past followed this method. However, the problem is that the demands for these interfaces are diverse, with many different companies requiring various methods, and creating specifications and holding meetings every time is difficult. What used to be achieved through a consultative body within a single industry now demands more flexible interfaces in the era of convergence. In fact, such considerations have existed in software for a very long time. In software, there have been various considerations, from functions, objects, and components to SaaS, to meet diverse requirements. Among recent technologies, mashups and cloud computing are also part of these considerations for reusability. Software changes rapidly. This is because its lifecycle is short, and the cost of modification is relatively lower compared to hardware. (However, blindly believing that modification costs are low will lead to losing in competition. Blind faith is absolutely forbidden.) In fact, these considerations have strengthened the flexibility of software products. Furthermore, within a single software product, virtual layers have been standardized, making transplantation easier. And these technologies can be universally applied to all technologies that use information. The communication methods for ATMs and telephone lines were different in the past. Whether it was voice or payment information, it was all ultimately the same signal. Ultimately, these changes led to the digitalization of broadcasting and communication. And cable, broadcast, and wireless moved down to the hardware layer and transformed into a unified IP network. The resulting software layer gained volume and became valuable as a single market. If the technology is open, many people will conduct various experiments with software here and create killer apps that no one expected. These changes can also be found in smartphones. What is the result of convergence created by the iPhone? A huge, open, single market created through the combination of computing technology and mobile communication. A massive software market volume, unseen in other markets that were fragmented by mobile carriers and consultative bodies in the past. It is the emergence of the App Store. It's not that there was no software market for feature phones in the past. What's significant here is that apps, which were merely one function of feature phones, became less dependent on the phone and created a huge market. The (open?) technology called iOS contributed to this. (In Apple's case, there is indeed dependence due to an intentional cross-platform strategy, but due to the nature of software, with the emergence of hybrid apps, perfect control is not possible, and in fact, Apple is also the biggest beneficiary of software de-dependence. If this is confusing, Android clearly illustrates this picture.)

** 1) SW is the adhesive that binds industries (services).**
Software is like a very flexible adhesive. To maximize efficiency, the use of standards and open, general-purpose technologies is important. If the needs of each service are incorporated, generality decreases. Even internet service providers are reluctant to create APIs for each of their services. This is because they might believe that investing their resources to expose their assets is not very beneficial to them. However, for a company with multiple services, these APIs are very important. Because they can reduce duplicate modules and respond to external requirements as needed. And to easily use these APIs and respond to complex demands, APIs must be standardized. This is precisely why software-level convergence is important. Each service can only passively create the APIs it immediately needs. However, in a diverse and standardized API environment, they too become beneficiaries. The problem is that this stage doesn't happen automatically. Because costs are incurred before the benefits can be realized. Furthermore, incorrect standardization or API management inevitably raises questions about utility. Therefore, these actions are carried out by a single organization with unified power. Amazon and Facebook can be cited as the best examples.

** 2) SW is the knife that cuts industries (services).**
Conversely, software is also a knife. Convergence and divergence are actually the same thing. Just as a carpenter uses both nails and a saw. When producing a single product, what should we do if we want to sell off some of our assets? We need to cut them. If you cut them, they eventually become independent modules, and these modules will have APIs or interfaces. Ultimately, it's good if standardized technology is also incorporated here. Among the companies that have entered the cloud, there is Google, which is a master of distributed computing. These were technologies for search, but they realized that if they cut and sold them, it would make money.

** 3) The potential of the SW industry: open to all industries but not subservient to any.**
You might say, 'Isn't it just at the level of SW services?' What happened when a general-purpose OS was installed in feature phones? And the Hyundai Santa Fe DM can now be started by installing an app on a feature phone. This is just the beginning. In the past, they would have attached an LCD to a remote control. You can control the TV with a smartphone, lighting can detect optimal brightness with a light sensor, and automatically turn off at bedtime according to the user's smartphone schedule. When you sit in a chair, it might find the optimal angle based on the time you've worked that day. The grumpy phone seen in Ghostbusters when I was a child becomes a reality. If a spam call comes, it might just curse and hang up. Commonly, computing technology is involved here. The sensor in the eye of a launched missile could become smart enough to return to the launch pad if the enemy raises a white flag. The prerequisite here is that if recognition technology, network technology, and middleware technology, which are commonly used in these technologies, are closed off by industry, then labor mobility and technology transfer will face difficulties. While one industry is struggling to integrate IT technology into another, the other might have already moved on to the next lifecycle. **The core of the SW industry, as always discussed even in unit development, is the elimination of dependencies. Well-made SW is beautiful on its own.**

** 4) Some areas of industries that are eliminated by convergence were originally not assets of those industries, but rather belonged to the SW industry.**
The reason why an integrated, SW-centric IT alliance is important is from this perspective. Of course, in this process, traditionally redundant industries will disappear. However, the reason they are eliminated is that they were not assets of those industries. Mobile carriers are originally network operators, and service or content industries are not their assets. SMS was a representative service, and its takeover by an IT alternative like KakaoTalk is a prime example. Of course, network operators can transform into SW industry players. Just as Amazon transformed. If you covet SW, you should transform into an SW business operator, not hate the SW business or protect your turf. The nation should also help with that. Currently, it seems that being in the telecommunications or broadcasting sector sometimes leads to reverse discrimination.

** 5) Is the Galaxy S3 a product domain? Or a SW convergence domain?**
The ICS upgrade for Galaxy S2 included a foreign app (SW) called Vlingo. It's a regrettable reality that such technology doesn't exist domestically. A large amount of context-awareness technology was invested in the S3. All those 'dormant whatever' features are context-awareness technologies. Whether it's a PC, a phone, or even a security chime, the principle is all the same. This time, the focus was not on hardware specifications. Although I was one who criticized Samsung for not having a big picture, the investment in SW can be interpreted as Samsung being well aware of its current weaknesses. Samsung's biggest weakness is SW, and the company must transform to be SW-centric to continuously create high added value. This time, they grasped the 'How' for the device research lab, but I was just disappointed that they hadn't yet shown the 'What' for Samsung Electronics as a whole. (I will write a post about this as well.) It can be seen that Samsung Electronics' devices were already created anticipating the power of SW convergence.

**3. From the perspective of national competitiveness, an IT control tower is needed to serve as the tower for SW convergence.**
However, in the era of convergence, incorrect convergence becomes a problem for national competitiveness itself. If an integrated organization managing convergence goes in the wrong direction, convergence is worse than doing nothing. Therefore, it must be very knowledgeable and have strong drive. And as mentioned earlier regarding dependency, it's difficult to exert competitiveness if it's subservient to other industries. The fact that the specifications created by the IPTV consortium for broadcasting have lost competitiveness as smart TVs in the current era of open OS can be interpreted this way, and if such environmental changes are detected, a rapid transformation is needed to adapt. This has become very long, but the **SW convergence paradigm is not about representing a single interest group, but a paradigm shift at the level of competitiveness by securing industrial

If Sung Apps had been created, how would the market have changed? (Though it's still a reality that telecom companies are the dominant force...)
P.S. In the next administration, would it be good to expect a CTO for South Korea? Honestly, I'm not sure if I'm in a position or at a level to offer an opinion, but I'm raising my voice, however inadequate. I'd like to hear many people's opinions and learn together.

titleEn: Galaxy Note 3G: What Consumers Want,
contentEn:
Interest in the Galaxy Note has been quite fervent, and at the same time, there's been a lot of talk and trouble surrounding it. Since the device I wanted was close to the Galaxy Note, I'd like to add a few words and briefly discuss the current situation of the Galaxy Note. First, while many users criticize the Galaxy Note without even trying it, I personally believe it's a device in a good position.

http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=5912095150

[Samsung Anycall SHV-E160S (Galaxy Note LTE)](http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=5912095150)

Brand
Samsung Electronics
SKT, Galaxy Note, Bar, Smartphone, Android 2.3, 1.5GHz Dual-core, 5.3-inch HD Super AMOLED, Tou...
[View Review](http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=5912095150&tc=6)
**1. Can the Galaxy Note be a Game Changer?**
**1) Is the size burdensome?**
In fact, just yesterday, I saw a lady in Bundang making a call with a Galaxy Tab, and I've seen many elderly people show interest in large, tablet-sized phones. Furthermore, a wider screen for web browsing, HD videos, and work is a welcome feature for many. An HD screen on a 4-inch device is highly likely to cause eye fatigue. When I used early smartphones like the Cellvic XG, MyCube, and Poz series, many friends asked why I used such ridiculously large smartphones. Eventually, the iPhone came out and shattered people's preconceptions about large touchscreens. I believe the Note's large screen size is a perfectly surmountable size if it offers users convenience beyond that. In fact, the reactions from other 5-inch device users haven't been bad either.

**2) Amazing S Pen, Wacom Hurray!**
Those who haven't used it tend to disparage the S Pen, but the S Pen's technology is Wacom's technology. It's one of the technologies I consider the ultimate interface. Electro-magnetic resonance (EMR) pen technology supports precise pressure and tilt detection, allowing it to perfectly mimic the effects of a real brush or pencil, making it a preferred technology among graphic designers. In fact, many people who draw game illustrations and webtoons that you see have a tablet equipped with this technology. Therefore, I won't discuss the completeness of this technology separately. If I were to compare the S Pen to a capacitive stylus, I would boldly say it's like comparing a professional drawing pen to a tree branch. If the iPhone's designer sketched digitally, they would have undoubtedly used a Wacom tablet. Some people say that capacitive touch and the S Pen cannot be used simultaneously, but there are already laptops like the TM2 that use both capacitive touch and a Wacom pen. The EMR pen activates when it comes within a certain distance of the screen, at which point capacitive touch is deactivated. This Wacom technology is quite old, and many companies covet it, but apparently, no one else can use it besides Wacom. That's why even Microsoft invested in an alternative technology called N-trig, but it can't match Wacom's performance. Of course, this technology isn't Samsung's. And the S Pen is not quite at the level of an Intuos, which graphic designers use for tilt detection. Still, with 128 levels of pressure sensitivity, it's slightly less than the ArtPad 2 I used way back in the 20th century, but it's more than capable of creating excellent images. For reference, the images in my blog's [Illustration] category are drawings made using a Wacom tablet, just like the S Pen.

**3) What changes when HD meets the pen?**
**- Direct use of PC web screens**
The true meaning of a larger screen and precise pen input is the ability to browse PC-based web pages without any inconvenience. Most current PC web services are designed based on a mouse interface. Wacom's S Pen can do everything a mouse can, from mouse-over effects to clicking small menu items. Even if current Galaxy or iPhone devices could full-browse PC web pages, the reason some areas had to be zoomed in via pinch-zoom and then touched was precisely because finger touch couldn't replicate the precision of a mouse. However, a pen can do that. Selecting all content without zooming. While this goes against the touch-based web design currently being considered, for immediate users, most of the web is not optimized for touch, so the benefits are very significant.
**- Development of new UX**
A combination of pen and touch, as announced by Microsoft, could be realized. Of course, the Galaxy Note has an either-or structure for touch and pen, so Microsoft's new patent cannot be applied. However, the fact that Samsung and Microsoft have signed a cross-licensing agreement for patents means that Microsoft's patents could be applied to Samsung's tablets in the future, potentially leading to entirely new UX. If anyone argues that the pen won't bring any change, I'd like to remind them of the changes the Nintendo DS brought.

**[MS's Touch and Pen-based UX planned for Windows 8]**

**2. But LTE tackled the Note's side**
**- Users want 3G!**
Another topic of this post, which has been praising the Galaxy Note, is LTE. It seems Samsung has created a wonderful device that could shed the stigma of copying the iPhone, but in Korea, someone strongly tackled it: LTE. Following my criticism of the KT Galaxy 8.9, I'd like to talk once again about the Note's story, ruined by carrier strategy.

**1) LTE for top specifications?**
They say LTE was chosen for the Note because it's for top specifications. But what about sacrificing the CPU for LTE? In Korea, Exynos was abandoned for LTE, and the inferior Snapdragon was adopted. For a higher HD resolution, a good performance CPU and video are very important. The need is even greater for the Note than for the Galaxy S2. Nevertheless, Samsung sacrificed performance for LTE network speed. The statement that LTE was chosen for top specifications somehow doesn't add up.

**2) Do consumers want LTE?**
That's a ridiculous claim. They can keep running ads to inject it into the public consciousness. In fact, they already are. But those who know, know the reality. Let me show you a few funny results I've seen recently.

**- Galaxy Note Recommended Search Terms Results**
{{IMG:1}}
Two of the recommended search terms are related to 3G. LTE isn't even there.

**- Galaxy Note search results on Joonggonara (used goods marketplace)**
{{IMG:2}}

Currently, 3G models are selling with a premium. Really, do people want LTE?

**3) Does Samsung not understand consumer needs or not intend to do business?**
Samsung is not a group of fools, and many bloggers who reviewed the Galaxy Note pointed this out, and even at events, 3G was mentioned, indicating they are well aware of consumer needs.

**3) Carrier pressure to make it a strategic phone for LTE**
The conclusion is simple. There must have been a deal or some kind of pressure from the carriers. It's incredibly frustrating. Clearly, buying a domestic model is more convenient than importing a Note from overseas through unofficial channels, so a certain amount of purchases will definitely occur. However, while precise measurement is difficult, it's clear that LTE has hampered the Note. If this model had been released with 3G, carriers would have been afraid of the Note consuming more traffic and using unlimited data plans.

**4. While carriers raise communication fees and strengthen control over service and device markets, the government stands idly by**
If the 62,000 won plan had been set around 55,000 won, I wouldn't be this annoyed. The 62,000 won plan is not unlimited either, but it allows a level of traffic that most 55,000 won plan users would find acceptable. The government, which claims to lower communication fees, is only lowering them in irrelevant areas. Data communication fees are now as essential as electricity. Perhaps those in power only consider voice calls as essential. The foresight of past governments, which worried about the problems brought by the digital divide, seems to be only concerned with digital control now. Data communication fees are an essential commodity, and I hope the government doesn't stand idly by in this situation where prices are increasing by more than 10% at once. And this money is felt by users as an increase in phone prices, becoming a reason not to choose Samsung phones, so Samsung Electronics should reconsider. Isn't it already the reason why the Note, which is more expensive than the Galaxy S2, feels even more expensive?

titleEn: Will 2012 Be the Golden Age for the Domestic Tablet Market?
contentEn:
**1. The 2011 Tablet Market Was Worse Than Expected**
The high expectations for tablets, hotly discussed at the beginning of this year, still seem quite disappointing even now, after the release of iPad 2 and the Galaxy 10.1 and 8.9. This is especially true and much more serious when limited to the domestic market. Compared to overseas, the iPad craze was much weaker, and in a tablet and pad market that hasn't taken off, no one is attempting to create tablet-specific apps or services. It's merely a slight modification of smartphone and PC services. You might say the iPad is different because you see a few around, but what people do with an iPad doesn't seem much different from what they do with a smartphone, and it hasn't replaced the PC either. Why did it turn out this way?

**2. What Users *Really* Want from Tablets**
**1) A Cheap Internet Browser**
What RIM and Amazon taught us in this year's tablet market is clear: tablets priced close to $200 caused a sensation. This means users aren't willing to spend close to $500 on a large smart pad. It's like looking at the netbook market. In fact, the exact position of the pad market is precisely that of the netbook.

**2) Content**
A pad market that hasn't achieved widespread distribution has ultimately led to a lack of content, and it seems a virtuous cycle like that of the iPhone has not been established. This phenomenon was even more pronounced in the Android ecosystem. As if to prove this, Amazon's Kindle is creating a sensation overseas. Amazon doesn't have fancy hardware like the iPad or Galaxy 10.1. Instead, it has a massive content market and shopping mall. And that, in fact, is the most crucial thing users want from a pad.

**3) GPS, High-Resolution Rear Cameras, and Gyro Sensors Are Not Needed in Tablets.**
**Duplication with Smartphones is Unnecessary.**
Amazon boldly removed these features. Why? It's not because those technologies are unnecessary. It's because users already have other devices that perform those functions. First, for GPS and rear cameras, SNS is the killer app. They particularly shine outside the home or office. This means they are not the main stage for tablets. Gyro sensors often appear in tilt-based games. However, one reason tilting became popular in games was that the screen was too small, and placing touch controllers on the screen made it look even narrower. While there are cases where the motion itself is a feature, like racing games that simulate a steering wheel, most games use touch rather than gyro sensors. In fact, killer apps using gyro sensors don't seem particularly necessary outside of browsing and camera use. A precise 9-axis gyro sensor? Is it needed in a tablet? I believe distinguishing between landscape and portrait is sufficient.

**3. Strategies of Domestic Players**
Having discussed my thoughts on the position of tablets above, I'd like to talk about the strategies of domestic tablet players and my personal outlook.
**1) Samsung Electronics, Indifferent to the Domestic Market: 'Just Do As Well As the iPad, What Else?'**
The Galaxy 8.9 and 10.1 are quite impressive hardware. However, the problem is that they are excessively all-in-one. Because they are tied to domestic mobile carriers, the price is also a bit strange. Furthermore, as a manufacturer, they lack content. As a result, they are likely to remain display items for those who already own them. This is because the iPad, which they considered a competitor, wasn't particularly cheap, so they only needed to match it. From the outset, Samsung seems to have little interest in the domestic pad market. After all, Samsung is a global company. A high-end tablet strategy at a high price seems natural for a company that doesn't possess content.

**2) Mobile Carriers: Let's Not Repeat the Smartphone Nightmare.**
Mobile carriers view tablets as another source of revenue. They control device distribution with manufacturers and won't sell tablets unless you subscribe to a separate smartphone plan. They try to convince consumers that tablets are cheaper if bundled with a smartphone plan, but everyone knows that paying 50,000 won every month for two years is more expensive than swiping a card for 500,000 won at once. They even bundle content into the device price. Moreover, the quality of most content provided is not very high, and the quantity is hardly abundant. Content with pre-determined profits is also very expensive, which inevitably hinders active distribution.
My reasoning for this is the carriers' reluctance to expand pad distribution through internet and WiBro bundles. There's clearly an effective sales method, but their hesitation suggests ulterior motives. As if to prove this, they launched the Galaxy 8.9 as a home pad and sell the Galaxy Tab and Flyer WiBro bundles without call functionality. It's clear they are more concerned about cannibalization and creating new revenue models for pads than expanding the market.

**3) SMEs: 'We Thought the Tablet Market Would Open Up. Google Fooled Us.'**
Android is open to everyone, allowing SMEs to release cheap tablets. However, their reliability is questionable, and without content and sales channels, the survival of SME tablets is not easy.

**4. Will It Open Up in 2012?**
The current situation looks bleak. SMEs lack the capacity to open it up, Samsung is not very interested in the domestic market and is swayed by carriers, and carriers are focused on discovering revenue sources rather than opening the market. Like with the iPhone, the domestic pad market seems destined to be isolated and quiet for a while. **Perhaps the turning point will be late next year when Windows 8 is released, or when HD-grade tablets under 300,000 won from China become available at E-Mart.**
Next year, mobile carriers are supposed to be unable to restrict devices, but we'll have to wait and see.
**The pad market will definitely come. It's just a matter of timing.** However, for now, I think it's too early to buy a pad domestically. Perhaps because of this, devices like the Galaxy Note, which fall in between, might sell better.

titleEn: [Infomark Wibro Egg Review
contentEn:
Last time, I criticized LTE, but I finally got a chance to experience WiBro. I was invited to an Infomark product review session, which gave me the opportunity to try out WiBro. As an SKT user, I didn't actually have much prior knowledge about the company. Anyway, there aren't many invitations, and even when there are, they're usually on weekday afternoons, which I can't attend. So, the condition of a weekday evening worked out, and I used my 'Oasis' (an early leave system at work, usable once a month) for the first time in a while to go out to Seoul.

 ﻿The venue was aA Museum in Samcheong-dong. I left work early and took a bus, but being bad with directions, I inevitably got lost. The place was further from Anguk Station than I expected. Anyway, the first things that caught my eye at the atmospheric cafe I arrived at were Infomark's pretty products. Several bloggers had already arrived and were taking photos. I'm not a professional reviewer, and I was so busy with work that I forgot to bring my camera, so I just took a few shots with my smartphone. You can easily find details about the appearance and specifications of Infomark's Compact Egg by referring to other bloggers' reviews. Actually, there's no need for a long explanation; if you use this pretty, small Egg, you can enjoy WiBro, which is installed nationwide, for 8 hours. You can think of an Egg as a portable wireless router.
 Anyway, rather than a spec review, I'd like to write about my actual experience and which users this product might appeal to. Today, let's start lightly with a review of my WiBro Egg experience.

http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=5953489383
 
  [INFOMARKKWF-B2700](http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=5953489383)
  
  Brand
  INFOMARK
  WiFi Wireless, WiBro, KT
  Rating
  
   
    
   
  
  
  [View Reviews](http://shopping.naver.com/detail/detail.nhn?nv_mid=5953489383&tc=6)
 

 ﻿

﻿﻿
**1. Subway Test, First Encounter with WiBro Was Highly Satisfying**** 1) Industry-standard micro USB. Ensures compatibility with other smartphone cables.**
 On my way home after the product review, my phone battery died on the subway. I remembered Infomark's Egg on the subway and took it out. Its charging cable is a micro USB, identical to the Galaxy S2. When I plugged the cable into my laptop and connected it to the Galaxy S2, it charged and booted simultaneously. Anyway, I secured a way to contact my wife until I got home. The fact that the Egg uses a micro USB port isn't a major feature, but its compatibility with most devices is a big advantage. Thanks to this, I don't have to carry a separate cable for my Galaxy S2.
** 2) PC web surfing with excellent speed**
 Since I had a seat on the subway, I decided to activate the Egg. I booted the Egg, selected KT's 5GB free event for a month, and entered my personal information, and it was registered very easily. Then the familiar Naver homepage appeared. Previously, when I surfed the web on my laptop connected via Optimus Q USB direct, it felt a bit sluggish, but the laptop connected to WiBro felt comparable to using it at home. It was a moment of realizing that WiBro was not originally a technology solely for smartphones. After telling my wife to talk to me via Naver Talk for PC, I enjoyed web surfing. I enjoyed it so much that I ended up missing my stop by one station ㅜㅜ  ﻿
**3) Both a drawback and an advantage. The Egg, as a separate device, brings the blessing of WiBro to all devices. For pad and laptop users... long live the Egg!**
The clear drawback of the Egg is that you have to carry a separate device. However, the advantage is that the Egg works with laptops, pads, and smartphones without distinction. My first impression of WiBro was 100% satisfaction.
**2. In-car Test**
 The second test was during my commute. It was to check for dead zones when traveling on the national road from Anyang Hogye-dong to Jeongja-dong. **
1) Slight dead zones occur underground and indoors.**
When I first turned on WiBro in the underground parking lot on the second basement level, it didn't receive a signal. I figured it was because it was an underground parking lot where even 3G doesn't work well. As soon as I saw the exit on the first basement level, WiBro turned orange and started receiving a signal. It turned green immediately after exiting the first basement level. 
**2) Usable reception rate, better than SKT's 3G**
After that, on the way to Jeongja-dong, I played Naver Music and passed through a few short tunnels.
 The music never cut out, and only in the middle of tunnels did the light briefly turn orange, indicating a weaker signal. And after arriving at work, there was no signal inside the company. In the restaurant during lunchtime, the orange light came on, but it was usable. WiBro, which has some diffraction properties, is insufficient in deep indoor areas but was sufficient for use while on the move. In addition, I tested it on the Yeongdong Expressway between Buksuwon IC and Yangji IC, and the signal was continuously caught in long tunnels like Maseong Tunnel, suggesting WiBro base stations are installed there. If the number of users increases like 3G, I think the nationwide network will become denser, and indoor base stations will also increase. I should ask KT if it's possible to install a small base station (gap filler) if there's a WiBro dead zone at home. 
** 3. Charms Felt While Using the Egg** **1) Fast Speed**
** ** It's fast. The actual usage speed was around 3Mbit/sec for downloads, which is three times the speed of SKT's 3G. However, the network felt more stable. I don't think a longer explanation is needed. Although LTE is said to be fast, the nationwide network isn't actually fully deployed, and if most usage is web surfing, the response speed of web pages during web surfing hasn't improved compared to the enhanced download speed, so users reportedly perceive it as slower. It would be interesting to compare the RTT (Round-Trip Time) of WiBro and LTE. WiBro showed quite immediate responses. Especially when viewing the Naver Webtoon app, it showed truly excellent speed. It was very impressive to be able to view it with almost no delay, and I felt a speed increase of more than 5 times compared to 3G. It also guaranteed a speed that allowed YouTube to be viewed in decent quality. It was proving the '4G right now' slogan. ﻿ ** 2) Easy Portability and Pretty Design**
 The advantage of Infomark's Egg, which fits perfectly in a pocket, is praised endlessly by other bloggers, so I don't need to explain it at length. It's pretty. They also give you a nice leather case. At first, I wondered why, but then I put it in the car and realized that without it, it would slide around and get scratched. I also found it interesting to hear that its design was 'chosen' by Apple CEO Tim Cook. The design truly expressed minimalism well, like the iPhone. (Everyone talks about Apple when it comes to design, and if they talk as if design is everything, I somehow think of iriver and feel a bit negative... but it's an undeniable fact that if functions are the same, good design commands a premium.) ﻿ {{IMG:1}}
** 3) Increases smartphone battery life** 8 hours of battery life, that's longer than my laptop. And by using Wi-Fi, you can also extend your smartphone's battery life. In areas with weak 3G signals, battery consumption for 3G communication becomes extreme, and the biggest culprit for draining smartphone battery life is the battery consumed by 3G. Ultimately, by using the Egg, you can also benefit the battery life of your Galaxy S2 or iPhone. ** 3. Overall Review**
**** **It's usable. There's also a first-generation Egg user around me, and they praised it endlessly, using it with complete satisfaction. With just a WiBro Egg, blogging is perfectly manageable. I haven't tried LTE, but considering that LTE's nationwide network isn't fully deployed yet, WiBro seems to have a good chance at this point. This technology, which has been out for over 5 years and commercialized in Korea for several years, made me resentful as to why it's only now getting a nationwide network and being pushed by KT. Furthermore, KT's WiBro in Korea is compatible with Mobile WiMAX, so it's now said to be compatible with overseas WiBro devices as well. In the next review, I'll compare it thoroughly with LTE, discuss which users it's suitable for, and what improvements would be beneficial, writing a story more in line with my blog's style. ﻿ {{IMG:2}} **http://opencast.naver.com/FS565** [Play This file does not support direct viewing.
