titleEn: The Legend of Dragonia Part 2, Chapter 3, Episode 3 - Ominous Star (1)
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}

For two days now, his mother hadn't gone to work at the castle. Benjamin, who was lonely without siblings, simply loved having his mother at home. He liked the songs his mother taught him, and most of all, he loved not having to eat all three meals alone, so he chattered incessantly like a skylark during mealtimes.
"Mom. Mom. I wish it could always be like this." A wide smile bloomed on Benjamin's face.
"You like it that much, Benjamin?"
"You always came home late, Mom, so we barely had time to talk. Adele doesn't even think about playing with me because she's busy feeding her own kids."
"Yes. That's Adele for you." Aisia looked at the ferret carefully tending to its young in a basket nearby and realized how neglectful she had been towards Benjamin.
"Son. Have you ever been outside Laodicea?"
"Yeah. Even though I look like this, I've been to the logging camp and the fork in the northern road, places other kids wouldn't even dare go." As Benjamin boasted proudly, Aisia smiled slightly and asked again.
"Hoho. Not like that. I mean other cities or other villages."
"Other cities? There's no way I could go. If I went any further, I wouldn't be able to come home that day."
"Right. That's true. Benjamin has to come home. Mom forgot." Aisia paused, then asked as if bringing up something she had held back.
"Benjamin, shall we go on a trip?"
"A trip?" Benjamin's eyes widened as he asked again.
"A real trip to another village."
"Wow! Really?" Benjamin was so excited that food splattered. Aisia stood up, wiped Benjamin's clothes, and said.
"Look, food splattered. Would Mom lie?"
"Are we really going to other villages and seeing amazing things like elephants?"
"Of course. There are many wonderful things outside."
"Can we take Adele too?"
"Yes. Let's go together."
"Yay!" Benjamin cheered with joy. Aisia had heard rumors that a traveling troupe had arrived in Nicopolis. She decided to join a familiar troupe, help with their work, and look for a place to settle.

The next day, Aisia went to the market for her trip. However, she felt a strange sense of unease in the streetscape. The usually bustling market was somehow quiet, and the prices of expensive foodstuffs had risen significantly. In particular, the prices of essential items for travel, such as dried meat and raisins, had become very expensive.
"Madam, why is this so expensive?" Aisia grumbled, reluctantly paying the high price. These were essential items, as they would need to eat on the road to reach other villages.
"Well, you see. As of yesterday, there were people who swept up all the foodstuffs. Thanks to them, we're at the point where we can't sell because there's nothing left, and what little there is, that's the last of it."
"Sigh. There's nothing we can do. Who are these people, anyway? They bought so much that they raised prices in a big city like Laodicea." Thinking that her plan was already encountering difficulties at the start of her trip, Aisia sighed and bought the food.
"Perhaps it's also because of the ominous rumors going around. There's a rumor that a great disaster will soon strike Laodicea. Some people are saying they're fleeing to the mountains, so it might be because of that."
"Oh, come on, Madam. Who spreads such ridiculous rumors? Is it another strange religious group?" Aisia waved her hand dismissively.
"Well, I thought these rumors would die down over time. But it doesn't seem to be the case. For several days, many people have left through the city gates. And yesterday, His Majesty also marched south, not north towards the Seres nation. There have been strange things happening all along, but yesterday morning, an ominous star appeared in the north."
"That happened?" Aisia was surprised by the news, as she hadn't gone out for several days after being shocked by her encounter with Dagmon.
"An ominous star?"
"If you look closely at the Traveler's Star, they say a faint, unfamiliar star has appeared. My eyes are dim, so I couldn't see it, but you're young, so you'll probably see it. Take a look tonight." Aisia felt an inexplicable sense of unease, but it was a city she was leaving anyway. She merely thought that she had to leave this place as quickly as possible.

That night, as darkness fell, Aisia stepped out of her house and was startled by what she saw in the northern sky. Instead of a faint star, there was a new star, unusually blinking with a brightness no different from other stars. It was known that encroaching on the Traveler's Star brought misfortune to those who traveled, but for gypsies, that star was a guiding star, a symbol for them. Though she didn't know much about astrology, Aisia felt uneasy.
"Mom, what are you looking at? Is there something in the sky?" Aisia, who had been gazing at the night sky, snapped back to reality at Benjamin's question.
"No, it's nothing. We have a lot to pack, and tomorrow we need to say goodbye to those who've helped us, so let's go inside." Aisia quickly led Benjamin by the hand, fearing her uneasy feelings might transfer to the child. That night, she went to bed quite late after packing. Just as she finally fell asleep around dawn, she was awakened again by an unexpected intruder.
"Thump, thump, thump." In the dead of night, when everyone was asleep, the sound of someone knocking on Aisia's door echoed through the street. Startled by the loud noise, Aisia shouted, "I'm coming!" and peeked out the window. A cart and a large man were knocking on the door.
"Who is it?" Aisia asked, not opening the door, but there was no answer, only the loud thumping on the door continued. She asked again, but still no reply. Aisia felt uneasy.
"Who is it, making such a racket in the middle of the night!" At the loud noise, lights turned on in other houses outside. Despite this, he continued to knock on the door.
'Who on earth is it, not even answering...' Although she felt uneasy, the mysterious man didn't seem like he would leave her doorstep. Finally, Aisia cautiously opened the door, but the man boldly pushed it wide open and entered.

titleEn: Legend of Dragonia Part 2, Chapter
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}

Aysia visited the tavern again the next day. She was surprised to see a "Tavern for Sale" sign hanging at the entrance. However, as she approached, the door was still open. Cautiously, she stepped inside. The tavern was dark, with the lights off, and no waitresses were to be found. In the silent tavern, only Gulliver remained, looking very apologetic, perhaps due to yesterday's events. Only after Aysia told him it was alright did his stern expression relax, and he handed Aysia a letter, which seemed to have been prepared in advance.
 -Prince Dagmon entered the northern avenue of the Laodicea territory yesterday. You should be able to see him if you wait on the central road of the Imperial Palace around tomorrow afternoon. A map of the way from the laundry room to the central road is attached.-
 Aysia was surprised to receive the letter. She had intended to meet Dagmon, but she hadn't expected to be able to do so this quickly. Feeling awkward being alone with Gulliver, Aysia couldn't have a long conversation, so she thanked him and stood up.
 All the way home, Aysia couldn't stop her heart from pounding after receiving the letter. She still vaguely felt her affection for Dagmon, her first love, but her fear was greater, and she still couldn't understand her own feelings. However, she resolved to meet him for Benjamin's sake. Aysia intended to leave Laodicea without hesitation if he showed even the slightest sign of not welcoming her and her son, but she truly hated the thought of such a situation and was even scared of it. Back home, Aysia took out clean clothes and ironed them.
 "Mom. What day is tomorrow? Why do you look so happy?"
 At Benjamin's question, Aysia's heart sank, and her face turned red.
 "Do I look like that?"
 "Yeah. You're singing a different song while ironing clothes. When I hear your singing, I know what kind of mood you're in, even if I don't want to."
 As Benjamin answered clearly, Aysia smiled and picked up the still-small Benjamin.
 "Really? So what kind of mood am I in?"
 "Hmm. A warm and exciting mood I've never seen before? Oh, I remember. I saw it once before. When the uncle lived with us."
 At Benjamin's answer, Aysia felt sorry for Mrs. Melchizedek. However, on the other hand, through her conversation with Benjamin, she was able to vaguely understand her own emotional state.
 
 Aysia waited on the central road of the Imperial Palace, as Gulliver had instructed. The central road was the direct path into the inner castle where the Imperial Palace was located, so several guards were firmly guarding the gate leading into the palace. After waiting for a long time, two guards approached Aysia.
 "Who are you, loitering here! This is the path to the Imperial Palace where His Majesty resides! Show your palace pass!"
 An older-looking guard shouted at Aysia. It was not unreasonable for a guard to look at Aysia, who had been loitering on the road for a long time, with suspicious eyes. Aysia, startled and frightened, presented her laundry room pass. The guard, taking the pass, knew that such a pass allowed movement within the outer castle without much trouble, so he frowned and, with a suspicious gaze, scrutinized Aysia's appearance once or twice before asking.
 "If you have no business, you should go straight home, not loiter in a place like this and draw suspicion!"
 The soldier yelled with a fearsome face, and Aysia replied in a timid voice.
 "I have someone I'm supposed to meet."
 He then scrutinized Aysia once more, gave an inscrutable smile, returned her pass, and said in a softened voice.
 "I don't know who the young lady is supposed to meet, but it's a big misconception that some high-ranking person coming out from inside would welcome meeting you. I've seen such young ladies sometimes, but I've never seen a good outcome. Don't do anything foolish, just leave. A young lady like you could meet a good man. If you keep loitering here, I might have to interrogate you."
 Aysia took her pass and had to leave in a hurry. However, she couldn't just go back, so she hid in an alley where she could see the Imperial Palace gate, peeking out to watch the road. But soon, her eyes met those of the fearsome guard who had been standing at the gate just moments before. Aysia quickly pulled her head back and hid again, but the guard clicked his tongue, pretended not to notice Aysia, and didn't even look in the direction of the alley. Perhaps he had spoken to the other guards, as no one looked towards the alley where Aysia was hiding. Aysia realized the guards' consideration and felt relieved.
 However, the guard's words bothered her greatly. It was certainly very common for young ladies to be betrayed by noble scions. Of course, there were also dream-like rumors of commoners marrying noble scions on white horses, but Aysia knew that these were just fantasies spread among girls. Aysia's mind became complicated.
 Fearing she might miss him, she carefully watched the face of every person passing on the central road. She almost spoke to a man who looked similar in age to Dagmon. As the waiting time grew longer, anxiety surged. Since it was a path within the palace, not many people passed by, but the thought that she might have missed him brought an unspeakable sense of disappointment.
 After standing and waiting for a long time, her legs began to ache, so she squatted down. Doing so, she suddenly felt so pathetic that she thought she might cry. Before she knew it, the evening sun was setting, casting long shadows, and Aysia truly just wanted to cry.
 'Like a real fool. What am I doing... What will I do after meeting him?'
 As the red sunset turned blue and the first stars began to appear, the Imperial Palace gate opened, and a man emerged. The moment Aysia saw his face, she felt as if her breath had stopped. It was Dagmon, a twenty-two-year-old young man who had shed his seventeen-year-old self. He was still dressed in simple traveler's clothes, and his face, unlike before, radiated a much more trustworthy light. Aysia could now see the strong light she had vaguely felt in him before, now clearly visible on his face. Just moments ago, Aysia had truly wanted to cry, but upon seeing him, her feelings turned to joy and happiness. His face still looked kind, unchanged from when he had whispered words of love to Aysia. She felt certain that he would call her name again at any moment.
 Just as Aysia was about to call out to him, she spotted a woman with him. Aysia paused momentarily with an ominous feeling and hid back in the alley. Besides the woman, there was also a pair of a man and a woman who looked like siblings, and they seemed very affectionate, as if they had spent a lot of time together. In particular, the woman closely following Dagmon looked beautiful even to Aysia. She had the same blonde hair and fair skin as Aysia, and despite being dressed as a traveler, she exuded an inexplicable dignity. Aysia, who had always played various roles, also had a talent for discerning people's hidden sides.
 
 Dagmon, having met his father, was not in a very good mood. He didn't dislike his father, but he couldn't help but maintain a love-hate relationship. Above all, his father's expectations were also a burden, and while his father tried to build a strong nation in his own way, Dagmon didn't like his father's methods. Even with Dagmon's warning that the two cities might self-destruct, his father remained stubborn.
 In the end, Dagmon decided he had to solve it his own way. If things continued as they were, countless lives of the people would be lost. He resolved to handle this matter in his own way, even if it meant being branded a traitor by his father. He believed this was how he could repay those who trusted him, and he no longer wanted to run away. After talking with his father, he felt even more certain. He didn't have much time.
 "What are you thinking about so much after meeting King Dagmon?"
 Sera, noticing Dagmon's different mood, asked.
 "This time, I'll have to ask for a favor from Princess Sera of the Ceres Kingdom."
Dagmon's voice was clearly audible even to

She pointed, but a more terrible pain surged from her chest.
'Right. It was obvious, but I had unnecessary expectations.'
Aysia thought this in her mind, but her breath caught in her throat, and her chest ached as if it were tearing. She was so exhausted that she squatted down and clutched her chest. She took deep breaths, repeatedly telling herself it was nothing.
"Are you okay?"
Just then, someone's worried voice was heard. Aysia, for a moment, wondered if Dagmon had found her and reached out, and she lifted her head with a hopeful heart. However, it was the soldier who had been considerate of Aysia.
"I'm... okay..."
Aysia barely managed to stand up. The soldier had an 'I knew it' expression. Seeing the soldier's face, she felt incredibly embarrassed and just wanted to run away from that spot.
Aysia trudged home with a heavy heart. She desperately missed Benjamin. Her mouth felt parched, and the pain in her chest wouldn't subside. She kept telling herself it was nothing, but tears soon began to flow.
'It's nothing... I'm fine, so why am I crying so much?'
In Aysia's memory, her moments with Dagmon played out like a sad movie. Her makeup was smudged, and her clean clothes were soaked with sweat. When Aysia returned home, she immediately hugged Benjamin tightly.
"Mom. I can't breathe. Why are you hugging me so hard?"
Benjamin was initially flustered and complained about Aysia's sudden action, but soon realizing his mother was crying, he said nothing and patted Aysia, comforting her as if she were a seventeen-year-old suffering from heartbreak. That was the last scene of the connection between Aysia and Dagmon, which the twenty-two-year-old Dagmon never knew.

titleEn: [iPhone Cult] Criticizing and Em
contentEn:
**1. Adherents of the iPhone Cult**
I have pointed out Apple's negative behaviors a few times in my posts. Each time, I received quite burdensome comments from those who love the iPhone. Nowadays, criticizing the iPhone feels like criticizing a specific religion. I'm not sure if this is a culture created by Apple or if it's particularly more severe in Korea.
And this feeling is not much different from the blind faith in a conservative party or the sentiment that "if it's S-Group, any corruption or whatever is fine." It seems the iPhone has already replaced a set of values. I have never stated in any post that the iPhone's product value or Jobs' business strategy is of low quality or will utterly fail. However, it seems there are some who interpret discussions about strategies I dislike and technological myths as a prophecy that the Apple empire will collapse. I merely stated that such monopolization and arrogance would become Apple's weakness and that it's similar behavior to a certain domestic corporation, not that I drew extreme conclusions.
So, this time, I'd like to talk specifically about its religious nature.

**2. In the Past, There Was the StarCraft Cult.**
When I hear about the iPhone these days, it reminds me of the time when StarCraft was immensely popular. Even those who didn't play games talked about StarCraft back then, and it indeed brought about significant changes in the gaming industry. Similarly, the iPhone has led users who didn't use smartphones to start using them, greatly impacting mobile devices and data plans.
And what emerged then was excessive blind faith in Blizzard. Statements like "nothing is a game except StarCraft" were common. This phenomenon was particularly severe among the quantitatively increased users who were new to gaming, rather than existing power users. The initial addiction was strong, and encountering a well-made game made everything else seem insignificant.
However, for those who knew that StarCraft was an evolution of existing 'craft-style' games like Dune, the impact seemed less. And then an RTS development boom began.
And what was the result? RTS did not become a major player in the game market. Instead, the online element, which StarCraft first introduced and pioneered, exploded, leading to the emergence of various online games, and diverse genres, especially MMORPGs, became major players. Of course, after MMORPGs first succeeded in Korea, Blizzard later released World of Warcraft, which achieved unprecedented success.

**3. The iPhone Cult Spreading Even Among Competitors**
They say the past is a mirror of the present. What lessons can we learn from this experience? All the imitations that simply copied StarCraft's RTS failed to survive. While it's true that the biggest shift was towards online games, StarCraft still holds a significant position and brought about many changes. The lesson here is that imitations, rushing to copy due to blind faith, failed because they couldn't find their own development and position.
My personal view is that the situation is identical to that time. The iPhone is essentially StarCraft. Like StarCraft, which has already reached the ranks of masterpiece games, the iPhone has ascended to the ranks of luxury goods based on its image alone. However, just like the RTS development boom that followed, there's a phenomenon of rushing to imitate the iPhone's device. But if we step back and think about it, why does the iPhone possess such astonishing explosive power? It's also because of online connectivity. Networks can give rise to various applications. Furthermore, adding location information to that connectivity can create new services. This is what differentiates next-generation mobile devices, and while we don't know what killer app will emerge in the future, it will certainly leverage these aspects.
That's why I've been thinking this lately. Copying the iPhone. What should be copied? If it becomes exactly like the iPhone, will a luxury phone be born? If its specs are better than the iPhone's?
The 'religion-ification' of the iPhone seems to have spread like a superstition not only among Apple fans but also among Apple's competitors.
This perspective prevents one from seeing the pros and cons of the subject. Whatever Apple does seems to become the right thing.

**4. Is We Rule an iPhone-Exclusive Game?**
Someone once told me that it was a blessing they bought an iPhone because they could play We Rule, which everyone else was playing, and wouldn't have been able to if they'd bought another phone. They didn't realize that We Rule wasn't made by Apple. Because for the creator of We Rule, the iPhone was just a good market, and if there was a better market for them, whether PC or Android, they could port it anytime. Com2uS was a powerhouse in WIPI but has now become a powerhouse in apps. EA and Activision are the same. Software is not exclusive to one platform. Of course, there are exceptions like Nintendo, where killer apps save the platform, but generally, that's not the case. In fact, multi-platform applications will significantly increase in the future.

**5. Apple's Monopoly Strategy and Developers' Burden, Fearing Multi-Platform**
Online games enjoyed on both iPhone and Android. It's possible. Of course, with Apple recently blocking cross-compilation, this need has hit its biggest wall in terms of cost. If converting Java libraries to Objective-C isn't possible, then a technology to convert Objective-C to Java using JNI, etc., will likely emerge. Since it's easier to secure Java developers, there's also a possibility of creating two separate versions. Considering portability, using Objective-C, which only Apple uses, as the main source is actually a burden.

**6. It's Not the iPhone Device That Creates Alienation and Belonging, But People and Their Culture**
Actually, I feel left out because I'm not an iPhone user and can't play We Rule, but it's not much different from when I felt left out because I didn't have a PSP and couldn't play Monster Hunter. Is this like kids who don't play Dungeon Fighter, or female college students in the past who didn't use Cyworld? Ultimately, the feeling of being left out is created by people, not by the device. The statement that Apple sold a culture is true.
I believe this is the part that competitors should pay the most attention to. Physically speaking, there's the iPhone device, then the software on top of it, and further on top of that, the Apple culture. However, leading domestic companies are so focused on the device that they are missing out on the software and the culture above it. This kind of culture is different from merely good service or marketing. Currently, Samsung doesn't have a particularly consistent image that comes to mind. Of course, even Apple's and Google's consistent images have many contradictions, but they have already deeply penetrated the public consciousness. In the case of domestic companies, contradictory images, such as that of the chairman, are intertwined, sometimes leading people to even have a negative image.
As an extreme example, those who love the iPhone don't even believe foreign reports stating that Android's mobile traffic, device growth, and app growth have surpassed Apple's. Even though these were the same sources that reported on the iPhone's success when we were 'in the well' (ignorant of the outside world). This means they are already filtering what they hear. What kind of hypnosis are they under? While this is certainly an abnormal situation, it is beneficial for companies. It's not just something to envy, but also something to benchmark. Personally, I don't think it's good for consumers to lose their discernment to this extent, but since consumption is fundamentally about self-satisfaction, it might be a natural phenomenon.

**7. Acknowledging Diversity, Desired by Users and Korean Society**
I also wonder if Korea, in particular, has a characteristic that makes it prone to such self-justification. As mentioned above, while it may be beneficial for companies, it doesn't seem like a good habit for wise consumers. Korean society seems to not recognize diversity once colors are divided, beyond those two colors. That's why it's divided into Apple fans and Apple haters, or conservative and progressive, orthodox versus heresy, leftists and reactionaries. Such religious beliefs prevent both sides from seeing many things. While beneficial for companies and political organizations, it's something wise consumers should consider. Because feeling betrayed after being hooked will only add to the disappointment. I don't wish for a day when either Apple or Android achieves world domination. The Lollipop 2 my wife bought yesterday was also really nice and charming. (Personally, I think the Lollipop's design is better than the iPhone's or other smartphones.)

There are plenty of needs for non-touch or non-smartphone devices, like Wine Phones for seniors or Lollipop Phones for children, but they feel thoroughly ignored. Is this solely the fault of LG and Samsung? I wonder if there's also a reason in our unconscious tendency to divide phones into 'iPhone' and 'other phones'.
The world becomes more beautiful when we can appreciate diverse colors.

titleEn: Legend of Dragonia Part 2, Chapter
contentEn:
{{IMG:1}}

When Aysia opened her eyes, it was already bright. She had a restless night's sleep due to a disturbing dream, so even though she slept, it didn't feel like she had rested.
"Oh my, where's my head? Oversleeping on a day like this. But why didn't you wake me up? Melchizedek!"
Aysia quickly tied her disheveled long hair and called for Melchizedek. But there was no answer.
'Did he go out for exercise even on a day like this?'
Melchizedek always woke up early in the morning to exercise and return, so Aysia didn't think much of it. However, when she opened the door to Melchizedek's room, her legs gave out, and she almost collapsed.
On the desk in the room, which was tidier than usual, lay two letters, and most importantly, his sword and uniform, which were always hanging there, were nowhere to be seen. Aysia, with a trembling heart, approached the desk, sat down, and picked up the letters. One letter was addressed to Aysia, and the other to Prince Dagmon. The sender of both was Melchizedek. Aysia, gripped by an unknown fear, hesitated to open the letters. Aysia composed herself, telling herself that nothing was wrong, and opened the letter addressed to her, but tears were already streaming down her face.
'Why am I like this? It'll be fine. Melchizedek is probably trying to surprise me again.'
Tears blurred Aysia's vision, making it hard to see the letter, so she wiped them away and unfolded the letter. On the white paper, Melchizedek's neat and clear black handwriting was visible.
As Aysia began to read the letter, tears burst forth again. Soon, she buried her face in the desk and began to sob bitterly.
"Mom! The soldier uncle brought a dress like a princess's!"
Benjamin joyfully opened Melchizedek's door, and behind him stood Vice Commander Galab in his uniform. He was startled to find Aysia sobbing bitterly and couldn't step into the room.
"Mom, why are you crying?"
At Benjamin's voice, Aysia turned around. Galab stood at the doorway with a stern expression, and in his hands, a remarkably white and beautiful wedding dress shimmered in the morning sunlight. Aysia silently hugged Benjamin tightly.
In the square, a public notice announcing Melchizedek's execution by hanging was posted. For treason against the country, public hanging was prescribed, and the body was to be dismembered and thrown into the field. The execution was scheduled to be carried out hastily in the evening. Normally, it would have taken several weeks for an appeal, but in Melchizedek's case, having been arrested on the spot and brought before a military court, no appeal was allowed, and only the execution remained.
What should have been a joyful day passed uneventfully into evening. The evening at this time of year, during the change of seasons, saw temperatures drop sharply, and the sunset was blood-red. On such days, not many people gathered at public execution grounds.
"Are you really sure about this? The commander even left a letter asking you not to come, sister-in-law, didn't he?"
"I can't. I've decided. I'll regret it my whole life if I don't see him."
Aysia's voice was hoarse, but her resolve was firm.
In the end, Galab couldn't stop Aysia. Melchizedek's comrades, who were originally supposed to attend his wedding, headed to the square of Laodicea.

For several days after that, it poured rain. When this rain ended, the temperature would drop noticeably, and it would be time to prepare for winter. A new recruit guarding the city gate grumbled about having to work in such bad weather. Then, even in the cold rain, he spotted a dozen or so people searching for something in the field.
"What are they doing in this rain? Shouldn't we report it to the castle?"
At that moment, the veteran soldier dozing beside him glanced over, waved his hand, and replied as if it were nothing.
"That? No, it's fine. Someone was executed as a traitor a few days ago, right? Starting today, it's the day they can retrieve his body. They dump the executed bodies near there, but the damage is severe, so it won't be easy to find. Especially since it's been raining for the past few days."
Only then did the soldier reply as if something had just occurred to him.
"Ah! Come to think of it, I attended that public execution a few days ago. That was the condemned man. But that hanging was really strange."
"What was strange about the hanging?"
The veteran soldier, bored, became interested as if it were a good diversion.
"I've never seen such a beautiful woman."
The soldier threw out the topic with a dreamy expression.
"A beautiful woman at an execution ground?"
"Before the execution, they can give the condemned water and food, can't they? A young lady brought food, and she was so beautiful, like she wasn't from this world. And her dress was like a wedding dress, I tell you."
The senior soldier said with an expression that implied he was talking nonsense.
"A beautiful young lady in a wedding dress at an execution ground! That can't be."
But the junior soldier continued.
"And on a day like that, there would hardly be any spectators, but the people who came to watch were so well-dressed, it was almost like wedding guests. And General Misraim himself attended."
Then the listening soldier also tilted his head and agreed.
"If what you say is true, it must have been a strange sight in many ways. Indeed, it's also strange that so many people are searching for his body even with this pouring rain."
The soldiers shifted their gaze back to them. The rain showed no sign of stopping, and it felt unusually cold.

Melchizedek was overcome with chills. He hadn't been subjected to particularly harsh interrogation, but his body was already a wreck. It was hard enough to breathe, and the hood placed over his head was truly suffocating, and his bound hands were numb. Melchizedek knew his fate that evening well. His name was called by someone, and then he was led out by someone else. He felt the cold air and sensed many people around him. He climbed the wooden stairs. The thought that this was the end overwhelmed him. His living breath, exhaled from beneath the hood, felt hot against him.
"The prisoner Melchizedek is to be publicly hanged as a traitor. Do you have any last words?"
Melchizedek tried to recall any last words but nothing came to mind. All he could think of was wanting to see Aysia's face one more time.
"I thought about what grand words I might say before I die, but now that it's time, I have nothing to say."
Melchizedek made a light joke, but the executioner proceeded impersonally.
"Then, the prisoner is granted a final meal. Is there anyone who has brought food for the prisoner?"
Allowing a condemned prisoner a final meal was traditionally meant as a meal to prepare for the journey to the afterlife. Friends and family would prepare food, or if that wasn't possible, the state would provide it. However, most condemned prisoners were too terrified to eat properly.
"The prisoner is granted a meal."
Melchizedek's hood was removed. The suffocating hood was suddenly gone, and for a moment, his eyes squinted from the brightness. And then, tears spontaneously flowed down Melchizedek's face at the sight before him.
His beloved Aysia stood there in a beautiful bridal gown, holding a food basket, and his friends and comrades in uniform stood in formation around the execution ground. The few spectators began to murmur at the strange sight. The soldiers felt threatened and tried to disperse them, but General Misraim instead restrained the soldiers.
Aysia approached the bound Melchizedek and silently laid out the food.
"I told you not to come."
Melchizedek's voice was choked, and he couldn't continue.
"How can you expect a wife not to see off her husband who is going on a long journey? I brought some warm soup and your favorite cookies."
"I like cookies? I never said that."
"Did you think I wouldn't know? You even ate Benjamin's share that I secretly saved before."
Melchizedek's face flushed slightly, like a child caught hiding something. It was true that he had tasted Aysia's cookies once and had liked them ever since. But he hadn't mentioned it, fearing he would be teased for having a childish palate.
Melchizedek eventually accepted the food and ate it in silence.
"Have some white bread too. It was just baked, so it's still warm."
As Melchizedek bit into the bread, the tears he had been holding back burst forth all at once. He felt ashamed and didn't want Aysia or his comrades to see him like this, but he couldn't stop them.
Then Aysia also shed tears and hugged him tightly.
"Poor man. It's okay. I'll be by your side until the very end."
"Aysia, I'm sorry. I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I promised to make you happy..."
Melchizedek cried, repeating only apologies.
Aysia held Melchizedek in her arms, stroked his head, and comforted him, also tearfully.
"There's nothing to be sorry for. I know you did your best. And thanks to you, I was the happiest I've ever been."
"The execution will now proceed. Step away from the prisoner."
As the executioner's command rang out, Aysia had to be led down from the execution platform by the soldiers.
"I love you, Melchizedek."
Those were the last words Aysia whispered into his ear before being led away by the soldiers. Melchizedek put the rope around his neck. He no longer felt afraid. He looked at Aysia and smiled.
Aysia, too, seemed relieved and smiled brightly back. Her appearance was like a white flower blooming among the crowd.
"Execute!"
As the executioner's voice boomed loudly, Melchizedek's footing gave way with a thud. As if on cue, a man's voice from among the ranks of soldiers standing in formation echoed loudly and long throughout the execution ground.
"First Platoon, attention!"
Melchizedek's comrades, in uniform and standing in formation, all snapped to attention. Immediately following, another command was given.
"Salute!"
They, too, saluted according to the command. General Misraim, who was observing the execution, watched the scene for a moment, then rose from his seat. And then he, too, saluted Melchizedek on the gallows.
In the execution ground, a man hung by his neck, and many soldiers saluted him. The spectators were speechless at the solemn sight.

"At ease!"
Again, at a soldier's command, those who were saluting dropped their hands in unison, and from the sky, large raindrops began to fall with a pattering sound.

titleEn: [Idea] Location-Based User Hunting Game
contentEn:
**First Written: October 13, 2009**
****
**1. Location Information 'Eat or Be Eaten' Game**
Similar to games like Janggi or Chess, only one user can survive in a single region, and this occurs within a limited range. The most basic concept is that when one user enters another user's region, the entering user 'eats' (captures) the user whose region was entered. This is similar to a moving pawn capturing a stationary pawn (or a battle occurring).
The overall status of participating users can be viewed synchronously or asynchronously, in real-time or periodically/non-periodically (participants can be seen by accessing the web). Separate from this status information, conflicts between users occur directly between their devices. The winner or 'eater' receives appropriate rewards, or absorbs the user's stats.
**It can be played as a team game until a specific faction wins, or until only one person remains, and there are traps or items specific to each region.**
******
****
**- A game originally conceived with a gambling concept**
A system where the winner takes all of the loser's stakes and pays a commission to the system. The final winner's stakes are proportional to the number of participants, making it highly addictive. The size of the stakes can also be adjusted by creating a system where the game can end after three or more victories.

**2. Avatar Raising Game Using Location Information in a Game Based on Real Maps**
* Character movement, outside of combat, doesn't involve actual physical movement; rather, the map changes as the user moves, which greatly encourages offline gatherings.
**- Raise avatars or monsters on mobile devices**
Through location information, combat is possible with nearby monsters or avatars. Appropriate rewards are given to winners and losers.
Among the attributes of avatars and monsters, 'combat range' sets how far away a character can engage in actual combat.
**- Regional shops, regional monsters, and other regional events**
Specific events occur in regions predetermined by the system.
**ex) - Rare items can be found in Hwanghak-dong Flea Market.**
** - In Yeouido, it's possible to collectively hunt a large mob called 'Gukgaeuwon'.**
In this way, it aims to foster offline communities among users, with the in-game map matching real-world maps, and in-game map events configured to reflect real-world information.
Even in areas where no events occur, characters can be raised through user-versus-user combat, mobs, or training systems. Combat is also possible with user characters not controlled by a user, but the rewards for combat with user-controlled characters are higher.
**Because it links with mobile devices, it aims to develop as an SNS.**
****

titleEn: SKT and Samsung: Ruining Android's
contentEn:
** 1. Android: Beyond the iPhone's Potential**
Android phones, often called the iPhone's rival and recently garnering more anticipation than the iPhone in North America and other regions, are soon expected to be released in large numbers domestically. Android is a more open market than Apple's App Store and an ideal platform for various experiments, so I personally have high expectations for it. This is because Android is thought to inherit the advantages of the App Store and the open-source spirit of Linux.

** 2. Samsung and SKT at the Heart of Concerns in the Domestic Android Market**
However, looking at the current trends in the domestic market, I feel that Android's image is being distorted by leading domestic companies like SKT and Samsung. And if Android settles with this image, I worry that its diverse possibilities in Korea might be distorted and die out, much like WiPi in the past.

** 1) Shrinking Software Market Feared Due to SKT's Android Device Monopoly**
First, what I want to point out is SKT's monopoly on Android devices. It's no exaggeration to say that SKT, which will bring in famous overseas devices, has monopolized most Android devices. Of course, this might be called a difference in sales capability and fair competition, but I worry that this move, like the WiPi market, will ultimately lead to a division of the software market between T Store and Show Store. Such actions risk making Android seem like a platform exclusive to SKT, ultimately significantly shrinking the Android market itself.
The reason Apple's App Store gained momentum in Korea is not due to Show Store. It's more reasonable to see it as due to global market power. With the introduction of the iPhone, KT easily acquired a large quantity of high-quality software and provided significant opportunities to domestic software companies.
The same will likely be true for Android in the future. The size of the market is crucial for a platform's software market.
Currently, domestic-exclusive software is obtained through Show Store. In the case of Apple's domestic market, only KT existed from the start, but** in the future, all three mobile carriers will be present for Android. If that happens, it's highly likely that domestic-exclusive markets will also be separated by carriers.**
** However, I strongly oppose this. The reason is not as a user, but for the sake of Korea's mobile software competitiveness. **What surprised us with Apple's arrival was not just the hardware, but the software. Here, the biggest barrier that always existed for Korea's mobile software was absent.
As I mentioned in my previous post ([A Look Back at 10 Years of Korean Wireless Internet Because of the iPhone](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/70075401680)), one was the expensive wireless internet fees, and the second was the narrow market due to dependence on mobile carriers.
The first barrier has recently been removed for all three carriers with the introduction of the iPhone. But what about the second? Are they planning to once again force software developers to choose between Show Store and T Store? **From the perspective of individual software developers, this limits the software market by as little as 30% and as much as 50%. If that happens, it means the market for hundreds, even thousands, of software developers could be reduced to preserve the profits of the three mobile carriers. **It might repeat the mistake of stifling Korea's wireless internet software competitiveness, which once held the title of 'world's first,' and ultimately getting beaten by Apple again. And such a market could ultimately lead to an inevitable weakening of competitiveness for domestic software companies.

** 2) Only Samsung Can Use the Android Trademark, and It Won't Supply to KT.**
The same goes for Samsung, which monopolizes the Android name and doesn't provide devices to KT. I know well that SKT has wielded power over Samsung as the '갑' (superior party) until now. However, Samsung's recent behavior seems to be about playing a power game through monopolization rather than fair competition in technology or products, much like the mobile carriers. The name Android is Google's OS and is actually a common noun that anyone can use. **To brand an OS name as hardware? This is proof that they are still stuck in a hardware-centric corporate mindset, not a software one. **What benefit is there in imprinting the idea that Android is hardware, not software, on users, and how can they claim to foster software competitiveness while doing so? **If they have that kind of spirit, they should be contemplating how to brand their own platform, Bada, to users and distribute it not just to the three carriers but worldwide – that would be the behavior of a software company.**
Furthermore, Samsung is so indifferent to KT that it seems like they might be abandoning their own WiBro technology. It's a foolish act to even use future growth engines as a bargaining chip due to a petty bruised ego from the iPhone. **What Samsung should do immediately is release a WiBro phone that supports Android-based FMC with KT. That would be the innovation the iPhone brought; releasing an iPhone-like Android phone for SKT is not innovation. **At best, it's just imitation and an expression of inferiority. Ultimately, with KT also seemingly planning to allocate LTE in the 800MHz band, Samsung's decision not to expand WiBro to KT means letting excellent technology rot and preserving circuit-switched networks according to carrier preferences instead of a true all-IP based network. And users will still pay expensive wireless internet fees with pay-as-you-go or half-flat-rate plans, making it distant to run MMORPGs on phones or use streaming services like YouTube due to pricing. KT's FMC strategy is actually linked not just to Samsung's profits, but also to the future of South Korea, more so than the iPhone.

** 3. What We Should Learn from the iPhone is Not Defense, But Paradigm Shift.**
I hope these two companies have learned something from the iPhone.** What these companies need to realize is that the real battle is not about defending the existing market by emphasizing their strengths or advantages, but about aggressively seizing the future through a paradigm shift themselves.** It's not that Apple is a small shop and can't forcefully break into the domestic market. Apple is not always as creative and magnanimous a company as people perceive. It acts with highly sophisticated sales strategies and uses massive capital when necessary. It's not a company that would lose a power struggle with Samsung or SKT. The reason it hasn't aggressively targeted the domestic market is simply because it perceives the domestic market as not valuable enough. And it's also true that our software competitiveness lags behind to that extent.** In this situation, shouldn't it be the rightful mission of domestic conglomerates to view Korea's software market as something to cultivate, not just something to consume? If the domestic software industry continues to be treated as secondary, a second and third iPhone shock will keep coming.**

** 4. One More Thing: A Plea to the Government.**
And in fact, one more thing... the government is the one that needs to know this. Seeing that not only mobile carriers but even the government is proposing new market-shrinking regulations, it makes me wonder if they intend to abandon IT altogether. At least the Ministry of Information and Communication had fined mobile carriers twice. But now, I don't know whose tune they are dancing to. I ask for efforts to expand the entire IT pie, not just to preserve the profits of a few large corporations.
**As one of the humble software engineers, I hope for magnanimous decisions and strategies from large corporations and the government. Honestly, as an IT professional, I am currently ashamed when I see the name 'IT Korea' in advertisements or on the internet.**

**2010.04.27 - [National Integrated App Store to be Created.](http://www.wownet.co.kr/news/vodnews/view2.asp?vodnum=41175)**
** : Contrary to my concerns, an announcement was made about an integrated store, not separate stores for each network operator. This is welcome news.**

+ Addendum (2010.04.28)** : There is a story that Samsung's monopoly on the Android name came from Samsung buying the exclusive rights from the parent company due to fear of licensing fees. However, I personally believe that while Samsung avoided the problem by purchasing the trademark rights, it still had the same impact on devices like LG Electronics' Andro-1, even if unintentionally. I believe the problem is the same whether the company that monopolized the Android name was Samsung or a small business from the start. I also think it would be good if Samsung Electronics released the Android trademark. (Of course, asking them to release something they paid for for free would be an unreasonable demand in the industry.)**
